Darkest Dungeon is one of the best games i've ever played, and i've played many.
From it's brilliant art design, sound design, and the characters. Everything is spot on. Even the enemies, the story itself, voice acting by Wayne June. It's all really well done.
If i have any complaint, is that it's heavily reliant on "RNG" (Random Number Generation). A dungeon could be a piece of cake, and that very same dungeon can destroy your entire party. There's so much uncertainty. However, if you change your mindset to treat each encounter as a gamble, where the outcome is all left up for chance, the game becomes far more enjoyable.
While sometimes unforgiving, Darkest Dungeon still keeps players coming back for more. Because it is just that good at almost everything.
All in all, it's a very good game, highly enjoyable, albeit sometimes frustrating depending on the player's luck.

Darkest Dungeon.
Probably one of my favourite, if not favourite games of my recent years, not only for its art style, its godly soundtrack, the enemy design and it's DLC.
It is a turn based Dungeon Crawler with various elements out of Lovecraftian horror and even derives itself from more traditional types of monster as featured within the Crimson Court DLC (Of which may not be so traditional upon further investigation.) Dotting you throughout different sections of your estate, the Cove, The Weald, the Warrens, the Ruins, the Darkest Dungeon and the Courtyard (Featured in the Crimson Court DLC.) You will earn Gold in return for completing quests and will upgrade the equipment and fighting ability of your flawed band of "Heroes".
Darkest Dungeon focusses on the futile nature of humanity, and delves into such matters as though it were something straight out of a H.P Lovecraft short story and that, dear reader, is exactly what it is. It delves into all manner of terrible things: the fragile nature of humanity; our addictions to activities or material possessions; our need to discover, and damns us for such things.
But! Do not think that it is a game that shoves it's themes of futility and hopelessness down your throat, for in order to see such themes and more of a similar nature, one must "read between the lines", if you would, even towards the end when things begin to become ever-so more terrible, it does not become something that will intrude and glare itself into your eyes. What’s more is that Darkest Dungeon displays moments of light and valour against the backdrop of despair in the many dungeons dotting the land, and offers brief moments of respite from the madness all around you.
In this game, you will be tested. You will feel frustration, and sometimes, you will be set back, but the game offers the opposite. The game will reward you, and you will be able to slay that accursed boss or enemy that has plagued you for far too long in the end.
Albeit. You will soon begin to learn just how terrible your wretched estate is. It will soon become increasingly obvious of your futility. And just when you realise it all: it will be too late.
As somebody that relatively enjoyed the stories of H.P Lovecraft as well as Edgar Allan Poe, I loved Darkest Dungeon, if my review was not obvious. And if I were to recommend it? I would. Definitely.

Turn-based game with a brilliantly dark and moody atmosphere.
I enjoy playing it because:
* I like the Lovecraftian backstory and the matching graphical and audio design.
* The idea of having the heroes suffer from all kinds of stress-induced quirks and disabilities adds a new twist to the well-known RPG-style "level up your party" type of game.
* The game is fairly casual in the sense that one can play for half an hour, leave it be for a week, and pick it up again - which perfectly matches my work-life-gaming balance. :-)
* While dungeon runs run the risk of getting boring after some time, due to the wide range of different hero and opponent classes there's sufficient variation to keep the game interesting for quite some time.
So if you like dark turn-based RPG-style games you should like this one, too.

A great farming sim, but so much more than that. This game is absolutely bursting at the seams with content. The amount of things you can farm, fish, mine, gather, craft, cook, forge, kill and loot is absolutely jaw-dropping. There is so much variety that you can always find something fun to do. One day you can be watering your parsnips and picking berries, and the next day you can be swordfighting undead skeletons in a dungeon.
It's all set in a perfect wholesome village full of people with unique, distinct personalities that you can befriend. Each month there are a number of festivals or events in the town where you can play minigames, compete in fishing contests with the townspeople etc. It all really helps create the feeling that it is an actual town filled with actual people, rather than just a cloud of 1's and 0's. I found the whole experience to be extremely immersive.
All this is topped off with a great soundtrack that really helps the lively, fun vibe of the game.
9/10

Where to start.... same writers blocka s you have a gamers block in game. "Where to start". I guess with the tutorial quests since you are locked in your ship until you learn the basics. It is a good concept. Sci Fi mine craft. But poor execution. Core game is collect and create. The Pro of that is crafting is fluid on the go. A lot of features are fluid and on the go...except for certain recepies that require a work bench or forge. That said, it KILLS IMMERSION. I can, 1 second create certain items from a menu anywhere, but need a bench or forge for other things? I under stand smelting etc. but I can't feel thaton the go is silly "sure 1 click, table done!" and the "need another table to create stairs" ...While I am collecting pieces of stairs in the real world.. kills immersion nonsensical crafting.
That said some item combinations make sense. For a fernace, fire and stone. Ok. But the entire concept of creating middle age items for me a robot in  a space ship (I chose robot race) is silly. I understand it is sort of survivalish, and I understand you evolve into greater things. But it just adds to yet another layer of "NON IMMERSION".
I would have prefered high tech right off the bat, fighting and surviving against enemies of high tech, bringing the battle to planets where I Command armies of less evolved beings to fight witht heir bows and arrows against the enemy, like landing on ENDOR in STAR WARS. But nope. We have you vs deformed llamas and swors...
Core game play leads to a lot of digging. And that leads to a lot of black screen. 90% of this game is pitch black, with you turning on flash light ever so often or placing a torch. It feels cheap and stupid. Quest 1) get ore for new forge. Took 1 hour in pitch black. PRO TIP: GO STRAIGHT DOWN. NEVER STRAY FROM A DIRECT LINE DOWN OR YOU WILL REGRET DIGGING YOUR WAY OUT. I learned the hard way. Spent 2 hours (your teleporter is disabled under the ground) diging my way out after 1 hour of finding 4 pieces of copper. This can lead to digging into water and drowning.... I recomend playing only on easy mode because you dont lose resources if you die. IF I died after 4 hour of game play and lost all my inventory, I would uninstall. If it had a better mechanic to make it immersion filled to lose that I would keep it. But the darkness serves NO PURPOSE but to cripple your mning efforts.
Example: games like  minecraft SMARTLY USE THE DARK To make enemies more aggressive and exploration a thrill. This game uses it for one purpose. SCREW WITH YOUR MINING EFFORTS. Enemies do not change in the dark. Nothing is effected in the dark except turning your entire screen black as you pass hours hodling down the left mouse button to dig a hole staright down until you reach the required ores you need. FUN. Also, they ripped off mine crafts mining sounds.
This was the uninstall moment for me (but I have not. I endured). Day 2 of play. Quest X) Collect x ore; I spend the next few hours in pitch black, turning on the light ever so often searching my path and ore. LEarned if I Stray from a straight line down, I will spend 2 hours digging up to get out.
Quest X-2) Go back get X ore. I have already some of it from first part, now just need to grab a few more of it to coplete. I do it. Wiser, I dig straight down for 40 min till I ind it.
Quest X-3) Collect X plant. Since it grows undergound. Here we go again...thankfully I already have a lot so DONE.
Quest X-4) Collect "CORE ORE" which is located...at the core of the planet. ...Oh hell no. Already I have 6+ hours of "black scrren occasional flash light" game play while holding down one mouse button. How deep to the core? Another hour of just straight up digging? Sorry but random caverns and underwater chasms and monsters ARE NOT ENOUGH TO SPICEN UP THE immersion to go down. Fak. I reluctantly do it though....
The terrain changes. What is dirt, will turn into brains on some alien planets. YEah, you dig through brains... But changing tiles is not enough exictement to keep one doing the same process over and over and over. I came here to be creative, not funneled into a core process that is about progressing your armor tree. Lots of little pixlated things to collect. Unlcoking "blue prints" is just a matter of "digging and touching" the item. THAT IS ANOTHER KILLER IMMERSION feature. It would have been cool to take things back to a mother ship lab to learn them. Mix raw materials, see what comes out, make a blue print out of it. I don't know, something more immersed than. "Held down left mouse for 2 hours. Got X ore. LEarned X craft"
Crafting as non sensical as it is. IS USELESS. Some key items are nice ot have and some are forced on you to have, especially to leave the first tutorial. But, all and all. YOu can't build a house for anything meaningful like Minecraft or Terraria. You can build your ship, but it is PURELY COSMETIC. No ship battles or anything of real advantage or game changing happens. There is a SLIGHT rpg weapons system with stats etc, but nothing worth writing about. You do not even have equip slots, just hot key use (they work more like spells not weapons).
The digging is odd. You can skip a saure and dig bellow the ground directly below you...yet you can not place a floating block above you (unless touching another part of the earth). Found that a little odd (something Trove does). But I regress, since it does not make sense to have a floating block, but this makes for ground structure Up building and not top down. The first time I wanted a floating block was to make a window to shoot an enemy through, a top piece like roof and bottom piece. I would have needed to build an entire attached suare around me then break a hole out. It is not a big complaint but it is there. All that trouble to build a house for nothing. Because AI is as dumb as they look. They are just static mobs that roam back and forth, some get agro on site, run after you, you can whack em. They back off. Charge again like they forgot you were there.... But glad they charge because hits don't really slow em and sometimes you HAVE to take damage. I wish combat was more attentive to strategy and push and pull, not "run up, hit, you hit". Building a house with threat of night creatures or day creatures attacking it would have been nice. But nope, just walk around hit mobs dig ore.  Takes the meaning out of a lot of the work you do.
It has a great sound track. Addicting game play for the same reasons as mine craft...That "plop" of bricks exploding and that "what is under the next layer" discovery. The rest. Either broken in execution or not that thrilling. I wish there was more meat on the bones. Like a larger base to travel back to. A mother ship giving you orders and more quest. So many times I felt alone. Bored. In the dark. Meaningless "going no where" goals. Armor crafting is nice, but if I wanted to spend hours crafting armor for upgrades, I could play any multitude of online mmorpg and have full multiplayer support and dynamic events...this...is pointless.
It is early, and things could be implemented by full release. So we will see (but I Doubt it, they already seem to have more emphasis on getting players to pay for hosting servers, and creating new "enemy" skins like lamas in jeeps. Penguins in tanks... cute, but irrelevent to your work.
Games that do it right still are minecraft (Working with real day and night consequences. Your house is your sage zone.
Trove: Goals that pay off with more relevent construction and combat. Multiplayer support doesnt make you feel isolated in an changing world.
Terraria: Housing serves a function that influences survival. Enemies with meaning.
etc etc etc...
I would not say stay away. But I would for sure say SAVE YOUR MONEY! you are not missing out on a single thing that is not already available for free or done better. Wait for it. Let it develop. And let it go F2P with purchases expansions if you want.

I'm a huge 4x fan which means I often end up buying bad ones. I'm happy to report that so far MOO has a great foundation.  The art style is spot on, the effects and graphics beautiful.  The sound is a great mix of old & new.  I'm definitely getting sucked in already and experiencing that great "just one more turn, just one more turn" feeling that a good strategy/4x game will give you.
Bugs - Nothing really noteworthy so far, just a bit of barely noticeable frame stutter on a large, well explored galaxy during AI turns.  There's some minor UI elements that could use some polishing/streamlining.
Some work needed - Diplomacy is a bit shallow, it would be nice to have some more subtle ways to make friends or enemies.  It seems like all the AI will do right now is get progressively more angry with you even if you don't do anything to offend them, even buying them off doesn't really do much. The auto-build is way off base for what new colonies need.  Pretty surprised that this got a public release without a working tutorial.....but that's the only real "buyer beware" I encountered.  Even as a 4x vet, I always like to give the tutorial a whirl just to get a feel for the game and all its features.
Wishlist (not really a knock on the game) - I know its probably a tall order with all the art & voice work required but even more different races would be amazing.  Bigger galaxies.  More ship variants.  I'd also love to see some sort of Ship Design Testing Room feature that you could access from the main menu that would take you straight to ship design and let you really play around with the ship building and then perhaps test them against some basic enemies.  I love the ship design part of a good 4x but I'd love to see some sort of testing lab feature to really get to play with various ship classes and loadouts.  With so much else going going on during a full game, you might spend some time on a new ship design, and never actually get to really get a chance to see if it performs well in combat.  A ship lab/fight AI ship minigame that you can access directly from the main menu would be a lot of fun.
Summary - great game, definitely recommend (even in early access), I'm having a lot of fun with it.  A few minor things to polish up and a few "above and beyond" things I'd like to see added.

After almost a year of buying this game, I'm writing this review. First of all, I know it has many changes from NBA 2k15 (specially in MyCareer) and that's why I had to learned a lot to get used to the gameplay. I didn't play all the game modes, just focused on MyCareer, MyPark and MyTeam. So i can't fully recommend it or not because i didn't try everything this game had. Anyways, I'm going to put the positives and the negatives.
On one hand, this game had many good features. The graphics: they improved it from the previous game (or maybe not, i just put better graphics on the options menu). Then the way you can control your player with more signature moves, dunks (two hands, right hand, left hand and flashy) and passes. Better AI on defense and offense depending on the personality of a player. Also the options you have in MyCareer during offdays.
on the other hand, there are negatives that I think many players have noticed. First, the linear story in MyCarer: you can't choose how your life is going to be in the future (except your team at college) until the end of your first season in the NBA. Then, the learning curve is pretty steep for new players that haven't play any NBA 2k game before. Also, is pretty difficult to obtain good cards if you only play MyTeam game. Is way easier to play other game modes in order to have a good team to play domination, road to the playoffs, challenges, etc. Likewise, and this is the main reason i stopped to play many hourse as before in the last two months is the hackers in MyPark. It's hard to play against them and I don't want to play with them because they are cheaters. Even there are guilds full of hackers.
In conclusion, NBA 2k16 with its pros and cons, it's the best sport simulation game. I recommend this game because there is not other basketball game that can be compared to this. I didn't reviewed it until now because i wanted to play as much as i can every game mode (that's why i recommend it too, too much content). Finally, i enjoyed this game: made many more friends and had competitive matches in MyPark and MyCareer. Thanks 2K sports.

Ok, so Trove is a good game. Quite good for its kind, in fact. Is it P2W? No. You don't need real money for more classes. People sell class coins (the things you use to get classes) in the auction house. You unlock that by getting mastery lvl 10. Paying really doesn't give that much of a bonus. The best thing (and in my oppinion the only thing you should buy if you buy something is patron. The other stuff is really just Random Number Generated luck based stuff. (Also known as RNG or chance)
Now, here is where RNG comes into play. RNG can play a big part in this game. If you want the coolest items in the game, you rely on boxes and your luck. Now these items im talking about are by no means the best items in the game. However, if you are one of those lucky people, those items can give you nice bonuses.
Now, the grind. The most dreaded part for most players. Once you get to Uber-1, thats when you really notice the grind to start appearing. However, your luck can easily be raised by something called 'Magic Find'. This has a chance to raise the stat of a random item in one of the dungeon chests you just opened. Magic Find is a stat that can appear on gear, gems etc. Also, special items and pets can increase it. Patron will also give you a nice boost to magic find if you are willing to put a bit of money into the game.
Now, the 3 main currencies. (For new players that dont know, glim that you get for various stuff is maining only for water travel and fishing) Okay, now flux. You get flux for doing a lot of stuff. Deconstructing, selling, doing dungeons, etc. It is a grind for a lot of flux. However, early/mid game can usually get most of the flux by deconstructing and opening boxes. Now, flux is used for just about everything that is not in the credits & cubits store, which i will get to right now. Every day you will get 500 cubits if you just play a little. Cubits are used for various things in the store, some more usefull than others. Now, Credits. You will get very few of these from the regular game. You get most from paying money. Most the stuff that you buy with them though, as I said earlier, really just isnt worth your money.
Finally, my rating of the game. I give it a solid 8/10. There are some tweaks that need to be made, yet there are still constant patches, updates, and sales. Of course, there is that every Friday stream that can give you rewards. Now, excuse me, i have to go play some more Trove.

This game is intensely good. The game encourages you to constantly gage how much challenge you're willing or able to take on and then always raise the stakes a little higher for greater reward. For instances, your choice of operator determines the starting difficulty and how it ramps up, while your vehicle determines the amount of firepower you can level at said challenge: more expensive operators face greater challenges for more rewards, while more expensive vehicles are substantially weaker and less durable but also grant better reward multipliers. This contrasts with other games that make you work to get the most powerful equipment; in this game, you get some of the most powerful things for free by default, and the rest are quite cheap. If you want to drive what is basically the Tuk Tuk from Just Cause 2, however, that'll run you a price so steep that it's 4x more than next most expensive vehicle, but it'll give you a 10x payout multiplier!
The number of completable objectives on each map is much greater than what you need to move on (and they can have good or dangerous consequences if you complete them), and you can often jump to the final payout mission well before completing all of the maps leading up to it. Every single object that breaks or person that dies adds to your paycheck, but you have to manage your ammo stores and your time may be worth more if spent on the objectives.
This creates a subtle ingraining of Brigador morality: Whatever it takes to get paid and get off world is paramount. You will be financially compensated for stomping on innocents, ramming through slums, and collateral damage, but you will probably find that it's not worth your time to go out of your way to do so. Civilians are worth so little to kill that shooting them on purpose may feel like a waste of resources. So, when you DO go out of your way to destroy the lives of the little people, there can be no room for doubt that you act as perversely as the Auditer or greedily beyond all reason.
Speaking of, the lore in this game is so good. Spacers in particular are genuinely unsettling in creative ways: their mechs are clearly backwards and all of their vehicles sport full-yellow paint jobs (the lore says that yellow on Solo Nobre is associated with peaceful surrender and that wearing it while fighting is utmost sacrilege; I wonder if the Spacers are even aware of that) but with bullseyes on the cockpits (which, again, appear to be on the wrong side of the mech). The aforementioned Auditer is merely the operator you can use to tour each map without worrying about hostile forces, but the lore makes an impressive effort turning him into an unusual and almost horrifying character.
If you do try to use a controller, definitely slow the game speed down. The aiming controls are much better suited to a mouse than a joypad, so a lower speed will give you some extra time to adjust the angle of elevation of your shots. For keyboard and mouse, I use Relative Controls for mechs/tanks but Screen Absolute for agravs (I may switch to Top Right Absolute but I have yet to try it).

I had an earlier positive review but I believe I reviewed it too soon. After beating Unity, I've decided it's one of the worst games I've ever played.
Is it the glitches? No actually. This is one of the least glitchy Assassin's Creed games I've played, but problems come from the fact that the game is just so very badly made from the core. Somehow Ubisoft managed to make one of the most frustrating and enraging games that I've played in my life.
For some reason it feels like Unity's sole purpose is to annoy you. Think you're doing well in combat? Get shot. Running away after a successful assassination? Get shot 6 times. Realize you have no smoke bombs? Get shot. Want to move out of the way of the guards? The controls don't let you - you waddle back and forth in the same spot, then attacked. Want to use the cover system? Use it, get seen anyway, realize you can't get out of cover, get shot. Want to take out a guard on the ledge? Climb on the ledge, take 10 seconds to kill him, get seen by all guards, get shot. Attack guards head on? Except you can't because you're sheathing your weapon for some unholy reason. Get stabbed then shot then plowed by an axe.
The enemies have laser focus vision and laser aiming that never misses except when you roll for some reason. They reload instantaneously, you can't use enemies as cover when getting shot, and counter all you want but in the time it takes you to start attacking the enemy you just countered is exactly the amount of time the game needs to attack you with another enemy. Sometimes you counter but your character does absolutely nothing in response, he just stands there and takes damage. Get level 5, full health upgrades, and still die in 5-6 hits. I just don't understand.
But then there's other problems: The collectibles swamp the map making it a Where's Waldo to find where you're supposed to go next (generally you want to fast travel so you aren't walking for 600 meters right? also for some reason when I would filter it to missions the main mission wouldn't show). Items are overpriced, and even with owning every Cafe I still can't make a substantial amount of money without what feels like MMO level of grinding. Without a substantial amount of money you'll be stuck with garbage armor and weapons. The weapons/armor price jumps are like this: 25,000F for second or third best items, 200,000F for best. You have to spend 200,000F on your sword, hat, gloves, boots, pants, and torso. Consumables cost too much and if you think you can just search guards to get consumables like you can in other games, think again! I forgot what that arm-crossbow that you get is called but the entire tutorial for that weapon revolved around it being a silent weapon you can use to kill people, well, silently. Strangely, whenver I used it, every guard's vision in the vicinity immediately turned straight toward me even if I had only a split hair sticking out from behind three walls. It isn't very silent and because of that went largely unused for me.
And the worst part about all of this? The story is good, and I really liked it. I just hate that this is a game I will never play again, and can't believe Ubisoft managed to make one that was this unbelieveably frustrating to me. I've never been annoyed with an Assassin's Creed game before, in act I've never been this annoyed with any game before. How did Unity do it? I guess it just isn't the game for me.
Then there's the price. I don't know why it's still $40 on Steam when you can find it for less than $20 on the PS4/Xbox one. If you absolutely must then get this game on sale, but otherwise you won't miss a lot of the 'grand' story by skipping this one, and you may just save your anger.

I'm a bored person, usually. I don't tend to see games in my library and immediately go "Yea, let's play that!"
Brigador has managed to not just be a game I play. Within two hours, it's managed to be a game I'll sometimes click on while paging through my list, and immediately boot up.
Graphically, this feels like looking at a 90s game, but you know how when you don't watch or play or read something for a long time, you come back and it really shows it's age? Brigador feels like a very old game that has somehow managed to dodge that effect. In a world of low-poly 3d and "8-Bit" in name only, this striks a very odd balance that I absolutely adore.
Lore-wise I'm very fond of what they do. Every vehicle, weapon, enemy profile, and article has a small chunk of lore, usually under a paragraph. I feel it fits the game's atmosphere, a mercenary isn't going to know much beyond their objectives unless the actively dig for data.
While I do love this game, it's not perfect, and the gameplay is where I actually have a few complaints. Mechs and tanks control fine, but inexplicably Agravs- armed hovercraft available to pilots- drive incredibly poorly on my machine. There's indication that moving forward in a mech moves you towards the mouse in an agrav, yet they seem to control like tanks no matter what I do. Effectively, this makes them much weaker tanks with the relatively nice ability of flying over low cover and not getting bogged down in debris.
Speaking of debris: in massive fields of it, and those do tend to pop up wherever you go, it's hard to tell what's a flat plane you can walk through, and what's still standing.
For a game with emphasis on destruction, explosive weapons and elements tend to be a bit lackluster visually. They're still very effective, but the actual blast seems significantly smaller than it should be.
Yet I feel like the best praise I can give here is that even though I have complaints, this is without a doubt my favorite game released this year. I've enjoyed my time with it so far, and the game seems to indicate that I have a very long way to go before I'm scraping the barrel. I hope this is a sign of the rebirth of content-rich singleplayer, because I would love to write more recommendations in the future and be able to say that this was the start of the trend.

I've been a long time fan of the series. But in the face of recent games like Endless Space and Star Drive 2 I don't see how this really contributes to the genre outside of "production values." There are significant aspects of the design and art direction that appear heavily cribbed from Stardrive 2 (which in turn cribbed from MOO2).
I do find the game enjoyable, but considering the overall design decisions I'd recommend Star Drive 2 or Endless Space over this for a modern space strategy game.
There's a few interesting ideas (fortifying starlanes), but these are harmed by many of the streamlining issues.
For instance not having fleet range like in many other space games turns it into "whack-a-mole" with the AI (and even worse with a human player).
The biggest faults which I do not see being handled with the planned features are tied to the end game. The effort to avoid steamrolling at the end game are very heavy handed with enforced turn limits and a 1 ship limit to Doomstars. These heavy handed approaches to ending the game at a set point don't work well when the AI and overall game mechanics lead to scattered empires that drag out conquest victories. (which is "fixed" by the hard turn limit)
Tactical combat is another area that could use some refinement. Although there are ship firing arcs the AI tends to circle and there's no fine control for focus fire on individual ships, the AI targets an entire group. Stardrive 2's combat seems to provide more benefit for not using autoresolve or the cinematic camera.
Some of these issues might be resolved with early access feedback. But some of these issues are simply fundamental flaws with the way that game mechanics have been streamlined.
So to make it clear, the game is fun, the game is pretty. I'm honestly not a huge fan of the cartoony art style and voice overs of this and Stardrive and prefer Amplitude's more grounded approach, but that is a matter of taste and not quality.
But overall, for a modern 4x game I'd recommend Endless Space over this title.

This game has been striped of all it's replayability. Two of my friends used to play this game with me, and now they have no motivation to continue.
I remember playing this game for days at a time, just exploring and finding interesting items and upgrades. I choose what I wanted to do and the game allowed me to make those choices. I remember traveling to a planet and getting punished for it because I wasn't ready, or geared enough for the challenge...
Now the universe is spoon-fed to you so you don't hurt yourself, and that's sad.
Now, you have no choice. You HAVE to do the quests in order to explore the universe further. But what is the point of exploring when there are only 5 different types Star systems? Firey, Frozen, Radioactive, Gentle, Eccentric. Once you've been to the 5 types there’s no point in exploring anything further.
Guns used to be special. Now you get one at the beginning and you can craft them whenever you want an upgrade. Bosses are NOT challenging like other reviewers are saying they are. They are instanced and spoon fed to you. You cannot face a boss without first having the armor for it since the NPC won't allow you to face the boss without having the armor! Why did the developers think it a good idea to reference World of Warcraft for this game?
You spend 10 minutes gathering fuel and you have fuel for life. But who cares? Because there is no reason to explore the universe.
I tried to get my friend (who had played this game previously with me) to play this game with me after the update, but he refused because the direction this game went in was so far away from what we previously enjoyed.
The art assets are still enjoyable, but the design has gone so awry. I used to enjoy this game but I don't see it improving. Remove the questing system, remove the star types and make this game an open world experience like it used to be.

Master of Orion (reboot), so far ...
(Editor's Note: I would classify this as "Maybe" as to "Do you recommend this game?", but there is no maybe catagory.  I would say on a scale of -10 to +10 it would fall around a 0 at this stage.)
Right now, what we have is a reboot of MoO II, with not all the functionality implimented, but with the graphics updated and reimagined.
UPDATE: If you are looking for a remake/update of MoO II, this is not it!  It is a reimagining of the franchise into a "beer and pretzils" game that can be completed in an hour or so, reguardless of size or complexity settings.  Not much strategy involved, just build and kill.  Die hard fans of MoO II will be disappointed.  If you're open to a simple, not very involved game, much like World of Tanks or World of Warships, then you might warm up to what WG is serving up here.
As I proceed further and WG adds features I will update this review.  The skinny on this "early access" (2/26/2016) is "Don't expect much right now."
Side Note: The early access also includes MoO I, II and III.  I have to say the folks at WG did a smashing job of repackaging these games.  MoO I and II run under Dosbox, MoO I is a bit finicky though and will crash on start up unless you set Dosbox to the game's original resolution (800x600).  MoO II runs flawlessly.  What really amazes me is they managed to repackage MoO III to run without having to install all the crap that it required when it was relesed.  My psyche still bears the scars of making my system unstable just to "run" (using the term loosely) the darn thing and arguing with the developers that it was a stupid idea to have 4 external dependancies.  Good Job WG!

Half Life (1998) is a classic for not only the FPS genre, but also to gaming in general. It was one of the first pioneers to have realistic and open ended level design and realistic/immersive atmosphere.
The game's graphics haven't aged very well, but thankfully the game comes installed with the HD pack, which updates weapon models and come NPCs to make them look crisper and not robot like.
But what really makes this game a classic is the gameplay and atmosphere. The gameplay is a mix of Run'n'Gun of older games (Doom, Quake) and the more realistic style of modern shooters. The balance of the enemies you will face on your journey is remarkable. They are tough, but the bullets you have to kill them seem about right. It is fun and with addition weapons you will get later makes it even more fun.
The A.I. of the soldier are also remarkable. They actually act as if they are soldiers in a squad, with them flanking and throwing grenades to weed you out.
The immersion of the facility you will be playing through is probably the best thing about this game. On my first playthrough, I barely noticed the story or stopped playing because I was so ingrossed. I think the limited graphics actually help the game here.
My only problem with this game are it's last couple levels. If you've ever played the game, you know what section I'm talking about. If you haven't, just remember that the ending is worth it.

I received this game as a gift and it might be one of the best gifts I have received in a long time (don't tell my family that).
This game is an unforgiving torture train though a Dungeons and Dragons type setting, with focus being on the dungeon crawling aspect and almost none on the role play side. You play as some sort of party leader, gathering troops and choosing their upgrades and where they should go, and what actions they should take. The fights are absolutely brutal, and the game exploits every possibly advantage to turn even the simplest encounters into a desperate fight to save what's left of your pitiful band of heroes. You are the manager of a murder grindhouse and only a good manager knows not to get to attached to his workers. Some heroes will die and you will fire some heroes. These negative actions are necessary if you want to polish your party into an elite force that will combat the hellish fiends you will find in the darkest of dungeons.
The artwork is unique and works so well for this game. The animation is subtle and could easily be improved in a sequel. What's fascinating is that none of the warrior classes are weak or useless. They are each unique and are necessary at specific time. It's your actions that make them weak. The powers you choose for them, the combinations you put them in, and how you react to certain situations is the blame for weak warriors. The most stand out thing about this game I feel is the audio. The music and ambient noise is wonderful, and the narrator is top notch.
If you like role-playing games even without the 'role playing' aspect, and really love number crunching strategy, get this game.

Amanita Design is single-handedly bringing the Adventure Game back into style.
Their previous game, Machinarium, blew me away with its creativity, soundtrack, style and charming little story. Their Samorost series is also a unique gem of a game series. Amanita continues to create great games with Botanicula.
Botanicula is like a blend of Machinarium, Samorost, and Windowsill. Like Samorost, you don't usually control your character directly, but interact with the environment, which allows you to progress. Other times you do tell the characters where to go and what to do, which is very much like Machinarium. And although Amanita did not design it, I couldn't help but think the game reminds me of Windowsill because there are so many clickable things on the screen, and clicking them yields fun surprises.
Cute, happy, creative and unique surprises.
There aren't any serious puzzles here like in Machinarium. It's much more casual. The focus is on interaction with the environment and exploration. You won't need to take notes to figure out the puzzles. Some will require you to make leaps of logic, but in the context of this strange world, it's never an unfair leap. In fact, it's usually a funny leap.
Happiness and charm are very rare in games these days it seems. The tone of Botanicula is happy, upbeat and humorous. I especially like it when the group screams. It's funny, and the surprises they uncover along the way are just as amusing. It doesn't become dark or scary until the last level, which is a surreal trip in and of itself.
Botanicula is a work of art and a joy to play!

From what I've seen so far Master of Orion is a modernized version of Master of Orion 1 with elements from Master of Orion 2. Artwork and general production values are extremely high, the voice acting is a nice touch.
I am an avid fan of both MoO and its sequel and so far I am enjoying this game very much. It has a slightly different feel than the originals but it's definitely a strong 4x title.
The realtime combat may be unexpected in a game calling itself a Master of Orion remake/reboot, but works pretty well and is in my opinion superior to the turn-based combat in MoO 2 which could sometimes turn into a chore especially in the late game. Starlanes are also something which I usually don't like and which are new in a MoO game but it works surprisingly well and leads to a lot of interesting gaming choices and opportunities.
Pros:
- Great visuals, awesome production values overall
- Very stable for an early access title
- Feels definitely like a MoO game
- The UI is modern and very user friendly
- The starlanes add a lot of strategic opportunities to the game
Cons:
- 4 races and a couple of features (like spying, several victory conditions etc.) haven't been implemented yet
- No tactical combat in multiplayer
Overall I am enjoying the game a lot and at least in my opinion it's a worthy successor. If you expect a 100% copy of the older games with visual improvements you'll probably not like this title, but if you are open to the thought of a new interpretation of the source material you might be in for a treat.

Summary: A good, real free to play and not pay to win moba style space-ship game, with pretty graphics.
There is no "farming" for currency, you just play, and if you play well, you get rewarded. RL money only gets you cosmetic skins or unlocking ships faster, and "the best ships" don't cost a gazillion credits to get. There are no OP ships, each one has pro's and con's, strategies and counters. And above all, teamwork will get you the wins.
At first most ships will still seem expensive, but the game just keeps throwing credit boosters and whatnot by completing objectives (again, just play normally and you'll get the goodies).
Game controls are good and learning to pilot the ship is quite easy, if you suck at flight sims like I do, you'll love flying here. Learning curve isn't steep, but mastering the game requires lots of experience and actively communicating with your team.
"Quickplay" should be your first choice until you get a good feeling of how matches should unfold, the AI is okay enough so you can learn the basics of PvP without being boring (plus, you still get rewards).
More details on the gameplay: 5v5, two side lanes, you fight for control over resource mines so your team upgrades faster and becomes stronger. Every few minutes there is the "Gamma Event", a big space station in the middle of the map becomes available for capture, the team that gets it will be boosted significantly for the next 3 minutes. Ideally you gain resource advantage, cap gamma, get rid of the enemy team and cap their base.
Simple enough yet it does allow for tactical flexibility.
Newb tip: Colossus ship isn't tanky enough to rush the enemy's line with, no ship is, follow your team.

Playing the game on Windows nowadays; it's by far one of my favorites and it's totally worth playing through a time or two. The strategy is nice and the turn limits force you to keep moving rather than move and overwatch each turn. If you have issues with timers they can be disabled with mods.
The events on the tactical map are one of the most chore things I have seen in a game though. Alien Hunters DLC is something that should just be left turned off after using it once because it breaks combat flow. Rarely the RNG completely hoses you on a randomly generated map. The battlefield combat is brilliant and the enemies actually are challenging. For the first good chunk of the game you will feel like you are actually outgunned and may even up until the very end when you rush into the final mission. There's also a wealth of mods such as the Long War mod (which fixes a lot of issues with the game). The storyline is overall very good even if it lacks replay-ability. Customization of your soldiers is a great way to give them a little life. I have fond memories of targeting enemies as they rush to the extraction point.
As to whether I recommend this game I suggest getting XCOM Enemy Unknown and XCOM Enemy Within first since for the price paid those are a much better deal. If you really like those then pick up XCOM 2 because it's a very unforgiving game that a lot of people will not care for.

A dark and gritty game, where you are constantly fighting against the odds, holding on by a tread. That is up to you, if you feel like tearing your fun from the claws of a brain eating eldritch horror, get this game. If you are just looking for some quick enjoyment, maybe skip this cesspool of insanity.

After finishing this game, I wanted to run out and plant a tree.  Seriously, though, this game is absolutely beautiful.  The character design is original and adorable.  The soundtrack and sound effects -- all done by the two people who make up DVA -- are perfect, and add to the naturalistic atmosphere of the game wonderfully.  The setting itself is fantastic and imaginative, with its little secrets and delights to discover.  You cannot imagine my reaction when the giant turtle revealed itself (you know the part if you've seen it), or when the lightning bugs land on the vines in the area under the frogs and crabs (again, you'll know the part when you see it).  The game also balances humor and terror very nicely.  The dream sequences are some of the creepiest game scenes I've ever seen, and the Zlos themselves are their own lovely brand of horror.  In short, this game was worth the price I paid for it.  20/10, would play again.

Being an old MOO2.EXE owner, I didn't expect much after MOO3, to be honest. That said, MOO:CTS (?) is a nice Early Access game, so far.
I think that it is a great 4X game that will disappoint some MOO fans, but I'm sure it is interesting to fans of MOO-clones such as Endless Space, Galactic Civilizations, Star Ruler etc., for perhaps the following reasons
- At this stage, it is a full game with tons of features already
- Nice art and sound, and (surprisingly) a decent AI with alliances and such
- It is not ground-breaking, nor experimental though, so it's easy to learn
- It is of a higher art and design quality than many other 4X games
- Space combat is RTS with an option for auto-combat
- Less micro management than old 4X games
For old MOO brats I'd say
- It is quite a shiny Disney evolution of a dinosaur
- Not so many fresh gameplay ideas so far
- It's like CIV4 and 5 are its best friends, MOO2 is its dad, and MOO1 its grandpa
- And quite some lack of depth, of story, due to Early Access, I guess
EDIT: Now that Stellaris is coming, I think that this MOO shows its weakness. Stellaris did show so far more fresh and interesting game mechanics, depth and even some story, while MOO:CTS seems to be rather a nice looking remake than anything that will push 4X forward.

I think it's fair to call this a stealth-lite game. But here's the thing about stealth games: most of them aren't really about stealth. They're more like an elaborate puzzle, where you have to figure out the exact route through a linear area of guard patrols.
Shadwen is no different. You follow a corriror or find an open-ish area, and you have to find the route through. Lethal or non lethal. But the time mechanic, where you rewind time if you make a mistake, makes this a hell of a lot more fun.
You can try multiple approaches, and keep going until you get a perfect sequence of kills. I wish more games worked like this, because it means the game never starts getting tedious from restarting checkpoints all the time.
Definitely worth a try.

I really appreciate that this game manages to make you feel like a badass based on your skill alone, and the devs didn't feel the need to implement skill trees or some sort of character progression system. It's unabashedly arcade-ish in this mentality, but it still manages to have a surprising amount of tactical depth when choosing how to approach groups of enemies or defended positions.
I haven't played the original release of Brigador but I think the complaints about it being hard to control are overstated. I started playing on the new control scheme but settled for tank controls for all vehicles. The absolute control scheme seems more responsive on a keyboard/mouse, especially for the agravs - it allows you to strafe and circle around your opponents with ease. I imagine the new control scheme would be great for a gamepad, though I'm still skeptical about the agravs. Anyway, my point is, the people who write this off because of the control scheme are giant babies. There's nothing wrong with it, and you have plenty of choices in how you choose to control your vehicle.
Music is another highlight for me. It's really well done retro electronica, cca late 70s/early 80s. Obvious comparisons would be John Carpenter movies, Tangerine Dream soundtracks, maybe Blade Runner in parts.
Overall probably one of the funnest action games I've played in the past while. It manages to recreate that satisfying MechCommander feeling of playing with giant robots, but replaces its clunky combat with sleek, streamlined, and surprisingly kinetic action - moves have heft and explosions feel punchy and dangerous.
With this re-release pretty much patching up everything people complained about, including adding an extensive tutorial campaign, even more vehicles, weapons, etc. as well as planning additional content to be released in the near future, this is probably the best time to get this game. I hope it achieves some sort of cult status at some point, because it really deserves it. This game is to the Desert/Jungle Strike series what Shovel Knight was for NES-inspired platformers, imho.

#Gameplay
A fun stealth based game that as far as I can tell doesn't use any scripted events, but rellies fully on the core game mecahnics. These are heavily physics based, but since the physics are reliable aswell as pretty realistic this works really well.
A fun twist is that we have to clear the way for a second unarmed character. The AI and simple waypoint system wrks pretty solid most of the time, but has some issues, especially on a no-kill run (once the NPC notices that the route it had planned doesn't work anymore it goes all the way back to its las hideout - thus sometimes missing the clear timeframe you were working towards).
There is a looting and crafting system in the game but aside from the grapling hook that is necesarry this is purely optional. It can save some time thought.
# Story
The games tells most of it's story via ambient dialog and some dialog between the protagonists. Sadly we do not really learn much about the player characters motivation. The ambient dialog makes a convincing case against the protagonists original plan, but since we know so little about the latter in the end the decission missed some emotional weight.
# World/Levels
The world looks really great: it is a belivable medivel world with more variation and assets than I had originally expected. Each Level has something unique, however the main interactible objects, foes and the gameplay stay the same making the world seem mroe repetative than it actaully is. Most levels have a pretty straight forward path trought them, however they are not actually as "tubey" as they might seem: while Lily the NPC we have to get trought the level has very little variation in her path we can actually skip back and forth qutie oben-world-like in most sublevels. There are some hidden areas with chests - but since the lotting and crafting they serve mainly to make the world seem more diverse and less linear.
# Archievements
As with most stealth games archievements are an essential part of this game giving the palyer to do more than simpyl paly through it once. The game offers the typical "pacifist" and "kill all"archives for each level aswell as a few playthrought-based trophies to go for. Other than these, there isn't anything really originial, hidden or  surprising.
# Graphics and music
Not much to say here. I like the dirty style that is much darker than that ofother frozenbyte games. The music kept me on the edge of my seat even in passages that took quite some waiting. Both really solid.
# Conclusion
Shadwen is a solid stealth game in a setting I have been waiting for for a long time. Including Lily gives it a unique twist. Even thought I enjoey stories that are somewhat hdiden and rely heavily on ambient dialog thereisn't really much story here. If the developers take this solid game and build uponthis I could see this (or rather its sequel) becoming the game everyone was waiting for with thief.

Now that the Up-Armored Edition has been released I figure it's a good time to review this. I've got about 70 hours in the game so far and don't see myself qutting any time soon.
Do you want to play a tank with a cloaking field and invisibly drive over your opponents? Do you want to be a multi-story mech bristling with lasers that wins through sheer firepower? Or maybe an agile anti-grav making hit and run attacks with corrossive chemical weapons? The huge amount of vehicles and weapons means you can play however you want. Huge levels with 100% destructible terrain mean you can carve your own path through the game, either through brute force or stealth.
There's also a ton of difficulty settings in Freelance mode in the form of pilots, each of which has a difficulty rating that is either stable or goes up steadily over multiple levels. In addition you can adjust the game speed in the menus to make things less hectic.
There's been multiple times I've broken out laughing during this game as I suddenly realize the absolute massive damage that's been done to the city during a fight. Though it might not seem like this game has much of a story, the info logs set up a surpisingly deep and darkly satiric setting. For example, you get extra pay for collateral damage. A civilian casualty is worth $50. A decorative shrub is $100.
Also worth mentioning is that the dev support has been incredible post release. There have been multiple updates including weapon rebalances to make sure everything in the game feels fun to use.
The controls may take a bit of getting used to if you aren't familiar with tank controls (however there are multiple control settings available). But once you do this game has a huge amount of entertaining content. I can't recommend this enough.

I picked up Shadwen during a sale for under $5.  It was a great purchase.  It's not a long game, but it is different to other games in the play style - it pauses whenever you stop moving.  To move the characters along when you want a guard to walk by, you can press a key to move time along but the pause feature gives you a chance to do some great moves with a grapling hook without having to reload a level over and over again.  Also, if things to bad, no reload necessary: press the rewind button until you arrive before the blunder.  Or if you want to try something, rewind to try different things whenever you want.
The only downside was that I never really found a use for a number of the items I found blueprints for.  Or, more accurately, I found uses, but never felt like using those.  I prefered the clever use of things in the environment.
Considering it does have moderate replay value, the $5 pricetag was perfect.  If you're looking for a game to play between some triple A titles, this is a fun one worthy of the few dollars it will cost!

Played through one full game last night as the Bulrathi.  This is definitely on the right track to relive the glory of the past MOO games.  It  should only get better.
Right now as it stands it played smoothly except they do need to may find a way to speed up the council voting sessions.  There was the only spot it seemed to dog down a bit on me with some time in between each one stating their vote and moving to the next.  Maybe a few more phrases would be nice during the voting too since I was already repeating their lines in my head on abstainting by the end.
The graphics are looking good.  The different lokoing ship designs I saw througout for each race are great.  The interface is overall a pretty easy to manipulate around to what you want.
Diplomacy is there, but definitely feels like it is still a work in progress.  It seemed pretty swingy at points for the way they got angry over things and was pretty hard to raise for me it seemed.  I do like how if you are friends with a race and you try to be friendly with their enemies they take notice.  There was always that aspect where wars and treaties were concerned, but just in general they appeared to pay attention to even the smallest trade of information.
Space pirates were kind of interesting, though never seemed much of an overall threat.  They did destroy a reasearch outpost on an asteroid field at one point on me when my ships were halfway across the galaxy hunting down the remanents of the humans.  Usually I hunted down where they were coming from, took out their base, and then found a planet in that system to settle to make sure they would not try coming back from there again.
I wasn't sure if the Council voting was at set intervals/turn marks or if something else was triggering when those came up.  So was a bit annoying at the end when it was down to me, the Alkari, and Mrrshan and we were all just hanging around for the next vote.  I was pretty sure I could win the next vote on my own, but requested/bribed the Mrrshan to toss their vote in with mine to make sure it was sealed.
Things not in yet, but are coming and will greatly improve the feel of MOO:
Spying:  There are some techs related to spying in the game right now, but none do anything since there is no spy network option.
Race options:  Currently not in are some of my favorites including the Klackons, Darloks (makes sense with no spying and that being their strength), Meklar, and Silicioids.  Also no cusotm race.  However, they are greyed on on the startup selection screen so you do know all of those are coming :)
Difficulty levels:  Right now can only play on average difficulty, which overall for veteran MOO fans or those that play other similar games a lot is just a walk through the park and enjoying yourself as you do.
Would like to see:
Planetary queue:  It'd be nice if I could queue up a few buildings/items at a time so I don't have to bounce back to the planets as often if everything is running well in the empire.  Obviously being able to modify/cancel the queued items will also be a plus in that situation.
Galatic laws:  I could see this being a pretty cool addition if done right and let the council of races have something else to affect the state of the universe and of course relations depending on which side of the voting you go with.
Technology splits:  I liked how some of the techs you were making the choice of which you would learn specifically and then you had to trade or eventually steal with espionage what you ddin't already learn.  I would like to see some more of those decitions within the tech trees, if it is possible wihout convoluting things way too far.

Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

I had this game sitting in my wishlist for a long period of time,
and when I finally purchased it, whoo~ boy was it worth my money.
Drive and maneuver many different vehicles, ranging from,
heavy mechs, tanks and anti-gravity vehicles.
Each with their unique gameplay mechanics, harpoints and maneuverability.
Equip them with dozens of various weapons, like, mortars, cannons, gatling guns,
missile launchers, rail guns, etc...
The sheer amount of unlockables is amazing, and I really enjoy playing the freelance mode,
where you choose everything, from pilot, vehicle, weaponry, sub-equipment and then a mission you want to tackle.
Upon successfully completing a mission, you'll get money, which you use to unlock items.
Brigador reminds me a lot of old games like Desert Strike, Jungle Strike and Urban Strike,
but instead of having "destroy these first", "then rescue this", "before time runs out destroy these",
you are given a vehicle, and told "hey this is your mission, do it the way you like, also, don't worry of destroying buildings".
The soundscape is fantastic, and together with absolutely beautiful 80's soundtrack, it all greatly falls into an one big great experience.
In the end, Brigador is a satisfying, game of wreacking havoc and destruction everywhere you go, no matter which vehicle you drive, in the neon light streets while blasting your cannons in unison with the great beats of the soundtrack.
Varlet/10

Shadwen is a nice little stealth/action game that has a lot of potential as it tries to mix together some core mechanics from previously seen games like Prince of Persia or Assassin's Creed. While I enjoyed playing it and do consider it a good game, it could be so much more with what it has going on for itself, but sadly it doesn't live up to all that potential (most likely due to it's low budget). Here are my thoughts upon why it is so. (Also note that I only played the 6 first levels and half of the 7th level, after that the game crashed and I decided to instead watch gameplays from YouTube to see the story as the gameplay had gotten a tad bit too boring for me at that point.)
The story isn't anything special really. Nothing too memorable or that new, which is always a shame when that happens. The character personalities are quite plain as well, with no real depth given to them unless you count the few lines of bantering in load screens between levels.
The gameplay is very repetitive as it's pretty much the same thing over and over again (killing guards/sneaking past guards in slightly different levels by using the same methods for the most of the time), though while I myself find it dissapointing it's not the big issue I have with it. The bigger isue here is that the AI seems to be quite wonky as the guards sometimes realize I'm sneaking somewhere closeby even though I didn't touch anything or do anything else that should make spot me. Not to mention that sometimes Lily just stops on her own and won't move even if I tell her to, and I have to replay the whole level just 'cause of that stopping my progression. There are also some weird sudden frame drops in the 6th level for some reason, while all the previous levels were all working very smoothly in that regard.
Some levels also were quite a bit too similar to eachother and they re-used the same assets a lot, making the game a bit too visually boring for my liking, though other than that the artstyle and the graphics were great to look at.
I don't know what's with the guards' sights as well. They might not see you if you're quite close and a little to the right or left of them, but if you're towards where they are looking at, they can see you from miles away. While it can be still dealt with, it can be quite an annoyance.
There are also the hint text boxes that bother me. Either I'm blind or there is no option to remove them, so the game keeps giving you hints about things you learned about ages ago already and sometimes they're even covering the items in your inventory and are making it hard to craft things. At least usually they disappear rather quickly,  but sometimes they can be stuck on your screen for up to around five minutes of playtime.
I might be nitpicking a little bit, but that's just 'cause I like what this game is going for and I just wish it could be more than what it is currently as it definitely has the potential for it. But anyways, I am still recommending this to anyone who likes stealth games as it can be a rather nice experience and the price isn't too bad.

Where to start.... same writers blocka s you have a gamers block in game. "Where to start". I guess with the tutorial quests since you are locked in your ship until you learn the basics. It is a good concept. Sci Fi mine craft. But poor execution. Core game is collect and create. The Pro of that is crafting is fluid on the go. A lot of features are fluid and on the go...except for certain recepies that require a work bench or forge. That said, it KILLS IMMERSION. I can, 1 second create certain items from a menu anywhere, but need a bench or forge for other things? I under stand smelting etc. but I can't feel thaton the go is silly "sure 1 click, table done!" and the "need another table to create stairs" ...While I am collecting pieces of stairs in the real world.. kills immersion nonsensical crafting.
That said some item combinations make sense. For a fernace, fire and stone. Ok. But the entire concept of creating middle age items for me a robot in  a space ship (I chose robot race) is silly. I understand it is sort of survivalish, and I understand you evolve into greater things. But it just adds to yet another layer of "NON IMMERSION".
I would have prefered high tech right off the bat, fighting and surviving against enemies of high tech, bringing the battle to planets where I Command armies of less evolved beings to fight witht heir bows and arrows against the enemy, like landing on ENDOR in STAR WARS. But nope. We have you vs deformed llamas and swors...
Core game play leads to a lot of digging. And that leads to a lot of black screen. 90% of this game is pitch black, with you turning on flash light ever so often or placing a torch. It feels cheap and stupid. Quest 1) get ore for new forge. Took 1 hour in pitch black. PRO TIP: GO STRAIGHT DOWN. NEVER STRAY FROM A DIRECT LINE DOWN OR YOU WILL REGRET DIGGING YOUR WAY OUT. I learned the hard way. Spent 2 hours (your teleporter is disabled under the ground) diging my way out after 1 hour of finding 4 pieces of copper. This can lead to digging into water and drowning.... I recomend playing only on easy mode because you dont lose resources if you die. IF I died after 4 hour of game play and lost all my inventory, I would uninstall. If it had a better mechanic to make it immersion filled to lose that I would keep it. But the darkness serves NO PURPOSE but to cripple your mning efforts.
Example: games like  minecraft SMARTLY USE THE DARK To make enemies more aggressive and exploration a thrill. This game uses it for one purpose. SCREW WITH YOUR MINING EFFORTS. Enemies do not change in the dark. Nothing is effected in the dark except turning your entire screen black as you pass hours hodling down the left mouse button to dig a hole staright down until you reach the required ores you need. FUN. Also, they ripped off mine crafts mining sounds.
This was the uninstall moment for me (but I have not. I endured). Day 2 of play. Quest X) Collect x ore; I spend the next few hours in pitch black, turning on the light ever so often searching my path and ore. LEarned if I Stray from a straight line down, I will spend 2 hours digging up to get out.
Quest X-2) Go back get X ore. I have already some of it from first part, now just need to grab a few more of it to coplete. I do it. Wiser, I dig straight down for 40 min till I ind it.
Quest X-3) Collect X plant. Since it grows undergound. Here we go again...thankfully I already have a lot so DONE.
Quest X-4) Collect "CORE ORE" which is located...at the core of the planet. ...Oh hell no. Already I have 6+ hours of "black scrren occasional flash light" game play while holding down one mouse button. How deep to the core? Another hour of just straight up digging? Sorry but random caverns and underwater chasms and monsters ARE NOT ENOUGH TO SPICEN UP THE immersion to go down. Fak. I reluctantly do it though....
The terrain changes. What is dirt, will turn into brains on some alien planets. YEah, you dig through brains... But changing tiles is not enough exictement to keep one doing the same process over and over and over. I came here to be creative, not funneled into a core process that is about progressing your armor tree. Lots of little pixlated things to collect. Unlcoking "blue prints" is just a matter of "digging and touching" the item. THAT IS ANOTHER KILLER IMMERSION feature. It would have been cool to take things back to a mother ship lab to learn them. Mix raw materials, see what comes out, make a blue print out of it. I don't know, something more immersed than. "Held down left mouse for 2 hours. Got X ore. LEarned X craft"
Crafting as non sensical as it is. IS USELESS. Some key items are nice ot have and some are forced on you to have, especially to leave the first tutorial. But, all and all. YOu can't build a house for anything meaningful like Minecraft or Terraria. You can build your ship, but it is PURELY COSMETIC. No ship battles or anything of real advantage or game changing happens. There is a SLIGHT rpg weapons system with stats etc, but nothing worth writing about. You do not even have equip slots, just hot key use (they work more like spells not weapons).
The digging is odd. You can skip a saure and dig bellow the ground directly below you...yet you can not place a floating block above you (unless touching another part of the earth). Found that a little odd (something Trove does). But I regress, since it does not make sense to have a floating block, but this makes for ground structure Up building and not top down. The first time I wanted a floating block was to make a window to shoot an enemy through, a top piece like roof and bottom piece. I would have needed to build an entire attached suare around me then break a hole out. It is not a big complaint but it is there. All that trouble to build a house for nothing. Because AI is as dumb as they look. They are just static mobs that roam back and forth, some get agro on site, run after you, you can whack em. They back off. Charge again like they forgot you were there.... But glad they charge because hits don't really slow em and sometimes you HAVE to take damage. I wish combat was more attentive to strategy and push and pull, not "run up, hit, you hit". Building a house with threat of night creatures or day creatures attacking it would have been nice. But nope, just walk around hit mobs dig ore.  Takes the meaning out of a lot of the work you do.
It has a great sound track. Addicting game play for the same reasons as mine craft...That "plop" of bricks exploding and that "what is under the next layer" discovery. The rest. Either broken in execution or not that thrilling. I wish there was more meat on the bones. Like a larger base to travel back to. A mother ship giving you orders and more quest. So many times I felt alone. Bored. In the dark. Meaningless "going no where" goals. Armor crafting is nice, but if I wanted to spend hours crafting armor for upgrades, I could play any multitude of online mmorpg and have full multiplayer support and dynamic events...this...is pointless.
It is early, and things could be implemented by full release. So we will see (but I Doubt it, they already seem to have more emphasis on getting players to pay for hosting servers, and creating new "enemy" skins like lamas in jeeps. Penguins in tanks... cute, but irrelevent to your work.
Games that do it right still are minecraft (Working with real day and night consequences. Your house is your sage zone.
Trove: Goals that pay off with more relevent construction and combat. Multiplayer support doesnt make you feel isolated in an changing world.
Terraria: Housing serves a function that influences survival. Enemies with meaning.
etc etc etc...
I would not say stay away. But I would for sure say SAVE YOUR MONEY! you are not missing out on a single thing that is not already available for free or done better. Wait for it. Let it develop. And let it go F2P with purchases expansions if you want.

Adventures in Babysitting, is what this should be called. I had high hopes for this game, considering I am a huge fan of the Trine series. Crafting, ya that is a waste of time, considering that if you plan on not killing anyone the only thing you can do is grapple, and pray the little girl isn’t seen. Which if you’re playing solo, the AI is one of the worst things about this game. I literally watched the little girl loop in between 3 guards for a good five minutes, and the guards were like, I think I heard a noise, too bad they just didn’t use their eyes to see in front of them.
The physics in the game is the best part, watching Shadwen swing on a rope like a yo-yo, as her lifeless body was a sheet of paper blowing in the wind. Every time I used my grappling hook I just laughed, and shook my head, and remembered why I should pirate games before buying them.

18 years after the release of this game, I feel a sudden desire to review it, as if anyone doesn't know about its acclaim already.
The videogame that marked Valve's global debut,
is an absolutely genre-defining release. Fresh for its time, unique, different, and still fun, it took the PC gaming world by storm in the late 90s, with its critical praise following it greatly into the turn of the century, with a large modding community and a great engine (GoldSrc) that carried a fulfilling lifespan until the release of its successor, the dominant Source Engine.
In HALF-LIFE, you are put into the shoes of Dr. Gordon Freeman, a 27 year-old theoretical physicist working for the mysterious BLACK MESA Research Facility located in New Mexico. After an experimental test goes wrong, Gordon is found fighting for his life, defending himself from hostile alien lifeforms crossing over to Earth from the borderworld, Xen, after the experiment creates a resonance cascade, opening an interdimensional portal between planets. Gordon meets many of his colleagues along the way, struggling for their own safety against the alien forces, and eventually, the massive military unit HECU, sent to wipe out anything related to the incident. Gordon travels through numerous complexes, canyons, and worlds in his quest for survival.
But that's the special thing about Half-Life: it never feels like you're just "playing as Gordon Freeman." It feels like every action is your own. Every step, jump, and gunshot is a power that YOU hold, not just something you're telling the protagonist to do. This is a goal that Valve had set out to achieve, a goal that was realized through the use of NO protagonist dialogue, an uncommon detail in FPS games at the time. This helped breathe life into the games motto:
The controls are great, with the same control scheme being subsequently used in most future Valve games. The gunplay is fun, with a fair amount of weaponry, both human and alien. The atmosphere is what I truly think makes the game. It brings such a feeling of desperation, dread, and isolation that I didn't quite get in the future titles. A true "you against the world" feeling, where every corner can pose a new threat. It's such an intense feeling of cold desolation, unforgiving and eerie as every footstep echoes throughout the metallic hallways that stretch deeper into treacherous facilities.
This is a game that greatly defined my vision of what games should be. It has so much heart put into it that it's mindblowing for a debut game. There's just so much life in Half-Life that I find myself replaying it every so often to this day. Despite its look, it never grows old. It may be difficult to get into if you haven't played before, but anyone who has played it could tell you it's worth the time.
There's not enough good things that I can say about Half-Life, but it's best if you experience it and decide for yourself. While not without its flaws, this is still about as close as I can get to considering a game perfection. Everybody should give this at least one playthrough in their lifetime.
