Verdict: This is game you should "play", not a game you should "buy"... at full price.... here's why:
If you're a long time player and fan of Xcom then this game is for you and you will love it, it has some new features and new gameplay mechanics which you will enjoy, but somethings will to some extent put you off and sometimes mad at it.
POSITIVE (Minors)
Visuals - This game looks amazing, the characters design, the armours, the weapons are superb, plus the customizations makes it even better, huge array of colours and modifications you can do, makes your squads unique.
The antagonists (enemies!!!) are also refined and give that extra feel of woe when you are battling them.
The maps are smaller (due perhaps to the countdown feature!) and more manageable, they are gorgeous!
Gameplay - Its interesting to the least, new moves and weapons, will make you say often: "wow!!... i can do that!!?" or "amazing!", and when you combine them in Overwatch to set ambushs, the cinematic scene its glorious.
The antagonists (enemies!!) are also smarter, they will work to flank you, support their teammates, hoard your squad to a small spot and throw a acid grenade just for 'lols'.
They will also flee when they're in a disadvantaged situation and regroup with other far away squads when they're isolated. This nice feature is exarcebated with enemy diversity within the squads, different type of 'aliens' work together to bring the most of pain to your heroes... and they will succeed.
Resource management is somewhat easy than previous XCOMs, as the mobile base of yours will be easily upgraded. The missions are enjoyable,challenging and doable...
however the difficulty of gameplay will not come from missions, and enemies but rather from some bizarre clusterf**k of things that in my opinion plague this game!
Soundtrack - Very nice! Its more moody and paced than the thrilled one of the previous XCOM, it will make you almost cry in those epic moment...i said almost :_(!!
NEGATIVE (Majors)
Performance
a) Pagefile - This game uses at very least 5-6 Gigs of Ram... all fine.. but when you read Pagefile numbers it reaches 6-7 Gigs of Pagefile!!!!... In 2016!!?  For a total of 13 Gigs of RAM + Pagefile!! ?? If it runs on a lot of Pagefile it can only mean one thing: Stutter!! Horrid gamebreaker stutter!! And if you put mods  it can reach higher.
b) Stutter, cutscenes - This game has a huge enjoyable cutscenes, when your squad drop from the transport in AO (Area of Operation) in zip lines, that is so awesome... until stutter happens!
Not only in in-game cutscenes but also in the plot cutscenes, which are excepcionally well made and one of the best parts of this game, but are dragged to the ground with stutter and small pauses! And it kills it!
c) Anti-aliasing - MSAA its a no-no, FXAA will help, but all AA in XCOM2 will drag your FPS to the 24-34 fps, VRAM even with 3.4 Gigs of use in its peak, does not seem to include AA... probably its all in Pagefile! The rest of graphics option seem ok!
Gameplay

a) Battle difficulty - The Devs right before launch thought the game was easy, so they made it more harder (not my words, google it!!), what resulted instead was a cringy set of combat never seen in XCOM.
The Missions themselves are not hard, BUT, the AI just for some reason overwhelms you with sheer numbers, and more often it pulls the heavy-hitters, that in some point later in the game its Gatekeepers, Sectopods and Andromedons in all missions!
From the simple beacon hack to the UFO 'break-in' raid... and early you just thought Codexes ( an antagonist...) were hard!
The Last Mission its absurd: you have to deal with the bosses, and... you guessed... a huge sea of enemies, which comes with all with the above mentioned... and more!
There was a beacon mission, when you have to run to it at the same time the enemies are going to it and destroy it. The AI distopic sense of gameplay balance there, just went up the charts, i have never seen such battle and it was soo cheesy, that that one beats the last mission on the matter of difficulty.
b) Can see enemies & shoot through walls - Another constant 'feature' its the shooting through the walls, and the cheating spotting of adversaries through them, by the heroes and enemies alike.
c) Super powerful squads at later stages -  the easiness wich you can reach full unstoppable power with your squads is a feature that i have mix opinions. You can enjoy the new armour and weaponary and its uses, but when at the same you can dispatch 5-6 enemies with at least a heavy hitter, in a ambush with Overwatch
its laughable, Grenadiers, Rangers and the Super Cheesy Gunslinger Build of Sharpshooter, takes some of the tactical aspect of the game.
But then you say:"... but you said the AI was also cheesy, so it compensates!", and you're right, but what happens next it that the AI compensates cheesiness over chessiness, and it bring more and more enemies, so in reality your advantage its lost.
You can see that, when in the last mission, one of your fully upgraded to an 'unstoppable-tank' Grenadier, gets overwhelmed by an absurd 3-4 fully upgraded advent basic troops plus 2 Heavy-Hitters! Thats the only way to kill him!
Even when you, prior to a mission, made a mission where you stopped enemy reinforcements for a while, i saw the AI pull reinforcements anyway! Wassup wit dat!!?
d) Lack of menus and of informative details - The game lack proper menus, for squad built and rooms management as well as shortcuts buttons to take were you want to go. You want to go a menu you have to click, click, click!
You have to manually, remove items, armours from each squad members in order to reuse them on other squad members.
Avatar countdown is also somewhat lacking, Comm Rooms and Towers and some of the most critical investments, but it doesnt get enfasized! I manage to pull myself of a predictament (lack of intel, and cost of Contacts), due to a hasty set of missions!

Oh boy, where do I  begin. I started playing XCom back in the '90s with XCom: Apocalypse, and that was awesome. Fast forward through the years and many disappointing "sequels", and finally the X-Com reboot comes around that we all wanted and almost all of us loved for holding true to the original.
So with XCom 2, I'm not sure what the ♥♥♥♥ happened or what these guys were thinking. The pacing of this game just pisses me off. Missions are forced with arbitrary timers, ever time I try to go to a supply drop I'm force-fed another mission, and whenever I try to do one thing then something else pops up in my face. What the ♥♥♥♥, guys? Really? Did you think that people hated the pacing of the XCom reboot so you had to try and rush it along? This is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
At the heart of XCom 2 is a great game wrapped up in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥, overly-rushed shell that feels like a bad Japanese stand-up arcade game where everything you do is on rails. I don't feel like I had the freedom of exporation and developing my own strategy like I did with XCom. Instead, it just starts to feel canned and rushed. It's a shame.
On individual missions, the early ones are WAY too ♥♥♥♥ing hard. I have a bunch of rookies, and they're already throwing aliens at me with psionic powers? Are you joking? Who did the level design and pacing on these? Because dude, you're drunk. The difficulty curve goes right up - there's no easing into this. Get ready for save/die/reload/die/reload/die/reload over and over. It's just too much. I get it if it's harder several missions in, but FFS, give us a chance to ease into this thing.
So overall I'm disappointed with XCom 2. XCom was damned-near perfect, and it was THE best reboot of any game ever, and it was amazing. But XCom 2 dropped the ball. They ♥♥♥♥ed with a formula for a perfect game, and what we get is something that tried to be more, but ended up being less. The small vids up in the corner are kind of lame, and the science nerd girl Shen is annoying as hell. The quality of the video is atrocious; I know what the devs were trying to do, but it comes off a lot worse than you think.
It's kind of sad, really. The joy of XCom is gone, and this version feels mechanical.

Seeing as how I have 850 hrs in 2k16, I feel I have played the game to warrant a full opinion and review on this product. This review will cover multiple aspects of the game, and will hopeufully serve as a guideline so that others can refer to it when necessary. With that being said, i'd like to stress that this review will focus heavily of the woes of the game, particularly for the PC audience. This review will cover 3 main topics: Gameplay, Gamemodes, and Community, as well as final comments and extra's. Each topic will then be scored out of 10, and at the bottom will be my conclusion as well as a TL;DR statement. Lets begin.
Gameplay: While the game's movement system is flawed at times, for the most part your controlled character is able to move fluidly and resembles the real thing. In game controls differ slightly from previous 2k games, but its nothing you can't learn relatively quickly. In regards to animations, the game claimed that "you would never be locked into an animation again" but that is simply not the case. there are countless times when you go up for a dunk, but your character will just throw the ball across the backboard, resulting usually in the other team grabbing aan easy 2 points. Animations can somethimes go a bit wonky, but for the most part it looks good. the same options that are available in previous games are available, and the game can be customized to fit how you want to play. There have also been multiple patches to the game, most of which are needed to fix game breaking bugs (See reviews below regarding Win10 bug) the gameplay is solid, but it leaves a bit to be desired. my score for the gameplay would be a mediocre 6.5/10.
Gamemodes and Online Functionality: NBA 2k16 features a plethora of gamemodes, each providing a different and fun experience... to console players. PC contains the same features that are present on console, however, with such a small player base, it is near impossible to find an online game in any mode other than MyPark. Modes like MyLeague (Previously Association), MyTeam, and Play Now Online all contain an online aspect, but it is barely played as there are not many players that aare participating ONLINE in those gamemodes. (These gamemodes are still fun in a local setting, but you are not playing 100% of the game) It is because of this lack of online functionality that I didnt fully enjoy my purchase. The gamemodes in 2k16 are great fun, earning an 8.5/10, but the online sections of the modes failed miserably, earning only a 2.5/10.
Community: Many players within the community are extremely helpful, and some can offer great advice and have a strong opinion regarding the state of the game. The PC community is paricularly special as we don't condone ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t from devs.  if your game sucks, we will tell you.however ther is a section of the community that spols it for the majority, and that would be hackers and cheaters, of which there is a significant margin of players that do so. Hackers ruin the game for so many, an its a shame that they exist, but the main cause that they do is that the devs have a terrible anti-cheat system, sometimes even banning those that did not commit any sort of unjust act. in addition to hackers and cheaters, there are also scammers that will attempt to trade with another member of the community, just so they can cheat them out of a card. iit is because of these types of people that the community is not where it should be just yet, and why i have to give the community a 6.5/10.
TL;DR: All in all, I would not recommend this game to anyone wanting to pickup a basketball sim. Rather, I would suggest you acquire this game by other means. If, at that point, you decide that you want to play modes such as MyTeam, and MyPark, even though they have a dwindling player base, then purchase. As of right now, this game is not for PC players, because it lacks suport in that area. I hope this review was able to inform potential buyers. Peace out ganstas.

I'm a big fan of grinding to get through games and experience everything they have to offer. Doing that will only end in tears here. I picked it up for the turn-based play and Cthulhu-mythos themes but was deeply unsatisfied with the gameplay and the amount of story mixed into it.

First and foremost, the thing to remember is that this game just launched in Early Access.  Comparing it to Master of Orion 2, while a natural instinct, would not be fair at this time because the game is just far too new and unfinished.
And the largest detraction I can currently label to this game is that it is very much unfinished.  At least four races are missing (possibly as much as eight depending on how far the developers intend to go), race customization is not yet an option and the racial traits thus far appear to be watered down, ship design and combat are not as intensive as they once were, and despite the wonderful narration and voice acting the story does not yet seem to be entirely in place.
Let's double back and remember, though, that this game is hot off the Early Access presses.  There can and will be additional content to come, and even if the detail work from before is missing the foundation for a game as great as MoO1 or MoO2 appears to be there: the races we know and love are present (mostly), the gameplay absolutely feels like a Master of Orion game, and there has been some evolution in how things are managed.  Did I mention that now there's a beautiful voice cast narrating and interacting in the game?
If you're looking for a re-skinned version of Master of Orion 2, I would recommend going over to StarDrive 2 for the time being.  If you're looking for a game being built on the same blocks as its predecessors, this is the game you want.  It would be fair to say it's more worth it when it goes on sale, but one way or another any MoO-loving, 4X-playing gamer will sooner or want this in their library.

There are some wonderful aspects to Unity, particularly in the environment and the detail that was put in the world. But there are countless annoyances throughout this game, and numerous problems and bugs that still exist. Optimization is still iffy, with framerate drops. There are countless graphical bugs throughout, from NPCs popping into existence 3 feet in front of you to thin white lines visible between some textures.
The biggest problem with the game for me, however, is that it's just not fun. The camera is clunky and often gets caught up on the environment. The combat itself can be fun and exciting in smaller groups, but is frustrating when you're facing against large groups. I've found myself mashing a button to drop a smoke grenade, which Arno would ignore, to attacks going through enemies without affecting them, to numerous gameplay mechanics which do not make an ounce of sense to me.
One of the problems throughout the AC series has been feature creep, but this game reverses that, to a negative effect. Enemies with guns are much more annoying as there is no effective way to dodge them. You can no longer grab another enemy and use them as a human shield (and in fact their bullets seem to go through their comrades and hit you anyway without a problem, which is particularly frustrating when you're surrounded by 10 guards and 4 of them are pulling out pistols), and your dodge move only works when you're near another enemy, not when you're trying to run towards a rifleman. The damage higher level snipers inflict is also riduculous.
Counter-attacks and parries that cause damage or instantly kill the enemy are out, as are kill streaks and combos. And under other circumstances, I would be alright with that, as previous games have often had straight-up combat being easier and much quicker than stealth. However, that combined with the other changes to the combat system just turns combat into a frustrating annoyance.
The changes to the stealth system is also similarly frustrating. In an attempt to make the game more difficult and challenging, the developers made it annoying. Hiding in crowds seems a lot more finicky, there's no tall grass to hide in, and you can't whistle to attract enemies. If you want to attract one enemy away from the sight of others, you have to stand in his line of sight and spin in place for a while until he notices you and decides to investigate.
Speaking of noticing and investigating, the co-op missions are also particularly awful. In order to increase the difficulty and encourage you to play them with multiple people (though you can play them solo), the enemies are horribly buffed, particularly in noticing you. You will be expected to sneak into a palace which has three guards at each entrance and overlapping snipers which have to be taken out at the same time or they will spot you. And then they will spot you on the other side of the street and immediately become suspicious and start shooting at you as well.
The storyline of the game is...mediocre. Nothing too special, though a bit more of a stronger personal story than previous AC games. However, I was disappointed with the treatment of the French Revolution. As with a lot of AC games, the actual historical events are often poorly explained or depicted, can be often played out of order, and they expect you to already know everything or just go with the flow. Not to mention the fact that the main character is locked in a prison during the lead-up and beginning of the revolution itself is horribly disappointing. You don't see a gradual transformation, you don't see people becoming more and more riled up and fighting back. It's just a cutscene and now it's the Republic, with the Reign of Terror, and that's it.
All in all, Unity is not horrible. It's a AAA game with a lot of resources put into it, but it's horribly disappointing compared to other AC games, and in an attempt to make the game more of a challenge, it was just made frustrating instead.

I would definitely recommend this game for a few reasons:
1. Master of Orion is one of my favorite games from back in the day
2. This new remastering of the game has similar elements to the first game, but a more fluid movement to all game mechanics
3. The mix of nostalgia and a game that could stand on its own is quiet apparent in this game, whether that be due to just game mechanics, such as the announcers, or the new diplomacy options/ more in depth solar systems
However, There are a few kinks in the armour, mostly just due to early access:
1. The game feels slow;
By this I don't just mean that it is running slowly on my computer, I mean that the fluid movement of the ships, as well as the movement of your screen accross the galaxy can be a little too slow for my liking. On the other hand, zooming out and then back in on the desired position does the trick most of the time
2. Some things are a little awkward
The diplomacy responses are too slow and awkward, especially when they say the exact same thing whether or not they like you or not. Another thing that bugs the heck out of me is that the galactic voting mechanism is really slow and almost painstakingly ridiculous if you stay and watch the entire voting process. The awkward silences and then feeling as though you are going to crash out of the game because of the silence just is a major turn off for me.
3. Diplomacy is iffy
If the diplomacy in this game was a little better, I would be completely and utterly in love with this game. However, when you are hostile with humans because you are colonizing too rapidly (Which I already hate that mechanic anyways) and then they agree to trade agreements and eventually alliances with you, it feels a little cheap. The other thing about diplomacy is what are the numeral configurations to why they are upset/happy with me? I get an up or down arrow telling me if i did something right/wrong, but it doesn't say how much each individual thing effects the relationship
Anyways, I hope you guys find this helpful; I don't mean to make it sound like I do no recommend the game, but there are some definate greviances that I have with the game, that will hopefully be fixed in the next few months as the actual game comes out. If you think it is worth the investment, you will spend a lot of time on it and definitely get back what you paid for it. If you wanna wait for the solo game to come out and not just the collector's edition, that will probably be a less problematic experience, that is if you are only in it for the new game. This constructive criticism isn't a knock at the producers, but just the fact of Early Access and that sometimes things just don't work like they are going to in the full game.
Hope you guys enjoyed and found this useful. Would probably rate the game(s) as a whole around a 7/10, mostly just due to the bugs of an Early Access game and the above mentioned things.

Bastion is one of those games that will always hold a special place in my heart. This game strikes so many notes in all the right places that one would be hard-pressed to point out its flaws. In terms of storytelling, Bastion offers up a tale that will keep you engaged until the oh so sweet end. The gameplay is superb thanks in part to fluid combat and numerous customization options. The gorgeous hand-painted visuals make this game look like a painting that has come to life. Then there's the soundtrack. Ohhh the soundtrack. Be prepared to get lost in audio bliss. Perhaps the most unique and welcome touch is the ever-present narrator who guides you through your adventure. It's one thing for a game to have great aspects to it, but it means nothing if they don't meld. Bastion is a game with a number of wonderful elements, the sum of which, equals a cohesive whole that you absolutely must experience. Grab a drink and pull up a seat. It's time to play some Bastion.

I appeared on the coast somewhere. I had no idea where, I had spawned with the minimum, two bandages and a roadside flare. I had no map to work out my location and nothing with which to defend myself. I ran over the hill and there was a small town. I was noticed by some zeds and ran away from the town. Let me tell you, these zombies do not give up easily. After a lengthy run throuhghout the countryside dodging in and out of tree. I was finally rid of my pursuers. Now where the hell was I,nothing but hills and trees to be seen. Well, more running. Eventually I come across a barn and once again I am noticed and chase is given. Another run through the countryside and more trees and hills later I find another hillside village. I begin creeping well before I get to it, I have learned something at least. As I get closer I notice the zombies milling around and go prone, crawling my way through the wet grass, skirting zombies and stopping now and thehn when they get to near. But then of course one of them would like to walk right where I am lying and I'm off for another run.
Yes there is a definate pattern forming here. Get lost in the wild, run and eventually discover some buiildings, get chased by zombies away from your finding and lost again you are. This goes on and on for some time. Eventually I died, one too many run ins with no means of fixing myself, my vision went all grey and blurred in and out of semi focus. Running around with your screen doing that you find yourself squinting at it, willing your eyes to make sense of what it sees and all the time fighting the headache which is arising from the disorientation this causes.
I died a few time s this way and learned to be extra cautious, more creeping and creeping slowly with the shift button held in too. Next time I spawned again somewhere on the coastline, I ran over the hill and noticed another small town. I crept up to it, slow creeping around any threats and found a dead man. Upon study I found out who he was and what he had died of, blood loss. And I also found a couple more bandages and flares. I proceeded to the building he was near and crept inside closing the doors behind me just to be sure. There was another dead guy lying near a table. I had hit the jackpot, this guy had been well geared up when he died, again from bloodloss. I aquired an alice pack, tool kit, matches food and drinks and weapons with ammo and a hatchet.
I was feeling good now, and I might add a touch over confident, which ultimately led once again to an untimely demise when I tried to take on everyzombie I saw with my hatchet. the first few were not an issue, hiding nearby I simply clouted them as they walked by and down they went. The next ones got the better of me, I was noticed creeping up on one and he ran at me. Hitting a slow ambling zombie with an axe is a walk in the park. trying to hit one running at full pelt in an erratic pattern is a completely different kettle of fish, he got me a few times, some of his friends noticed and joined in the fun and games. I hit and ran, got my gun out (my guy stops running to do this!) and shot which only alertedmore of them. I ran to the sea and in I plunged. Now zombies are not bees and the characters in this game are not fast swimmers. The last of my health left me as I tried in vain to doggie padlle away from the voracious horde.
I have given ot a positive review because it is a rather marvelous creation. The map is enourmous and will take a good long time to explore. It looks good too, as you crawl through the long grass you push it down, flattening a trail as you go. Vehicles are good in the fact that you can store things in them too, load it up with weapons and food and you have a mobile home. However they are rather difficult to drive and you want to be extra careful with them as the last thing you want to do is crash into a wall whilst trying to escape from a horde of zombies and put it out of action.
This is a survival game and it will test you to your limits, if there ever was a zombie apocalypse it would not be a walk in the park and this game does a grand job of highlighting that fact whilst also reminding you that it is after all, only a game.

Having bought the game shortly after v1.0 came out, I have witnessed quite a number of changes in the game's design, mechanics, and the way it's best played. And what can I say....from already great this game became ever better!
While it has become a ritual to watch players groan about changes introduced or new features added (I can't think of any other game where this is the case), the new slings and arrows, let alone outrageous fortune, hurled at the player have inevitably added novel layers to the gameplay. Layers that would punish sticking to the old strategies - but always could be used in the player's favor, too, by adjusting playstyle and party composition and gauging risks anew.
As others have said, risk management is everything. This, rather than the supposedly merciless RNG, lies at the heart of DD gameplay. In fact, I would argue that DD is a quite calculable game. Don't hesitate to retreat if things get dire and there are team members you'd like to keep. Even on the default difficulty settings, which is what I absolutely recommend simply for having the full experience, most of the times it's pretty straightforward - play it safe, know what you do, and equip your team appropriately, and you'll hardly lose anyone even in champion dungeons. Run around in the dark at the lower end of character, skill, and equipment class for the dungeon level - and risk to fail horribly. Of course, one might also turn lucky and return laden with those fabulous treasures you can find in the dark. Just don't expect it.
Of course, outside of NG+ this is nothing that could not be made up for by a bit of grinding. Yes, it is grindy. And I DID fail horribly more than once and spent over a dozen of hours to regain my lost items and beloved characters after the most abysmal defeat alone. Still, it is the haunting, intense atmosphere created by the ineffable art style that makes losses feel all the more desponding, and wins hardly triumphant. Although these moments are there, too.
In short - get the game and play it! It's a unique experience, and the mixture of competing feelings you'll have once you finally make it past the final boss is worth every minute, let alone every dime, you spent on it.

After playing through this game I really wish I had the chance to play the first, but seeing as I did get to play the second one lets just give you the review for that. In this game you are going to get the chance to play as a couple of different characters, but mainly you are going to be playing the part of Max and his wife Lara. The game starts of where the two are on vacation, and it turns out that there has been an art theft in the city you are staying in. You are asked to check it out, it seems routine enough, but as so many gamers can tell you, that mindset will always doom the characters. As the mysteries deepen, and the players involved become more complex, you might have to end up having to put the fate of one or more individuals on the line.
Graphically this was a great looking game. Each character not only looked different but their different styles, it gave them instant depth, and you quickly learned to trust some characters and be weary of others. The different venues that you will be going through were also very well done. You will be traveling to museums, harbors, houses, churches, ruins, and more, each captures an image in your mind that reinforces the mood of the game at that current moment.
Now lets get to one of the well done, and sadly tangled pieces that hurt the game overall. As many of you know, I am a SUCKER for fully voiced dialogue, and this game has it, the unfortunate thing is that there are quite a few times during the speeches of the secondary characters where the order in which the subtitles and audio files DO NOT match up. This caused quite some confusion for me the first time, and then later on when it happened, a couple more times, it was just a distraction that took me away from what is otherwise a very solid game.
The controls are very straight-forward. You are going to be pointing and clicking your way through the game. You will need to do this to combine items, solve puzzles, talk to individuals, and of course move around the screen. It's also a idea to use the 'J' key to pull up your journal, that thing had a tendency of saving my♥♥♥♥♥when maybe I didn't read through something thoroughly enough.
So as mentioned before you are going to get to play as a couple of characters, and the story that they are all a part of is something that had me wanting to keep playing the game. Now for some reason there were times where I didn't have a choice as it seemed the ability to go back to the main menu disappeared. I would just get a black screen, but if I hit the ESC key again I could go back into the game. If you too suffer from this, have no fear, if you move anywhere in the game, which causes a change in scene, the game autosaves. So what you can do is once you hit the black screen just Alt-F4 out, and the next time you play you can just click on the continue option.
Enough about the main menu issue, though. Let's get down to the game. There's going to be an artist flare to the whole thing, which plays nicely into the fact that Max is one hell of a painter. In some regards this level of polish in the game is what I had expected from Moebius Empire Rising. The character animations, though sometimes a bit slow on the walking aspect, where spot on. There was emotion in the characters, but not completely over the top. Each character had such a unique personality, I believed each and every one of them. I started to fear some of the characters, and started to really get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at others. So the developers and writers of this game were spot on. The degree of difficulty in this game wasn't extremely high, but there is something about this game where it was no walk in the park, there was a scoring mechanism added into the game after a while, but it wasn't anything that would stop you from being able to further the story if you were not perfect.
I wish I could tell you about some of the characters, some of the twists, some of the puzzles, and all the rest, but that would be a grave injustice. You see, even though the audio files might have gotten mixed up, and maybe there was a weird bug with the main menu, I was still able to get through the entire thing, and at the end I wanted more. That's the kind of game that I love to play, and I hope that we can see more from this game, and more of this type of game in the future. This game, hands down, gets a score of 9.3 out of 10.

I rate the game Fractured Space 2.5/5 Not that great.
Fractured space is an online, multiplayer, team-oriented (only 2 teams play at a time) space combat game wherein each player controls a fairly large capital ship. While the graphics are fantastic and the variety of ships you can play is good, this game still becomes boring and repetitious quite quickly. I don't know if there are any better games of this type out there which also involve each player controlling a big capital ship but I do know that there are a lot of things this game could have done better, at least so far.
It can take a long time to find people to play with (which means lots of waiting in game lobbies looking at boring menus) and the game is further hampered by many poor design decisions and a confusing menu interface. Areas to fight in are fairly basic and battle scenarios are overly simplistic featuring space stations which are arranged in amazingly simple and symmetrical patterns. The constant symmetry of the battle areas makes matches more fair but drastically decreases gameplay variety. Each battle area is arranged too much like every other battle area which this game has to offer making matches that much more repetitive. And since the battle areas are arranged in such basic patterns and because the game modes are so simple, the game becomes tactically simplistic and thus that much more boring for it.
As a result of this game's ultimate tactical simplicity, victory can usually be achieved in 1 of 3 ways during the course of most matches; 1) Have a generally more competent team than your opponents. 2) Have more battle ships than your opponents. or 3) Have an extremely competent player using a repair ship on your otherwise incompetent team. Ultimately, after some repetition the game starts to feel like a longer, slightly more complex game of rock, paper, scissors.
Worse still, there are not many game modes to choose from (which does help funnel the few players this game has into the few game modes which remain). There is no capture-the-flag style mode, no escort a weaker ship mode, no cooperative fend off waves of zombie AI ships mode, no free-for-all mode, etc. (at least not the last time I played). To make matters worse still, it is possible that this game may have pay-to-win elements when it comes to buying access to additional ship types (I don't know for sure myself as I never bought any access to the advanced ship types). It is possible to upgrade your ships but getting in-game currency for upgrades either requires you to play many, many matches (grinding) or paying actual money for it (hence pay-to-win allegations).
It's really too bad because this game's core concept is an intrinsically good one. The graphics are amazing and the sound and music are okay too, though the music is done in a minimalist style. The controls are good and make you feel as though you are piloting a big, ponderous capital ship. What's really gone wrong is much of the implementation of the game's core concept.
As a result, Fractured Space stands as a nifty sort of online game experiment, albeit a failed one but I think that this same sort of game could certainly have been done a lot better, especially if players were given far greater access to and control over ship customization options (a big part of the game could have been about trying out different parts for your ships like in Mechwarrior Online or Gear Up) and access to more map creation utilities (so people could create or at least recommend or choose more of their own map designs/layouts). As it stands though, Fractured Space feels old and tired and boring despite the fact that it is a fairly young online game. I hope it will improve further as time goes on but I seriously doubt it actually will.

This may be the only game I regret getting from the Humble Monthly Bundle pack, and not knowing about it before then. I had never seen a single image of this game or of its indev version Matador. I had not seen this on my Steam reccomended list, curators list, or on RPS. I wasn't scouring, but still. I regret getting this in a bundle, because I know I'd have purchased this the moment I saw it at $20, and I would've bought it sooner then that at the current $14.
Brigador is almost a simple concept; you are a mercenary pilot, and your contract is to topple a South American style dictatorship on a far off colony world. You pilot a mech walker, tanks, tiny power-suits, and even anti-gravity tanks [all in three distinct enough factions]. The weapons feel very real, the controls are incredibly solid, and the combat is incredibly refreshing and difficult. For anyone who fell in love with C&C games like Red Alert or especially Tiberian Sun, they will be visibly aroused by the graphics. The description by devs that this is a 'Kool-Aid man simulator' is remarkably applicable, as the best tactic is often to rush through an apartment block flanking your foe.
I am not even finished with the campaign, of which there are literally a dozen tutorial levels that actually have meat, and two dozen actually missions with 4 different starting configuartions each to complete. You earn money, and funnel that back into puchasing pilots and gear to use in Operations, something almost akin to Diablos dungeons. You can purchase packs of anywhere from 2 to 20+ levels to run through any pilot configuration you choose, earning money based on how difficult you've made it for yourself. That makes for a very nice feedback loop, much nicer then, say, Diablos. You earn only pride for beating a Hell level run with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ motorcycle, but you crave that pride. Like starting a Dwarf Fortress map on a glacier, just because.
Another aspect I find absolutely incredible is the dev team. For a small team to place this much effort, polish, and obvious enthusiasm into a $20 package, rather then a watered down $40-$60 game with in-game purchases and DLC level packs gallore. This is an incredible amount of game for the money. Not to mention how responsive to community I have seen them be. Two separate devs came to answer an angry thread about a particularily tricky level, and both took a lot of time to explain as best they could to the player, but also preserving the experience. They didn't say "Yeah theres a command we use to skip levels...". To take the time out of their day like that as a developer is unique. Assasins Creed devs don't do tech support.
All in all I highly reccomend this game to several people; Mech enthusiasts, C&C junkies, lovers of strategy, lovers of finely crafted menus and UI's, and fans of Just Cause. Just cause they're pretty similar with the dictator thing.
12/10, cannot wait to see what this team does next.

Where do I start? I was expecting an action packed multiplayer Sci-Fi MOBA, with real strategy needed to overcome the opposition and win the game. But this game simply wasn't that, at all. The game isn't bad in itself; the graphics are amazing, the soundtrack is great, the game runs smoothly, the tutorial is informative and you really feel a rush of excitement as you first gain control over your ship. It's just awesome at first. However, as soon as the tutorial ends the game gets worst; and it's because of the multiplayer. Since PvE in this game is just SO damn boring you have no option but to hop into multiplayer (which you should be hyped for anyway considering that is the core of this game).
After waiting 10 minutes of queue time, you finally get a chance to play and then
, you are defeated by a tank ship with better firepower than an attacker ship or oneshot by a stealth ship with infinite missiles or whatever P2W bonuses you can think of. And believe me, these ships are purchased with real money. Try having a good game when around half of both teams members are AI because this games toxic playerbase is SO small, and any actual players in this game are just SO OP because they decided to spend some cash, meaning you can't play this FREE game AND have a chance at actually winning anything, unless you dip into your wallet. That's P2W.
If you're lucky, with a credit boost in a good game you might make approximately 10K credits or so, but there's no point because a new ship costs millions and a grind like that won't make much difference in battle anyway as this is a MOBA, a TEAM GAME, and you need a good team that uses strategy to win, not just good ships (sadly that's not how this game works...). But there is no strategy if half your team are AI that do nothing but traverse the map in circles, or your team also happens to be weak af whilst the other team obliterates you with their P2W goodies.
Also, for a MOBA, the map is incredibly small, and games are quite short. It's obvious that this game focuses more on a straight-up standoff between ships, and the strongest one wins (let me remind you that these are usually the 'money ships') and there isn't really any strategy involved. If you love team-based games with a heavy focus on strategy, this game isn't worth it. If you're looking for a game to waste time in (hey, it's your life not mine) then go for it.
+ Stunning graphics, really detailed ship designs and action animations
+ Great soundtrack
+ Performance is good
+ Informative tutorial
- P2W has a lot of weight in this game. Too much
- Extremely low playerbase, resulting in long matchmaking times and a lot of AI opponents in PvP games
- Community is toxic, with hackers taking advantage and devs doing nothing to stop it
- PvE is incredibly boring (imo), and the AI could be better
- No sense of strategy; the more expensive the ship the better chance of winning
- Map is very small, despite the game having a space theme (space is meant to be vast and expansive right?)
- Games are very short for a MOBA, too short for any sort of 'team plan'
- Grinding for new ships legitimately is excessive and annoying

I can not in good faith recommend this game to anyone who claims to be a fan of strategy games or X-COM as a series. After a successful campaign played, and several others started and promptly aborted, I find myself looking back on my time with this game as being utterly wasted and unrewarding. Here's why.
If you are a fan of strategy games, like myself, and know nothing of the X-COM series, you're better off either getting the original, Xenonauts or the 2012 remake that this game is a sequel of. The former two actually reward tactics and strategy, while the latter is at least fun, despite its tactical shallowness. This game features none of the fun of its predecessor. Both games claim to be in the "hardcore" spectrum of games, and while games like the original 1994 game earn that moniker by presenting the player with difficult, but ultimately winnable scenarios that have multiple solutions based on player skill, this game earns it by merely presenting the player with a series of weighted dice rolls.
XCOM 2 loves its dice, and this becomes apparent right from the beginning of a campaign. Skipping the tutorial (a multi-hour affair valuable only to someone who has never touched a strategy game before in their life), the intro campaign mission on anything but normal difficulty will rapidly introduce you to XCOM 2's idea of difficulty. Your soldiers, at their basic state, will hover at a
chance to hit any enemy with a
- while your enemies don't have better chances, provided your soldiers are positioned adequately, they are more than equipped to mitigate their own failings - even basic enemy patrols at the beginning of the game will often include an officer enemy who, provided the AI doesn't make a stupid decision (another dice roll), can mark one of your soldiers, making them much more likely to take a hit from any enemy, and shoot, all in the same turn. If you don't find yourself against one of these officers, you might find yourself up against a Sectoid, whose cover-ignoring psionics can make your soldiers panic, waste a turn and reposition to an often-disadvantageous position where they'll likely be flanked and killed with little effort from your foes.
The player, conversely, is presented with few tools to mitigate the abhorrent effects of the game's RNG - when 66% is the best you can expect on a flanking shot from even a middling range, the only reliable tools at your disposal are grenades and melee, and the latter has the unfortunate yet obvious side-effect of forcing your units into close quarters, making it suitable only as a finishing touch to an engagement. An enemy introduced fairly early into the meat of a campaign, as well, can, without prior warning or indication, block even the most veteran Ranger's blade and deliver a counterattack, usually resulting in the death of your unit, so melee is hardly a reliable friend in tactically adverse situations. Reliable damage-dealing abilities and player-controlled psionics are also options, but only at a point in the campaign where a player has already dealt with the worst that XCOM 2 has to offer.
And worst it is. The first 10 or so missions of any campaign are guaranteed to be the most brutal on offer of any that you will deal with over the course of the game. Simulating scarcity by giving the player an under-equipped force is one thing, but how the player is expected to deal with it is ridiculous. Off the battlefield, on the world map layer of the game, the player is expected to amass resources, develop better equipment and try to foil ADVENT (the alien antagonists) and their Avatar Project, a constantly ticking clock at the top of your screen that is introduced within the first few missions. The problem with all this is that, like everything else in the game, your progress will largely be decided by dice rolls. "Investigation sites" pop up on the world map, and the player can spend in-game days following these leads for a variety of resources and rewards. These are entirely random, and the first few sites a player can access can determine the fate of an entire campaign, thanks to ADVENT ramping up their forces far faster than your own if things play out poorly. Getting an incredibly valuable engineer as your first site can make all the difference in whether or not you can take 5 or 6 soldiers into combat instead of the base 4, or if your units will be expected to fight Vipers, Faceless or Mutons with conventional weapons or Railguns. Getting supplies (the game's currency) or recruits as your first few sites, on the other hand, can mean being dangerously underequipped for the next several missions, resulting in inevitable casualties, and the casualties are indeed inevitable. Unlike in its immediate predecessor, where unit damage resulted in a brief convalescing period for unarmoured units or MECs, units that take a single hit in combat might be put out of action for close to an entire in-game month; an almost-unacceptable loss when a campaign only spans maybe 6 or 7 months. Mitigating this requires devoting engineers, personnel vital to construction and therefore progress, to medic duty, something that probably should have been relegated to scientists, who have comparatively little else to do, and only one building to supervise compared to the 4 or so vital buildings
the attention of an engineer. The game, therefore, punishes you for even trying to mitigate the effects of a combat RNG failure by stalling your progress, either through bad design or through malicious intent.
The illusion of choice on the strategic layer is, therefore, just that - an illusion. A player can decide to rush down certain avenues (psionics vs. weapons vs. armor vs. squad buffs, for example), and the lacklustre DLCs add additional paths to prioritize, but any of these options have the same result on the battlefield; you'll either stomp your foes or be stomped. There is no middle ground in XCOM 2, thanks to the sheer cruelty of its dice rolls. Until one researches the top tier of armor and weapons, or obtain fully kitted-out psionic soldiers, one can only plan for the eventuality of losing a veteran soldier, which can happen in the short and brutal span of a single enemy turn, if the dice will it so.
The campaign itself is predictable - relatively open-ended campaign missions only serve to bracket the purpose-built campaign "levels", much like its predecessor, and the story doesn't go in any particularly interesting directions. The characters aren't anything special, but neither were they in the first game, and characterization is only a bonus at best in a strategy game, so no points are lost on this. For all its focus on the "story", however, the campaign manages to end on a definitively lacklustre and humdrum final mission, something which almost every X-COM clone or remake has had an issue with. Gone are the days of taking the fight to the aliens, using their own technology to make a spacefaring vessel and bombing their base on Mars to kingdom come (the original game's ending) - this game's final mission has none of that intensity, and even has the gall to end on a cliffhanger, despite plans on forthcoming expansions or DLCs being apparently relegated to third party development in the form of the Long War team.
That I've been motivated to write so many words on this game should speak to my devotion to the series and to strategy gaming in general. So few games with the production values and expertise put into XCOM 2 come out in the genre that it would be tempting to give it a pass purely on that basis. However, a focus on brutal RNG in place of difficulty through good design prove to be crippling flaws to what should otherwise be a fantastic game, to say nothing of further development on it being apparently outsourced.
Final score: 4/10, with prejudice. Not worth full price by any means, and certainly not worth an extended period of time.

I appeared on the coast somewhere. I had no idea where, I had spawned with the minimum, two bandages and a roadside flare. I had no map to work out my location and nothing with which to defend myself. I ran over the hill and there was a small town. I was noticed by some zeds and ran away from the town. Let me tell you, these zombies do not give up easily. After a lengthy run throuhghout the countryside dodging in and out of tree. I was finally rid of my pursuers. Now where the hell was I,nothing but hills and trees to be seen. Well, more running. Eventually I come across a barn and once again I am noticed and chase is given. Another run through the countryside and more trees and hills later I find another hillside village. I begin creeping well before I get to it, I have learned something at least. As I get closer I notice the zombies milling around and go prone, crawling my way through the wet grass, skirting zombies and stopping now and thehn when they get to near. But then of course one of them would like to walk right where I am lying and I'm off for another run.
Yes there is a definate pattern forming here. Get lost in the wild, run and eventually discover some buiildings, get chased by zombies away from your finding and lost again you are. This goes on and on for some time. Eventually I died, one too many run ins with no means of fixing myself, my vision went all grey and blurred in and out of semi focus. Running around with your screen doing that you find yourself squinting at it, willing your eyes to make sense of what it sees and all the time fighting the headache which is arising from the disorientation this causes.
I died a few time s this way and learned to be extra cautious, more creeping and creeping slowly with the shift button held in too. Next time I spawned again somewhere on the coastline, I ran over the hill and noticed another small town. I crept up to it, slow creeping around any threats and found a dead man. Upon study I found out who he was and what he had died of, blood loss. And I also found a couple more bandages and flares. I proceeded to the building he was near and crept inside closing the doors behind me just to be sure. There was another dead guy lying near a table. I had hit the jackpot, this guy had been well geared up when he died, again from bloodloss. I aquired an alice pack, tool kit, matches food and drinks and weapons with ammo and a hatchet.
I was feeling good now, and I might add a touch over confident, which ultimately led once again to an untimely demise when I tried to take on everyzombie I saw with my hatchet. the first few were not an issue, hiding nearby I simply clouted them as they walked by and down they went. The next ones got the better of me, I was noticed creeping up on one and he ran at me. Hitting a slow ambling zombie with an axe is a walk in the park. trying to hit one running at full pelt in an erratic pattern is a completely different kettle of fish, he got me a few times, some of his friends noticed and joined in the fun and games. I hit and ran, got my gun out (my guy stops running to do this!) and shot which only alertedmore of them. I ran to the sea and in I plunged. Now zombies are not bees and the characters in this game are not fast swimmers. The last of my health left me as I tried in vain to doggie padlle away from the voracious horde.

Yes, absolutely yes, I -can- recommend the new Master of Orion (4?) already now with tons of content still missing
I consider myself a longtime fan of the series (by which I mean Master of Orion 1 and 2) and yes I was certainly not sure what to expect when I heard Wargaming Net had picked up the rights.
Though I was happy Orion was finally seeing new life.
For the most part? They've played it pretty safe,  you'll recognize the technologies, the alien species (based on Orion 1's style/look) being able to design ships and put them to good use.
You'll reckognize tiny little details like the Master of Orion 1 colonization theme when establishing new colonies.
You'll see creatures like giant "Space Eels" and many many other things you'll reckognize from the originals.
That said? There have been changes, there's now a space-lane system (that you might reckognize from other4x games) rather than the fee jump where you want (that's within range) , to me this works, though you'll have to play the game differently (fortify key systems to avoid the enemy pushing through)
So, if any enemy empire has hidden their weak/developing systems, behind an wall of fortified systems? That's to bad, you won't be able to hit them.
As before you can simply "roll" the dice to see who win starship battles, or duke it out. Though ...the "tactical" combat leaves much to be desired for now, I imagine this will improve.
Had they simply stolen "Sid Meier's Starships" combat, I would've happy with it.
The game is still in early access, but it's already really well polished, there's obvious stuff missing (features and more playable aliens).  The potential fall for this series was a HUGE one,  I'm happy this game doesn't disappoint.
Is it the deepest space strategy game out there?  Absolutely not, and that's a good thing in my mind. It's easy to get into, and there's definitely a lot of strategies to master.
On a scale from F to A, I'd give it a B minus. I expect this grade to improve :D

One of my most enduring memories as a young PC gamer was sitting in front of my old 386 well into the early morning hours playing Master of Orion.  I still have my old floppy discs for it, and the manual which was absolutely necessary to pass through the regular security checks the game ran to prevent piracy.  And it was a masterpiece, one only exceeded by Master of Orion 2 in the canon of space 4x games in my estimation.  After the absolute travesty that was MOO3 I thought we would never have another one to rival the first two.
Until now.
This game is EARLY ACCESS.  That has to be emphasized.  There are races not yet available for play (The Darlok, Klakon, Meklar, and Silicoids), I've had one solitary CTD, and a few graphical glitches here and there but on the whole this is already an amazingly polished title with astounding voice acting (by such luminaries as Mark Hamill and Alan Tudyk) and gorgeous graphics.  I enjoy just sitting on the main game map, watching the stars twinkle and shine, the nebulae shift and flux, and my ships flying through the space lanes with a massive bow shock in front of them as testament to their faster than light speed.
This is the first game since the old MIcroprose days to capture the FEEL of Master of Orion.  Everything about it is immersive, from the extraordinary animations for the alien race leaders you meet, the constant chiming in from your advisors (some of which are voiced by big Hollywood names ... hearing Alan Tudyk as the Psilon advisor just makes me smile every time he speaks up).
There is no proper campaign at this point, but plenty of open, free space to play around in, conquer and be conquered in turn.  You can play a game from beginning to end already, through conquest, diplomacy, research, economic might, and several other victory conditions of your choosing.  The game map on Medium or Large is huge, and I know there was some concern that it was only going to contain, at maximum, 100 or so star systems but believe me when I say that at the pace this game plays that is an ideal number.  It feels as grand as games offering thousands of systems to conquer and plays at a more thoughtful pace requiring more attention to detail (unless you automate production and let the game do it for you, which is an entirely viable strategy, focusing your own attentions on matters of military and diplomacy as your governors churn out buildings and units like there's no tomorrow).
I had some concerns about the ship design system.  There are still aspects of it not in game, but I will tell you straight away that it lacks the complete customization of a game like the GalCiv series.  You won't be putting together the building blocks or your ship here, choosing from hundreds of hulls and nacelles and fiddly little bits.  But it still manages to be intensely satisfying, with lots of graphical bells and whistles (I especially love the Psilon ship designs which harken to the flying saucer days of 1950s alien conspiracy theories).  I felt no great lack of customization in the end and the polish on these ships outshines much of what players could manage on their own.  I suspect there will be more hull designs to come, more options to choose from, but again it is still Early Access.
In short, if you loved the original MOO or MOO2, if Civ5 was your cup o tea, or if you relish getting stuck into the kind of gaming experience that will have you plastered to your PC for hours without a break and every minute of it spent feeling like you ARE the emperor of a burgeoning space-faring race out to charm, deceive, or otherwise conquer all who dare to raise a laser cannon or tachyon beam against you ... this IS the game you've been looking for.
For all the supposed successors to Master of Orion that have come and gone over the last 20 years, this is the first one to do it justice since MOO2.  What Wargaming have made is a clear labor of love and it retains enough of what made MOO the father of the 4x genre while blessing it with enough that's new to bring a much-loved franchise into the 21st Century.
Buy it.  NOW.

ADDRESSING THE COMPLAINTS:
If you plan on playing Ironman mode; DON'T.  If you plan on playing on Legendary difficulty; DON'T.  If you plan on playing with a make-shift handicap; DON'T.  At least not at first.  Majority of the people complaining about the difficulty of XCOM 2 are idiots who routinely ♥♥♥♥♥ed about how easy XCOM 1 was and then proceeded to play at max difficulty thinking it would be a cake-walk.  They rightfully got smacked in the gob by the sequels challenges.  You should have a game completion under your belt before playing Ironman or Legendary, so that you know the full extent to what the game offers.  Without experience in playing XCOM 2, you will lose multiple, multiple times within the first few hours.
For those saying that the game "runs horribly", despite a few absurdly long load times (coming back from missions takes a solid minute, to a minute and a half for some reason for me) this game is fairly recent, and was designed to be a PC exclusive, taking advantage of PC exclusive graphical features.  If you're running this on a 760, or even a 950, expect to be disappointed with the framerate.  I was running it on a 1050ti and I just barely managed to average around 50 FPS, though I was playing with substantially higher settings, including Screen Space Ambient Occlusion, High shadows, High textures, at 1920x1080, etc.  If you have a 1060 or better, then feel free to ♥♥♥♥♥ about the framerates, but overall, I have found that this game tends to have a fairly consistent framerate, though after long hours of playing it also tends to become more inconsistent.
NOW THAT THAT'S OUT OF THE WAY
This is a worthy successor to the original XCOM that released back in 2012 (has it really been that long?), in more ways than one.
-GAMEPLAY-
The gameplay from the original is still intact, but there's a significant difference; concealment.  Some missions will start your units out in a concealed state, and some abilities allow your soldiers to conceal themselves.  This creates a level of stealth that has virtually been absent from the entire X-COM franchise, strangely enough.  You can create ambushes, use scouts to (try) and achieve the objective unseen, if it's planting a bomb or hacking a computer, and you can have them conceal themselves to hide and avoid enemy fire.  This greatly changes the beginning of most missions, and makes them more fun in my opinion.
There are some annoying features that I have to get out of the way though, the first being the very annoying pauses that seem to happen ALL the time.  For some reason, the AI camera will pause before playing an in-game cutscene if you've been revealed, run into a new enemy unit, or sometimes if it's waiting for the AI to ends its turn.  Overall, it seems that this is either a bug with the ambient narrative setting (I had it turned on, haven't tried it with it turned off yet), or just a large bug in general.  It doesn't break the mission (that comes later), but it does become frustrating, since all that time adds up.  Another thing that bothers me is that sometimes, albeit rarely, units will get "stuck", unable to act in any way what-so-ever.  Not all of them, just one, maybe two if you're really unlucky, and nothing you do besides reloading an earlier auto-save can free them.  Perhaps they're just bugs with the map, but it seems to happen at random, which is especially scary during evac missions, since you cannot evac them.
Back to the core mechanics; a loot system has also been integrated, where you can now modify each classes weapons, offering a wide variety of gizmo's and gadgets to add to your guns to increase aim, increase crit chance, magazine size, or something that offers a small little bonus like reloading not spending an action the first 2 times on a mission.  Among those, there's also the Proving Grounds and Guerilla Tactics School, where you can customize your soldiers in their special abilities/bonuses, as well as adding new gear to your arsenal.  Things like exo-suits with mounted weapons and unique ammo types are only a small selection of the large amount of different gadgets you can make, some more useful than others, others more specialized.
Speaking of the soldiers, they are far more customizable now, with full-body, name, color-scheme, biography, and even personality customization.  Indeed, this seems to be the most in-game customizable XCOM yet.  Your soldiers will be instantly identifiable in the field with that cool new armor combination you gave him, or that incredibly ugly color scheme you slapped onto him.  Either way, there's a lot to take away and personalize here that gives each soldier a level of intimacy and personality to make you become genuinely attached to them.
Outside of the new mechanics and customization, they've also added a procedural map generation system, which I must say, I did get tired of all the samey-feeling maps from XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but here they all feel different enough that you don't start questioning whether you've played this exact map setup before.  It creates a more enjoyable, immersive experience to be going from China to Africa and not see the same city layouts as before, which is something that has plagued the series for years.
-THE ALIENS-
The alien design is great, in particular, the design of the ADVENT forces, a gene-spliced mingling of human DNA, which you'll soon come to find out more about.  The sleak, geometric designs of the ADVENT forces gives them a visibly clean and intimidating vibe, where they may be the most basic cannon fodder you'll come across, they still know how to aim and flank.  Aside from them, the real stars are the Andromedons and Sectoids, the former of which feels very reminiscent of a Big Daddy from bioshock, although far more menacing.  The Sectiods, for that matter, are also much more intimidating, wielding potent psi powers and having reasonable health, they remain a fairly consistent worry on the battlefield throughout most of the game, primarily in the beginning.  Not to spoil too many of the games surprises, but you'll see a plentiful variety of aliens throughout, though perhaps it's just because of the luck of the draw, I seemed to run into fairly few of a certain kind.
Each alien also has their own behavior in battle.  The ADVENT forces will routinely use cover and try to out-flank you, exchanging gunfire in a standard affair, though the Sectiod's are unpredictable and will try and scurry around the environment, flinging psi powers at you and taking shots at you every now and then with their wrist-mounted blasters.  Chryssalids have a new ability, in that they can burrow (oh joy!) into the ground and wait for you to come a little too close before popping out and ambushing you, sort of like their very own "reaction shots" as they burst forth and rush you to deal an attack.  Chryssalids are far less deadly though, and I don't think I lost a single soldier to one (probably due to my hatred/fear of them and targetting them first).
-GRAPHICS-
The game looks great.  Colors are evenly distributed and vivid in the designs of the environments and the units, not to mention the core designs of all the units all stand out phenomenally well, the animations standing out on their own as wholly impressive.  The subsurface scattering is most instantly noticeable on the Sectoid's, which gives them a lively flare, their translucent skin and skeleton-like bodies create an immediately concerning visage.  Maps look very slick and polished, environments are substantially better than they were in the previous game, and the destruction is a lot more in-depth, with gradual and sectional destruction of environments rather than before where you either destroyed it or didn't.  Overall, it looks as good as it plays.

Shadwen feels like a superhero stealth game. The fact that the game freezes time unless you're moving or explicitly waiting means you can take your time and carefully plan out every single action, pulling off ridiculous stunts like swinging from the rafters down to loot a chest right between two guards, or use your grappling hook to Spiderman your way around the level. It's amazing! I absolutely loved it - I'd never considered real-time pause for a stealth game before, but it works excellently. The fact that you can instantly rewind everything makes it all so playful as well, and eliminates the impulse to save-scum.
The core mechanics are solid fun; and the levels are reasonably challenging, since your main goal is less getting through the level than it is getting Lily, your little companion, through the level safely. If the idea of a game built around an escort mission worries you, that's totally fair, but Lily isn't an obnoxiously terrible companion like you'd find in other games. She's pretty good at heading for the exit as fast as she can, so much so that for most of the game I forgot you can specifically send her to certain spots, and instead followed her to the exit when the level design was confusing. She also never triggers guard alarms, though she will avoid their lines of sight and won't move through the level unless she's in the clear, so doing a non-lethal run means distracting the guards from her path.
The narrative is very, very minimal - you get some idea of what's going on through guard banter, and it's fairly subtle, but beyond that the entire game is about your slow progress through an occupied city to a castle, where you're hunting the king. I enjoyed the minimalism and the lack of explicit explanations, and I thought the Shadwen/Lily dynamic was nice.
I did have a few issues. For one thing, the art assets were very limited - you can tell they reused as much as possible, to the point that there are two enemy types and two hiding spots (bushes and haystacks) in the whole game, which can lead to ridiculous situations like bushes growing inside of castles or haystacks at every street corner, because there just aren't enough art assets. Most of the levels are built from the same few sets of brick, stone, walls, and props; it does get a bit boring to the eye after a while. Although the stuff that is there looks quite nice for such a small indie game - some of the backdrops and architecture are really nice, and the characters look good, so it's probably for the best they didn't try to make too many assets.
By the fifteenth level, some of the gameplay did get a bit repetitive too - there are only so many ways you can distract guards by knocking things around and swinging from the rafters with your awesome grappling hook. But overall, I had a lot of fun with this game, and it didn't quite overstay its welcome.

Brigador is, on the surface, an isometric shooter in the vein of Desert Strike. You drop into a zone and complete any number of objectives before exfiltrating. You can blast everything in your path, but sneaking is usually an option with the right vehicle. There are a gazillion unique, and well-designed, vehicles you can unlock, divided into three categories; tanks, mechs and antigrav.
Categories of vehicles all share common traits but they come in all shapes, sizes and forms. Hulking heavy mechs like the Touro are the most straightforward; good for overall mayhem with heavier weapon mounts and strong hull and shields, while smaller vehicles like the Mongoose powersuit require a much more subtle approach, sneaking around and ambushing lone units before hiding again. A fast, light antigrav like the Rope Kid might require you to stay on the move, doing hit and runs, 'knife-fighting' or do repeating jousting attacks with short-range, high power weapons.
This is where the beauty of Brigador lies. Picking a random vehicle and figuring out what loadout and tactics work best for that particular one is really fun. If you've mastered one, you pick another and find that it's a whole different game. Some are harder than others of course, but you are rewarded accordingly for picking harder vehicles (and difficulties). Mastering a hard vehicle is truly satisfying.
The campaign takes you through a lengthy tutorial (introduced in the Up-Armored relaunch) and a series of missions featuring a few vehicles with preset loadouts for each. It works well for demonstrating the diversity aspect of the game, but the meat of it all lies in Freelance mode. This is where you pick a vehicle and loadout and go on operations through a varying number of districts. The more you do in a row, the more cash you will make for unlocks, but ammo, hull and shields carry through each level. Dying before a run is complete will forfeit most of the rewards. The pilot you pick sets the difficulty and also determines the reward multiplier, which stacks with the multiplier set by the vehicle you're piloting. Pull off a long, difficult run with a tricky vehicle and earn massive rewards.
Weapons are as varied as the vehicles themselves, including cannons of many calibers and ammo types, machineguns and autocannons, mortars and howitzers for indirect fire, along with energy weapons of multiple types. They all do differently against shields, hull, and cover, and behave differently in regards to range and firing arcs. Weapons also have penetration values so depending on the circumstances, you might be able to take shots through walls or take out multiple enemies with one shot. Figuring out how the shooting works is a learning experience on its own, and may lead to some frustration as you might for example shoot over low-profile enemies despite aiming straight for them (tip: aim slightly in front to get the right elevation in such circumstances, or behind to avoid shooting under antigrav vehicles). You will also have to take care standing clear of obstacles (not always easy since you tend to look at your target instad of your own vehicle) as you fire since a building might not only block your shot but might turn your own awesome firepower against you (looking at you, siege howitzer). Explosive hazards are not always easy to see or identify, and you might walk into an exploding fuel pipeline or two before you get the hang of it, but destroying such hazards have an intrinsic value in that it distracts enemies and might set you up for a tasty ambush.
This game is a gem; the developers, Stellar Jockeys, have been working hard on new content over the past year, keeping their ears open and have lovingly crafted a hell of a game. With the recent re-launch things have only become better, adding much needed polish and a proper tutorial. The background lore can nearly be ignored since focus is on gameplay but if you care to look you will find some very cool stuff there too. I can recommend reading the ♥♥♥♥ing amazing Brigador novel by Brad Buckmaster. The soundtrack by Makeup And Vanity Set is killer as well. Brigador is a goddamn miracle.

Coming from a user who started playing this game in 2010 on the stand-alone client.
Pros
1. Hit register never fails. If you didn't get the shot you missed.. period.
2. Doesn't take a lot of time to get in to the groove of the game, but mastering it takes much longer.
3. Can run on low-end (2011-2012 amd/nvidia chipsets ) PC's perfectly on high/medium settings.
4. There is always some kind of event or give away.
5. As you rank up, you receive items to help you throughout your experience.
6. There is missions/quests to help you rank up faster, so less time worrying about how low your rank is.
7. Built-in enhancement system for your character(s) (You can pick more than one character). These enhancements are class-chosen (Assault Rifler, SMG, Sniper) and so on. The enhancements are things like accuracy, firing your gun faster, reloading faster, throwing grenades farther, so on.
8. A fresh experience for a player who has played common FPS's.
9. It has a tutorial that gives you free in-game points.
Cons
1. Poor in-game recording tool. You will be better off using tools like Fraps and ShadowPlay.
2. Slightly P2W, but you can easily destroy enemies who have equipped pay-to-win items.
3. The game mechanics a majority of the time are highly unrealistic, compared to games like CS:GO. Please don't say this game is a copy of CS:GO, dear god it was released 5 years before GO.
4. Extremely limited PVE mode. It is a deathmatch mode where you can go up to vs. 8 bots, and the more kills you get, the higher their difficulty increases.
5. The weapons are not permanent in any way. There is quanity (guns purchased with points) and days (equipment purchased with points/ real money or guns purchased with real money). ***tl;dr ***
Wait for the full release. Game is unfinished, unbalanced and too easy at the moment. Buy only if you A) Want to support the developers or B) Want to experience all the patches that will come untill release. At this time the game will give you about 10 hours of fun before you will realize that it needs to be finished to give you about 100+ more. It plays well though and I like it a lot.
*** See the bottom for updates. ***
First impressions from Early access, review will follow when the game will be released.
If you cannot bare bugs, strange behavior and missing depth to some parts of the game elements then DO NOT buy this game yet, except you would want to support the developers.
* This game is a lot like Endless space when it started, but has a lot more potential. The tactical combat mainly is going to be better in my opinion due to the possibility to control the ships. The production values overall are higher.
* Game lacks depth at the moment which is coming in few months I hope but is very well playable now. I will repeat myself here; the game is very similar to how the Endless space was at launch.
* The art and voice overs are TOP quality. Music reminds me a lot of Star Trek for some reason.
* Graphics are OK for a 4X game but in my opinion the ship models could use some work, especially at the strategic layer.
* If you want to experience full depth and engaging game from the start then you should wait a bit... I suppose the game will be feature full in the summer.
* Strategic game is turn based and tactical combat is RT with pause.
* Map options are limited at the moment. Map size, difficulty and number of races mainly.
* If you like 4x games in general then you will most probably like this game too. The gameplay is fluid and quite fast, no HC micromanagements at the moment.
* If you are expecting a graphically updated MOO 2 then you will be disapointed. This game is going to be a bit different. This is in no way a clone of the old MOO games. It uses the same basic structure but the feel to it is not the same.
* Game is not finished; you can see it mainly in tactical combat which is lacking a lot. And the combat is not turn based (maybe it will change?).
* Research and race stats are done differently than in MOO2.
* No NPCs yet.
* The voice overs can be a bit annoying if they will not fit your "expectations" from how you have imagined them in MOO2 for example.
* This game is, in my opinion, for new generation of players. It will have a lot in common with MOO2 but will never be the same...
I like how the game is looking now and what potential it has so I recommend it in general but be careful here. Even though it fits my "needs", it may not fit yours. Do a bit of research and watch a lets play on youtube first.
*** Updates: ***
So after playing a bit I've found following things that will be worked on most before the release, or at least I hope so.
* Espionage is missing at the moment, but the foundations are there. You can build and research upgrades for your spies.
* Ground combat is a placeholder at the moment. No armies battling at the moment, only simple explosion animations.
* Tactical combat is a bit better than ground combat but it's still a place holder too.
* No story at the moment as far as I can tell.
* Races are not complete, the racial stats are too simple at the moment to be considered finished.
* No race specific tech at the moment.
