Master of Orion 2 is my definitive favourite strategy game, no 4X game has ever gotten as close to near perfection as far as I am concerned. I have played MoO2 for probably thousands of hours since I first bought it about 18 years ago, and still play it a couple of times every year.
From the first early teasers I was really hoping this game would be a true Master of Orion sequel. I went in to play for two hours. Forced myself to stop just before the 2 hour mark due to feeling VERY, VERY dissapointed, then I went to watch several youtubers to see more of what the game has to offer.
*The races are dumbed down variants of their own MoO2 counterparts, the traits are little more than minor stat buffs in different fields. Not game defining traits that you based your core strategy around, and give each race a unique play style.
*Technology has a civ-style tech tree, which do feel bland, thin and very constricted. I am happy they decided to hold on to one of MoO2s defining features, that you could only choose one discovery per technology. In MoO2, that was something that further allowed you to gradually define your empire and playstyle as the game progressed. However, this feature feels somewhat dumbed down in this game, as at the first tiers of research you get all the discoveries, cutting out some potentially very difficult decisions. Later on you will need to make choices however, which is nice.
*Combat is very boring. While you CAN control your ships to some extent, especially if you repeatedly pause and overview their orders, they fights mostly manage themselves rather quickly.
In MoO2, combat was a great, it was the climax of the game, where you finally got to test your ship designs against the enemy, and where your actions and tactics mattered the most. It was far from perfect, but it had potential to be FUN. There were definitely possibilities to improve, perhaps by getting rid of the coarce grid, reducing fleet-sizes or making huge fleets easier to manage, adding MORE weapons types, tactical options, etc, etc.
But rather then keeping what was good and improving on it, they decided to make combat uninspired, dull and nothing like Master of Orion 2. (It is pretty tho).
*Ship customization was the last huge feature of Master of Orion 2. Each ship had a maximum mass, and you could add ANY mix of weapons and modules into it. Mostly, each type of weapon was interesting and offered a unique tactical option. The process of creating ships was always interesting and challenging.
This new Master of Orion does, very unfortunately, dumb this down... I feel constricted when it comes to customization. Weapons feel bland and lacks uniqueness. This lack of interesting ship design also further hurts the already boring combat.
I was hoping for a reinvention of one of the best games in history, an improvement on what already was great. But this is not that, at least not yet.
If they want to get my thumbs up, and amount to anything but being another failed MoO2-clone in my opinion, they need to do a total design-makeover and adress the immense dumbing down of the races and technology, find a better and more interesting way to design ships (likely with more subsystems and weapons). And most important of all: make combat something that is actually something more then a mere cinematic experience with minimal interactions.
I will ask for my moneys back, but I will keep my eyes on the game. Perhaps eventually it will grow to finally be a decent game. But I doubt that will happen, as major design changes rarely happen this late in production.
[EDIT] Thinking about it some more; this game is actually not that bad if you don't compare it to MoO2, there are no obvious game-breaking features that actually ruins the game. If you are in the market for a uncomplicated, mainstream space-4x, you might very possibly enjoy the game.

I wake up on my dead grandfather's derelict farm. Around me decay has claimed most of the property; the fallen limbs of trees scattered about like lifeless soldiers on a battlefield, weeds growing mockingly from their corpses. I shuffle uneasily past the grim scene and make my way into town. Rude teens scoff at my dusty overalls, my calloused hands. The debaucherous glowing faces of daytime drunks and self-interested egomaniacs sneer at my passing and huddle in my wake to add fangs to their slanderous rumors. I seek shelter in the town library, surely a safe haven, but a prissy woman shoves me out of the way as if I were nothing but a door; inside the curator won't speak to me unless I bring him gifts. Deep in the mines I watch as the playful veneer melts under the grim darkness and lava floes.
As I drag my weary body back to my uninviting straw mattress I realize -- Stardew Valley isn't a farming simulator; it's a hell simulator. What, oh, what have I done to bring me to this woeful fate? Alas, what can be done but to work the land, to toil eternally under the sins of my former life? Axe, hoe, pick - these are the tools of my salvation. As I watch the seasons roll past, as my hands twist themselves into massive bleeding blisters I begin to understand that I was always here and here I shall always remain.

Ok, serious time. This is my personal favorite game. It holds this title as it represents the spirit of the underground market that it hails from, and as such stands toe-to-toe with any triple-A game and stares them down to their knees.
The world is developed and rich, even as it falls apart you can see the ghost of what it once was and what you stand for in it. Bastion tells the story very well, in the midst of gameplay VIA Logan Cunningham, regarded by yours truly as the man with the sexiest voice in the history of anything. Heavy character exposition is delivered very cleverly, instead of in a big boring cutscene almost entirely unnesential to gameplay it is delivered in the grind areas where you will be bored to♥♥♥♥♥♥and with open arms welcome the story of the characters and learn to love them. Also, the grinding mentioned before is only for indesicive people who can't decide on a weapon they love with all their heart. Which brings me to weapons. There are so many weapons and each has a cemented niche. It's one of the best feelings ever to pick up a gun and fall in love with it, and have it evolve with the story because of your hard work filching upgrade materials and grinding on proving grounds. Some of the best weapons include:
A sniper rifle that can be upgraded into essentially a machine gun that shoots explosives
A knife that turns you into a wall of stabbing and pain
Two revolvers. Enough said.
A shotgun that turns into a wave of bullet that washes enemies off the unstable ruined landscape.
A machine gun that upgrades into a hideous beast that pukes out a storm of bones that seek out enemies.
Make no mistake, this isn't a gun game. It can be if that's what you want. It's strong all around and it is easily my favorite game. It's still my favorite game even after things like bioshock infinite. Make no mistake, I like Infinite too, but if it came down to it it'd be Bastion in a heartbeat. If you do not own this game, buy it and finish it. If you are dissapointed, I am genuinely sorry.

As someone who was born in '96, I didn't really get to experience the games of the 90's until I was much older. Now that I am, going back and playing these games for the first time is very interesting and unique experience.
When I heard that this game won over 50 game of the year awards and is said to be one of the best games of all time, I wasn't entirely sure why, until I played it of course.
It's very adrenaline fueled adventure, like being in a sci-fi action movie. From the moment Gordon Freeman accidentally ushers forth the Green Apocalypse, to the ending where that mysterious timelord threatens you before putting you on ice, the story and action doesn't stop. The first person perspective really puts you into the world of The Black Mesa Research Facility, making this a personal journey for every player. Brigador is, on the surface, an isometric shooter in the vein of Desert Strike. You drop into a zone and complete any number of objectives before exfiltrating. You can blast everything in your path, but sneaking is usually an option with the right vehicle. There are a gazillion unique, and well-designed, vehicles you can unlock, divided into three categories; tanks, mechs and antigrav.
Categories of vehicles all share common traits but they come in all shapes, sizes and forms. Hulking heavy mechs like the Touro are the most straightforward; good for overall mayhem with heavier weapon mounts and strong hull and shields, while smaller vehicles like the Mongoose powersuit require a much more subtle approach, sneaking around and ambushing lone units before hiding again. A fast, light antigrav like the Rope Kid might require you to stay on the move, doing hit and runs, 'knife-fighting' or do repeating jousting attacks with short-range, high power weapons.
This is where the beauty of Brigador lies. Picking a random vehicle and figuring out what loadout and tactics work best for that particular one is really fun. If you've mastered one, you pick another and find that it's a whole different game. Some are harder than others of course, but you are rewarded accordingly for picking harder vehicles (and difficulties). Mastering a hard vehicle is truly satisfying.
The campaign takes you through a lengthy tutorial (introduced in the Up-Armored relaunch) and a series of missions featuring a few vehicles with preset loadouts for each. It works well for demonstrating the diversity aspect of the game, but the meat of it all lies in Freelance mode. This is where you pick a vehicle and loadout and go on operations through a varying number of districts. The more you do in a row, the more cash you will make for unlocks, but ammo, hull and shields carry through each level. Dying before a run is complete will forfeit most of the rewards. The pilot you pick sets the difficulty and also determines the reward multiplier, which stacks with the multiplier set by the vehicle you're piloting. Pull off a long, difficult run with a tricky vehicle and earn massive rewards.
Weapons are as varied as the vehicles themselves, including cannons of many calibers and ammo types, machineguns and autocannons, mortars and howitzers for indirect fire, along with energy weapons of multiple types. They all do differently against shields, hull, and cover, and behave differently in regards to range and firing arcs. Weapons also have penetration values so depending on the circumstances, you might be able to take shots through walls or take out multiple enemies with one shot. Figuring out how the shooting works is a learning experience on its own, and may lead to some frustration as you might for example shoot over low-profile enemies despite aiming straight for them (tip: aim slightly in front to get the right elevation in such circumstances, or behind to avoid shooting under antigrav vehicles). You will also have to take care standing clear of obstacles (not always easy since you tend to look at your target instad of your own vehicle) as you fire since a building might not only block your shot but might turn your own awesome firepower against you (looking at you, siege howitzer). Explosive hazards are not always easy to see or identify, and you might walk into an exploding fuel pipeline or two before you get the hang of it, but destroying such hazards have an intrinsic value in that it distracts enemies and might set you up for a tasty ambush.
This game is a gem; the developers, Stellar Jockeys, have been working hard on new content over the past year, keeping their ears open and have lovingly crafted a hell of a game. With the recent re-launch things have only become better, adding much needed polish and a proper tutorial. The background lore can nearly be ignored since focus is on gameplay but if you care to look you will find some very cool stuff there too. I can recommend reading the ♥♥♥♥ing amazing Brigador novel by Brad Buckmaster. The soundtrack by Makeup And Vanity Set is killer as well. Brigador is a goddamn miracle.

This game is a masterpiece and (IMO) vastly superior to it's predecessor. Most of the negative reviews stem from 2 camps.
1) Technical issues - which are mostly fixed. I only had 3-4 crashes with no progress lost, in my 52 hour playtime.
2) Time limit on some missions - While it does make the game harder, I actually enjoyed this kind of missions. I played on hard difficulty, and I hate timers in any game, so it is saying something.
That being said, there were parts of the game that I did not quite like.
a) RNG is at it's core, so you will have scenarios where you miss an enemy point blank while the enemy hits you across the screen, while you're behind cover, for critical damage, killing you. But apart from CTH, Critical, damage range on weapons, there is the hacking ability. Which almost always fails, at first, and when it does the enemy gets stronger for some reason. Even at later levels hacking the 2nd bonus is at 50% after full upgrades. A lot of other unnecessary RNG placed in a tactical game which is a really weird point to focus on.
b) Wish you could skip more missions without being punished hard by doing so.
c) Building facilities and managing power could have been made less tiresome.
Other than that, the game is pure goodness
1) Tactically demanding combat
2) Challenging scenarios which requires good positioning and good planing in order to succeed.
3) Blowing up walls to enter a building, take the objective and get out feels very satisfying.
4) Lots of enemy and skill variation
5) Story is descent enough
6) The difficulty curve might be steep at some points, but it's nothing that ruined my fun with the game
7) Dressing a Ranger class in Power ranger-like suit and make them run across the map to one shot enemies with a sword feels as awesome as it sounds.
8) Animations are awesome!
This is definitely the GOTY for me, despite the bugs at launch, it now plays very polished and is a ton of fun (bits of frustrations included)

Shawden is the kind of game that at first looks and feels very sloppy, and very "meh". The graphics are a bit last decade (and the few FMVs (who even uses those anymore?!) look two decades old), the controls feel clunky and unpolished, the basic idea of the game boring, and the gameplay itself needlessly difficult at points.
Big emphasis on "at first". Once you get the the idea, get the hang of it, get used to the controls (at least with a gamepad), actually starts being really addictive. I recommend giving this game a chance for at least a couple of hours before dismissing it. What feels clunky and needlessly difficult at first will actually turn quite natural and even clever gameplay mechanics. The idea behind the stealth mechanic hides a surprising amount of tactical depth that is not necessarily apparent from the beginning. The shock of "omfg, is this really a huge escort mission?!?" will soon pass, when you get the idea behind it.
There are three ways to play the game: Complete stealth, complete slaughter, or a mix of both. I found myself liking the complete stealth approach the most.

After countless hours of playing, can I say that XCom 2 is a successful follow-up to XCom: Enemy Unknown and XCom Enemy Within? Yes... and no. This is a long one, but hear me out.
XCom 2 picks up years after the first game with the assumption that, cannonically, the humans lost the first-contact war and are now being quietly shepherded to their deaths. You are tasked with building a resistance force to take on the aliens and take back Earth. You'll recruit new soldiers, scientists, and engineers, build and research upgrades, and fly around the globe to collect resources and fight pockets of ADVENT.
This all sounds great on paper, and for the most part, it is.
The story, while not out-of-the-park amazing, has some interesting twists and turns to it, though it suffers from stagnation on the in-between phases like the first game. There are some interesting moments that stand out and add a sense of intrigue to the game that wasn't quite as present in the first. Unfortunately what this game does lack is a sense of the unknown, which was a big part of the creepy, ethereal atmosphere that made XCom: EU really tick and added a layer of tension to the combat-scape.
Being able to customize your characters and save them to a character pool is a welcome addition to the game and helps build a sideline narrative for the game as you play through each mission. I always feel a little excited to see a character pop up in a new playthrough from a previous one.
Combat flows in a similar fashion to XCom: EU. Everyone takes their turn on one side, then everyone takes their turn on the other. Each character has a range of abilities based on their classes and can use them to their advantage (I'll touch a little more on combat later). The character classes are great this time around, with most abilities (but not all) having a place in one build or another. Sharpshooters still reign suppreme though, so make sure to have a few hanging around the barracks. Despite this, each class felt like their roles were important on a squad, not just a meatbag with only slightly different abilities that shot every now and again, kind of like how the supports felt in XCom: EU. Specialists are essential for almost every mission, being able to hack terminals or heal teammates from afar and provide additional protection for essential or heavily injured characters. Grenediers shred armored units to pieces and can lay waste to large areas with grenades. Sharpshooters deal massive single-target damage or can supress an area with their hand cannon. And rangers can clean up the flanks with their shotguns or swords or remain invisible to sneak around and grab an objective quietly.
Enemy classes also recieved a substantial boost to their numbers and a number of upgrades for existing classes. By-and-large these additions are a welcome improvement and add more layers of consideration during combat, and each of them have devestating abilities that you need to work through in order to succeed.
The combat is, for the most part, quite satisfying. The cinematic camera is a nice addition but does not always work quite as intended, clipping through walls on occasion, and animations are sometimes delayed and stilted. Additionally, as is the nature of games that use RNG, sometimes battles can feel entirely unfair, especailly when a string of bad luck ends in an unavoidable squad wipe. But, again, that is the nature of RNG-based games. You are supposed to work with the hand you're dealt, success or failure. If this is not your kind of thing, then you will likely not enjoy this game.
That aside, the overworld map has been completely changed, becoming more dynamic and giving you more agency in where you go next. Pick a mission or scan site and get to work.
The biggest complaint I have is how many mods I needed to get the game to be playable from a quality of life standpoint. Health bars do not show numbers, instead showing abstract bars. The camera is locked to 90 degree rotations, key information is sometimes awkward to reach, and other minor gripes and concerns. Thankfully there is a massive modding community that has numerous fixes for pretty much everything at this point. At the end of this post I will like to my personal collections of mods. A lot of these things should have already been fixed, especially after a year since launch, but have not been addressed.
DLC is nothing noteworthy but if you're looking for a little bit extra it's an interesting pickup.
One last thing to touch on is performance. Unless you have a render-farm level system, you will not be able to run this game on maximum settings. It is poorly optimized, and does not run well on mid-tier machines unless you tone down the settings. Just be warned.
That aside, this game really is fantastic. If you are willing to look past the small flaws you will find a game truely worthy of your time and investment. Battles are tense and exciting, and numerous improvements in gameplay and enemy variety have been made across the board from the first game. The story has potential and leaves room for more development.

Fractured Space is fantastic. It's an extremely addicting MOBA based game that focuses on ship piloting and team strategy. There are many unique ships that allow for you to play a role that is pivitol to the team. Teams are 5v5, so there is no solo act. You fight with your team, or you lose.
With that said, the game handles matchamking poorly. People just brand new to the game will be thrown into matches with players with hundreds of hours played. It's not fair to either party.
Teams are therefore improperly balanced and lead to just bad games. It's hard to find games where you feel like it was a hard fought win or loss. Those are the games that really are fun to play. Instead it become demoralzing as you lose over and over and leave each game feeling cheated. If you group up with friends, your party can be split so that matchmaking MMR is balanced. It can be infuriating. I find myself becoming angry over undeserved losses, and I want to blame teammates. However I was in their shoes once, and I was learning the game too. Some people learn faster than others. I myself am very competitive and don't like losing games where one team is clearly better than the other.
Just keep this in mind as you play. Try and have fun, and improve what you can do. It doesnt fix the problem, but it helps you from getting angry.
The game is fantastic when played at a properly matched level. Good graphics, effects and awesome sounds immerse you in this ship to ship warfare. You can always play bots to give yourself the feeling of winning again.

This is a game that I have been looking forward to for at least 2 and a half years. I have wanted to have a game on the PC that had the elements of harvest moon (for the little bit I played of it), Animal crossing (<3) and Rune factory. I was super excited when I was approached by Leth (publishing manager at Chucklefish) at the beginning of December to help him and ConcernedApe (developer of the game) with bug testing and QA. 400+ hours later (off steam and on steam), I still love the game.
Farming. The farming is fantastic. It is to me one of the main elements of the game, and it's just a joy. Being able to design your farm any way you want it... yes please. Planning out what to buy every season, where to plant them, on top of the thrill of when you can harvest and reap on the gold... it's so enjoyable and addictive.
Fishing. The fishing is outstanding. From playing WoW and Runescape.. or any game with fishing, the fishing in Stardew Valley is so much fun. At first, the fishing is challenging, but as you progress your skill, you become a pro in no time.
Mining and combat. Mining and combat is incredible. Going deeper into the mines can be tough, but if you're prepared with your food and weapon in hand, you can fend off the creatures and get your sweet ore/minerals/gems that you want to bring back to your house and possibly hoard. (Hi, I'm Bexy, and i'm a hoarder.)
Social. Social interactions are great. Being able to become friends with the people in the town, and eventually being able to get into relationships with people and having a family with them.. what's not to like about that? And what's great is that it gives great replayability because you can have different saves with different spouses! The backstory for each of the characters too is so in depth and well thought out, you will be silly if you don't shed a tear maybe once or twice.
Main story. The actual main story is well rewarding, and once you "complete" it, you can still continue on your adventures and farming life with no problems, hell you might even discover new things afterwards, I sure as hell did!
Yes, I was a tester for the game. Yes, I have played for ridiculous amounts of hours. It may feel like i'm being a bit overzealous with this. However you have to remember, I was a tester. I tested the crap out of every aspect with this game, even though there were massive game breaking bugs, errors, glitches, crashes. I still love this game. I reported many a bug, and ConcernedApe was quick to fix them.
And that's the thing, not only is the game amazing, the developer is too. ConcernedApe works around the clock to make sure that bugs are fixed in quick time in order for us to have an amazing experience with this game. And that's true. The experience that you have with this game IS amazing.
Minutes playing turn into hours. Hours turn into "oh no it's time to sleep".
You will forget about time. You will forget about sleep. You will forget that dinner was about 5 hours ago but you couldn't' remember because you were too busy trying to fight off 12 bats that were clobbering you inside the mines while trying to gather that 1 diamond waaaaay in the back

Darkest Dungeon is a Lovecraftian-themed turn based RPG, if you somehow didn't already know. The game follows the main theme of your heroes being actual people who fight, argue, and have their own needs. The game itself isn't necessarily complicated, just takes some getting used to. And you may have heard people complaining about the RNG (random number generator) in the game. I'll admit it does get obnoxious from time to time, but because of the randomized nature of the game it makes all the lucky hits, heals, or dungeon layouts all the more meaningful. The game has a steady, not to slow and not too fast difficulty curve. The game never holds your hand, but doesn't leave you to die. There are situations where you may lose some of your favorite heroes to a boss, and you'll need to level up more characters. Yes the game is grindy at some points, but it doesn't focus on it. On a side note, the soundtrack to the game is great. Not the best OST out there, but certainly among the better ones I've heard. Tunes are crafted to match any scenario you may encounter, all of which are well orchestrated to match the depressing and foreboding tone of the world.   This leads to the artstyle, which, unlike the music, may be my favorite. All characters, environments, and enemies are made perfectly to match their sorroundings as they should, and everything is just nice to look at. Not nice to look at as in pleasent, because honestly I don't think an amalgamation of rotting corpses and mangled spines is nice to visualize, but in the sense that everything is drawn very well. At no point is the game necessarily lackluster, but it can and WILL frustrate you, so take that as you may.
Overall a fresh idea executed very well. I'd say an 8.9/10

It's not often that I call a game where you play a teenager trying to mend a post-apocolyptic world "memorable," but Bastion is the perfect example of a game, and a story, using tried-and-true narrative and world building elements and working it into something fascinating.
You are The Kid. While you were napping, the earth quite literally tore itself apart in an event known as "The Calamity." Everyone you've ever known is dead. You go to the evacuation point, the Bastion, and with the aid and advice of a few other survivors, seek to find the objects that can rebuild the Bastion and restore the world as it was before.
This all comes as fairly cliche, but Bastion avoids feeling trite because it feels so earnest. Most of the game is told as a tale by the rough-yet-endearing stranger you meet in the opening chapters, and despite how grim the situation comes across as it unfolds, it is presented to you in a way that feels warm and personal, and comments on almost everything, from what combination of weapons you choose to whenever you're redoing a challenge for the second (or even third or fourth) time. In fact, I'd feel the voice acting of the narrator, who for a long time is the only voice you hear in the game, is what carries this story, alongside a beautiful graphic design thats reminiscent of watercolor paintings and a beautiful soundtract that seems to focus on acoustic guitar.
The gameplay is also incredibly polished. A top down-combat game (which I must recommend a gamepad for), Bastion is aided by a large amount of customization, allowing you to switch out weapon upgrades and levelling perks (the latter of which represented by drinks you select in a distillary which give you everything from more health to the ability to shoot spikes at enemies whenever you take a hit) whenever you return the the game hub, allowing for constant experimentation. Of added interest are the vigils, simple challenges one can complete for rewards, and a temple that allows you to make the game harder in various ways, while multiplying experience and monetary gain in whatever way you see fit, including making enemies faster or having them drop explosive bombs when they die.
Bastion works because of how honest it is about being a labor of love. Every detail is put forward in a beautifully polished and memorable manner. Play it, explore it, and find out just how enjoyable the end of the world can be.

ADDRESSING THE COMPLAINTS:
If you plan on playing Ironman mode; DON'T.  If you plan on playing on Legendary difficulty; DON'T.  If you plan on playing with a make-shift handicap; DON'T.  At least not at first.  Majority of the people complaining about the difficulty of XCOM 2 are idiots who routinely ♥♥♥♥♥ed about how easy XCOM 1 was and then proceeded to play at max difficulty thinking it would be a cake-walk.  They rightfully got smacked in the gob by the sequels challenges.  You should have a game completion under your belt before playing Ironman or Legendary, so that you know the full extent to what the game offers.  Without experience in playing XCOM 2, you will lose multiple, multiple times within the first few hours.
For those saying that the game "runs horribly", despite a few absurdly long load times (coming back from missions takes a solid minute, to a minute and a half for some reason for me) this game is fairly recent, and was designed to be a PC exclusive, taking advantage of PC exclusive graphical features.  If you're running this on a 760, or even a 950, expect to be disappointed with the framerate.  I was running it on a 1050ti and I just barely managed to average around 50 FPS, though I was playing with substantially higher settings, including Screen Space Ambient Occlusion, High shadows, High textures, at 1920x1080, etc.  If you have a 1060 or better, then feel free to ♥♥♥♥♥ about the framerates, but overall, I have found that this game tends to have a fairly consistent framerate, though after long hours of playing it also tends to become more inconsistent.
NOW THAT THAT'S OUT OF THE WAY
This is a worthy successor to the original XCOM that released back in 2012 (has it really been that long?), in more ways than one.
-GAMEPLAY-
The gameplay from the original is still intact, but there's a significant difference; concealment.  Some missions will start your units out in a concealed state, and some abilities allow your soldiers to conceal themselves.  This creates a level of stealth that has virtually been absent from the entire X-COM franchise, strangely enough.  You can create ambushes, use scouts to (try) and achieve the objective unseen, if it's planting a bomb or hacking a computer, and you can have them conceal themselves to hide and avoid enemy fire.  This greatly changes the beginning of most missions, and makes them more fun in my opinion.
There are some annoying features that I have to get out of the way though, the first being the very annoying pauses that seem to happen ALL the time.  For some reason, the AI camera will pause before playing an in-game cutscene if you've been revealed, run into a new enemy unit, or sometimes if it's waiting for the AI to ends its turn.  Overall, it seems that this is either a bug with the ambient narrative setting (I had it turned on, haven't tried it with it turned off yet), or just a large bug in general.  It doesn't break the mission (that comes later), but it does become frustrating, since all that time adds up.  Another thing that bothers me is that sometimes, albeit rarely, units will get "stuck", unable to act in any way what-so-ever.  Not all of them, just one, maybe two if you're really unlucky, and nothing you do besides reloading an earlier auto-save can free them.  Perhaps they're just bugs with the map, but it seems to happen at random, which is especially scary during evac missions, since you cannot evac them.
Back to the core mechanics; a loot system has also been integrated, where you can now modify each classes weapons, offering a wide variety of gizmo's and gadgets to add to your guns to increase aim, increase crit chance, magazine size, or something that offers a small little bonus like reloading not spending an action the first 2 times on a mission.  Among those, there's also the Proving Grounds and Guerilla Tactics School, where you can customize your soldiers in their special abilities/bonuses, as well as adding new gear to your arsenal.  Things like exo-suits with mounted weapons and unique ammo types are only a small selection of the large amount of different gadgets you can make, some more useful than others, others more specialized.
Speaking of the soldiers, they are far more customizable now, with full-body, name, color-scheme, biography, and even personality customization.  Indeed, this seems to be the most in-game customizable XCOM yet.  Your soldiers will be instantly identifiable in the field with that cool new armor combination you gave him, or that incredibly ugly color scheme you slapped onto him.  Either way, there's a lot to take away and personalize here that gives each soldier a level of intimacy and personality to make you become genuinely attached to them.
Outside of the new mechanics and customization, they've also added a procedural map generation system, which I must say, I did get tired of all the samey-feeling maps from XCOM: Enemy Unknown, but here they all feel different enough that you don't start questioning whether you've played this exact map setup before.  It creates a more enjoyable, immersive experience to be going from China to Africa and not see the same city layouts as before, which is something that has plagued the series for years.
-THE ALIENS-
The alien design is great, in particular, the design of the ADVENT forces, a gene-spliced mingling of human DNA, which you'll soon come to find out more about.  The sleak, geometric designs of the ADVENT forces gives them a visibly clean and intimidating vibe, where they may be the most basic cannon fodder you'll come across, they still know how to aim and flank.  Aside from them, the real stars are the Andromedons and Sectoids, the former of which feels very reminiscent of a Big Daddy from bioshock, although far more menacing.  The Sectiods, for that matter, are also much more intimidating, wielding potent psi powers and having reasonable health, they remain a fairly consistent worry on the battlefield throughout most of the game, primarily in the beginning.  Not to spoil too many of the games surprises, but you'll see a plentiful variety of aliens throughout, though perhaps it's just because of the luck of the draw, I seemed to run into fairly few of a certain kind.
Each alien also has their own behavior in battle.  The ADVENT forces will routinely use cover and try to out-flank you, exchanging gunfire in a standard affair, though the Sectiod's are unpredictable and will try and scurry around the environment, flinging psi powers at you and taking shots at you every now and then with their wrist-mounted blasters.  Chryssalids have a new ability, in that they can burrow (oh joy!) into the ground and wait for you to come a little too close before popping out and ambushing you, sort of like their very own "reaction shots" as they burst forth and rush you to deal an attack.  Chryssalids are far less deadly though, and I don't think I lost a single soldier to one (probably due to my hatred/fear of them and targetting them first).
-GRAPHICS-
The game looks great.  Colors are evenly distributed and vivid in the designs of the environments and the units, not to mention the core designs of all the units all stand out phenomenally well, the animations standing out on their own as wholly impressive.  The subsurface scattering is most instantly noticeable on the Sectoid's, which gives them a lively flare, their translucent skin and skeleton-like bodies create an immediately concerning visage.  Maps look very slick and polished, environments are substantially better than they were in the previous game, and the destruction is a lot more in-depth, with gradual and sectional destruction of environments rather than before where you either destroyed it or didn't.  Overall, it looks as good as it plays.
I'd say it would be hard not to recommend this title, especially with the cliff-hangar they left it on.

I once wrote a review for "Half Life" when I was about 4 hours into the game. Having finished it just now, I'd like to do a new and more appropiate one. This one's gonna be long, so bare with me or move on ;)
"Half Life" was released in 1998, way back in the past when Valve still used to make games and I was only 6 years old. Half Life was, as you probably already know, at it's time revolutionary for the fps genre and has since influenced arguably every game, not only fps game, which contained elements of the half life formula.
But here is the thing: "Half Life" did this in 1998. I have played this game 18 years after it's release and this review is for gamers who want to play it after the same amount of time or when even more years have passed.
To understand my impression, I want to explain that my fps game experience is quite limited: I have never played "Counter Strike". I have never played "Battlefield" or "Call of Duty" or any "Wolfenstein" or "Quake". A little bit of "Unreal Turnament" when I was little but I can hardly remember that.
The only fp shooters that I had played before HL were "Mirror's Edge", "Bioshock Infinite", "Portal" (1&2) and the "Metro" games of whom I loved all three. They were atmospheric, had great GREAT stories and good gameplay, each in their own way.
And then I bought all the Half Life games during a sale being curious about the hype and wether it's actually justified.
So here are the things I liked:
The pacing (as long as it wasn't hindered by the controls- more about this later):
Action packed fight scenes were often broken up by environmental puzzles, platforming passages or simply the search for the corridor which would lead me further. This kept things nicely varied.
The level of realism:
I liked the lack of a compass, of an intrusive quest log leading you to the next level like a child, of a healthbar above enemies and auto generation- all mechanics that got introduced in later games and which I probably wouldn't want to play without for ever, but having such a "natural" gameplay was kind of nice for once.
The level design:
The levels varied a lot in terms of scenery and things like verticality- again more variety which I appreciated. Also no backtracking, which should be selfevident but I feel like it has to be said nonetheless.
Weapon variety:
Not only was I equipped with all the killing tools a gamer heart can desire (plus some which one wouldn't even expect), but every weapon did also have it's purpose. I only found myself neglecting the shotgun almost completely which might even have been a mistake. I switched freely between around 14 weapons (beat me if I'm wrong), which raised the interest level along with the other plus points.
And here are the things I disliked about Half Life:
The controls:
As I have said before- I have never played counter strike, so Half Life's controls really felt uncomfortable to me. Here I have to admit: Not expecting to find any major changes in comparison to other fps I skipped the tutorial, which made me get stuck at a point, where I needed to crouchjump in order to progress. So I won't criticize HL for a lack of accessability.
But because I played it in 2016 I have to compare it with the controls of the fps which I have already played. And in comparison to those, HL'S controls are, at least to me, very uncomfortable. Because of the walking on jelly or whatever it is I never felt like having full control over Mr. Freeman. It was more like navigating another person through an obstacle course, hoping that he will act your command out just in time so that he doesn't bash against a wall. i know that you can walk and crouch and that the jelly then disappears. I also know that the unresponsive movement is supposed to represent how one can't just stop on the spot coming out of a jogging motion. But there is a reason why later games didn't have this mechanic- neither did System Shock 2 btw which I played for a short time- it doesn't work that great. People commented on my old review that this motion system is very common in modern shooters and named CS as an example without giving another one when I asked for it. Because CS is running on the source engine just like HL one can't really let that get pass as an example.
My point is that the movement didn't feel good; it provided an additional challenge which I hadn't asked for and don't consider necessary. Having thought back, I remember that "Portal" being built with source aswell, has the same movement scheme- but I never noticed it there because in those two games it doesn't become such a pain in the butt.
The story:
I'm not saying that today's fps stories are better (even though "Infinite"'s and "Metro"'s were in fact more interesting to me), but they are surely better put into play. What people often praise about "Half Life" left me quite desinterested: The story sort of runs beside Freeman- there are no dialogues, no facial animations and no plottwists. You see what happens around you and sometimes people talk to you, but there is no depth. The story is just enough to carry the game through. But I don't consider this to be a huge minus because I don't think that Valve aimed at any monumental story arc and targeted gamers who were more interested into the gameplay rather than character development.
The style:
I consider videogames to be a medium of art which, if it wants to tell a story of any kind, needs a style and graphics good enough to let the player immerse himself into the game. I am no graphic fanatic but at a certain level of muddy textures and bland lighting i can't dive into a universe- except if the story makes up for it; which it doesn't in "Half Life".
As you might have noticed, more or less all of my minus points for "Half Life" are due to it's age. And I know that. And I don't say that "Half Life" wouldn't have caught me in 1998. But games tend to age far worse than books or movies due to the huge improvements which were made in terms of graphics, gameplay and storytelling during the last 20 years. And because of that, at least to me, "Half Life" didn't hold up so good. And I don't like people, who played it at it's release, bashing on the ones who play it today and therefore fail to see what gamers of the 90s saw in it. By the way I CAN see what made it great in the past. It just doesn't make it great anymore.
Here is an example: I love the "Mass Effect" trilogy more than any other video game and played "Mass Effect" (1) back in 2009 or so. And it was already quite clunky back then but I didn't mind. I had a wonderful experience with it and loved the story aswell as it's universe. But when I recommend it to other people I warn them about it's age and tell them if the game's mechanics are too clunky for them and graphics too dated they might want to start off with part 2. Of course I am happy for everyone who can look beyond it's flaws which came partly with it's time. But I wouldn't condemn anyone who is put off by it's age.
I recommend "Half Life" for people who are curious about gaming history and who want to play HL for research more than entertainment. And for those who are not bothered by the critique points which I mentioned.
Other than that: I wouldn't bother and rather wait for HL3 just like everyone else. I am going to dive into HL2 shortly out of couriosity, so maybe this will hook me more:)
Thanks a lot for reading, sorry for any grammatical or vocabulary mistakes!

Brigador is exactly the kind of game I would've played the absolute, er, beans out of in the late '90s on my PSX and would still remember fondly (and play, occasionally) today, exactly in the same vein as Front Mission 3, Nuclear/Soviet Strike, FutureCop LAPD, G-Police, WipeOut, Colony Wars... I don't mean to imply it's anything like any of those gameplay-wise (it's not completely unlike FutureCop, but it's nowhere near a clone of it), but it's just so well-produced, charming and engrossing like those examples and definitely has a special feel to it. It's also pretty difficult at times, which would've also been appropriate in that era.
The gameplay itself is properly great and much deeper than you might expect; there's all sorts of different tactics to use including hit and run stealth (which I find the most fun but also very difficult to pull off properly), tons of weapons and vehicles, great attention to detail in both the design and writing of the entire game and an awesome soundtrack. There's a
of game here, I've played a fair bit and I haven't even finished the campaign yet.
What I love about it is it's maybe one third straightforward isometric twin stick-ish shooter, one third tactical combat and one third puzzle; each campaign mission gives you four pilots to choose from and each presents a wildly different strategy, working out how to complete the mission you just aced using the aptly-named Treehouse, this time using a tracked motorbike with a tenth of the durability and damage output (but ten times more speed) will have you scratching your head for sure. It never gets old! Then there's the Freelancer mode, which is actually the meat of the game, where you get to choose your own pilot, vehicle and weapons and therefore set your own challenge.
The only downsides I can think of are the weapon sight lines can be hard to use at times, especially against Agravs (floating enemies), I've died more than once by accidentally launching a huge artillery shell at a building I'm practically inside because of this. It's difficult to tell which weapon will fire on which mouse button, I feel this could've been handled better, but I get around this by giving most targets both barrels until I learn which is which so that's a minor one. Explosive scenery has also killed me a number of times because it's hard to focus on shooting a large group of enemies and moving at the same time, but you work out how to stop doing that after a few times. I think that's it, I haven't encountered any bugs, cheap deaths or poor balance in my time with it.
In summary, I'd recommend this so strongly that I've bought two copies of it besides my own (technically one was in the Humble monthly but still counts, damn it) to distribute and will buy more when it's full price again to support the devs.
Although I feel like I haven't said enough about the quality of the writing. Fortunately the Brigador wiki has a lot (if not all) of the lore and intel transcribed so you can see that for yourself even before you buy. I'm fairly sure this gave me goosebumps the first time I read it, being so vivid and evocative as it is (spoilered, but doesn't give away any of the story, in fact there's not actually a story to spoil):

This game is awesome. That's it. It's awesome. Everything about it is fantastic with the exception that vehicle customization is somewhat limited. Two weapons plus a special. But that is compensated for by the sheer number of vehicles and weapons so it's a rather moot point and you will surely find a vehicle that caters to exactly how you want to play - and there is a huge variety - hover cars, tanks, walking mechs, and others.
Ok, on to the details:
The graphics are great. Dated in the same way something like Super Meat Boy is dated but perfectly fits the game. Obviously intentional. It's dark and usually night-ish time for some reason. Everything can be destroyed. The only problem with this is that you'll enjoy destroying things so much you'll run out of ammo :) If there's a story, I can't find it. I feel like I am playing the bad guys because I am often romping through residentail areas destroying houses and stepping on fleeing people. Awesome. It's kind of refreshing. The music fits the environments and graphics perfect. Its dark and snythetic 80's dystopian...something. I don't know much about music.
The missions themselves are all "destroy the thing". This is good because shooting guns is awesome and exploding things is great. The only issue with this that I have run into is that some of your objectives blow up real good. I say this is an issue because I've been in situations where I have run out of ammo, the ammo depot was destroyed, and I only have stomp left. My own fault. Again, see my comment about shooting everything.
The learning curve in this game is sort of high. Think of it as a twin stick shooter but the direction of your guns is often independent of the direction your legs/treads are facing. This means you can move around in one direction and shoot in another. This might take some getting used to if you've not played other games that work like this. But there are excellent tool-tips throughout the missions. You walk up to these objects and some text is on the screen. At first I wanted this gone so I could just play but the implementation is perfect and few games do this right. There are even reminders about past tips that are situated perfectly. It's like the game read my mind and was never annoying or patronizing. The text is only on the screen so long as you are close to these objects and the tips/instructions are always helpful. Perfectly designed so if you want to skip it you can and if you need the help, they actually provide good help. And you can go back to these objects at any time if you get lost or need help.
The mechanics in this game also exceed what I was expecting. Mechs can crouch!!!! This helps you avoid fire. Your weapons have an extreme range limit (usually). Far too often you play top-view games like this and your cannon fires all of 60' and disappears. In this your guns may as well have unlimited range - which is how it should be. It means you can properly snipe and use stealth to kill things from far away. Most vehicles have some kind of grenade. Some are smoke or EMP. The arc is helpful. And if you are smart about it, things like smoke deploy multiple projectiles over time so you can move your reticle to spread out the smoke grenades. Very smart and allows for a higher skill ceiling. Going back to movement of your vehicle, it all feels really good. With weapons/turrets separate from treads/feet, they have differing turn rates. Machine guns might turn faster than a cannon (or a mount turns at different speed - not sure yet) so you have to factor that in when maneuvering. You need to keep an eye where your feet are facing relative to your guns. Also, where you point your cursor is where the gun fires on the ground so you can hit small things on the ground quite easily but if the cursor is beyond the target, you could easily shoot over it to hit something behind.
If there was one thing I would add to this game is co-op multiplayer (either local or online or both). Also, if the maps are any bigger than I've experienced (about 2/3 the way through the campaign), a minimap would be helpful but I've never really gotten lost at all. There are indicators at the edge of your screen where stuff is. Sometimes finding/getting to the exit after completing the goals takes a minute but that's it.

Just to make things painfully clear: I'M NOT "UN-RECOMMENDING" THIS GAME SOLELY BECAUSE OF THE CREATION CLUB.
Okay? Okay. Now, on to the actual review!
I can't in good conscience recommend Fallout 4 for a vast array of problems with the game. First of all, the charm. Or rather, the lack thereof. See, Fallout New Vegas had a certain charm to it, despite its horrendously fûck-ugly graphics and characters with universal radiation-induced downs syndrome. The whole cowboy shtick weirdly enough fit the game, and it was filled to the bloody brim with interesting dudes and dudettes to get to know (I'm lookin' at you, Victor!)
Fallout 4, by contrast, doesn't have a single goddämn interesting character of the entire lot! Frankly, just the fact that Preston Garvey exists is yet another reason to burn Bethesda at the stakes, along with George "I'm Too Fûcking Retärded To Do Anything Right" Lucas and Uwe "I Need To Be Tortured To Death For Being A Worthless Trashcünt" Boll. Seriously. Burn 'em all, I say!
Anyway... as I was saying. Fallout 4's "charm" is nil. Null. Void. Zero. NONE. IT DOES NOT EXIST. The characters are all ENTIRELY interchangeable, and none of them has any real personality beyond a few extremely basic traits, all of them verbal.
Next up, the story. FNV's story was, by contrast, a lot more complex and interesting. At the beginning of the game, all you really know is that some dude who smokes a lot and wears a really fûck-ugly suit shot you in the head and left you for dead, but you (fûckin' somehow) survived. That's literally all that's established at the beginning, and I LIKE IT. It makes the story unclear, but it gains clarity as we explore it.
F4's story, on the other hand, is that we're a recently widowed person who's completely obsessed with finding a child that was taken from us an entirely unclear amount of time before we begin the search, and who by odds would most likely be dead by now. But we're determined, in the way only extremely poorly written parents are in extremely shïtty game stories. Seriously, the way your "character" constantly whines about how he or she lost a child is downright fûcking PATHETIC.
Just the fact that you can't even avoid the whiny bullshït your character spews in every dialogue about their missing child makes me wanna crucify the story "writers" with rusty nails and then set them on fire. This is literally the worst goddämn gaming story I have ever seen. If the writers weren't fired (out of a cannon) for this ultra-garbage, then I am even more severely disappointed in you than I would otherwise be, Bethesda!
Anyway... moving on from that shïtpile called a "story", we have an actually positive remark about F4: the guns. Or more precisely, how guns handle. See, what FNV was severely lacking in was the ability to modify your weapons. Sure, you could slap on a choke and extended tube mag on a hunting shotgun and wreck shït up with it, but that was literally the only way to modify weapons: 2-3 mods per gun, MAX. That does NOT make for good customization options, especially since every single mod in FNV was absolutely guaranteed to be 100% beneficial. There were no drawbacks whatsoever to modifying ANY of your weapons in that game.
F4, on the other hand, both punishes and rewards you for every mod you attach or remove from a weapon. Sure, adding a longer barrel to your shotgun tightens the spread, but it also adds weight and makes the weapon much less effective when fired from the hip. And yeah, making your 10mm pistol fully automatic ramps up your rate of fire by a fûck-ton, but it also consumes ammo faster, and has much more recoil, as well as lower damage. And obviously, I like it. It's a lot of weighing your options, thinking about "pros vs. cons", etc.
But that also leads me to a MAJOR gripe I've got with F4's arsenal, namely the variety. Or rather, just like with my point about "charm", the extreme LACK of variety in the game. Let's throw out some numbers here... in Fallout New Vegas, you had access to over a HUNDRED different weapons, and that's not even counting the unique variety ones (such as Ratslayer or Lucky). Almost all of these weapons also had access to alternative ammunition, from high quality, hand-loaded semi-wadcutters and junky surplus rounds, to armour-piercing rounds and even Dragon Breath shells for ballistic shotguns!
Fallout 4, by comparison, has less than HALF of that. Yeah, I know, you can modify weapons to a greater extent than in FNV and theoretically create HUNDREDS of different weapons by using weapon mods, but that doesn't excuse the fact that there is a severe lack of variety with the BASE weapons, and the combinations that're actually viable are few indeed. For examplé, there are no longer any 10mm sub-machineguns, no pump-action shotguns, no .22 calibre stealth pistols, and absolutely NO FEED-LOADED WEAPONS OF ANY KIND. Which honestly pisses me off to an extreme extent! My absolutely favourite weapon in FNV was the Medicine Stick, a feed-loaded .44 calibre repeater. When loaded with .44 SWC ammo, it was a BEAST of a weapon!
Fallout 4 also has a retärdedly pathetic variety in terms of actual armour types. Sure, how armours actually WORK has been significantly improved, but there's still a severe lack of variety. In FNV, you had the basic leather armour to start with (more or less). But later on, you got access to metal armours, combat armours, reinforced metal and leather armours, and a whole slew of various faction armours to let you blend in and disguise yourself. In Fallout 4, you have leather, metal, combat and raider armour. Two of those types are entirely USELESS, and I'll let you figure out which onees. (Spoiler: It's the metal and raider ones. Metal weighs too much, and raider is even worse than leather for protection!)
Which in turn leads me to ANOTHER thing about Fallout 4 that pisses me off to no end: FACTIONS! Another idiotically excluded feature from FNV, F3, F2, F1, etc. that Bethesda were just way too goddämn lazy to bother with including. There are no factions in F4. NONE. And don't tell me the Institute, the Minutemen, etc. count as factions, because THEY DO NOT. Aside from them all having PRESET ATTITUDE VALUES, there is ZERO difference between institute synths and raiders. They're both gonna be 100% hostile towards you, all the time, every time. You can't decide that "fûck it, I'm-a be a total doüche and join the bad guys now!" in F4.
Unless you dïck around with mods (which I'll add SHOULD NOT BE NECESSARY TO PUT THE "ROLE-PLAYING" INTO A "ROLE-PLAYING GAME"!) you literally can't change anyone's opinion of you in any significant way whatsoever. Sure, you can still murder people, but there is no justice system or karma system. If you murder someone, one of two things will happen, based ENTIRELY on whether or not you get caught doing so: if not caught, nothing happens. AT ALL. The person's dead, that's literally it. If caught, everyone nearby will IMMEDIATELY turn hostile and attack you, even if only ONE person saw you, and was in no way able to warn anyone else before attacking you.
That's the ENTIRE EXTENT of the "role-playing" you can do in Fallout 4: murdering people for no reason.
Moving on... one thing I do feel has improved in F4 is how the economical aspects are handled. In FNV, it was retärdedly easy to amass enough money to buy the entire universe and everything in it. In F4, by contrast, it's insanely difficult to earn money, and everything is ridiculously expensive if you don't have the right perks/stats. Which I actually like. It's more like it was in F1 and F2, wherein stim-paks could cost you a motherfûckin' FORTUNE early on, but became less inaccessible the further you progressed into the game.
All in all, I wouldn't recommend Fallout 4 to ANYONE. It's a shïtty excuse for a Fallout game, and even on its own, it's an extremely mediocre experience. 3.5/10
(Also: WHY THE FÛCK IS THE WORD "DOÜCHE" CENSORED?!)

On one hand, DayZ is a military simulator, with all the makings of one: Bullet drop, the constant need for camouflage, and a mind-boggling ammunition system that, while being fair, forces memorization, as each weapon has its own independent ammunition. Sorry, but no shared ammo between multiple assault rifles. That M4 and AK-74 each need their own magazines.
On the other hand, DayZ is also a game of survival in a brutal apocalyptic world. Not for a single second will this game hold your hand. You'll be required to cross large stretches of zombie-infested terrain to find food, water, and weapons to survive. It could be argued that your fellow survivors are just as dangerous as the infected. The big question that will ultimately shape your experience in this game is whether or not you will make an attempt to reach out and help your fellow player in his or her mission to survive.
As you play, you will generally find that it seems as if the whole game is against you, and is actively attempting to either starve, shoot, or slash you to death. You wouldn't be wrong. Supplies are scarce, and zombies are common. Depending on your server population (and the nature of its community), you may also have anything from massive friendly settlements to small, trigger-happy groups of survivors attempting to forge their own way in the world. The farther you move from urban environments, the harder it will become to find things like weapons, ammunition and medical supplies. This will, eventually, force you into a situation where heading into a city is your only option. This by itself is not necessarily a bad thing: Guns, first-aid supplies and even army uniforms are all rather common in these areas. The only thing to be wary of is the watchful eye of a potential sniper.
Your enjoyment of this game will stem only from your eagerness for realism and/or your hunger for a challenge. Play this game at your own risk, for it will be a long, difficult journey. But, if you are successful, you will have accumulated knowledge and power, the likes of which few survivors have ever seen.

This game is a masterpiece and (IMO) vastly superior to it's predecessor. Most of the negative reviews stem from 2 camps.
1) Technical issues - which are mostly fixed. I only had 3-4 crashes with no progress lost, in my 52 hour playtime.
2) Time limit on some missions - While it does make the game harder, I actually enjoyed this kind of missions. I played on hard difficulty, and I hate timers in any game, so it is saying something.
That being said, there were parts of the game that I did not quite like.
a) RNG is at it's core, so you will have scenarios where you miss an enemy point blank while the enemy hits you across the screen, while you're behind cover, for critical damage, killing you. But apart from CTH, Critical, damage range on weapons, there is the hacking ability. Which almost always fails, at first, and when it does the enemy gets stronger for some reason. Even at later levels hacking the 2nd bonus is at 50% after full upgrades. A lot of other unnecessary RNG placed in a tactical game which is a really weird point to focus on.
b) Wish you could skip more missions without being punished hard by doing so.
c) Building facilities and managing power could have been made less tiresome.
Other than that, the game is pure goodness
1) Tactically demanding combat
2) Challenging scenarios which requires good positioning and good planing in order to succeed.
3) Blowing up walls to enter a building, take the objective and get out feels very satisfying.
4) Lots of enemy and skill variation
5) Story is descent enough
6) The difficulty curve might be steep at some points, but it's nothing that ruined my fun with the game
7) Dressing a Ranger class in Power ranger-like suit and make them run across the map to one shot enemies with a sword feels as awesome as it sounds.
8) Animations are awesome!
This is definitely the GOTY for me, despite the bugs at launch, it now plays very polished and is a ton of fun (bits of frustrations included)

Copa Petrobras de Marcas is a game based on the well-known rFactor engine by ISI, and that is a big thing in this game: this engine is known for its lifelike physics simulation, tons of customisation options and modding features. The result is that the game offers a solid, reliable driving experience similar to games such as GTR and F1 Challenge 99-02, though in a different scenario: Brazilian racecars and circuits, recreated with great attention to detail - thanks Reiza Studios!
It is important to notice that, as a serious race simulation, the game requires a steering wheel if you want to enjoy what it has to offer. Graphics are a bit outdated, but the overall driving experience, the sound and the detailed models make up for it. On the other hand, the game doesn't require a Master Race desktop setup.
If you're Brazilian, you know what to expect. If you're not, it's chance to know some tracks popular in Ayrton Senna's country, and take some popular vehicles such as the Focus, the Lancer and the Corolla for a drive. In the real competition, these cars are equipped with a similar engine and a fixed ratio gearbox (this aspect was thoroughly recreated in the game).
Most importantly, Copa Petrobras de Marcas is free to play. Not the microtransaction type, it is actually free! Great driving model, accurate vehicles and tracks, realistic sound and a highly competitive AI for free - quite a deal, aye?

After countless hours of playing, can I say that XCom 2 is a successful follow-up to XCom: Enemy Unknown and XCom Enemy Within? Yes... and no. This is a long one, but hear me out.
XCom 2 picks up years after the first game with the assumption that, cannonically, the humans lost the first-contact war and are now being quietly shepherded to their deaths. You are tasked with building a resistance force to take on the aliens and take back Earth. You'll recruit new soldiers, scientists, and engineers, build and research upgrades, and fly around the globe to collect resources and fight pockets of ADVENT.
This all sounds great on paper, and for the most part, it is.
The story, while not out-of-the-park amazing, has some interesting twists and turns to it, though it suffers from stagnation on the in-between phases like the first game. There are some interesting moments that stand out and add a sense of intrigue to the game that wasn't quite as present in the first. Unfortunately what this game does lack is a sense of the unknown, which was a big part of the creepy, ethereal atmosphere that made XCom: EU really tick and added a layer of tension to the combat-scape.
Being able to customize your characters and save them to a character pool is a welcome addition to the game and helps build a sideline narrative for the game as you play through each mission. I always feel a little excited to see a character pop up in a new playthrough from a previous one.
Combat flows in a similar fashion to XCom: EU. Everyone takes their turn on one side, then everyone takes their turn on the other. Each character has a range of abilities based on their classes and can use them to their advantage (I'll touch a little more on combat later). The character classes are great this time around, with most abilities (but not all) having a place in one build or another. Sharpshooters still reign suppreme though, so make sure to have a few hanging around the barracks. Despite this, each class felt like their roles were important on a squad, not just a meatbag with only slightly different abilities that shot every now and again, kind of like how the supports felt in XCom: EU. Specialists are essential for almost every mission, being able to hack terminals or heal teammates from afar and provide additional protection for essential or heavily injured characters. Grenediers shred armored units to pieces and can lay waste to large areas with grenades. Sharpshooters deal massive single-target damage or can supress an area with their hand cannon. And rangers can clean up the flanks with their shotguns or swords or remain invisible to sneak around and grab an objective quietly.
Enemy classes also recieved a substantial boost to their numbers and a number of upgrades for existing classes. By-and-large these additions are a welcome improvement and add more layers of consideration during combat, and each of them have devestating abilities that you need to work through in order to succeed.
The combat is, for the most part, quite satisfying. The cinematic camera is a nice addition but does not always work quite as intended, clipping through walls on occasion, and animations are sometimes delayed and stilted. Additionally, as is the nature of games that use RNG, sometimes battles can feel entirely unfair, especailly when a string of bad luck ends in an unavoidable squad wipe. But, again, that is the nature of RNG-based games. You are supposed to work with the hand you're dealt, success or failure. If this is not your kind of thing, then you will likely not enjoy this game.
That aside, the overworld map has been completely changed, becoming more dynamic and giving you more agency in where you go next. Pick a mission or scan site and get to work.
The biggest complaint I have is how many mods I needed to get the game to be playable from a quality of life standpoint. Health bars do not show numbers, instead showing abstract bars. The camera is locked to 90 degree rotations, key information is sometimes awkward to reach, and other minor gripes and concerns. Thankfully there is a massive modding community that has numerous fixes for pretty much everything at this point. At the end of this post I will like to my personal collections of mods. A lot of these things should have already been fixed, especially after a year since launch, but have not been addressed.
DLC is nothing noteworthy but if you're looking for a little bit extra it's an interesting pickup.
One last thing to touch on is performance. Unless you have a render-farm level system, you will not be able to run this game on maximum settings. It is poorly optimized, and does not run well on mid-tier machines unless you tone down the settings. Just be warned.
That aside, this game really is fantastic. If you are willing to look past the small flaws you will find a game truely worthy of your time and investment. Battles are tense and exciting, and numerous improvements in gameplay and enemy variety have been made across the board from the first game. The story has potential and leaves room for more development.

Shadwen is a third person stealth game with some unique elements. You play as the assassin Shadwen, who ends up escorting the young girl Lily through a variety of pseudo-medieval levels. Along the way you can either murder everyone in sight (traumatizing the poor girl in the progress) or use less-lethal methods to clear the path for Lily.
The visuals are rather dated and many animations look pretty poor. Art direction is rather boring too.
The sound effects, music and voice acting are all passable, but not particularly memorable.
The gameplay in Shadwen just isn't very good. The concept is interesting enough, but the execution leaves a lot to be desired.
For starters, the AI guards have ridiculously narrow view cones and are some of the dumbest NPCs I have ever seen in a stealth game. The game only has two different enemy types, which aren't really very different anyway. The level design is pretty bad too as pretty much all the maps are extremely linear and rarely interesting.
The escort mechanic is rather poorly done too. Lily's AI is pretty terrible and probably for this reason the developer made her completely invisible to enemies. She will only progress if enemies aren't watching, but this can still lead to situations where she really should have been spotted.
For some unexplained reason Shadwen also has the power to stop/rewind time, which does make it easy to pull off superb stunts. Too bad you rarely need these fancy acrobatics, as the dumb guards and boring levels often lead to rather uninspired gameplay.
The game also has a rather superfluous crafting system that let's you unlock new traps and tools. This system feels rather tacked on and is almost completely pointless if you are going for a non-lethal run.
There are no difficulty levels and overall Shadwen is a pretty easy game, especially if you are willing to murder a guard or two. Even a non-lethal run wasn't particularly challenging.
The controls are decent enough with mouse + keyboard.
The writing is ok but the background story is never properly developed.
The physics are pretty terrible and highly unrealistic. The rewind mechanic is also rather glitchy and poorly implemented.
Overall Shadwen is an extremely disappointing game. The concept is interesting but everything else about the game is either unpolished or poorly done. I would not recommend the game, even to the fans of the genre. You should play the similar (but far superior) Styx game series instead.

This is a controversial opinion I know, but .. .
I just can't play this game.
No it isn't broken or buggy, merely that the graphics and sound are just so bad by today's standard that someone like me, who didn't play Half Life (or Doom or Woldenstein or even Star Wars Dark Forces) during the FPS boom of the late '90s, are  completely lost.
Yes, I know what this game did for the industry, especially for later shooters.
But just because a game has a great legeacy and a lasting impact does NOT make it playable to a modern audience.
A hallmark of a great game should be that it is, was and will be playable at any time in history, regardless of graphics.
FF6 and, to a lesser degree, Pokemon Red and Blue are still playable today due to the simplicity of 16-bit, 2D graphics.
On the other hand, practically all 3D games from the 1990s are unplayable and frankly ugly to the modern gamer's eye.
Even that aside, the story is an afterthought being not especially riveting or intriguing by even the standards of the game's creators; Half Life was a technological marvel of the time, thus the story was second to the gameplay experience.
My final score, devoid of any nostalgia is a 3/10.

I greatly enjoyed this little gem of a stealth game.
There are 2 ways to play: Ghost or Assassin.
Ghost style means you're distracting the guards for your little friend Lily to slip past them toward the exit.
Assassin style means leaving nothing but bloodstains behind you.
(you can technically do a balance of both, but if Lily sees you kill someone, you're locked into the 'killer' route, and it denies you an achievement :P)
Personally, I did the stealth route first, then did a slayer-speedrun, this is the order I recommend it.
Story is revealed by overhearing the guards, and chatter between chapters, based on your path through the game.
Gameplay is like Thief meets Prince of Persia (Sands of Time).
Time stops when you do (unless you hold the key to allow time to continue, such as when waiting for a guard to pass, or get into position), so you can have some pretty slick acrobatics with your grappling hook.
Expect to 'die' a lot when you're learning. You can turn on the guards' field of vision, but personally I only found it distracting when doing a stealth run.
Speaking of 'combat', you don't so much fight guards as ambush them. You can't even win a 1-on-1 fight. Even attacking an enemy from the front makes them block it and raise an alarm. Of course, you don't have JUST your trusty dagger, drop crates on people, set traps, run them over with carts, etc. Some of the best moments in the assassin path involve setting up a rube-goldberg like chain of events, ending with four guards standing under a falling barrel.
Overall, 8/10.

On your way to this deed you encounter a little orphan, Lily, who you escort for the whole game. As escort quests go this one is not that bad as Lily is kinda smart and as long as the way is clear she'll go where she needs to go and she's basically invisible for the guards.
Every level you have to remain unseen and clear the way for Lily to get to the exit. You clear the way by either providing a distraction, so the guards will look another way, or by killing the guards so they won't see anything ever. You have your trusty rope that clings to wooden surfaces with which you can move things or reach places. Similar to Superhot, time moves only when you move (or you press a designated button), and you have unlimited rewinds whenever you get seen or mess something up. The levels are well made and remind me of Styx a little bit with their verticality, and the game is a quite fun stealther overall. It also has crappy animations, so so graphics and little variety, so well...
There are two or three endings, depending on whether you kill the king or not and whether you let the escorted girl know you're a killer. One playthrough should take more or less 7-8hrs, then all chapters are available for chapter select if you want to hunt some achievements. Shadwen is worth a try if you're a fan of stealth games (and it's on sale).
I liked:
* stealthy stealth
* ai of Lily, doesn't make the escort a drag
* the story (it's very simple, but changes based on whether your stealthy or murdery)
* good level design
I disliked:
* occasional glitches
* the rope animations can be crazy (not in a good way)
* most of the levels look the same
Get this if:
* you like stealth games and it's on sale
Don't get this:
* if you're easily bored (this is more puzzle stealther than action stealther)
* you can't overlook some glitches

I like playing Assassin's Creed games. I like playing what I call, collecting games. I like running around cities or places collecting things, doing missions, ect. You go talk to someone, there is no cutscene, just them talking to you while you stand there. Then you go and do some task for them (pick up x, kill y, ect.). That is pretty much it. I couldn't bring myself to continue playing this game.
The combat has changed a little bit, it is a little bit harder in a good way, but my camera felt so zoomed in during combat that I would get hit by guys off screen because I couldn't see them so that I could counter them. That was pretty lame.
The only innovation I saw was the detective missions where you go and look for clues for a crime in several locations. That is pretty cool.
Overall a pretty bland game in my opinion. You are best skipping this entry to the Assassin Creed series.
