This is going to be a long review so in short: Half-Life is a classic game, that everyone who likes the FPS genre should play. The price is right, the game is entertaining, and the series of more recent games (Half-Life 2) it leads into are incredible, historicaly, gameplay-wise, and story-wise. Worth your money; you'll enjoy it.
In a little more detail: I played Half-Life first, around 2 years ago and I've since logged about a hundred hours in the game. I've played through it 9 or 10 times. I had been needing something new to play after finishing Portal 2 and Half-Life was on sale. I asked a friend if I should play it and he said no - that it was boring, but the price was so good I bought it and tried it anyways, and I was immediately hooked. I've since bought the game for several friends, and it's the first title I bring up to anyone asking for a game reccomendation.
Half-Life is an old game. I'm not going to pretend that I would be thrilled with this game if it had come out yesterday. If I bought this game in 2016, let's face it, I'd want a refund. The graphics are extremely dated, the movement is a little tough to get used to, and the AI is seriously lacking. Gabe Newell would be getting an angry email.
In 1998, when it was released however, Half-Life was a revolutionary game, with unique and new methods of story telling, exciting new mechanics, and realistic AI. The ability to jump was still a relatively cool new development in the gaming world, and the ability to crouch-jump was very new. Half-Life has a large variety of interesting weapons, and the enemies move and interact with the player in advanced ways for a 90's game. Enemies will follow you, take cover, switch between different types of attacks, call in other enemies, and more. The puzzles in Half-Life are what 90's gamers would have wanted. While jumping puzzles nowadays are lazy and annoying, they were popular in the 90's in the FPS genre, because being able to jump at all was still somwehat of a novelty. The chapter "On A Rail" is my LEAST favourite chapter, and annoys the hell out of me, but like the Ravenholm chapter in Half-Life 2, it would have been an exciting way for gamers to test out a fun new game mechanic. The story is told entirely through Gordon's eyes, which creates a level of immersion that had never been seen before in the FPS genre, and that still holds up today. Even despite dated graphics, I still found myself deeply engrossed in the game's world. Half-Life was one of the (if not the) first FPS game to be highly story-oriented. Prior to Half-Life, the FPS genre was not usually chosen for story telling. Valve took the FPS genre to the next level by creating a game that is dynamic in BOTH gameplay, and story. My apologies if that paragraph was a little messy; I have a lot of thoughts.
Now I hear you, it's not 1998 anymore, so whether or not Half-Life was a good game THEN is only part of the story. Half-Life can be a revolutionary game-changing (no pun intended) game and still suck to play today, and the reviews section is supposed to give you some idea of whether or not you actually want to spend money on this game and play it.
Half-Life is worth a play, 18 years after it's release, in 2016, and it's worth paying your ten dollars to get to do that, in my humble opinion. People dont play games out of context. When I bought and played Half-Life the first time, I bought it to enjoy a classic game. If you expect to play a game with the same graphics quality as Portal 2 then you'll be dissapointed. If you expect to play Half-Life as it is (an 18 year old story-rich FPS) you will be blown away. Half-Life shattered my expectations for what an 18 year old game could be. Don't pretend the game is something it's not.
If you're alright with playing an old game, Half-Life will not dissapoint. While some aspects of the game are dated, the core principles (weaponry, characters, story, and gameplay) stand up to time beautifully and the parts that do not (some puzzles, designs of some rooms and levels) do not take away from the over-all experience, and are still fun.
Half-Life is fun, stands the test of time where it needs to, bears a great deal of gaming-history, and is the opening installment of one of the most (in my opinion) great game series of all time. For anyone who actually read this far: remember when there were rumours that Half-Life 3 would be released in February 2015? That was funny.

All right, from what you can probably glean about this game from the screenshots and the other reviews, it's a cutesy anime style roleplaying game starring little girls with swords and magic.
What you can't see though is the amazing swordplay that said little girl is capable of, and which you have to master.
You'll see people call this game 2D Dark Souls and there's a reason for it. If you rush into fights you will get you♥♥♥♥♥handed to you. You have to study all your moves (frontslash, backslash, downslash, uppercut, followup, cartwheel, dodgeroll, etc) to know how you can use them effectively against certain enemies. There's no button mashing in this game, each attack (other than the normal slash) needs a certain simple button input in order to be executed which is easy to learn but difficult to use effectively.
Take the starting green slimes for example, if you watch the way they move you can see how simple it is. They hop until they get to melee distance and the strike. If you strike at them though they might react in order to avoid that strike, they may jump back whereupon you will need to use your frontslash (attack button + the direction you are facing) which has longer distance than your normal slash, or they may jump high up and go for a counterattack on the way down whereupon you will need to use your uppercut (attack button + up) and juggle then in the air, or they may jump behind you whereupon you will need to use your backstab (attack button + the direction you are not facing), etc etc.
This might sound complicated but it really is simple. This game is hard, but not because of hard hitting enemies or damage sponges (although enemies have varying degrees of damage depending on the attacks they use and their level and you will need to level up and keep your equipment up to date in order to keep up with them), it's hard because of their AI and the moves they use which you have to counter with your limited arsenal.
Seiously if you want to know what this game is all about, put it on the hardest difficulty and go 1v1 with a kobold.

Colin McRae Rally
You hear that name and instantly awesome true Rally experiences come to mind. Harsh terrain, realistic and believable damage to your car as you make stupid mistakes, and a fairly competitive AI that makes it a nice challenge all-in-all.
That isn't this game. This game is a mobile port. It isn't (at all) what it tries to advertise itself as. Handling is simplified, damage is merely cosmetic at best, the terrain looks horrible. Remastered is a term many low-resolution games use these days to try and bring these experiences to the modern PC, but Colin McRae Rally doesn't manage to do any of it.
It lacks features that previous games in the series. You can't customize your car's behavior before a stage. Repairs are fairly unneeded as they don't impact gameplay, and fixing the "engine" costs the same amount of time as fixing the "suspension" or "wheels".
There isn't much else to say. This game was trading on good memories of the Colin McRae series and it's just a cash grab. It's lame, it doesn't feel like a rally game, and overall it's a perfect example of what is happening to Steam's storefront where publishers and developers have no shame about what they try to do with their advertising.

First of all i love this game, i sincerely love this game.

The dungeons you fight in tend to look similar, sometimes you need to go in the same dungeon multiple times, and exploration is a necessity as you dont get levels quite the same way as a normal rpg. There are collectibles known as "Mark of Heroism" that will increase your maximum achievable level by 1 and increase the amount of money you can carry, so exploration is extremely important, however exploring too much will deplete your mana and it will be very hard to advance or backtrack, always have some mana restoration items on you.
Platforming can be difficult at times, especially with moving platforms because even if you go at the same speed as the platform you still slide as if it was solid ground and you will fall off alot.
Combat is actually amusing, i have a few things to say about it, while it has faults like, turning and timing are difficult to get used to, and combos are extremely difficult. It is still very well balanced, even if you are overpowered, you can still get destroyed very fast, the team aspect of the combat to me is amazing, if you do not fight as a team with the AI that controls your members, you will die, and you will die fast, you have to cover for your teammates so they can cover you. you will often get comboed by your enemies, so try not to fight too many at the same time and try to keep some distance from your teammates otherwise you all get hit by the same attacks, magic is unblockable along with some specific attacks, so it is just a matter of who gets the first hit.
It is a shame that it was cut down during development, i read up about the game and i read that it was originally going to be 20 hours long, but was cut down to 5 hours. It really feels unsatisfying because there is alot of items that do nothing and sort of just exist, they are actual items, like "water of life" "white whale oil" and more, seemingly usefull and valuable items.
Once again i love this game, and there seems to be an expansion called Fortune Summoners Plus, that adds a randomized dungeon and some extra items and spells, and has a little bonus to the main story, but it is only available in japan or through japanese websites, which, frankly... sucks!

Great utility for managing multiple monitors. This kind of functionality has been sorely lacking in Windows for a long time. I've owned a couple business laptops over the years that used Nvidia's nView desktop management software (which is only available for their workstation-type Quadro cards, unfortunately), and this is definitely a good substitute. It's a bit less polished than nView, but that's to be expected when you're comparing it to workstation utlities. It fixed the biggest problem I had with multiple monitors, which was simply getting programs to always start up on the active monitor.
Now, why I actually need an additional piece of software in order to make this happen is beyond me. You'd think someone at Microsoft would've noticed by now that new windows almost always open on whatever particular monitor would be least useful for them to open on.
^^^^  If anyone wants to mention how annoying this is to someone at Microsoft so they can fix it, I would much appreciate it, and while you're at it, let them know that whenever I click "End Process", the computer does the exact opposite, almost every single time.
I feel like I'm under a lot of pressure to write a fair, objective, and highly informative review, based on the facts of my user experience... it probably would've been easier if I had just typed "10/10 - would buy another monitor again", or something stupid like that, rather than actually trying to tell you why I like this software.
Display Fusion does a lot of other great stuff too, and a more dedicated reviewer would take the time to tell you, dear reader, about all of it. Don't give up; you may yet find the work of such a dedicated reviewer. The last paragraph of this review will not provide an new information and is essentially a rewording of the first paragraph of this review.
Don't let the comparison to nView deter you - this is a little less polished but it probably does more overall, if you take the time to customize it. Best software of its type that doesn't require a workstation card, as far as I know. A lot of the functionality feels like it should be a component of the OS itself, in my opinion.

I initially purchased this game in a bundle with two other games published by Carpe Fulgur almost a year ago and wasn't really too keen on playing it, though after finally giving it a shot I would say I wouldn't have minded paying for it separately. The game more or less is in line with other Carpe Fulgur games like Reccetear or Chantelise, with the cute, girly anime aesthetic and lighthearted tone and simple story, but I learned pretty quickly that the game is deceptively deep, as well as difficult and outright mean in places.
At first, the controls and physics of your character feel sluggish and clunky, but after about an hour of messing around, as well as fighting some monsters and learning new abilities, the combat and controls are extremely satisfying. You start with a simple slash attack, jump, flying jump-kick and dodge roll, and all of your combat abilities are activated by using the control stick and attack button with combo inputs, sort of like a fighting game with quarter-circle movements and such. As you level up you gain more and more attacks and abilities, you eventually turn into a total badass, being able to attack while rolling, getting a few more attacks that you can combo into, stabbing behind you and being able to change direction quickly, and you start to realize that you have much more mobility and range than you thought.
Funnily enough, there is also a combo meter that builds up as you strike enemies without being hit, which is really puzzling at the beginning of the game when you feel so slow, but as you get more confident with the combat you can rack up combos in seconds and get a bunch of damage bonuses when fighting groups of enemies or even bosses if you learn how to string your attacks together. One important thing to note is that you'll likely have to constantly remind yourself to play slower, judge attacks, and block often, as enemies have greater attack range and are generally faster, not to mention that you have a sort of input queue, so button-mashing and getting impatient or greedy is a great way to get yourself killed.
As you get further into the game, you'll be introduced to your second and third party members, one being a support spellcaster and the other being an offensive mage, each with their own abilities that they will unlock as they level up, and you are given the option to take control of any of the three members as well as customize which spells they use and how often. As fun as it is to play with the starting character alone, having even one other party member to sling spells, buff, or heal takes a lot of the pressure off as enemies start to scale pretty roughly as they get stronger, use status effects, get a lot more mobile and aggressive, or just show up in larger groups.
Though not really a core element of the gameplay, your father owns an item shop in your new hometown, and each day you can help out by collecting a specific item to add to the shops inventory, allowing you to purchase an unlimited amount of special items dropped from monsters or carried by stores in other towns. Each town has a pretty fair distance between the other, so being able to save time by buying a specific item from home is a neat mechanic, as it encourages you to fight monsters, collect items, and explore dangerous areas thoroughly.
Another element of the gameplay that encourages exploration is the Mark of Heroism, an item that increases your level-cap and allows you to reach a higher level. Generally, I dislike RPGs with level-caps or similar limitations, but I feel it really works well in this game, as it doesn't reward mindless grinding in easier areas or relying too much on your stats to carry you through the game, instead expecting you to dive into dungeons and learn to play better in order to make progress. Not to mention that collecting each Mark fully restores your HP and MP, giving you some extra longevity if you start to get lost in a dungeon or run out of items.
The story is pretty simple and straightforward, though the dialogue and characters are charming and don't make the game feel like a chore to sit through. You play as Arche, a young girl that moves into a new village to attend a magic school, though after the first day she realizes that she doesn't have an elemental stone that would allow her to practice magic in the first place. She then explores a cave after hearing she might be able to find one for herself, only to find that the stone is sealed, with an elemental spirit attached to it. With the stone essentially useless, Arche has to find three crests in order to break the seal and actually use the stone, which serves as the main conflict of the story. Throughout the story you explore new areas and find new towns, with each "chapter" having a different focus. At first you can only visit a few locations, but as you make it through the story you can freely explore areas that are made available if you feel you've missed something.
The flow of the gameplay and story essentially hinges on the events of each day, with the first few days slowly introducing characters and the basic plot, and then further on you start to get into the meat of the game, getting two other party members and going dungeon crawling to solve various problems. The issue I have with the flow of the story is how it affects the gameplay. Entirely too often you will have a party member leave you, forcing you to play alone for a portion of a dungeon or new difficult area, and the game constantly swings between casual fun and teeth-gritting frustration when you encounter new enemies, bosses, or lose party members. Depending on how much trouble with the game you're having, it takes about 10 hours to finally get your three-girl party assembled, with the game essentially teasing you by giving you scenarios where you play as one or two separately, which can be incredibly frustrating in specific dungeons.
In conclusion, the game is harmlessly cute and fun with plenty of cool mechanics, good graphics and sound, and a surprising amount of content. Even at 15 hours I feel like I might only be approaching halfway through the game. The only complaint I really have is that it can be a bit frustrating and difficult, so you'll just have to grin and bear it even if you are good at platformers and action-RPGs in general.

First off, it's a 2D RPG/Roguelike/Bullet hell game. This is actually a really good combination, the combat is fun and very simple whilst still having a fair amount of depth to it. You can deal incredible amounts of damage very quickly with wizards, heal your teammates with priests, or stun monsters and tank with the knight. Or you can rush dungeons with rogues. Or take event bosses with an Assassin. Or clear dungeons with an Archer. For every playstyle, there is a class.
The economy in this game is based off of stat potions. These increase your stats permanently, and are always in demand due to perma death. The least rare and thus least valuable potion is the speed potion, with the holy grail of pots being the life potion. Trading with other players is a fun process, albeit long. Unlike other economies in other games the currency in this game is always being destroyed so it retains it's value instead of constantly being inflated. This makes each boss fight that much more intense knowing that even though the risk is high, the reward is much, much higher.
However the bad in this game is Kabum. The developers of this game have constantly shown they don't understand what the player actually wants. I've stopped playing this game simply because Kabum is terrible. Things they have done include accidentally releasing a warrior kit bundle for 1 gold (premium in game currency worth roughly 1 cent). This instantly tanked the price of the kit and screwed up the economy for a bit. Another thing they did to mess up the game royally was removing the ability of gland mobs to drop pots. This made the price of stat pots rise until they reverted back to the original model. Again, screwing up the economy for a bit.
Altogether a good game ruined by a bad developer.

I can't remember the last time a game made me cry! This has got to be one of the most heart-felt story-driven games I've ever played! I personally am not that big of a fan of the show, but holy cow did this give me a new appreciation for the franchise as a whole. This game features a man named Lee, who ends up in a car accident after getting arrested by the cops for felony. The accident was caused by walkers, zombies who have breathed new life and continue to inhabit it for the soul purpose of, what else, eating their victims alive. Throughout the story the game presents you with choices for your character to make. Some are ordinary and produce opportunities to learn about other characters, while other choices are timing and must be answered or else you choice will remain dormant. I really like this feature and it can show us how well we as people would do if we were ever thrown into a zombie apolcalypse. What's really cool is how some of these choices can create different outcomes that effect the story's plot to extent. It would of been nice if this was exploited a little futher, but this is the first game in the series so improvements are bound to be made. Over the course of these five episodes you also interact with a little girl, who evidently becomes your legal guardian. The situations they put you in whether hostile or laid back both make for a great parenting simulator if you can believe that! The pacing seems fluid as it gives you an opportunity to explore and observe the country as it falls in the hands of the walking dead. the graphics give me that Borderlands feel with the sharp outlined textures of each character model. Everything about the game from beginning to end feels like a satifying journey. Regardless if you follow the show or not, this game will win you over in a heartbeat.

Let me start by saying that I am a fan of the X-Com franchise
and I like it that an AAA game like this runs on Ubuntu Linux.
However I do not recommend this version (Xcom 2), as I got frustrated playing it.
The last (X-Com Enemy unknown/within) also had some bad points, but not as much.
Firstly X-Com 2 contains a lot of bugs (even the game was released already a year ago), like:
- sometimes the game wont start.
- when it starts ok, the keyboard sometimes wont work (only mouse works).
- the animated camera movement (zoom in/out) can set its position/view to wrong coordinates.
- the GUI sometimes displays buttons on top of eachother, so you can't press the button underneath
- before a mission starts the button to release items of non-active soldiers will sometimes abort the mission, thus making it impossible to release items for that mission.
- often the game will let my laptop hang (probably due to overheating).
- enabling autosave seem to cause a more frequent hang situation (SSD issue?)
- a few times the game simply crashed.
- using the mouse to select a movement path might exclude locations which should be reachable.
- when high up a building you can see stuff floating in the air, which clearly should be at the ground
- the physics engine will show weird impossible animations
- a viper can take a soldier (Tongue Pull) through a walled corner
- an enemy can sometimes shoot through walls/roof
- enemy (and you) can detect (and shoot) through doors
- standing next tile to enemy in plain sight and still its not a target
- sometimes an enemy is made visible upon shooting another, then disappears after the action.
- an enemy robot "Advent Mec" can jump high and stay standing in mid-air.
Then the bad game mechanics:
- the chance to hit is too much random, even with over 90% chance a sniper might miss 3 times in a row
- note also that reloading a save game will deliver different random results, which is ofcourse nice to create higher chances.. but also means the randomness statistics can not be valid.
- when a soldier dies, one or two will get panic and be useless and so most of the time the whole team will be dead.
- a sniper at a roof in half-cover cloaked behind a wall, can still be seen and shot dead by one shot
- a sniper behind a tree in full-cover is unable to hit an enemy at a line straight through the tree, even though the soldier animation shows he/she is looking around the tree.
- an enemy group might detect my movement and get an extra movement turn to hide, which is uneven advantage.
- red squares denote tiles that (your soldiers know) are seen by enemies, but moving your soldier will erase some of those (so I have to remember which were red squares for the whole turn).
- those red squares do not seem to be updated correctly, as sometimes a square next to it is also seen by the enemy.
- in most cases the shown possible movement path excludes red squares, but sometimes they include them.. I have to check closely each time.
- the game allows different building types, but only a few are essential and the rest can be discarded as useless.
- the same with certain items/weapons, they are not relevant (eg vests cost utility spot but only get you one/two hitpoints)
- to do certain actions in the GUI you need to press buttons a lot, while it could have been made eassier/faster with a single button.
- very nice animations appear before/after starting missions, however they get bored quickly.. pressing Esc skips them but can also abort starting the mission.
- the help inside the game is very bad (eg. choosing between special abilities and building needs many google searches to make them clear).
- some missions are impossible
- the computer AI's turn and executing of storyline scripting takes a significant amount of time
- AI detection is too simply.. when not cloaked the enemy will detecting you when in range (even through high cover)
- when still cloaked, the AI guard movement is guided towards you.. making it more difficult to sneak past.
So the frustration causes me to:
- reload back when one of my soldiers dies or a mission can't be completed ok.
- disabling the autosave (which overwrites itself after a few minutes) and manual save before/after each mission.
- restart the laptop after each hang.
- restarting the game after crash.
- hit escape to skip the animations, but not the mission.
- keep the amount of actions to a minimum, as there require many mouse movements+clicks.
- keep google search open to help me find info about each new selection opportunity.

XCOM 2 has a soft space in my heart. I've tried the first XCOM, I mean, the REAL first XCOM. As much as the die-hard fans rave like rabid dogs about how amazing it is, my simple, casual, millennial mind simply can't sit down and grasp how it works or how to put up with god awful graphics (and trust me, I've played stuff like Populous, so I've got some resistance compared to my generation.)
When I first found XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within, I had literally no idea what I was in for. What I found was a great "Dress up these people and make them fight aliens" strategy game I immediately fell in love with. Making everyone look like celebrities was my best choice, and having secret agent Ben Affleck kick doors down whilst Jeremy Renner did wierd magic stuff was just hilarious.
So, I was stoked for XCOM 2. Despite my usually harsh view on the videogame industry, I even pre-ordered a couple of weeks early, I was so damn excited.
On launch day, I was... satisfied?
XCOM 2 is buggy, feels somewhat unfinished in some areas, with some oversights included and overall loses a couple of elements of strategic depth for more "Pfft, that's XCOM"-ness I was growing somewhat tired of. That being said, I still adore this game. The graphical upgrade is immense, and my soldiers look sillier than ever thanks to the impressive range of mods available for this game. Even in vanilla, this game still entertains me. XCOM 2's take on top-down strategy gets me immediately feeling like a strategic genius when I manage to get a grenade thrown through a wall to tear down cover for someone else to take a shot.
Despite it's bugs, flaws, and it mistakenly thinking that everyone who plays it will spend six hours on every mission like some sort of chess grandmaster, playing on a lower difficulty to get to grips with the game and just having some fun with the characters makes XCOM 2 a worthy sequel to it's predecessor, building on the lore and gameplay of the first, elevating the stakes and making you feel that much smarter when grenadier Michael Bay blaster launchers an entire house to dust.

Despite some of these shortcomings I do enjoy the game. Shadwen is fun to play, nice-looking, the soundscape is fine and the female protagonist doesn't look like a porn star. I got the game cheap when it was on discount, so I think I got my money's worth.

Very mixed. Nice work from a small indie studio. Nice level design and attention to environmental detail. Good character animation. Gameplay is a bit disappointing however. It feels like Thief or AC at first but for a stealth game it’s a bit frustrating. Lighting conditions, distance and cover don’t  do much for you and are inconsistent—at times you will be shot by a guard who catches a glimpse of you from half way across the level while you are motionless behind a stack of crates. Other times you can cross a brightly lit hallway 40’ in front of a guard looking your direction.  You will die hundreds of times playing this game but fortunately there is a kind or rewind action that lets you back up immediately without having to start from a checkpoint.  The AI has the perpetual problem of stealth games by being incredibly stupid while at the same time having superhuman senses. Pull a crate off a ledge and have it smash on the street a few yards from guards and you’ll get, “Did you ‘ear som’fing?”  But try to slip past a dude in full plate armor and he’ll whip around like a cobra.
Stealth is further frustrated that the time between “Did you see that?” and DEAD is about two seconds.  The levels are full of all kinds of wonderful nooks and crannies perfect for hiding in except these are useless. The guards will march right over to you no matter how hidden you are. However, duck into a shrub (game asset) and they will be completely flummoxed. So unfortunately, the lovely levels are completely meaningless to game play. The AI is only concerned with game assets.  They will often shoot you around corners, or through objects. They have a Detect/Kill reflex that might be ok for a SiFi killer robot game, but is frustrating in this setting.
More problematic is the game is clearly trying to have you be “good” and not kill the guards, but like so many stealth games with a non-violent path (i.e. Dishonored) there is little provided for you to do that. You have a wide range of loot you can gather to make all sorts of lethal bombs and traps and as the game progresses you’ll encounter barrels of gunpowder, precariously placed wagons, and all sorts of fun clever ways to kill the guards but almost nothing for the non-lethal path other than make a noise, hide, wait…wait… wait…GO! Over and over. This is further complicated by the fact that any dead guard detected by any other is a Game Over as well—even if the guard has killed himself by knocking a box on top of himself. Plus the little girl can’t ever see any dead bodies or you’ll get the “bad” ending.
Further, the game is one long escort mission with a little girl that you aid early in the game. Rather than tell the kid to beat it, this assassin on this super-deadly mission let’s her tag along. Looking at the promos I thought the girl WAS the point—rescuing the rightful heir before her evil uncle has her killed or something. That would make sense. But no she’s just a street urchin our hero escorts on this deadly mission. What?
The game has a strange freeze-action play style that seems to be inspired by Kill Bill/Matrix. The game is  paused unless you are moving or holding down the “wait” key. I found this very distracting and constantly kept me thinking about the game mechanics instead of getting drawn into the story.  Secondly your character has a Spiderman-style “grappling hook” that the game designers obviously intended you to use constantly but the combination of this tool and the stop-motion action made it annoying and frustrating to use.
Do yourself a huge favor and assing Crouch/Sneak from the default Ctr to Caps lock so you can toggel it on and off instead of holding it down for 90% of the game.
So for the price, this game is well worth it and will keep you occupied for 10 or 12 hours depending on your play style. Its disappointing in that it came so close to being an exciting game, but fell just short—kind of like our hero missing her landing by a few inches and falling on her face in front of a guard.

I bought this game because it looked good, I was looking for a casual game to play, and it was cheap.  As I read reviews, the biggest complaint was that controls were terrible and it was really hard to actually hit enemies.  I also noted that players making such claims had generally logged under 1/2 an hour of play time.  I now have 13+ hrs of game play and rest assured, once you get a better bow, targeting gets much better, plus your special abilities also make it easier to hit and kill enemies.
Another complaint is that the voice acting is terrible and that the translation from Russian to English is pathetic.  Although it's true, I'm actually finding it endearing.  It actually fits the game, the graphics, and the story.  It's quite funny!
In terms of game play, it isn't just hack and slash.  There is definitely some strategy involved as the authors have created situations in which you can't simply charge in.  There are also some non-fighting puzzles involved.  I heartily recommend this game (4 out of 5 stars).  It's fun, funny, and the plot is fairly interesting (based on a Russian fairy tale) with casual game play so you can play for 15 minutes or 5 hours at a time.

Three Heroes is a short indie-RPG developed by Cats Who Play and released Sep 16, 2015.
You basically have a fairy tail start, the archer and hero Alesha has come out of retirement because bandits attacked him and he turned them into pincushions.
He goes to get the help of his two other friends Dobrynya who fights with a staff weapon, and Ilya whom fights with the bread and butter: sword and shield.
Each Hero has a different fighting style, and a set of talents they can choose between while leveling up. Experience is granted from kills and completing quests. Just a pro tip right now: You cannot unlock all of the skills to max in a play through, so choose wisely.
As a whole, I didn't find the game to be too unpleasantness, for the first hour or so Three Heroes is very entertaining! But then you start to feel like somethings not quite right... It starts with the awkwardness of the controls. Don't jump... just don't. it slows you down, the only time you'll use it is if you're stuck on something. Also you cannot move and attack (which is agony for someone who loves to kite in video games).
Lastly the music gets a bit repetitive (so I turned it off), and the voice acting is borderlines awkward and annoying, and awkward and funny. It's right inbetween.
The 3d models are rough around the edges, and one of my favorite effects, is when you use a special pole vaulting animation with Dodrynya, when after he launches himself HE RAGDOLLS when he hits the floor. It's hilarious, I love it!
So here's the thing... I've played some games which are right in between being good and bad and I decide I think they're bad because they weren't interesting, or had mechanical problems which took me out of the game.
This game is definitely in between, some mechanical things should be ironed out. But It's clear the developers are actually trying. Each character is distinct and different and has different controls. (And making a whole 3d game as an indie team? it's pretty uncommon to make a game which feels like it came out of the Play Station 2. Most indie dev's will make an RPG maker for the hundreth time, or go a pixil art so they don't need to 3d model or program as hard.
Kudos to  Cats Who Play for actually taking this route with their game. It won't appeal to everyone, some people will probably hate their game. But as long as I can recognize the good with the bad, I enjoyed my time with the game, it didn't over stay its welcome, and if you're looking to support an indie dev, go ahead and give Three Heroes a try.
Thank you for reading, as always I'm Atratzu and I approve this review.

TL;DR: Solid stealth-puzzle hybrid, recommended on sale due to short length and little replay value.
Shadwen is a competent mashup of genres and mechanics. It's a stealth game with light puzzle elements where you must use mobilty and physics objects to distract guards, creating a path for your AI companion (Lilly) to move safely through the levels.
The graphics and art are pleasing to look at. It has a great, relaxing nighttime vibe, similar to Thief 3. The story is simple, you are on your way to assassinate the king when you find Lilly being harassed by a guard. From that point on it's up to you whether or not you let Lilly know you're a killer, hide your tracks or simply avoid guards altogether. Any additional details about the world are revealed through conversations between guards, again similar to Thief.
The game is short, roughly five hours for a first run. Additionaly, the only real replay value is in the form of achievements. It's up to you whether that matters or not. Shadwen is also fairly easy. This is either going to be a positive or a negative depending on what you're looking for. It's a good late-night game, easy to look at, calm atmosphere and not too demanding.
The main mechanic of the game is that time only moves when you press Q or when you are moving, similar to Superhot. This lets you observe your situation in relative safety and execute complex grapple-hook manoeuvres. The grappling hook is used extensively to make use of the great deal of verticality present throughout levels. It's also your main tool to create distractions by pulling wooden objects.
The idea of a five hour escort mission would probably put most people off, but the game is rather forgiving and the mechanics are just solid enough to avoid frustration. That said, there were some moments when getting groups of 3 or more guards out of the way was finnicky and Lilly would refuse to move on.
Lilly herself cannot be seen or harmed by guards, only you can trigger a fail state. That alleviates a ton of potential frustration from having to rely on companion AI. The game also has a Prince of Persia style rewind mechanic with infinite use, allowing you to immediately rectify mistakes or failures. This a godsend when dealing with physics objects.
Shadwen has a pseudo NG+ where your inventory and gadgets are saved as you progress, allowing you to replay chapters and checkpoints at any time with all your items. However, it also keeps track of whether or not you have killed and if Lilly has seen it. This means you're best off going fully non-lethal on your first run, in order not to block any potential achievement progress.
Pros:
- Looks great, runs great
- Interesting mechanics
- Great atmosphere
- Stress-free, casual stealth experience
- Customisable difficulty
- NG+
Cons:
- Relatively short
- Little to no replay value
- Heavy dependance on AI and physics
- One big escort mission
- Not recommended if you're looking for something challenging
- Not much point in crafting or using gadgets
- NG+ keeps 'killer' state, can block achievements

Brigador is a vehicular shooter with a killer aesthetic and tight gameplay that rewards good play no matter how you go about it. Smart, stealthy players will have a serious challenge ahead, but the payouts will be massive. Not up to the crazy hard, grueling endurance runs? No problem. Grab a big mech with a big gun and wreak havoc and guess what? You'll still get paid, and you can do it in three missions.
This isn't really a twin-stick shooter; WASD are your chassis movement controls and your turret/torso are controlled with a mouse. I definitely do not recommend using a controller at all as you'll lose some serious precision which you'll need. There are options to significantly reduce the game speed if needed, so if you're jonesing for a controller game Brigador will do in a pinch.
The Freelance mode, with static maps but random enemy placements, will be the meat of your time with the game. Pick any vehicle, weapons, and level setups you've unlocked and GO!
The campaign is decent fun, with unique and static scenarios. You'll be rewarded very well for each level and vehicle pair you complete, so if you're enjoying youself, go back and clear the level again with a completely different vehicle.
The Deluxe Edition is well-worth it for the music alone, and the Audiobook is great military sci-fi fun.
I wholeheartedly recommend Brigador to anyone who likes action games. $20 is a steal for how much you'll get and there's more to come; the devs have been releasing more pilots, vehicles, and missions since release, along with balancing and the like.

Darkest Dungeon is a rather difficult RPG with gothic and lovecraftian horror elements. However this time it is not you, who follows the steps of a true hero, but your job is rather to to manage diffrent "Heroes" which have unique Quirks and of course a speciffic class. Your task is to stop, whatever it is, that your ancester awoke and basically restore peace to the monster plagued hamlet.
The thing I like most about this game is the atmosphere. The visuals and the sound create an immersive experience. The Narrator is plainly genius and the sanity system is well done. The difficulty is harsh, but after some time, you´ll see your own improvement. The Boss battles are very special, as they have very unique patterns. As you will do them blind on your first attempts, give it enough time, to figure their patterns out. Your first party might fail, but as long, as you managed to get enough informations to design new strategies, you got a step closer to victory.
Many commentors before me have complained about the RNG in this game, but I think it is, to some degree, an important factor of this game. With experience you´ll learn to rate the danger of an encounter, but you can never exactly predict the outcome. The game will remind you very often, that your heroes are not immortal and that their will to fight may falter. This is necessary to create the atmosphere: the dungeons are terrible, the slightest misstep, wrong Judgement or sheer bad luck can lead to an untimely end of an character. While there are ways to mitigate the danger, and you WILL improve on that, there is never certainity, that everyone will return save and sound.
I would recommend this game, if you
- like RPGs especially those who are challenging
- are into (lovecraftian) horror
- like to mange your units, base and resources
- like exploring and dungeon crawling
you might want to reconcider, if you
- absolutely hate it, when your heroes die
- prefer a more relaxing setting or a simple difficulty
- give up easily and get disheartened by failure quickly
I hope this review was helpful to you.

Ok, where to begin. I suppose I should mention before anything that this is purely a mobile port taken straight off the app store and shoved into Steam for what I can only assume is a quick bit of money making. The price itself isn't all that bad and if you don't have an iPhone/iPod etc. and you want to play this then fine, but go into it with the certainty that it is a mobile port, the feel and style of the original seemingly lost to the pages of gaming history.
To get the full experience you'll need to play through championships to unlock other cars/rally's etc. Not a bad mechanic in itself but this game makes it feel like such a chore. First the AI is humorously slow, on my very first attempt i beat them by a minute and a half (and while I may be mistaken I couldn't for the life of me find any option to up the difficulty). Secondly there is no sense of speed while driving, I remember the original leaving me on the edge of my seat, sweating trying to work out what just happened. This just left me feeling like I was stuck in traffic during a long drive home after an exhaustingly long day of work. Now it is perhaps worth noting that my experience and therefore memory of the original may have been skewed by a 6 year olds sense of wonder and far too many Smarties, but I am not quite yet senile so I doubt it is that skewed.
It has some positives, like the version I played on an iPod I was impressed by the audio, each time I passed some fans I got a little kick out of the cheers and sounds of horns but alas this kick fades way before I reach the next cluster of my adoring groupies. The handling is average for a mobile so as far as you approach the game expecting that it’s not too much of an issue, though I still feel like I have more chance of power sliding driving at 40 KM/H in that traffic I mentioned (I feel like the game has assists enabled but no way to turn them off…).
And that I feel is as good as any point to leave this review on, what is a pretty good mobile game somewhat unsurprisingly makes an entirely dull PC game. Good day folks

I can't remember the last time a game made me cry! This has got to be one of the most heart-felt story-driven games I've ever played! I personally am not that big of a fan of the show, but holy cow did this give me a new appreciation for the franchise as a whole. This game features a man named Lee, who ends up in a car accident after getting arrested by the cops for felony. The accident was caused by walkers, zombies who have breathed new life and continue to inhabit it for the soul purpose of, what else, eating their victims alive. Throughout the story the game presents you with choices for your character to make. Some are ordinary and produce opportunities to learn about other characters, while other choices are timing and must be answered or else you choice will remain dormant. I really like this feature and it can show us how well we as people would do if we were ever thrown into a zombie apolcalypse. What's really cool is how some of these choices can create different outcomes that effect the story's plot to extent. It would of been nice if this was exploited a little futher, but this is the first game in the series so improvements are bound to be made. Over the course of these five episodes you also interact with a little girl, who evidently becomes your legal guardian. The situations they put you in whether hostile or laid back both make for a great parenting simulator if you can believe that! The pacing seems fluid as it gives you an opportunity to explore and observe the country as it falls in the hands of the walking dead. the graphics give me that Borderlands feel with the sharp outlined textures of each character model. Everything about the game from beginning to end feels like a satifying journey. Regardless if you follow the show or not, this game will win you over in a heartbeat.

My experience in basketball games ranges from the NBA Street games (you know, the best ones) to 2K15, and now 2K16. There have been stellar reviews for 2K16, praising it for the most quality basketball game thus far. Well I have to say, all in all in comparison to its previous installment, I'm not impressed.
Yes, 2K16 has an actual story to its game (a Spike Lee Joint apparently), but the story is streamlined in various ways. This is not necessarily a good thing. Regardless of your nationality or ethnicity you get the same family, the same hometown, and the same story. It feels lazy and borderline offensive even. Kind of feels as though 2K Games thinks only black people are playing basketball, which is just kind of stupid. Not to mention that the story takes too much out of your hands. Want to pursue your education first and hone your skill with your college basketball team? Too bad! Spike Lee says you're off to the NBA! Unprepared I might add, because you simply aren't of the appropriate skill to handle these kinds of games yet. Almost like you should have stayed and honed that skill first. Oh well, too bad that option wasn't available eh? Kind of makes the time you took deciding on which college to go to pointless.
Aside from some random cut scenes with the cringeworthy cast of characters (Jesus your in-game girlfriend [another decision you weren't allowed to make by the way] is downright nightmarish), the game basically falls back into the same game NBA2K15 was, with minor tweaks.
That's the best way to explain the game as a whole, minor tweaks. Nothing special, but I suppose if you missed out on 2K15, then this game will be a newer experience to you. It's not a bad game, just not good enough to warrant calling it a brand new game.

I've been using DisplayFusion for a few years now, and it's exceed my expectations in nearly every way. Anyone with 2 or more monitors should have it.
What I was looking for was a simple way to manage multiple monitor profiles because the Windows display management is severely lacking. It was a pain to connect to my HDTV, enable the display, change the audio device, and then disable my other secondary display. You're talking at least 5 separate steps to get it working correctly.
DisplayFusion made it so incredibly easy to bind a hotkey for this function. When I want to play Big Picture, I hit the hotkeys and it enables the display, makes it the primary, disables the other, and makes my desired playback device the default. On top of that, it was super simple to set up. In about 5 minutes I had it working like a dream.
Doing a little MORE digging, I found a user-made function that can do all of the above with one simple keystroke AND launch Steam in Big Picture directly. Better yet, there's a remote App for iPhone that allows me to call this function while sitting on my couch. Even better, I can use the app to switch Audio Devices on the fly when I need to hook up my headphones to avoid annoying my neighbors.
These functions alone have made this software absolutely worth the price. I'd pay double the asking price to have them.  The window management and advanced snapping functions are the cherry on top of the cake.
It's an exceptional software, well-supported and does exactly what I wanted and more. I could not possibly be happier.

OKAY, so it came to my attention that so many people are putting not recommended because of paid mods. But I'm just gunna ignore that fact because WE ALL KNOW CREATION CLUB SUCKS. And you can get free mods from Nexus.
Fallout 4 is an exellent game. I'm nearing 500 hours on it. Yes, it has it's bugs, as every Bethesda game has, but for what it is it's an exellent game. I really enjoy the voiced characters and the life that most characters have. The story is engaging and it still allows you to make impactful choices.
Each companion is unique and have their own personalities, I love the affinity system and how it plays with the romance option. Not to mention the returning characters.
There is much customization with your character and the armor system gives you an ability to make a unique looking character each play through.
Unless you decided to mini nuke them, the bosses are satisfactory in challenge and there's just a lot of neat behind the scenes things.
I'm in love with the settlement building. And with various mods you can really go to town.
Honestly, playing through it with the language filter and the unofficial patch first round, then tweaking the game with mods to how you see fit is the best way to go about it. (unless you don't mind profanity, then just get the unofficial patch)
I love the way you can mod weapons, armor, and power armor as well. Also, the whole power armor system was well designed.
Of course, there are the flaws, especially because Bethesda is known for buggy games.
Sometimes I'd have to force a cut scene to trigger in second and third play throughs, and I miss the karma system. I also miss the old way of leveling up, but the leveling system isn't bad.
While the dialogue can be overly simple in selection, they still have that witty dialogue that gives you chuckle occassionally.
All the Fallout games I've played thus far have been excellent thus far. There is no reason to push people away from a game because a stupid decission on the developers part. Just don't buy stuff from the Creation Club. walla!
Fallout 4 is defintely worth a go.

Bugs, dodgy UI decisions, and some supposedly core mechanics that defy the games core philosophy.
That philosophy is a good one, reward the players ability to assess and manage risk on multiple levels, with many hidden/not obvious variables at work that are there to significantly reward you for doing something "right", and more lightly punish the "wrongs", missions are risky stuff, but if you open your eyes, ears & mind a little, are always within your control more so than ADVENTs.
Hacking & Stealth mechanics were not given this treatment for whatever reason, their success or failure is largely out of the players hands unless they plan to alt-f4 or reload a save.  Which will get boring real quick and put you off these mechanics, because those load screens are looooooong.  Hacking especially is far more advantageous to the enemy AI than it is to the player, especially if you attempt the t2 hacks, the enemies rewards for your failure massively outscale your own rewards for success, and it costs the player a valuable specialists action points for the turn too.  Xcom would not actively train specialists other than for combat roles if they were being practical under these conditions.  They might turn that GREMLIN budget over towards teaching their veteran soldiers how to just check their damn corners & ledges for once in their short lives.
Gripes aside, Chess 2 is a great successor to Chess 1 and I would pick it up the moment it next goes on sale.  The problems i mentioned can be fixed (other than the terminal case of loading-screen) with some ini edits and/or community mods very easily, and should be.  Grab yourself a copy of notepad++ while you wait for the download, you'll want it for later.  Personally recommended only because tweaks are easy, fix the balance issues that I percieve, and allow a really impressive degree of customisation.
tl;dr good game but don't bother hacking something unless its close to 100% chance or has no failure penalty and stick to the center of the roads for stealth because reasons.

Is it worth my time? I myself dont usually indulge in games that I wont get to play for at least 100 hours, but long story short it is a very fun and interesting little gem.
What is the gameplay like? Its a top down space pirates game where you can play it like splinter cell, or hotline miami. It basically lets you play it either as a stealth game, choosing lethal/non-lethal/ghosting, allowing you to choose silenced (or not) guns, melee weapons, bombs, and many futuristic gadgets. But if thats not really your stuff dont worry, you can also play it as a Hotline Miami except its in space. Beware though, this game has permadeath. In actuality that was quite a good design choice, but if thats too much of a deal breaker for you no worries, the game allows you to disable that through the menu if it really bothers you, although it advises you not to as it would make the game much less dynamic and varied.
Is it replayable? Unfortunately, not really. In 20ish hours you can finish it, and after that I didnt see much else that would keep me playing it. The devs could certainly extend the interest of maybe a second playthrough (clocking in from 5 - 15 more hours then) by allowing players who beat the campaign to use cheats, like making your own character (making a glorious self insert or crossover between games now possible), letting the player pick any item in game to use, be able to edit the attributes of any item, etc...
Level design? This game is about infiltrating ships and screwing around with them. Then after doing that, clicking on certain outposts to liberate them, providing you with more and better gear for your next infiltrations. Its a roguelike of sorts, if you are seeking a game about space exploration or something this game isn't that at all.
Lore? There is some lore indeed. You must speak to certain characters you can find in the outposts to put the lore together if you are interested. The world the game has built (and its story) is quite compelling, even if the game itself isnt that big or complex.
I think those are about the basics that someone with some money to spend and not much patience to give would need to understand if this game could be appealing. For those that played the game, or just want to read a really throughout guide, thanks for sticking so far. Now lets begin.
The game presented itself beautifully. There was no hand holding, from the start you were out by yourself free to explore and discover. And by that I mean discover the game's mechanics and how stuff works. I didnt feel lost, and I felt a great urge to just go around and test out things myself. You might be surprised to find out you could do certain stuff you didnt knew you could even after finishing the game once. Read a guide if you buy the game, it could potentially show you some things you might have not thought of doing yourself while playing it.
The soundtrack was? It fitted the game, but I guess except for one song I wouldnt really go out of my way to listen to it. It does the job but isnt exactly spectacular.
This game has exemplar design for what stealth games could be. By having permadeath and no saving the game forces you to not simply bash your head continuously in the wall and hitting quickload until it works (the way it happens with many stealth games), this is amazing because the experience becomes a lot more dynamic, a lot of times you would find yourself considering to kill when you decided to be a pacifist, or throw yourself out the window into the vacuum of space and failing the mission, to avoid something worse from happening since there is no magical rewind button, just like you would if you were in that actual situation. Yet at the same time the game balances that out, you go in missions knowing fully what will await you inside the ship, you can stop time to decide what to do next or align a perfect shot or use the right gadget when you find yourself in a difficult situation unexpectedly, time also slows a bit when you are about to do an action such as hitting someone or when someone has seen you while you were sneaking around. But even so its not necessary to use this mechanics in order to play it, it allows for many different playstyles that each have their own benefits and shortcomings.
My only criticism of this game is that I wish there was more to do after finishing it. Really, it was an amazing experience, something genius that I have no idea how someone came up with. It does last about as long as it needs for what it tried to do, but I wish so hard that the game was larger and had more content, Id pay for a ♥♥♥♥ing DLC playing as Fiasco making a name for herself,
, seriously I wish so hard this game was longer.
But in the end I just really want to thank the devs for making this amazing little game. Hopefully they profit well from it. Just give a free copy to some big letsplayers on youtube and you will see the money flowing in no time. Now I finish one of my rare reviews, with a lot of love.

Don't let the cute visuals fool you, this game is great, tricky but rewarding controls and combos give the combat a lot of depth, and the enemy AI is intelligent and aggressive enough to make you have you actually play well to push through.
The games strongest feature is it's combat and it never ceases to escalate the fights as you play. Every monster has a decent set of moves and will use them to the best of their ability to shut you down, you won't be button mashing through these enemies. One of my favourite features is that while most enemies have one or two palette swap variants, these variants usually have very different movepools, often changing how you approach fighting them and always keeping you on your toes.
Be prepared for some nail biting difficulty and some very very clutch moments against bosses and even certain trash mob encounters. The pain is worth it however because coming out on top feels great. (and even if you fail, the game is very lenient allowing unlimited retries)
Get ready for a lengthy, charming campaign, with a lot of exploration and quests to do, sadly the game is mostly linear and you'll discover most secrets and optional content on your first playthrough, but I myself clocked around 30 hours on the first run, so you get your moneys worth.
Some small weaknesses though, a lack of fast travel between save points means that giving up on a dungeon run forces you to redo the whole dungeon again, which becomes an issue lategame as the dungeons get HUGE. Additionally, there are only about 5 tilesets for dungeons, so a lot of them end up feeling samey, and even in the same dungeon you'll often do loops and get completely lost due to a lack of decent landmarks.
This is a really underrated title. I'd liken it to titles like Hyper Light Drifter, Cave Story and Axiom Verge, but replace serious dark storytelling with a lighthearted, cute story.

I've played this game through about a dozen characters, each of which has built his own legacy of murder and success in their attempts at liberating their galaxy.
I've played a hitman with a heart of gold, knocking out enemies time and time again and only leaving dead the right people at the right time.
I've played a teleporting pickpocket desperately shunting himself accross time and space until the only thing of value a spaceship has left is the very people on it.
I've played a murderous lunatic, gunning down enemy after enemy, loudly blasting away to the cadence of alarm yells and activated shields.
I've played a sociopathic hacker, turning turrets against their masters and making people shoot themselves with hacked shields.
This game BEGINS as a relatively simple puzzle challenge where you almost always have a solution, even if the solution tends to be near-suicidal or self destructive; where stubbornness can take you a long way, but knowing when to fold your hand will save your life.
The game CONCLUDES with players one of two ways: They put it away for being repetitive, or become performance artists of mayhem and murder, their minds filled with the rhythmic wub-wub of the trance music as they teleport, hijack, club, trap, stab, and shotgun their way through spaceships, taking their bounties, or, for the particularly ambitious, taking the whole ship with them as though it were nothing.
Buy it. It's a hell of a lot better than most of the open world garbage out nowadays.

Shadwen is at most ok.
You are given enough tools to fool around, but the thing Shadwen does worst is what it was supposed to be: a stealth game.
This is mostly due to the rewind mechanic. There's no tension when you can stomp around like a pig and the moment they hear you, you just rewind time. The tension from stealth games is to not be detected, here you just rewind until you get away with whatever you want to. There's so much room for error, so why bother being careful (i.e. stealthy)?
There's a storyline incentive to be sneaky, which is the only reward for you to get creative, but if you don't care that much you may just stick a knife into everyone's neck. It's way easier to pounce and kill.
By giving players all the tools to breeze through the game, Shadwen does itself a disservice and I don't think any player will care enough to play it without those tools. A waste of time for everyone involved.

This seemed like a great game from the screenshots and videos, but I'm left disappointed with it.
While I haven't played MOBAs much to know if this is standard fair for this genre of game, this game, at least in it's current form seems far to simplistic.
Aside from the training/practice map and possibly the 1v1 PvP (which I haven't tried), there seems to be only one map to play on and only one match type, conquest. Meaning the variety comes soley from flying different ships.
Granted I only played free, I'm not sure that paying for DLC unlocks anything game mode wise, map wise etc, all indications seemed to be just other ship variants/types/skins.
While I can overlook these shortcoming and enjoy it for what it is, the ships themselves (free ones at least) just aren't really interesting to pilot. There's a quick and light primary attack, a heavy attack, a ranged missile/fighters attack and then a couple of per ship specialty abilities.
Annoyingly, there appears to be no point in levelling or upgrading ships. It all seems to revolve around tweaking weapons and abilities slightly, not really improving them at all, just changing them to have a DoT or AoE effects but with reduced impact. I'd call it side-grading, not upgrading your ship, and from what I experienced it doesn't change the ships play style much.
Honestly, Star Trek Online (another free to play game), an over 7 year old MMO (that doesn't focus entirely on space combat, there's gound combat and stories to do etc etc), does star ship battles far better than this title that's dedicated to it. Ships in STO fly very similarly to Fractured Space yet they have a ton of equipment, crew, abilities and weapons that can all be customised to such an extent that with the one ship you can switch loadouts and change from being a damage dealer to a tank or space wizard or some combination in between, you can really tweak them to how you want to play.
Fractured Space on the other hand is just far to restrictive on this front and while I enjoyed playing it, this game is far to shallow to keep me interested.
It looks great with ultra everything settings and is what drew me to it initially, but unfortunately that's about it.
The free to play aspect of this game seems ok. It's not too in your face and if you like it I can see how spending a bit of cash will be worth it to unlock other ships. But with such similarities just between the free ships I just can't see a reason to drop money on this title.
It's been fun, but time to uninstall.

Right from the start I got the sensation of a tactical turn-based game like Shadowrun or Tactics series, mixed with the atmosphere of older Thief games; particularly Thief: Deadly Shadows. While I haven't completed it yet, here are some pros and cons I've noticed:
Pros:
* Runs great: On my mid-to-lower end laptop, getting 60fps in anything is a blessing and there hasn't been a single hiccup.
* Innovative amalgam of features: From rewinding time a la Prince of Persia to the default timefreeze when you're not inputting anything, you have every opportunity to master each level
* Audio: I think the soundtrack, though minimal, is great and the voice acting is up to snuff as well
* Graphics/models: The models look great. No, they're not hyper-realistic but they are excellently designed and animated. You can really appreciate them up close when timefreeze is active
Cons:
* Repetition: By the 5th or 6th level, you'll find you can easily master each hurdle the guards throw at you. From what I've read though, changing your play-style (stealth vs killmode) can drastically change your experience which I intend to do after completion
* No manual save/save on exit: The checkpoints save your game so fast that its actually difficult to tell if it saved or not, which doesn't give me a ton of confidence when exiting the game
* Story: So far I actually love the dialogue as it sets a gerat tone and highlights the understated relationship between yourself and the girl you're escorting. However, very little (if any) backstory has been revealed thusfar and I really don't know WHY I'm doing what I'm doing.
Overall, this game is worth the experience for the pricepoint IMO. If you find it at a discount or bundle, all the better!

So there i was, aimlessly wandering the wastes of the Steam store, seeing if i find something that stands out. Something that manages to impress me. Something that isn't just a generic clone of something else.
And then i found this. Looked interesting, so i thought i'd give it a whirl. And very quickly, i found myself thinking "Good heavens, why have i never heard of this game, before?".
Truly, i had found the very definition of a hidden gem.
It has the vibe of the original Syndicate. It has the music (And the somewhat cryptic lore/plot) of Hotline Miami. And rather gracefully, it brings these elements together in a mech/tank/hovertank action game where you level entire city blocks.
A quick run-down of the setting: The game takes place in the city of Solo Nombre, on the planet Novo Solo, an off-world colony far from earth.
A while ago, this colony was taken over by a dictator simply known as "Great leader", who turned the colony into a North-Korea style, hyper-isolationist city-state.
Tonight, he has died.
Pretty much immediately, you have a rebel uprising happening, loyalists trying to cling to the old ways, a highly advanced outside faction called the "spacers" using the opportunity to essentially invade, and your employer, a shady corporation, hiring mercs to "represent their interests" as well. And it's all happening in one night. A battle royale to be sure!
Oh, don't worry though, despite the game being set all in the same night, the devs were kind enough not to give us time limits. (Thank you devs!)
As for the gameplay, it's quite a good mix. On easier difficulty settings, with stronger vehicles, you will pretty much steamroll everything, but get fairly small rewards. The higher the difficulty gets and the more challenging the vehicle you pick, the more you will have to play it smart and carefully, but the richer you will become. It's quite charming that way.
Anyways, i'm truly hoping that this game gets a bit of a late updraft in popularity. Maybe it's just me, but i had never even heard of it before i randomly stumbled upon it in the store, the other day. And for a game this fun, that's just not right.
So yeah, a clear thumbs up. I heartily recommend you give this game a whirl, and i hope it's been successful enough for the devs to make future titles!

Brigador is an excellent isometric shooter about ~ D E S T R U C T I O N ~
You can drive a tank, hovercraft, a big ol' mech or a tiny sneaky one, but at the end of the day, the goal (and gameplay) is to shoot your enemies, rolling and stomping through the buildings (and ruins!) of the bases and towns you'll encounter in missions.
=> Vehicle urban warfare, gone dystopian sci-fi. <==
There's several original elements regarding Brigador:
1) The music: well-fitting neon 80s tunes!
2) The isometric view: allows you to properly see the combat unfolding.
3) The collateral destruction: every cannon shot that misses or pierce through will strike the buildings, vehicles and barriers around. When everyone is shooting high-caliber machineguns, mortars are flying, the scene is definitely gonna be apocalyptic once the firefight is over.
4) The lore. It's not the first thing you'll notice, and it will take a while to get into it, but it's crafted with such care it's well worth it.
If Brigador was food, it would be that odd looking meal you think is bland, but with every bite it gets better, it's actually pretty damn good, and a real killer by the time you finish the first plate.

GMod Tower was an addon way back when in Garry's Mod, starting in 2009. I joined about a year later when I got Garry's Mod on my first account, and I loved it. It featured a great community, one of the best I have seen in games, it was like a convention in a way, everyone was friendly to everyone, because we all shared a common interest. The tower was host to all sorts of fun events, not even including what the community did on their own. When the first tower was shutting down, my friend and I started a cult to meet at the fountain as the server repeatedly crashed, all wearing the same mask and hat, until the world was ripped apart under our feet.All these events don't even include all the minigames that were there. In the addon there were portals to other servers where you could join others to fight zombies, race in go-karts, kill eachother, race in balls, survive a virus outbreak, or join the pigmask army to shut down a chimera. The addon was amazing, going through 2 iterations of towers crammed full of game references, and all the fun you could fit in 2 skyscrapers.
Now the servers are gone. The addon in Garry's Mod is gone and dead. This game strives to be what that addon was. I have my skepticism, but without support, this game will never be anything close to what it has to be. But at the same time, I think the developers know what they're doing, and will give it whatever they can to make this game what it has to be. The addon died for this. Let's hope it's good.

It may have been mainly due to the associated audiobook's relentlessly grim and gravelly narration and story focus, but this is the first game I've come across that left me moraly conflicted enough to question whether I should be playing it. It wasn't the actions of the game (shootling, stomping toops and civilians alike) but the wider economic conflict between the exoplanet collony and the nebuleous corporation which frames your actions as a 'brigador'. I imagine its what it might be like being a soldier in North Korea, or other isolationist dictatorship, with no knowledge or ability to completely trust in either narriative about the conflict.
Mechanically the gameplay is initailly awkward but fun once you adjust for the movement controls (or change setting in the options menu), and the aesthetic is right up my alley (doubly so the music) but the core gameplay feedback feels like its fighting itself. This is especially apparent when you switch to heavier mechs with louder weapons, the one vs all setup is particuarly punnishing when you summon 1/3 the map to your position and have low mobility which means your supertank is actually a death trap, forcing you to sneak through each level. This design feature is perhaps understandable,  and unavoidable, but I still wish there was some obvious solution or alternative mech to make campaign runs easier.

I was very hesitant to buy this game, having read the negative reviews, worrying that I would find this too punishing to enjoy. Here's the thing, this game will punish you when you make a mistake, and it will punish you when you do everything perfectly, and you're going to love every minute of it.
If you enjoy Roguelikes, buy it, plain and simple. The setting is inspired by the Cthulu mythos, set as a roguelike turn-based RPG. Each time you go into a dungeon and come back, it fills one day of in game time. Every new day, you're able to recruit from a fresh new band of starry-eyed adventurers, which is perfect, becasue everyone you know and love is going to die. You pick a group of 4 adventurers, across an assortment of different classes, and set off into clearing the monsters that are infesting your ancestral homeland, in the hopes that you can blaze a trail to take on the titular "Darkest Dungeon."
The majority of the gameplay will be your four man party walking along a 2d path, and combat. A dungeon starts out with a mini map, that is set in a grid. The grid has several points you can travel to, if a path branches, you have to choose which way to go down. Once you make your decision, you begin to move your party down a 2d path. Along this path, you'll come across traps, monster attacks, and curios. Curios are objects you can interact with, if you choose to interact without using an item...you're usually in for a bad time. But the use of wares that you buy before starting the adventure, things like shovels, bandages, anti-venom, using the correct one will usually nullify any negative effects...or not. The combat is turn based, and turns are taken based off a  characters speed. Once all of your party members and monsters have taken an action, it's time for the next round.
This game does a masterful job of knocking you on your♥♥♥♥♥when you get overconfident. There will be times, after trials and tribulations, you've finally honed a group of griseled, veteran explorers. You've found it, THE PARTY COMP that no one else knows about, and you're the genius, you're able to mow through mobs. Then it happens, you come across a curio you've never seen before, you interact with it, it gives a warning, you ignore it and proceed, and then one of the hardest boss battles is thrust upon you. When your characters die, they are dead, for good, so at this point, you have to make a decision, how much do I have to lose, before I cut my losses and run? You weren't expecting an intense boss fight, you weren't ready for it, your torches are extinquished, your party members are starting to lose their sanity, your most veteran healer just died. What do you do? Do you still try and slay this monster or cut your losses? These are the decisions you'll be forced to make, that will knock you off your♥♥♥♥♥ This isn't unique either, you can run into another boss fight, as just a random enemy encounter, without having to interact with some odd looking curio. Or even if you let your torch get too low and get unlucky, and the monsters ambush you and get a tree extra turn, or even just an unlucky crit, and that knight you've spent a dozen hours leveling, is now dead on the floor. You will lose you're most beloved adventurers, you will mourn their deaths, but you will train others in their place, and press ever onward, a game of absolute attrition at times.
One unique aspect, one that was a main selling point, was that hit points are not the only thing you have to worry about. Characters have a stress meter, certian attacks, or events will directly effect a characters sanity. Once they hit a threshold, they'll have to make a good ol' fashioned saving through, as their mettle is being tested, to see if they break under their mental pressure, or come out of the ordeal a true hero. Most will falter, and break, your characters will lose their sanity, and begin to take actions on their own, or refuse certian commands from you. This game does an amazing job of really hitting home that these dangerous adventures into caves and ruins filled with monsters, takes a trmendous toll on a persons sanity. You'll have to rest your characters, either at a church or a tavern to lessen their stress. On of the best little flairs that is an example of this, the darkest dungeon exists of 4 seperate journies. Members who survive one journy into the darkest dungeon, will absolutely refuse to go back again on the subsequent events, that what they witnessed is so horrible, they're mentally scarred for life.
Dark souls made me see the beauty in pain. Darkest Dungeon made me revel in it. Buy this game, you wont regret it.
