Every once in a while a game comes along and does something so ingenious you wonder why it hasn't been a part of every game of that genre to begin with.
For the stealth genre, that game is Shadwen.
Most stealth games encourage you to play perfect from start to finish, and failing to do so means completely breaking the stealth experience, usually blasting loud buzzers at you and berating you until you either sit in the corner like a good little player or restart the whole level to try and perfect the whole thing.
Shadwen subverts the entire problem by taking your mechanical ability out of the equation and instead makes the game completely about your macro-level decisions.  Even if you do get spotted because you didn't see a guard hiding around a corner or whatnot you can reverse time immediately and play it out perfectly.
Some reviewers might call this easy, but really if you think about it any stealth game is easy if you have infinite patience.  Shadwen's time mechanic is really just a way to streamline your experience into more than just tons and tons of waiting.
And if this sort of waiting is the kind of thing that drives you away from stealth games, then maybe stealth games aren't for you.  But maybe Shadwen is.  This may well be the last stealth game I ever play, because I can't go back to the standard wait-and-retry.

This game is a successor to the popular game mode "Gmod Tower" in the game Garry's Mod. Or should I say "was" popular as the game mode was shut down in order to begin development on this project. The core of Gmod Tower was socializing in the hub area, customizing your character and personal apartment, and participating in minigames to earn credits.
I wish I could say I have any expectation of this game reaching the same level as the game mode it was based on, but I'm not sure it will. The playerbase is kinda dead at this point, pulling in only approximately 77 average users across any number of servers (And that average has been dropping by about 20 users every month). The physics in the new engine just feel "off", it's especially noticable in games like ball race. I can say I think condo customization has gotten a bit better, albeit at the expense of player customizability. In it's current state I'd say there's just nothing to bring you back to it aside from the stray update or two, which even then will only get you back in for a few minutes before you realize there's not much substance there and leave for another month or two.

I've been using this software for a long time outside of steam, and it has made my life a lot easier. I use 2 monitors and all the utility DisplayFusion gives is just amazing, and I recommend this software to every single human being who wants a permanent license on their steam library and uses 2+ monitors.

I dislike most Japanese media... but I freaking love this game.
TL;DR - Must have for lovers of action RPG's. The game is not impossibly hard, people just think it is. If you spam buttons in this game you will be pulverized. Planning your attacks is very satisfying and required.
It has entertained me for far more hours than shown only because I was offline. The gameplay is what makes it all worth it. Many people rating will be commenting that the game is too difficult even on easy and while there is some truth to that this game is designed that way. I cannot stress enough that this game is far from impossible. If someone is claiming the game is extremely hard even though they are good at the game... sorry... they aren't. The game is extremely punishing but rewards you if you are skilled / prepared. The controls are extremely responsive outside of the sliding that happens while you are moving fast or falling but your speed is something you can control. With that out of the way, my pros and cons.
Pros:
-Difficult. Enemies have telepathy (I can't describe it any better.) You will have to outsmart the last boss and you'll have to outsmart that level 1 slime too... every time. I'm going to slaughter the easy stuff but I still need to execute the mechanics to hit it. There are no free kills here.
-Satisfying combat. Similar to the above comment, combat is very satisfying. Enemies do not let you hit them. It will take either a block and quick return attack or a combined effort with your party to HIT something let alone kill it. Juggling is equally as fun and skillful as it is required.
-Nostalgia. It just has that older RPG vibe that reminds me of the games of my childhood. This might not apply to some of you but it was a very important part of the game to me.
Cons:
-It ends abruptly. This angers me and the company behind it is done. Carpe Fulgar is just a localization team... they don't actually make the game. Sadly there will be no follow up.
- Enemy infintes. There are some psudeo infinite combos the enemies can get you caught in. They are rare but when you die without being able to put up a fight it is frustrating.
- Can't remap all the controls. It's annoying but I got over it. You could of course use a program to swap keys if you wanted but that's a lot of work. Not acceptable in the modern PC world but this game was from a Japanese Doujin company. They understand little in the ways of proper PC gaming.
Those are my main points, I play this game for the gameplay. As for the story and art I'm not an expert and it isn't my prefered style by any manner but you know what? It grew on me. I like every bit of this game. It has excellent sound design as well. If cute, little, ludicrously overpowered girls is your thing then you need look no further.
Or if you just like good combo action RPG's you need look no further either. 9/10

The story seemed mostly anime ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. The delivery was also strange, since it relied to a lot of voice-acted exposition (in japanese)
combat! Especially at the start, I was being overwhelmed by the non-standard shooting of the game and all the chaos on the screen to understand what the heck was going on with the story.
Not my thing.
The music I found pretty generic, which is unfortunate. (I've been playing Einhander which has a really awesome soundtrack). One of the reasons I'm not really playing more of this, for now. I've finished the game on all difficulties, and I'm not much of a score attacker, so...
The visuals are a mixed bag. As in, has some pretty "heh, okay" stuff, and then has some really awesome stuff. The visuals effects are really great at spots and actually made me try to recreate some of them myself. Not many games make me do that! (let me say the lens flare is reaaaally bad, though).
The distortions and flow effects are particularly cool!
The environments (aside from the beautiful ending zone) were a bit uninspired, for me.
So yeah, I really enjoyed the effects (models are also cool!), but the visuals weren't very striking otherwise.
The gameplay seems very unique. You have basic forward shooting, and then have to lock-on enemies and missiles to fire your homing energy things. You also have melee attacks (very important) and a chargeable special attack.
Enemies have 4 bullet types: weak bullets you can destroy with your forward shooting; yellow bullets you can destroy with melee; missiles you can destroy with your homing energy; red bullets you have to dodge.
This is a bit too much at the start, but it gets very fun once you get the hang of it!
It gets even better when you start to pay attention to the score. The game doesn't seem prone to min-maxing, destroying every enemy, timing every moment, etc. A looot goes on throughout. But you build a multiplier (resets when hit) that is maxed at 16 pretty quickly. When you melee kill an enemy, the multiplier drops, but the death gives you more points. So it's then a balancing act of building up your meter and trying to kill as many enemies with a single melee attack to maximize the score.
Again, overwhelming at the start. But, trying to go for the harder Easy mode achievements and replaying the campaign you'll get the hang of it!
This seems to be how the game is meant to be played. It's more of an arcade experience. Which explain the very short campaign (can take ~30minutes once you've beaten it a few times). The first time it may have taken me 1-1.5 hours because of deaths and difficult controls. I expected to have only finished the "opening act" when I saw the credits...
I did get my enjoyment out of it, in many ways! Unfortunate that there are so few people who have replayd the game - there are 2 mechs you can played with; On hard mode, one mech has 130 leaderboard results, the other only 30! And you don't need to finish the game to get there... I feel like people are just finishing the short campaign and putting it aside. That barely lets you "get" the combat system, in my opinion! So yeah, anyway, rant's over.

The game features some nice updates since the first part: hacking, soldier customization, even the increase in difficulty and the change in settings where you are always being pursued by the aliens (which I personally do not like, but am willing to accept). Visuals look great too. If I were to base my review just on gameplay, the review would be positive.
However, the game is still very buggy, even though it's been a long time since the original release. This is the reason why my review is going ot be negative. It has problems setting resolution (requiring me to reset the game resolution every time I launch it), the support for gamepads is buggy (I don't use a gamepad, but I have a few joysticks connected and the game assumes I'm using them, even though I have Mouse as the control scheme - the buggy controller support results in inability to name saves, because edit boxes behave as if the left arrow were pressed all the time), the game crashes once in a while - and those are just the biggest problems. These problems seem to have been known for a long time, so it doesn't look like they are going to be fixed ever.
Then there are a few intentional interface design decisions that make things difficult. Texts are rendered on floating screens with a pulsating random effects - making it painful (literally) for someone like me, whose eyes are not perfect. Fortunately, this can be turned off by directly editing the config files. The transitions between different parts of the ship interface may look great, but seeing the same transitional 5-second animation for the 50th time during an evening isn't fun. And again, there's more.
So overall, the gameplay is great, but the technical problems make the game so much worse than it could be. Thumb up for just the game contents, but thumbs down for the technical problems, resulting in an overall thumbs down.

Got it for $30 on steam sale expecting 2k16 to have their bugs figured out.
First, the audio stutters often. It happens more often half way through the AI's offensive set, like it's thinking of the next play while sacrificing processing a smooth audio. Music, crowd, PA stutters while shots & player voices have a second delay (imagine hitting a jumpshot, then a second later "....swoosh"). There is a fix where you go into the Roaming Folder, go through 2k sports up to 2k16 video settings folder & editing the audio settings (turn off optimization) - but this only minimizes the stuttering.
Gameplay: same old clunky animations getting in the way of controlling how accurate your player's position is. There are still running animations that dramatically moves your player way out of position or hardly moving at all. Clipping is still a concern, usually hands floating through the rim causing goaltending or arm & ball through defender's body. 2K14 called kickball several times a game, but 2k16 goes a few games before calling it on the shoe only. The rules state any area of the leg is a violation, though there are exceptions for accidental (foot on ground and ball hits it) kickball that are difficult to program. But the ball goes off defenders knees & thighs often enough. Spacing means almost too much: every open shot is ez even if you're off - but the defender is barely in your area and your easy layup bounces out.
MyPark: I was doing ok at the park when there were actually people online (15+). But usually there's only 4-8 people mostly playing half-court. But then I was plagued with another bug. 2k16 never had a problem my first few trips to MyPark, although I couldn't change the camera angle. But the last few times, I spawn on the court, walk around and find and "Got next," take 2-3 minutes for the new game to load, and all of a sudden my controller goes dead & I can only use my keyboard/mouse. There's no menu options, so all I can do is force-close 2k16. When I return to MyPark, I have to wait for the AI version of my custom player finish the match. Before this happened, I've seen other players remain in one place for the first few possesions before playing - were they the actual players or did they have the same controller issue and switch to AI?
Pretty disappointed even for $30. I even spent some money on attributes before the MyPark issues got worse.

Having played all previous games I had high expectations for Unity but due to all the launch negativity I decided to leave the game until now hoping that all the issues would be fixed. One concern was the performance issues but it ran fine on my mid-high end system. However during the course of the play through it has become evident that they just abandoned the game, constant issues with buggy quests and AI made it a frustrating experience.
Its hardly recognizable as an assassins creed game and hard to believe it was developed by the same teams that handled previous games.
There is only one real environment and whilst its beautifully done it does start to feel very samey after a while and it left me wishing for the variety of previous games.
The one main feeling i'm left with after playing this game is why there is so much missing that has grown to be part of AC games :-
* No Horses/Carriages
* No area control !
* No Crafting
* No Treasure Maps
* No minigames
* No Unlockable Inns
* No Brawling
* No Sailing ?! (I know its kinda outside the scope of the story but seriously France has a rich naval history and this would have been ideal excuse to add this).
* No upgradeable base as with previous games (the cafe/creed lair is a poor imitation).
* No allies system like Brotherhood.
Somehow they also seemed to make combat more clunky, weapon and item selection was done better in previous games and the camera seemed awkward too -- someone tell them sequels are supposed to improve things!
Another area that suffered badly was the enemy AI -- it really is a joke in unity, far worse than previous games. Simply jumping onto a roof is enough to leave an enemy dumbfounded as to where you are !
Whilst some might be happy with the addition of Co-op its not something i'm interested in and i felt annoyed at the constant pushing of the Co-Op modes even to the extent that you cant unlock stuff without doing the co-ops missions.
Whilst there was a fair amount of side-content it felt very MMO-ish in nature with a vast majority being variations on defend NPC/steal something/kill someone
Yet another premium game with microtransactions -- sad times :(
Feels like they cut corners in trying to rush this one out the door and also pushing the co-op in a bid to capture a different market.
By FAR the worse the in the entire AC series -- Bought discounted for only £20 and still feel robbed.

tl,dr: The story is well made.  Keep your AI on the fighter as much as possible.  And probably keep the difficulty on easy.  The enemy AI in this game punishes you for almost any kind of movement.
ADDED:
I would like to add this to my original review.  The gameplay is well made.  The problem is that the AI will punish you for any normal action.  Jump over an enemy?  They react almost instantly and will wail on you for it.  You can't get a single string of attacks in even on easy mode.  They can, and likely will, beat the living daylights out of you.  Bring healing items at all times.
Original:
Fortune Summoners is, from what I played, a good story.  It isn't a good platform RPG for those wondering about the gameplay.
Reason: It's the difficulty and the controls.
First off, the difficulty.  The enemies can deal a significant amount of damage in such a short amount of time.  Not only that but they can knock you down or render you unable to even fight.  All this in normal difficulty.
If it were only the difficulty this game would be fun.  It's not.  The controls for the fighter are so contrived and stiff it makes even the most simplest of fights like a battle for your life.  I generally run past them when I am given the opportunity.
Am I being too hard on this game?  No.  The game is making it hard on itself.  The first boss you will encounter will decimate you if you play the fighter.  Try fighting with those controls with actions that are hard to fire off.
Although, credit due where it is given.  Their AI for both the enemy and your allies are well done.  Especially for the fighter.
Returning to the first boss fight and letting the AI take control of the fighter while controlling the mage/healer.  The fight is much, much more easier.
Still, I intend on playing this to the end.  But I am going to keep the difficulty on easy and I'm going to have the AI control the fighter for any available moment.

"Fortune Summoners: Secret of the Elemental Stone" is a sidescrolling action RPG developed by a japanese indie developer Lizsoft and localised by Carpe Fulgur. In this game, you follow the story of a young girl named Arche, who will learn new things, make new friends, and go on a grand adventure in order to reveal the secret behind a certain artifact, along with her hidden powers.
When I saw this game in the Steam Store, it looked interesting and unique, so I bought it. After playing it, I must say that I really loved it. This is in my opinion a one of a kind game, which is a combat-based platformer wih an anime art-style, classical music and action jRPG elements.
The audiovisual presentation is really good. The music is really good, and is a joy to listen to. It is mostly made of classical-style compositions, which are definitely vivid and not generic. The visuals, bearing a 16-bit aesthetic, are gorgous as well. They are colourful are well detailed, characters are pretty well animated. The actual anime artwork of characters in the game is actually really pretty as well. The enviroments are varied, every area looks interesting and unique. You will travel through mountain paths, dungeons, watery caves, medieval cities and more.
The combat system is quite nice. The game is quite challenging, as the foes and level design do not hold back. Enemy AI will make them block, jump, evade and use attacks depending on the situation, just pressing the attack button repetitively without any other action(like with ettins in Hexen 1) will not get you anywhere. A lot of enemies require different tactics to beat them, so use you brain effectively there. There are even a few bosses indluded, be prepared.  Over the course of the game, you will have two playable sidekicks added to your party(and a third one, that is passive). You can play as one of the three people in the party, without spoiling anything, one is a powerful short-range attacker, second is a mostly healing mage, and the last one is a mostly offensive mage.  Don't worry, they definitely are not plagued by the likes of retail version Daikatana sidekick AI, they will not get blocked by geometry and will follow you without having to babysit them. Just like the enemies, they will do things depending on the situation. If someone in the party is hurt, someone will heal you with a spell, if there's a lot of enemies, they will use powerful attacks, if there's a tough enemy, they will use buff spells, and so on. During the game, you can adjust what the AI is supposed to be doing with just a press of a few hotkeys. You can set their behavior to follow you, stop dead in their tracks or just fight whoever they want without needing to follow you. What kind of magic spells they are allowed to use can be managed too, you can set to not use magic, only heal, use powerful attacks, use buff spells, and burn their magic power as fast as possible. You can also set the camera to be static, dynamic or locked onto an enemy. Arche, the sword using character, relies on not so easy to pull off button combinations to perform attacks, later in the game she learns more combos, making fights easier. Mages generally rely on holding the button and letting go of it to cast a spell, so playing as one of them an letting Arche go berserk could be easier for some people. There is also a quickheal button, status effects are cured before wounds, mind that. Don't forget that during battle, applying items takes longer time.
The game is a metroidvania, therefore it's not a linear platformer where you just hunt the exit. You will go around towns and dungeons, and look and ask people around to ask for clues in order to progress through the plot. The game often involves puzzles, where you push things to solve them. In some cases, the game might get too cryptic, but that's not that much of an issue. You can only save in certain spots, however if you all your characters get K.O.'d you are given the option to restart at the beginning of the last room you were in, or be taken to the last safe area you've been in at the cost of 10% of your money. When a character gets K.O.'d, she can not be used at all. The only way to revive her is to use a special item or return to a safe area, or perhaps find a regenerating spot.
The story, due to involving cute little girls, is somewhat light-hearted, but it is actually interesting and gripping. During the course of the game, some serious business will be going on, especially at the end. The game is quite humorous, some adult jokes are even thrown in, so the story absolutely is not bad. The characters have their distinct personalities, the main protagonists consist of an energetic, brave and spontanous girl, a shy, but kind-hearted girl, and a cynical, easily annoyed, somewhat selfish, yet intelligent and helpful girl, and a cheerful cute animal, who speaks.
You will level up and gain new items as you progress, some of them have unique effects, so make sure to upgrade your characters correctly. The world contains a lot of secret areas and items, look them up, they totally can be helpful! There's also a few sidequests, so after you beat the game you will still have some things to do.
There is also a bonus mode, where you can see the characters autoplay an early portion of the game without your input. Unique, but not very exciting, to be honest. There is also a versus mode, where you can fight against characters from your party(except that you can totally have four of the same character on the battlefield). It is either AI vs. AI, or player vs. AI. Can be 1v1, 2v1 or 2v2. There further you are in the game, the more features that mode has. It is kind of cool. You can have fun with it.
Game does not support Steam Overlay, and can run in a window, fullscreen(with bad resolution for some), and fullscreen with border, making the whole game take place on a square in the middle. However, you can still use F11 to make screenshots, so for that matter you will be fine, check guides on how to inject them into Steam.
In conclusion, this a very great game, that sadly is not very well known. If you like challenging games, anime artstyles and not too serious stories, go for it and buy it, you will be in a treat!

I really like XCOM Enemy Unknown with Enemy Within expansion. Long War mod for it is a real treat and makes the game even better if one can handle the higher difficulty. In my naïveté I decided to get XCOM 2 as soon as possible. They can't possibly break the solid foundations of XCOM EU, can they? Well, they kind of did.
I have to say something about the performance. Back when the game released my PC was on the minimum side of the requirements spectrum. I heard the stories about the horrible performance, but still I soldiered through the first 23 hours and blamed the sub 30 framerates on my potato PC. After a long break, an upgrade, and 130 hours of Witcher 3 on high with constant 90 fps I decided to go back and try XCOM 2 again. Unfortunately, I am not impressed. The framerate is all over the place. From time to time it even tanks to 15 fps for some reason. It's Unreal Engine for crying out loud! How much power does it actually need? There are also bugs and crashes. One particular crash made me chuckle. At least on my system the game crashes on the cinematic after the first tutorial mission. I had the same problem with XCOM EU! Are the devs making this on purpose?
After years of playing catch-up hardware-wise I can deal with bad graphics and low framerates, but the gameplay of XCOM 2 is also testing my patience. The biggest problem is the fabled LOS that is utterly broken at times. Shooting through walls is not uncommon. Just now I played a mission where most of the shots were taken through brick walls. You just never know if this amazingly looking piece of grade A cover will shield you from incoming fire.
Mission timers are also a miss. Not only do they force you to recklessly rush the objective only to activate all the surrounding enemy pods, they also are a detriment to the newly-introduced stealth mechanic because they start ticking down even when your team is still undetected. I guess that the aliens rig their stuff to explode regardless of guerilla activity.
However, the worst sin of all is the fact that the game feels just unfun and tedious to play. The strategic layer forces you to scan a location for multiple days just to get something as mundane as money, while bombarding you with reports of new locations to scan. The problems with LOS and a number of alien units that appear early on and can instantly incapacitate a soldier (Vipers, Stun Lancers, Sectoids) can easily turn a mission into a squad wipe. I do realise that I should just 'git gud', but it wouldn't hurt to have some fun while I'm 'gitting beter'.
This is the last straw. I'll try to fight the game one more time and hope it gets better. If it doesn't, it'll end up in the bottomless pit of games that I wasted money on. If it does, I'll change my review. I won't hold my breath, though.
For now - don't bother with this game.
Edit:
It did not get better. I just cannot deal with this. It is not even about the difficulty. I would rather play XCOM: Enemy Unknown ten times over with the Long War Mod than this on baby difficulty. Cheap tricks to crank the challenge, glitchy LoS, performance issues (maybe it is just me, but still) - just some reasons why I am not going back to this waste of money and space. I got burned so much only with Rome II, and supposedly the latter got better. We shall see.
Moral of the story - do NOT preorder or buy day-one, kids.

First of all, before i begin i would like to adress the point of view in wich i am reviewing Fallout 4:  as first person shooter enthusiast. As such, comments such as "it's bad because it's not rpg enough" don't make sense to me. I also want to stress the fact that Fallout 4 is the first entry in this franchise that i played. Having stated the above, time to begin my review of Fallout 4.
Fallout 4 is a surprisingly rich game. By rich i mean it has decent shooting mechanichs, an interesting universe and a formidable story. I will be looking at this game form the folowing parts: gameplay, soundtrack and story/campaign.
Gameplay:
Fallout 4 feels like one of the most generic shooters available, as the shooting mechanics in first person, and 3rd person aren't anything special. However the VATS system does bring some life into the game. Don't get me wrong, the gameplay isn't bad at all, but it's nothing special as many other games have been released with much better shooting and movement mechanics.
Soundtrack:
While Fallout 4's gameplay isn't so amazing as others, it's score is more than just good. The talented people form Bethesda made a score for this game that fits so well with the story, i was very tempted to review both as one. However since we are here i will express my feelings while playing the game. The first surprise i had was when i started the game and heard the intro soundtrack. It gives a feeling of hope and dreams in this post apocalyptic world.
Story:
Where do i begin? Maybe from the fact that 100 hours later on a single character, i have finaly finished all? the quests in the base game. 100 HOURS! Some games aren't worth the 2 hours steam gives for a refund and this one took 100 hours of my life in the first week. Without any spoilers, you are one of the "Vault dwellers" (those who survived the nuclear blasts in vaults). From that point, you make your own moral code, own decisions and own story.
In conclusion, Fallout 4 is a game with a decent gameplay, and a mesmerizing story that has a score that enhances even more the experience. If you like playing a game for it's story and aren't afraid to have a weaker than usual gameplay experience, Fallout 4 is a game that you must play. Still, try to buy it on a sale. 30 Euros is too much for this game. anything below 20 is just right.

Remember those oldschool isometric shooter games like Soviet Strike, or those oldschool mechwarrior games with tank controls, and heavy weaponry? Brigador is like that, except now you can decimate the entire map leaving nothing but piles of rubble, kill all the civilians, and destroy enemies using structures as cover, and explodable buildings, like gas stations or power plants to ambush enemies looking for the sound of an explosion. Don't like a wall? Smash it with your mech's feet, or ram it with your hoverbike's bumper. Can't get a guy hidden behind a wall? Blow up the powerstation and cause a chain reaction that blows the wall and your enemy hidden behind it. It's not easy, though, it's not just circle strafing and aiming in the center. Sometimes you have to use distraction and stealth, to out think the enemies looking to outnumber and destroy you.
A large variety of different vehicles, from battle vans, and exoskeletons, to hover jets, and giant mechs, and anything inbetween, The mainstory missions have a set selections of vehicals, with set weapons, that varys the level strategies, but with all the money you earn blowing anything up, and even for killing civilians, you can pay for different pilots, vehicals, and weapons to use in contract missions.
The visuals are perfect, retaining that oldschool sprite 2d style graphics, while adding in modern touches, like 360 degree veriable  rotation, instead of that lame 8 direction forcing you to go back and forth to hit the right angle.
Definately get the soundtrack, it's excellent.
Edit: You even get the Up-Armored Edition LP included when you get the soundtrack for free!

Brigador is all about being a mech pilot. Now, when you think about being a mech pilot you'd usually think Mechwarrior (or Steel Batallion) and naturally, a cockpit view. That's always seems like the way to go with games about giant walking battle machines, but have you ever thought about how much you are missing, with a camera fixed like that? In those 3d games, you are limited either to pilot's cockpit or to your mech's neares vicinity (in 3rd-person mode), with all interesting stuff left out as blips on the radar. Even if you're involved in some close combat, you don't really see more than a handful of enemy machines at once.
In Brigador, thanks to its isometric perspective, you can see everything around you. You also can take a peek a screen further. You see what you're doing, you see what your enemies are doing, nearly at all times - this allows you to take on lots, lots of enemy mechs at once.
Realistic? No
Fun? HELL YEAH! It really gives you feeling that a lot is going on.
Of course, you have a single digit chance of winning a battle against 20 or more machines in an open field. There are two things which can help you with that. First, your mech's special abilities: smoke grenades, EMP grenades, thermo-optical camo, audio-kinetic pulse - they differ from machine to machine (and can be swapped). Second, your environment: buildings, industrial facilities, plain old walls, lush forests - these will readilly take a hit for you. At which we come to another cool feature of Brigador - fully destructible environment. You can make a hole in almost any wall, make a nice pathway in any forest, or cork-open some apartment building with a side of your mech. The cool part about this is that destructions are very detailed, as all structures have multiple destructible sections with several damage levels, which surprisingly adds to the feeling of weight of your mech and the destructive power of its weapons. And it's always fun to dissect a factory in a half and see what's inside. But it's not a visual feature only - this allows you to try whatever tactics you want, whether it's luring your enemies out, sneaking up to them, bottlenecking them, retreating from them ASAP, gathering them up near a gas station and blowing it up, you name it.
The cool part about it is there are almost no encounters dragging on for too long. They are all short and violent, in a matter of a minute you either win, retreat or blow up.
Of course, the amount of possible tactics is limited to two main factors: your machine type and its equipment. Speaking of machines, Brigador goes above and beyond - you have bipedal mechs, hover tanks, normal tanks, armored cars, killdozers, and even a threaded motorcycle! Speaking of equipment, you have three slots: primary, secondary and special ability. Special abilities are limited to 4 types. The guns, however, are plentiful, as you have cannons, laser guns, railguns, howitzers, rocket launchers, mortars, machineguns of different caliber and effect.
So how to familiarize yourself with all this equipment and figure out best configurations? That's where we approach game modes. Brigador has two of them - campaign mode and freelance mode.
Campaign mode is where you play through the story missions, with 4 pre-defined vehicle configurations available for each. This is a good place to get familiar with all weapons and chassis, as well as the maps (and also earn some money for freelance mode). This is also where we come around the fact that Birgador has very oldschool composition - you select Campaign mode, then select a mission from a list, then select a mech. That's it. The story, if any, is in a text box to the right of the mission. Which is bad. On the other hand, if you're tired and all TL;DR, you can jump straight into action without any obstacles. Which is good.
Freelance mode is where you go all nuts with customization. You hire pilots, buy chassis, buy equipment, unlock missions and engage - pretty much everything you would like to do in a game about mechs. The only complaint here is that missions are procedurally generated and start on the easy side. If you come to freelance fresh from the end of campaign mode, and go with the first suggested pilot, you'll be wondering why all you have to do is fight human targets
. That's because the freelance mission difficulty is tied directly to the pilot's stats. So, pay attention to Start Difficulty, Max Difficulty and Increase Per Level stats of the pilots and pick the one that suits your skills.
Both modes reward you with multiple types of missions - stealth, heavy close quarters combar, hit and run missions, etc. The missions are not all about engaging the enemy, but also about managing your mech. This is especially true for the freelance mode, where you have to clear several goals on several maps in a single mech. Your hull, your shields and your ammo are limited. There are two main ways to restore ammo - from reloading stations on the map (which are guarded), and by scavenging your destroyed enemies (which needs some precision damage control). If you don't blow them up to the bits you can get their ammo and their shields for yourself. This is important to know, as you can easilly be left without any ammo in the middle of your operation. So lots of times you'll have to plan your shootouts and keep some balance during combat, all so you can disable enemy vehicles and get to them to replenish your shileds and guns. Try doing this during a combat with multiple machines for the most hardcore action.
To make your experience smoother, the game offers rebindable keys for keyboard, and rebindable buttons for your controller (which is a rare find these days)
Speaking of sound, firing your guns is very, very satisfying. Explosions and destuction sounds are also good. The music in game is your synthwave/retrowave mix - it's very upbeat, compells the gameplay well, and gets you in the mood very quick. Which is all it needs to be.
There are not to many games in the mech combat genre, and even less games which offer a level of fun, action and attention to detail Brigador offers. It makes even sadder the fact that this game could really use more sales, as at the time of review SteamSpy estimates it to be around 18k. If you ever thought that giant battle machines are cool, you should definetly give Brigador a try.

As a long time user of RPG Maker 2000, it's great to see this available properly now. I can't even begin to guess how many hours I put into it throughout the years. Countless thousands though, that's for sure.
Having recently moved over to using VX Ace as my main RPG making program, I don't know how much I'll use this any more, but there is still so much I prefer about this version. It's probably still my favourite, partly because of nostalgia, but partly because it just works without much stress.
It's a lot simpler to use, and is of course far more limited in what it can do (since the scripting isn't here), but VX Ace felt like it over-complicated some of the things that were still possible in this version, especially making custom graphics.
If you're looking for something to play about with, and don't care too much about making something that's completely unique and customizable in EVERY little way, this is an instant recommendation from me. Very easy to learn, and you can still do some amazing things once you master it (especially Switches and Variables).
But if you want to go deep and mess with scripts and higher quality things, RPG Maker VX Ace is the obvious superior choice, as it can do everything this one can, and infinitely more.
(There are of course also RPG Makers 2003 and XP, but I have very small experience with those, so I can't compare)

This is one of very few action RPGs with a compelling story and good characters. If compelling stories and good characters are what you're looking for, play it. It's good. It's really good.
It's not a stereotypical action RPG either. You start with your character waking up in his bed with all the world except the 10-foot radius around him just gone. When you walk, the world floats up and pieces itself back together in front of you. It's not only a cool visual effect. It's also part of the story's worldbuilding and a metaphor for the main character trying to piece his life back together after a catastrophic event that evidently left the world wiped out.
Gameplay-wise, the action is skillful and fast -- much more skillful and much faster than I could handle at higher difficulties (note: difficulty levels are built into the game's lore, so that's pretty cool too). It's also fun and responsive, though the isometric perspective combined with the colorful levels and masses of objects and enemies alike moving around the screen at once, it can get confusing. It's never so confusing that it becomes unplayable, though. It just starts to feel a little like a bullet-hell shooter at times, and it's not even a shooter.
The music's not getting out of here without a mention. I got the soundtrack in one of the Humble Bundles, and I've listened to it far more than any other video game soundtrack (except perhaps Metal Gear). It has an electro-western feel to it that's a bit difficult to describe. The lead acoustic guitar is tuned down to something odd that I tried out on my own guitar (note: just a simple open strum sounds cool in the tuning Bastion's music uses). There are vocals in a few of the songs, and they all come in at exactly the right time for the meaning of the song and the context in which they're played to punch you right in the feels. Sometimes, the music fits so well (mostly the instrumental stuff) that I didn't even realize it was there. It's incredibly unique for a game in the fantasy genre, and the same could be said of all the game's design, from art to writing to music and even to gameplay to an extent.
Each weapon feels different and serves a different playstyle, which is more than can be said for nearly any other game in Bastion's genre. The Cael hammer, the default weapon and the one I used throughout nearly the whole game, feels like it has weight and power packed in every swing. The sword is quick and slicey, the guns are suitably punchy, and the bow is precise enough to feel great.
If you thought Diablo was the king of the action RPG genre (any of the three), I request you try Bastion. At least in my opinion, it completely demolishes all three Diablo games in every area on which it contends (Bastion has no loot system, so there's no contest there): story, characters, art style, music, worldbuilding, combat, and probably a few I missed.
Play Bastion. You'll be doing yourself a favor.

In short:
The good:
-Amazing space battles that look gorgeous and are for the most part quite well balanced.
-Movement, sound, and visual effects are wonderfully immersive and make you feel like a capital ship captain.
-Ship-specific weapon alternatives and crew system add some breadth for tweaking your gameplay style.
-Not pay-to-win at all. Most pay options are purely cosmetic.
-AI, while inconsistent, allows for a comfortable environment to learn in.
The bad:
-In game currencies are in a state of perpetual flux- some are being phased in and phased out on a regular basis.
-AI inconsistencies lead to some bizzare team stacking issues.
-The community (specifically other players) are extremely toxic at times, even in casual matchmaking. Takes a lot of the fun out of the game. You can vote a player a poor sportsman at the end of the match, but im not sure that does anything.
-Low player numbers, while offset by bots, means matchmaking can often take quite a while.
TLDR: Would recommend for epic capital ship space battles that are wonderfully immersive. Just be prepared to deal with a small and toxic community.

If you have a slow computer now, maybe wait to buy this game. Otherwise, I would heartily recommend it

This is the first AC game I couldn't bring myself to finish. I liked most of AC1, a LOT of AC2, nearly all of Brotherhood, much less of Revelations, a small chunk of AC3, most of AC4 and loved Rogue.
Though none of the games in the series are perfect Unity definitely flies furthest from that goal with an insane amount of bloat and zero polish. I tried to play the game twice, both well after initial release. The first time after just finishing Rogue and the second time months later after I felt like I could really get myself into an AC game again. Both times I stopped with the thought "what's the point?"
To me, Assassin's Creed has always been my go to game to scratch an itch. An itch to complete. In a way, I treat AC games like a project where my goal is to reach that satisfying 100% feeling - starting from being a moderately badass assassin into a full blown super killing machine, collecting thingy-ma-bobs, looting chests, running rooftops, capturing territories and killing waves of fools in ultimate style. Unity definitely doesn't lack things to do, but absolutely destroys any fun in doing them.
Side content is more plentiful and more pointless than ever with most chests and side-missions providing scraps of money for completing them and little more than a couple of lines of NPC dialogue to go with the latter. The Murder Mystery and Nostradamus missions were more enjoyable to solve (provided you didn't look up solutions online) but again provided lackluster rewards. Often the game would tell me to upgrade my gear before attempting a mission that gave me... the same level of gear recommended to complete it. You can, of course, ignore these warnings about gear level and complete these missions anyway, but even if the gear you get is better than you current stuff it won't matter for very long, which brings me onto my biggest problem with Unity.
Balance. It's all ♥♥♥♥ing over the place (excuse my french, hoho). Unity seems to have attempted to revamp it's equipment system to work more along the lines of looting-focused games or MMORPGs every bit of equipment is given a rating out of 5 "stars" which determine it's general tier of usefulness. Armour pieces even have some more interesting stats tied to them like running noise or extra ammunition carrying which should, in theory, allow some personalisation of style. The problem is that the progression of this gear is entirely botched. A few hours into the game I'd bought a "4-star" weapon and was one shotting every guard in sight (while before I was being pleasantly challenged by large groups of enemies).
Moreover, despite this wide array of gear promoting personal playstyle it seems Unity actually provides fewer combat tools than ever to change up the way you play. Combat in AC games has never been difficult, but at least each new release gave me a few more ways to kill my enemies efficiently or stylishly. Changing from using a sword to a short dagger, then disarming a polearm dude and sweeping the guy with the big axe off his feet then smashing someone's head in with a counter attack and finally throwing a knife into back of that cowardly guard that tried to run was FUN. You could certainly make the combat boring by just holding the counter button down but the point is being "better" at the game meant being a cooler killing machine. In Unity, I hit people until their health bar hits 0 then try not to hit them again so i have to watch the same finishing animation regardless of the weapon I chose - all while rolling about like a maniac trying to get close enough to the guy who's decided to walk back and shoot me.
It's easy to see the scope that Ubisoft wanted to achieve with Unity. Hundreds of weapons, armour pieces, side-missions, coop, hiests, and a massive realistic city. But it feels like no one actually sat down and played it, because Unity doesn't feel like a fun game with endless content. It feels like a chore, wading through endless unpolished content, hoping to see light at the end of the tunnel and be done with all this crap clogging up my experience.
All I can say is that I'm glad I never played before they patched out the need for using the companion app or their "initiates program" because "social" chests in AC4 were already rubbing me the wrong way. It's weird because Ubisoft all but scrapped the modern day gameplay in Unity (I actually liked those sections, by the way) but instead of focusing on the history and story they spent all their time moving that modern day gameplay into actual annoying IRL rubbish. Something which no one ever asked for, and as I'm sure they know now, no one likes.

Overall: Would recommend. A solid stealth game with a number of unique elements.
Pros: Interesting blend of mechanics. It's a fusion of a stealth game and an escort quest, but a well done one and the mechanics work together well. You play a sneaky assassin with a grappling hook breezing through the levels to murder a king but you must escort a little girl around/through the guards. The core patterns work well, the basic jumping, sneaking, and stabbing is fun. There is also a rewind mechanic where you can undo any actions that don't go the way you want.
The achievements can push you to go a kill everyone, or spare everyone run but there isn't any other gameplay hooks pushing you towards a direction you are free to do what works for you.
Cons: Controls are a little clunky and there are gameplay bugs, but the rewind mechanic forgives the vast majority of issues since you're allowed to freely rewind time if the character misjumps.
Gameplay can get a little repetitive as there are only two enemy types and new mechanics are rarely introduced but the core gameplay is solid enough to carry it along. Crafting is also a little weak, I think I used it once over the course of the game.
Overall though it's a solid pickup and well worth the price point. It won't keep you for more than 5-6 hours but it's a highly enjoyable 5-6 hours.

A good game that is held back by how frustrating it is.
The character of Shadwen is amazing to play, once you get used to her weird mechanics. She has an amazing grapple ability which is really exciting, and her assassination animations are fun to watch. It's very satisfying to silently swing through the air and land on a guard's head. What is really hard to get used to at first is how time stops unless Shadwen is moving. This is really great for landing that perfect jump or making sure you are landing on the right guard, however it is a completely UNNECESSARY ability considering you can also rewind whenever you want. Didn't stick the landing? Just go back two seconds and readjust. Instead you get this awkward start/stop stutter effect throughout the game that sort of hinders it. True, by the end when you get used to it it can be really amazing, but honestly it would have been more fun at the start if it didn't exist. Or even if you could just toggle it.
However what really, absolutely, and completely holds this game back is LILY. This tiny HELLSPAWN. I am trying so hard to protect her innocence and keeping violence out of her life, but she just decides to run after me constantly so she is always within sight of my murderings. The system to control Lily might as well be non-existent. You can sometimes tell her to go somewhere, it doesn't always work, and the second she gets there she turns around and runs back at you full speed. So if I am trying to hide three bodies I have to keep spamming the T key to try and get her to stay on the other side of the room, which is very hard to do while moving a body. I usually had some success by running to the end of the level and then back tracking, taking guards out as I went, so that Lily would be trapped at the beginning. Overall I am still recommending this game, because it has amazing visual style, mixed in with some really great assassination mechanics. As it is it's only so-so, but worth it for the chance to be Shadwen.

In Darkest Dungeon, it's best to treat a dungeon run similarly to playing a hand of poker.
You know what's in your hand (your characters and abilities), you know what's available to all players (health points, attack types) but you don't know what the other players have (when they miss / do critical damage). It's all about assessing each situation and managing risk. Generally when you suffer serious defeat, it could have been avoided. Greed, optimism and bravado are serious enemies in this game.
You'll hear a lot of complaints about the randomness of the game. It's true that it plays a large part of the mechanics. It seems unfair, especially for the first few hours. Once you realise how it impacts the game and how it is communicated on the UI, you can take steps to mitigate it. Some actions have wild variance whereas others are more dependable. A good example is the difference in healing between the 2 healing characters (Occultist and Vestal).
Another large complaint is the grind in the game. It can take a long time to progress, especially if you suffer a setback. I have only played on the default difficulty and I do agree that there is too much grind. I intend to try out the radiant mode which apparently reduces this somewhat.
Onto the positives, I feel the execution of this game is top notch. The character design, voice acting, environments, animations and the narrator (in particular) all work extremely well together for an immersive experience. I really appreciate the work in the character design, making each character unique and also avoiding the trap of childish character design that so many titles fall into.
The gameplay is a lot deeper than it seems initially. It is a turn based strategy game, and at the start it seems like you just select attack or heal, etc. However, you soon realise that there is much more to the gameplay. I found that one of the major decisions for a successful dungeon run is the party composition. Also of importance is the positioning of each character as well which actions you use. There is a lot of depth in combining these characters and abilities. The choices you make in this regard can contribute to major success or defeat.
The major mechanics work well together and the content is generally well balanced. I do feel that it can be too difficult at times; especially if you are building up a party to take on a boss, losing a key character can set you back a fair amount of time. However, the developers have been adding mechanics and rebalancing over time. It’s great to see developers supporting a game long after release.
Overall, this is a unique game made to a high standard. I recommend it thoroughly, but selecting the appropriate difficulty is one of the most important decisions to make.
Always remember to keep your bravado in check!

Imagine a Russian version of Mad Max.
With giant bugs.
In space.
Now make it a thousand times better.

It's ultimately worth a buy, worth a play.
+++PROS+++
I like stealth games, and this one's spin on stealth was enjoyable and to be learned from. You play as an assassin, but the main challenge is clearing a path for a little girl; getting yourself through would be easy.
The game cuts out waste. Doors and switches trigger automatically, and you can rewind time by the frame to correct mistakes; no deaths or respawns. Time does not move unless you move. This does, however, make it more like a puzzle game.
Escort missions are traditionally dreaded, but the girl's AI is written in a way that she will never cause you trouble and you will actually like her for how "smart" she is. She will never get caught and the game only ends by your own mistakes.
The story is simple, nothing too fancy, but the setting and world building works very well, even if conventionally told through NPC dialogue.
---CONS---
The gameplay can get repetitive. The levels are pretty open and you have freedom to choose how you want to do things. That said, things are so loose that you can bumble around blindly until the girl moves forward. I found myself often dangling crates in front of guards, making a racket, gathering all guards to me while they stupidly looked at my floating crate and wondered what was going on.
There is a crafting system, but I hardly used it. I just didn't need the items. So I just ran around the whole game with a grappling hook and never used the knife either.
The morality system is like many; a trite, binary kill or spare. Whether you want a bad ending or not, having this system makes players commit entirely to one route. It is also upsetting when you're an assassin and you never get to kill anyone. In this case, it was also easier to not kill anyone, not harder. Lastly, the endings upset me. Was I being punished with a less desirable ending for sparing everyone? Or is the characters' parting the happier ending because it's good for them? Am I supposed to believe the girl was better off alone?

The game features some nice updates since the first part: hacking, soldier customization, even the increase in difficulty and the change in settings where you are always being pursued by the aliens (which I personally do not like, but am willing to accept). Visuals look great too. If I were to base my review just on gameplay, the review would be positive.
However, the game is still very buggy, even though it's been a long time since the original release. This is the reason why my review is going ot be negative. It has problems setting resolution (requiring me to reset the game resolution every time I launch it), the support for gamepads is buggy (I don't use a gamepad, but I have a few joysticks connected and the game assumes I'm using them, even though I have Mouse as the control scheme - the buggy controller support results in inability to name saves, because edit boxes behave as if the left arrow were pressed all the time), the game crashes once in a while - and those are just the biggest problems. These problems seem to have been known for a long time, so it doesn't look like they are going to be fixed ever.
Then there are a few intentional interface design decisions that make things difficult. Texts are rendered on floating screens with a pulsating random effects - making it painful (literally) for someone like me, whose eyes are not perfect. Fortunately, this can be turned off by directly editing the config files. The transitions between different parts of the ship interface may look great, but seeing the same transitional 5-second animation for the 50th time during an evening isn't fun. And again, there's more.
So overall, the gameplay is great, but the technical problems make the game so much worse than it could be. Thumb up for just the game contents, but thumbs down for the technical problems, resulting in an overall thumbs down.

Definitely worth a punt, but a bit too expensive for the amount of content. I'd recommend keeping on a wishlist and picking up in a sale.

1998 was the year of
(the original one with the top-down view),
and
. Vangers didn't catch on much back then, because there wasn't any genre it fit. Even if it does some things similarly to GTA (open world top-down driving game with missions and unstructured gameplay), its premise and game world are much more confusing, and most reviewers and players couldn't warm up to it, though some did. (Actually, that probably hasn't changed.)
What sets Vangers apart?
Voxels: Vangers has been implemented with a voxel-like world (that was before the prevalence of polygon-crunching graphics cards), which means that the terrain doesn't have a surface made of textured polygons, but is sculpted out of tiny cubes (like square pixels make up a digital photograph, but in 3D). (Think minecraft with finer grains.)  This means that you can deform the terrain: vehicles leave tracks, weapons make craters, you can move under water, through tunnels (sometimes hard to spot in the top-down view) and, with the right equipment, even burrow along like a mole. Unfortunately, this is also the reason why Vangers still runs at 800x600: if you upped the resolutions, either everything would be very small, or the Voxels would appear larger, and everything would still be blocky.
SciFi: Vangers is set in a confusing world, or rather a "Chain" of worlds (do read the "preface" eventually), with seasons that affect gameplay, weird installations, the purpose of which is initially unknown, and strange creatures that talk in riddles. You need to discover much of  the gameplay as you go along.
So how do you get a feel for the game? Review the controls in the options - you will need to move, turn your vehicle over and use the KiD a lot. Set the game to fullscreen. Then click yourself (somewhat to the right) through the prologue into the buying screen, pick up a shipment of Nymbos, exit the burrow, click on the lower right panel to set your compass for Incubator, and take off. (I set my camera to zoom and tilt, but not to rotate, because  it is very easy to get disoriented.) You'll find that with your small, lightweight car, terrain matters a lot. There are roads, some obvious, some not so much, and unfortunately, you need to stay out of the way of stronger Vangers for the time being. Reach Incubator, sell the Nymbos, get some Phlegma, trade it back to Podish, buy better cars and equipment, ask the councellors about the things you saw, figure out how they work and how to reach other worlds in the chain, take part in races, take down other Vangers and loot them, become a motorized Scifi mercenary.
If you like off-road driving and can keep going in the  face of confusion (and if you don't mind a time machine trip back to when screens had 15", 640x480 was a good game resolution, and 800x600 looked definitely wonderful - and games had to ask before saving 64MB of persistent world),
will reward you with huge and deep world full of surprises -- and driving.
I can safely say that there hasn't been any game like Vangers since 1998, because if there had been, I would have played it. (
, also published by Buka, comes close, but it doesn't have voxel terrain and isn't nearly as strange as Vangers.) I'm very happy that it has been overhauled to run on modern systems.
P.S.: I just found my old Vangers mousepad with the yellow and blue liquid and the floating mechos!

I really like XCOM Enemy Unknown with Enemy Within expansion. Long War mod for it is a real treat and makes the game even better if one can handle the higher difficulty. In my naïveté I decided to get XCOM 2 as soon as possible. They can't possibly break the solid foundations of XCOM EU, can they? Well, they kind of did.
I have to say something about the performance. Back when the game released my PC was on the minimum side of the requirements spectrum. I heard the stories about the horrible performance, but still I soldiered through the first 23 hours and blamed the sub 30 framerates on my potato PC. After a long break, an upgrade, and 130 hours of Witcher 3 on high with constant 90 fps I decided to go back and try XCOM 2 again. Unfortunately, I am not impressed. The framerate is all over the place. From time to time it even tanks to 15 fps for some reason. It's Unreal Engine for crying out loud! How much power does it actually need? There are also bugs and crashes. One particular crash made me chuckle. At least on my system the game crashes on the cinematic after the first tutorial mission. I had the same problem with XCOM EU! Are the devs making this on purpose?
After years of playing catch-up hardware-wise I can deal with bad graphics and low framerates, but the gameplay of XCOM 2 is also testing my patience. The biggest problem is the fabled LOS that is utterly broken at times. Shooting through walls is not uncommon. Just now I played a mission where most of the shots were taken through brick walls. You just never know if this amazingly looking piece of grade A cover will shield you from incoming fire.
Mission timers are also a miss. Not only do they force you to recklessly rush the objective only to activate all the surrounding enemy pods, they also are a detriment to the newly-introduced stealth mechanic because they start ticking down even when your team is still undetected. I guess that the aliens rig their stuff to explode regardless of guerilla activity.
However, the worst sin of all is the fact that the game feels just unfun and tedious to play. The strategic layer forces you to scan a location for multiple days just to get something as mundane as money, while bombarding you with reports of new locations to scan. The problems with LOS and a number of alien units that appear early on and can instantly incapacitate a soldier (Vipers, Stun Lancers, Sectoids) can easily turn a mission into a squad wipe. I do realise that I should just 'git gud', but it wouldn't hurt to have some fun while I'm 'gitting beter'.
This is the last straw. I'll try to fight the game one more time and hope it gets better. If it doesn't, it'll end up in the bottomless pit of games that I wasted money on. If it does, I'll change my review. I won't hold my breath, though.
For now - don't bother with this game.
Edit:
It did not get better. I just cannot deal with this. It is not even about the difficulty. I would rather play XCOM: Enemy Unknown ten times over with the Long War Mod than this on baby difficulty. Cheap tricks to crank the challenge, glitchy LoS, performance issues (maybe it is just me, but still) - just some reasons why I am not going back to this waste of money and space. I got burned so much only with Rome II, and supposedly the latter got better. We shall see.
Moral of the story - do NOT preorder or buy day-one, kids.
P.S.

Unlike X-COM Enemy Unknown, this game isn't actually fun. I would be more Ok with this if it were appropriately named -  X-COM 2: Load & Reload.
It adds a lot of pointless, negative, and frustrating mechanics to what should be a very cool game, like having to spend 10% of your days in game collecting your monthly budget or watching a snake alien pull a character through a bush, tree, bush, bench, and van in one shot with it's *tongue*.
The game sees those as barriers for bullets, just not for tongues or human bodies unless you're moving them.  I think that summarizes whats wrong with the game - you get punished for everything and rewarded for nothing, even in ways that don't make sense internally.  Much like XCOM EU had the stupid premise of aliens invading across interstellar distances but Earth, where there are literally tens to hundreds of millions of soldiers, you can only bring just FOUR so the humans on the human homeworld are always outnumbered.  That could be forgiven as making the game a challenge, but this game goes so far out of it's way in unecessary ways it stops being enjoyable.  This is the real crux of the game:  most people will not enjoy the endless saving and reloading that is the core and in some sense only mechanic characterizing the game.
Also, it still has game breaking bugs - I quit after not being able to finish a mission after four attempts because it would hang half way through it, with the game menues still working but the Alien turn never completing.  Just play XCOM EU on a harder difficulty setting.  If you do buy this game, avoid activating the Alien Hunter's mission until you're in a 'win more' position.  It can easily break your forward progress and ruin your game with no real way to recover.

Highly competent shooter in 3D and 2D planes that is fairly unique due to its changing perspectives. The tutorial is explained quite well, and the prologue will get you used to the action.
The maingame has six levels. The story plays out while you are gunning and dashing, and I could barely pay attention to it. There is a lot going on here. Using dash along with lock-on, regular bullets, and the sword plus putting in an EX attack now and then really makes for a crazy experience. And this is a Japanese experience through and through. There are even a pair of cute cyborg sisters in this, and an extensive though entirely obscure plotline that has been crafted with some care.
The technical details about the game seem great as well. 4K 60FPS is easy on my 1070, and overall while simple in some ways, the aesthetic is really well done and even gorgeous in some spots. The sound is decent, the voice acting is fairly competent in Japanese, and I can't find too much to complain about here. This shooter is well worth your time. The story is a bit deeper than most shooters, and you might want to go through the game on easy to get a bit more of it while you are pummeling the bad guys.
The difficulties really get pumping on higher modes. Too much for me, so I am glad there is an easy mode. You will be working your sticks and triggers in this game big time. I cannot even imagine how this was playable before on the buttons.
Other than that they have some galleries and different modes for you to play. All around the new update has made this a a much better experience. They tuned a lot of things, and gave existing owners a free update. Still worth it if you don't own it for about ten bucks. Recommended.

A fantastically challenging isometric game of total annihilation.   Depth of game play including many different mechs, weapons, and levels of challenge.   Varied maps to play and overcome.
To me, this harkens back to Bullfrog's Syndicate from 1993 - a cyberpunk-style thrill-a-thon, merciless and brutal, but instead of having a squad of mercs you'll tackle the levels with an assortment of vehicles.  An assortment of weapons (primary and secondary) plus defensive mechanisms, mixed and matched across several different chassis and control schemes.  The neon overtones and slick screen movement, combined with total devastation makes for a graphically enjoyable experience.
Top-notch soundtrack.  Great music, very much in the 'Outrun' or 80s synth style.  Never gets old.
Brigador is a quality product from an indie development team.  It's a game that plays wonderfully on my archaic beast of a computer, built some 8 years ago, and that's worth mentioning as not a lot of gamers have newer rigs.  A game that deserves more recognition and gameplay - but don't give up if you are frustrated with the controls at first - Brigador's control scheme is worth mastering.

Armed with your choice of war machine and war crime-generating devices, smash your way through a city in uproar. Capitalise on environmental destruction to flank your foes and bring ruin to those who would stand against your employers.
Brigador is a game of a mould less often seen these days - the kind of game that expects you to learn its rules and adapt to it, instead of holding your hand and making concessions for your comfort.
The districts of Solo Nobre are hostile places, their inhabitants moreso. Be smart in the application of your firepower, lest you be buried under bodies and a storm of retaliatory fire.
This game has tank controls. Learn them. Love them. For goodness' sake, use a mouse and keyboard if you can; you'll have a much more pleasant time of things. Typically, it will take about an hour to get properly accustomed to them.
For those willing to invest the time and effort, you will be rewarded with a warcrimes simulator put together with care and attention and a tactical arcade shooter with a surprising amount of depth.
The only issues I, personally, have with the game are that the sound could be punchier in places and that the heavier vehicles are slow to traverse the larger maps, which can lead to a lot of dead time wandering about when you've cleared a sector of enemies. That second one is less of a complaint than an observation, though; that's just how it's going to be in those cases.
In conclusion: If you're willing to get over the initial learning curve, this game will handily provide you with hours of fun.

The first of all is how the game controls in regards to movement. You will slide... A LOT. I am pretty sure it is impossible to not slide a significant distance unless you land at a 90 degree angle to the ground. This is not too big of an issue for most of the game until it tries to give you platforming challenges. 95% of all difficulty in any platforming section of the game is simply trying to not fall off of platforms after jumping. It is honestly so bad that many platformers I ahve played that have a ice physics gimmick level have less sliding then this game does.
My second complaint is with status conditions. Simply put they last FAR too long. Earlier today I was playing the game and my main character got put to sleep, too lazy to swap characters for the rest of the battle I grabbed my phone to check my email. Seeing someone asking me something on email I typed out a short paragraph reply and sent it back to them and then set my phone down and still had about 10% of the time left on sleep because nothing was focusing on that character. Not to mention that status conditions are spammed like crazy and are often on aerial enemies which are already stupidly annoying to hit as you have to chase them around the screen for a few minutes unless you are lucky enough to bait them into an area with a low ceiling.
You should not feel bad about dieing in this game as it is hard and takes some patience but even with that I would say that about 1/3 of the times that I die I feel that it is not my fault that I died becuase of annoying aerial AI or bad movement controls etc which is not a sign of great design. And even then a significant number of my "game overs" are simply my giving up out of being annoyed and letting things kill me just so that I can warp back to safety.
Overall great game that I highly recommend but be prepared to be very annoyed at points.

I was bitten by the Shadwen bug and I am smitten.  This is one of the best games I've ever played!  In terms of mechanics and style, it IS the best game I've ever played!  I'm a stealth nut for one, so maybe that is a factor, but I really think this is a huge step in the right direction for the stealth genre and possibly many other "adventure" avenues.
Some people can't wrap their head around the time freeze function, and they give bad reviews, or they talk about the NPCs being dumb and scoff at the mediocrity.  Like, does that really F'ing matter?  It's a game!  The true joy comes from how many ways you can do one thing.  Maybe you got to already enjoy the cerebral part about it.  Maybe some people don't have cerebrals, I don't know.  Some people talk a lot of hate while at the same time commending it, so why?  I'm here to say, This game f'ing rules!
I've played a lot of stealth and this one is by far the most original.  Simple concept, simple rules at your disposal, yet so immensely engageing.  Swinging from your grappling hook is an art, as well as how you get your orphan to the end.  I wish you could do this kind of thing in say, Batman, or Assassin's Creed, or any other stealth game.
I know it's not perfect.  I think that Shadwen is the first of it's kind and it has a lot that it could offer in future titles that could add some more depth and range.  It's going to spawn some interesting games in the future I think.  It's not perfect, but that goes for a lot of first titles that then become an epic series later on, and I love a good niche.
So for all you nay-sayers I say "STOP CRAPPING ON SHADWEN! IT'S SOMEBODY'S HERO AND WE WANT MORE!"

Although steam says I haven't played this game much, I've put about 1000-2000 hours in total using DayZ Commander. Now, being based of a Military Sim. There is some amazing gun play, tactics and all around great fun to be had. Although there are some very bad bugs and glitches. If its not glitching off a ladder and dying or lagging through walls. (Every hardcore DayZ player has had this happen to them.) Its also got a very steap learning curve. Don't let that turn you off to the game though. DayZ is all about a game based around survival. Your set in a place in Russia, so anyone who doesn't know how to read russian is gonna have alittle harder time remembering the towns. (Although after 10 or so hours, it isn't hard.) Your set in the middle of nowhere with next to nothing. You have no objective except survive the zombie infested island. You have no idea where to go, so you start running, you found a house! Grab the beans, soda and pistol of the ground. Suddenly your a threat. You meet another player, a not so friendly one at that. People call him many names, but the most common. Bandit. He wants your items, are you going to get shot, or survive. Either by running or taking the fight to him.
Now, that we're done with the little story. Back to the review d:
Yes, considering it is a mod. There are going to be bugs, and more then likely you WILL get mad. Its only normal.
Some annoying bugs are -
- Getting one hit by zombies and dying
- Glitching off ladders and dying or breaking legs
- Reloging and your items be missing from inventory
- Glitching through walls
- Zombies hitting you through walls
- Zombies having horrible pathing
- Zombies glitching though floors
Those are some annoying bugs, that happen normaly. But if you can look past that, there is a silver lining. Once you get passed the bugs you find an amazing experence. Just image finding a friendly group of people, running up north, getting end-game loot and finding another squad of people and having a huge gun fight. Like I said before, the gun play is amazing. So naturaly so are the gun fights. Then you find a heli, go help freshspawns or kill them(Hero/bandit), then a rogue sniper takes all you guys out. Its fun. But I highly recommend you get some friends, get on skype/teamspeak/vent etc etc and play that way, as its much more enjoyable and way easier.
If your brand new to DayZ here are some beginner tips -
- G = Gear
- / on numpad - Changing optics on weapons
- Q , E - Lean left and right
- Right click to aim
- Hold right click to zoom (can do while aiming)
- There is no autorun feature
- Z , X , C = Changing Stance
- . and , = Changing channel to talk
- / not on numpad to talk
- Capslock - Voice chat
Those are gonna be some basics your gonna need to know. Well, I hope this review helped out atleast slightly. I fully recommend this game. Just remember. Its ok to get mad. . . Cause you will, I promise. :P
EDIT - This game is also very badly rendered. Meaning, anyone who doesn't have a decent computer are going to have trouble running this game. Although not impossible, you will have to get used to it. I get a solid 30 fps and about 15-20 in large citys. Which isn't very good. But its playable. Just like the bugs, if you can get passed that. There are many adventures that await you in the DayZ.

Amazing multi monitor tool. Each monitor can get its own taskbar which only lists applications running on that monitor. You can also set an individual wallpaper per monitor, or, one that stretches across all of them.

If you have AMD Eyefinity or nVidia Surround, DF can virtually split the combined monitors again -- with optional bezel compensation -- so you can have  the full view, but still have logically confined monitors that correspond to the physical frames. Even mismatched monitors of different resolutions and locations are supported.
Another feature which I use a lot is the window location: you can optionally set it so certain applications (wildcards are supported) always open on a specific monitor. I use this to move all my windows games to the left most monitor.
If you have two or more monitors, you want this. Promised.
