As much as I want to recommend this game.  I simply can't.  It is a fun game and unique being a JRPG action based game.  The story is great, the characters are colorful and it's not bad in that department.  What it fails in is it's playthrough.  Some parts didn't make sense at all where to go next and some parts totally made sense.  I found myself looking at a guide vs the clues it gave me for my next objective, the game could have worded it better.
Another aspect was control.  I'm not sure about KB but I'd recommend a controller.  Even with a 360 controller, the control was sometimes very stiff.  In most action games I've played, if you have to button mash and change directions the character would usually do that automatically, here it does not.  You have to stop turn then resume your attack if you want to change directions.  A thing someone can forget in the heat of battle.  Also jumping/attacking just feels sluggish and inaccurate.
Finally, the enemies.  While at first it's not bad at all; about midway point through the game.  The stupid switch gets turned on....BAD!  I've never seen such enemies become super smart on normal mode.  They know when your gonna jump (they counter it), they know when to avoid a trap just at the right moment, they know when to dodge, and know when to attack.  It's like super smart, I'm only human!  Also enemies are VERY relentless AND brutal.  They will chase you down, spam attacks, while at the same time predicting your every move.  Amazingly, it was only boss fights that weren't as brutal compared to normal enemies.
I got this game for $10 and for the most part it is worth it, but if you can't get past these flaws.  If controller or really unfair enemies isn't in your forte then don't get this game.  On the bright side, the game is VERY forgiveable about restarting as you'll resume in the last room your in.  This doesn't change how I feel, doing this just makes the game feel sorry for you and is frustrating to retry something just because the enemies are brutally unfair.

A breaker-style game with powerups and permanent upgrades but there are enemies that can fire back while you play.
The first mode (of two) is a campaign mode where you play through a set of levels, beat the boss level, then repeat with a slightly larger set of levels. As you progress they introduce mechanics and enemy variants (such as enemies with periodic invulnerability, enemies that fire at you, background enemies that slowly repair things you don't destroy, and two-way wormholes).
The other mode (tower attack) is a traditional score attack mode with that sends you through stages one after another. No upgrades, only temporary powerups are dropped.
In campaign mode, destroyed blocks and enemies drop XP that you have to collect before they drop into the void. You use XP to purchase permanent passive and active abilities. However, you can't replay stages to grind xp and you can't refund to get xp back. Any upgrades you choose are final. The levels weren't especially difficult/frustrating for me until the final boss in campaign mode.
I didn't really enjoy the final boss.
I wasn't going to replay the dozens of levels in the campaign just to get a better setup for the final boss fight. Luckily, I figured out enough of the easier patterns that I lived through it. Beating the game restarts the campaign but you keep upgrades and gold.
I lost track of the ball a lot until I turned 'minimise effects' on. Even with that on I still lose track occasionally. Maybe partly because the ball pulses and when you hit the wall sparks fly so it takes me a sec to figure out where the ball is heading? The glowy visual effects make it look flashy but I'd prefer to have the option to turn it all off so I could see better.
Sometimes the screen is so busy I have to focus on only the ball and just randomly use active abilities to make sure I use them all before I lose the life. I didn't buy the kamikaze ability for that reason.
Worth a look if you want a breaker with decent enemy and powerup variety. The store page has gameplay video clips that show how the game plays and some of the earlier bosses are. Also good to look at to check if you might get distracted by all the flashy explosions.

the game's fairly easy if you're just going straight through the story, and a satisfying challenge for those wanting to get all the achievements and stray beads. Okami's a fantastic entry for those new to Kamiya's character-action games, and a fantastic experience for those already familiar with his other works. i simply can't reccommend this enough, especially for the asking price.

I have no idea where to start this review. Hacknet is the kind of hacking game that's just.... Mysterious.
Everything from the music to the story helps set the odd yet brilliant atmosphere.
Before I contunue this review,  have to say this: I've never known a lot about hacking. Sure, I know how the command terminal works, but that was about it. So, with little knowledge of hacking, I took a dive down the rabbit hole.
Probably the most important ascept of the game is how open it is. You get to do whatever you want, and you don't have to rush any of the missions. In exchange, you have to figure out a lot by yourself. Usually you're given a link at the start of a mission, or in between missions, and then you have to work your own way from there.
This combination of having to work things out yourself and the freedom that it brings is genius. It is very satisfying and rewarding when you finally figure out how to get the mission done.
Furthermore, the commands were very easy to learn. It is a lot to take in at first, but getting the hang of it is quite easy.
Gameplay aside, let's talk story.
Hacknet is completely driven by the story behind it. I just have to point out how well the story actually is. To understand everything you'd have to do a ton of hacking and searching, but not doing so won't result in confusion about the ending.
This is yet another expample of the freedom you are given.
Sadly, it isn't quite as long as I expected. The main storyline took me about 6-7 hours. Luckily, there's still Labyrinths DLC and workshop extentions.
Finally, you don't need knowledge about hacking at all. It all works out fine.
Pros:
+Good story
+Awesome music
+User-friendly interface
+Lots of freedom
+Steam Workshop
Neutral:
+-Easy to learn, hard to master
Cons:
-A little short
-Confusing at the start
8/10

The game story is fairly well made, other than the fact that it takes every opportunity to force you to explore a hardcore dungeon. I was kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at the 'hot springs arc', the part where the party of adventurous magical school girls goes to an Onsen for a field trip and I was so keen on seeing the artworks for that but...
I had to explore 2 dungeons before getting to the Onsen and guess what happens when I get to the Onsen? ****SPOILERS**** The Onsen is dry... ****SPOILERS END**** Now here we go to explore a few more dungeons. I stopped playing for quite a while after that.
It may sound easy to you, 'pfffft... a few school girls clearing dungeons, it'll just be one of those easy Japanese made weeaboo games.' Well, you are wrong, for the most part. There is a reason why I chose to call this game "Kawaii Souls". Because it's hard as♥♥♥♥♥♥ therefore I hereby make a Dark Souls reference. I play on normal and the monsters are so hard to kill, oh my god, I sometimes contemplate killing myself. But it's a good point, to some, the combat AI is amazing. I feel like the AI learns the way you fight, and calculate strategies on how to break the way you fight. Normally there would be a sequence that each mob follow in combat situations in other games, and you just have to figure out that sequence and you'd get through the game easy. But it's the complete opposite in this game, if you don't constantly improve and change the way you fight, the AI would kill you off, easy.
Other than the amazing...ly hard combat, the dialogue and story is quite good too. The humourous and cute (omg the babbling Sana, so cute, kya kya) dialogues always cheer me up after spending hours trying to clear a dungeon. But sometimes I wonder what's actually keeping me here playing this game...
Overall, 8/10 game with over 20 hours gameplay. Would play again.

Lots of reviewers bash Fortune Summoners for its "unfair" difficulty, but that is not true. This game is hard and sometimes frustrating, but if you think it's unfair then you need to practice more and stop mashing buttons mindlessly, because it's not going to work in this game. The good news is that once you start figuring out how to beat each type of enemy properly, it becomes incredibly fun. It gets a LOT better and easier once you get the 3rd party member and more skills/spells though, too bad it takes a while.
You will have to master the controls, your available skills (each one exists for a reason, do not ignore them), strategies for each enemy, item/mana management, and your ANGER. No, really, you WILL get mad at times and you WILL want to just jump at that little ****er with all guns blazing, but that will only make it worse. Stop, think, try different approaches, observe his movements, defend, and most importantly: do NOT be stingy with recovery items and mana. They are there to be used and abused. Do not expect to get by most fights without recovering or using spells.

This game is disappointing and tiring.
The gameplay is not uniform. Once you watch a 10 minutes long cut scene and in the next instant you have to make a split second decision that affects your story. Not even enough to locate a keys on a keyboard. Sometimes you don't even know you have to do something. Movie just stops, and you have to guess that you're back in control. Sometimes this controll is limited to just one button, moving forward.
There is a lot of difficult choices in the game but more often than not, choices make no sense. This is no rpg. This is a train simulator. You ride along tracks and occasionally you can choose to turn right or left. Often there is even no way to guess where that would lead you. You cannot examine your options. Even if it's a rare occasion where you have time to do so.
Dialogues are similar. Sometimes there is just no right option. And sometimes even if you think there is a right option the tone of your voice is different than you'd expect. For example instead of calming someone it sounds like you are blaming them.
There is also problem with pacing. Once there is nothing to do. You spend a few minutes just looking around for that one action that would move the story forward and it's just boring. On other occasions there is so many things happening at once that you are just not prepared to handle it. Fortunately in the most hectic parts you have more that one layer of quick time events you can fail. However some of these QTEs can affect your story so don't count on that.
In conclusion this game reminds me a little of Resident Evil 4. Especially that one moment where you watch a 3 minutes long cut scene, you put down your controller, take some popcorn, a guy jumps on you with a knife, press LT+RT to not die. You died. And now imagine a whole game based around this concept.
This game would be better if it was just released as a movie. And even then, story is not that great. Just watch it on youtube if you must.

I've played this game multiple times now. After beating it on my first playthrough on Veteran difficulty, I tried doing Ironman runs, but I rarely even go to magnetic weapons or plated armor (tier 1 upgrades). Frustrated, I deleted the game (even though I really enjoyed the first normal playthrough). When Long War 2 came out, I reinstalled it and tried Long War 2, but I quickly realized that Long War 2 is nothing for me, so I started a normal playthrough again, this time on Commander though. With everything I learned before, especially from my Ironman runs, I managed to get through commander fairly easily, so before completing that playthrough, I started another one on Commander Ironman. And I beat the game.
This playthrough was one of the most satisfying, terrifying and intense experiences I've ever had. In the past it always seemed stupid to me to have a mode like this for a game that is so RNG heavy, but if you know what you're doing you can play around that. And the game tells you that Commander is only for people who already know the game.
I also found out about all the little secrets the developers put into the game to make it as unfrustrating as possible. For example when you miss shots, an invisible counter goes up and increases your chances for your next shot until you hit something. When you are in combat against an enemy squad or two, the game will make other enemy squads move away, so you don't have to fight too many enemies simultaneously, and when there are too many enemies active at the same time, not all of them will try to kill you. Some will just run towards some cover, other will go into overwatch.
There is still plenty of times where you'll feel like the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting you. You will miss 90% shots, you will get hit from enemies even though you were behind high cover and the enemy very far away.
The game also still has tons of bugs, some really annoying bugs and even some that affect the gameplay in a very bad way. Once I had a soldier on a roof, which got destroyed. The soldier fell down, but then got stuck in terrain. I couldn't move that soldier away from there, and it was an escort mission, so I HAD to evacuate that soldier. Luckily I could free that soldier with a grenade (which did damage to him), but that's obviously stupid. The game still struggles sometimes with performence, sometimes the game gets stuck for a few seconds because it doesn't know what it's supposed to do or something. When you click "Make all Utility Items available" the mission will just cancel a lot of times. There are multiple places where sounds can get stuck. The list goes on and on.
You have to keep in mind though how big and complex this game is. The game offers a great amount of enemy types right at the start, and for most games, that would be fine. No one would really complain if those were the only enemies in the game and if they just got more health and damage later. But no, the game keeps introducing new enemies right until the final mission, which is really impressive in my opinion. Those new enemies are also extremely crazy with devastating abilities and tons of health, but the thing is your soldiers will get SO powerful during the game that you will still be able to completely destroy them, and this is just awesome. It feels so satisfying, because you actually made so much progress with all your soldiers AND the enemies did as well.
The systems of the game are really well thought out. The base building, the world map, the avatar project. There is a timer that starts after a few hours, which if it runs out, you loose the game. But the timer is really generous and it is just there so that you can't just build and research until you get extremely powerful, but are forced to go for the enemy blacksite facilities every now and then. But as I said, the time is generous, and it brings a strategic element to your base building, like in RTS games, where you have to decide how greedy you want to be and what path to focus on. And there are plenty of ways to delay or lengthen the timer btw.
I think X-Com 2 is a brilliant game. Even the story was really cool. The character customization is very impressive for a game like this and makes your soldiers much more important to you. Also nice soundtrack.

I love this game so much, I don't even know why, and my friends are very sick of me talking about it, haha. Maybe it's because I don't play a lot of arcade shooters, or maybe it's because I love things that involve Japanese story-telling and voice acting.
This game is an amazing, bright, sparkly, shooting-slicing-destroying fest that is not too hard for beginners like me (although I did have to beat it on Easy before I could beat it on Normal - Hard might be beyond me for a while yet). The controls aren't hard to learn, although I'm still improving on their use, and the view and targets are always changing, so it's never ever boring. It's very smooth even on my three year old laptop on max settings, although it runs a little hot after an hour or two. The voice acting is pretty good, and once the game is beaten there are all kinds of goodies to look at in the Gallery, like the art stills, the mecha models, and concept art. I also love the music to bits and have imported it from the game files to my iTunes so I can listen to it all the time. It's exciting, scintillating hyper dance music with solid tunes, and the final boss music makes everything 100x more badass and was honestly what kept me going when I tried and failed to beat the final boss so many times.
Only a couple things that detract from my experience: it can sometimes be difficult to tell exactly where your own mecha is among all the movement and health bars and explosions on the screen, and the plot twists generally come when I'm trying not to die horribly and can't read the subtitles; there are still some sections that I haven't seen all the dialogue. Also, maybe it's just me, but sometimes the 'skip cutscene' button doesn't work right away. Lastly, although I think I understand the story and it works, it really feels like the final story arc in a much longer series, and like there could be a sequel, which makes me feel like there should be more game somewhere. But that one's a really minor thing, and could be interpreted as a good thing, if we eventually do get more game. Maybe?
Another thing is I really like the achievements chosen for this game; it might be a little thing, but it keeps me coming back to play the game again and again, trying for something new every time. Or sometimes I just play a level to help me wake up in the morning; it really shakes out morning brain cobwebs. It's not very long - about 45 min without dying or cutscenes - but that doesn't bother me.
tl;dr I love this game to a disturbing degree and highly recommend it if you have a controller.

XCOM 2 is a triumphant continuation of the pulse pounding and harrowing action of the reboot, be it megre victory on the ground or the dramatic logistics of the world map. It builds on its predecessor in all factors of gameplay and design, with few missteps. Prepare to lose hundreds of hours of your life once more, with a key twist. XCOM is no longer the vanguard of humanity against an unknown threat. As many players experienced on their first campaigns, the alien threat was for more powerful than they expected, resulting in early and decisive defeats. Firaxis assumes the player experienced this, and in XCOM 2, you play as a Resistance movement, striking the Alien occupiers from the shadows.
On the surface, 2 is a significant graphical step above its predecessor. Higher resolution textures, and (surprisingly) fantastic lighting make individual soldier and alien models gorgeous (check my screenshot collection for some great shots), and level layouts are well lit and colorful. In general, 2 is more colorful and detailed- vibrant and shiny environments and soldiers, as opposed to the somewhat muddy original. Don’t get your hopes too high- this is still a game played from a high-overhead perspective. It’s just nice that zoom in shots still hold up, detail wise. Similarly, the new aesthetic the team decided on is distinct from Enemy Unkown. All of the original aliens received amazing updates- not just ability wise, but in armour and even physiology. The advanced Mutons and Chrysalids give returning players a ‘Oh,♥♥♥♥♥♥ they’re back!” followed by a  “OH ♥♥♥♥, WHAT IS THAT SUPPOSED TO DO!!!”. Soldiers have a huge array of new customization options, my personal favorite part of this sequel. Gun and armour camo (as well as alternate pieces for every armour set), head and face pieces, even a ‘stance’ option that gives them some twitchiness or swagger on the field.
The updated graphics come with a cost- 2 is a bit of drain to run on older systems (my old GTX 760 and FX6300, 8GB of DDR3). While the graphical updates warrant this; there were some significant performance issues on launch- random framerate drops, long load times, buggy audio, and frequent stuttering. These have been mostly resolved, but my new GTX1080, i76400k, 16GB DDR4 setup still had framerate dips.
Sound effects are very good, with  heavy hitting firearms, and shrieking lasers. Soldiers also have a multitude of languages to choose from, with multiple accents for each language. The soundtrack is nothing short of fantastic! Hopeful, terrifying, heroic, apprehensive- Tim Wynn hits all the right notes and seldom misses. The mission planning and extraction themes are of particular note, with me sometimes wishing for longer load times as I excitedly air drum after a successful mission (EVERY successful mission).
Down to brass tacks. I’ve played 2 campaigns in full, and am currently playing a heavily modded one. One easy (and save-scummed), one medium, and currently on hard. I am DEFINITELY not an authority on inner-workings and mechanics, and on the lower end as far as player skill goes. That being said, I adore the action-impacted tactical gameplay- which leaves you rubbing your head in thought and nervously sweating at the same time- a pyramid of empty stress-water bottles next to you (or is that just me). The combat encounters play out very similar to EU. Turn based, soldiers and aliens trade fire, grenades, psychic abilities and buffs and debuffs as a team. Individual soldiers and their unique abilities (achieved as they gain experience) amplify their teammates, or save them from horrific deaths. A Sniper can be upgraded down the gunslinger skill-set, and starts blasting enemies with a revolver as they get too close, fire on her, or stack in a rapid volley of hits. Be wary, many enemies have brutally effective abilities of their own, to be learned through trial and error. The tactical and rewarding combat is enhanced by the fact that: a) you are so drastically outnumbered and outgunned, making victory even sweeter, and b) you once again develop a true attachment to your customized and veteran soldiers.
The strategy portion of the game also nails the themes of disempowerment and scant resources, fighting a guerrilla war against a juggernaut threat. Your mobile base allows you to wheel and deal, building up a world wide resistance network. You still have to make difficult choices, abandoning areas of the world to alien control, and using precious intelligence resources to counter alien operations against your movement. The research and engineering mechanics work the same way as EU.
XCOM 2 is the natural progression of Firaxis’ take on the series, and a must-have for strategy gamers.

This game has an innovative, somewhat interactive, narrator who reminds me of Morgan Freeman, and if that's not enough, the soundtrack is incredible. Really just an amazingly well done game. This game is well paced, challenging enough and graphically very pleasing. The real game starts after your first run (first game). Once you are familiar with all mechanics and possibilities, focus on some of the achievements to create your own unique and challenging game. With so many different options you can try different playstyles and new tactics.
I disagree with many negative comments below, complaining about some of the mechanics etc. It is just a game after all, not a real-life simulator ("turn-based" is already a strong indicator of that simple fact). Imo the main fun comes from the huge diversity that the game offers in terms of tactical possibilities and difficulty levels combined with achievements. Many games today spoiled the idea of achievements by adding hundreds of useless medals etc. that mean nothing. This game however, through intelligently set achievements can create a totally new, entertaining and refreshing experience. So you get few games in price of one!
If the first run was too simple, try to finish the game without increasing the squad numbers (stay with 4 soldiers only), increase difficulty to Commander +, play Ironman mode, try to finish it by June or mix these challenges into a new unique game. You will discover that some class abilities that you used to find useless, suddenly become very useful and fun to try (in my case pistol-oriented sniper spec or guardian specialist). You might discover that some of the abilities are extremely powerful but in order to use them you have to change the whole playstyle and specialise all soldiers in a new way.
Of course there are some irritating things but they do not change much the overall experience. Things I would like to get better:
- missclicks are unavoidable (especially in some situations) and soldiers run to a wrong position (hex). In Ironman mode I was playing as if I had to disarm a bomb, checking my every click... there should be some option to secure players decision.
- it is currently very hard to know what a soldier will be able to see once he moves to the desired position. In many situations I was surprised to see that the soldier didn't see enemy. I would turn camera around, check obstacles, walls etc and yet, many times would be wrong. On some occasions I'm actually convinced it was a bug, as there was nothing in the line of sight and still one of my soldiers couldn't see enemy standing in open. Reloading can help with that, but it is anti-climatic or impossible on ironman mode.
Hope to see even better remake of my old favourite "Terror from the Deep" now...

Brigador Up - Armored Edition Review - This update to Brigador refines the gameplay that was already there. The beginning of the campaign now spends much more time explaing its control scheme and tactics the player can use with the different vehicles. After not playing for a couple months, Brigador is still fun and refreshing.
Brigador is a fun game and it's also really cool. The scenario is crafted in a way that feels familiar and fresh at the same time. It would be cool if they created DLC or another game that was related to Brigador's universe. As for the gameplay, It tends to be varied probably because of all the options available to the player once he or she has some mastery of the controls. Yes, mastering the control scheme was tricky for me and I still need more practice. However, the contols aren't complicated in the least so people willing to invest a little time into the game are bound to unlock more satisfaction than the intial frustration that may come during the early sessions.
This game isn't perfect. It could use a little more depth like a deeper managerial aspect. However everything that's in Brigador is top notch.
I'll leave you with a phrase that sounds foreign to my Steam filled ears. Brigador is a bargain even at full price.

The combat is pretty cool. When you're the swordsgirl, it's almost like Super Smash Bros. This is definitely not a button mash game, and the game is most rewarding when you improvise your combos. As with most RPGs, you can always grind if it gets too difficult, which doesn't seem long if you see it as an opportunity to hone your sword skills.
The thing that stands out in this game is the AI. Some enemies have perfect reaction time, which makes it seem like they can predict your moves and counter whatever you do. If you like learning enemy patterns and countering them, this is the game for you. Even if you suck, your allies are strong enough that they can bail you out.
Money is plentiful in the game, so you can always adventure with good healing items. You'll still need to save up for better equipment, though. You won't have to worry about permanently missing any items, but a walkthrough will make sure you get them all. In fact, I highly suggest using one with maps for the dungeons. I find myself going in circles a lot because I forget where I had already explored.
The cute art and dialogue makes up for its lackluster plot, which ends on a bit of a cliffhanger. I heard that the developer(s) won't make a sequel because it didn't sell well. It's a shame, because the swordsgirl learns some very cool magic spells, but the only good time to use it is for the final boss.

Okami... Oh Okami. I love this game, I love it so much. I know the number of hours I have played it on Steam doesn't look like much, but I got this game shortly after it came to the Wii and have played over 300 hours on that version. I've played it so much the disk has been worn down and one of the cutscenes has been permantly altered with a textureless rectangle that covers half the scene.
What is Okami exactly? Well, I heard someone describe it as Bayonetta meets The Legend of Zelda and after playing Bayonetta for the first time yesterday, I agree with that statement.The fighting in both games are rather similar with the battles taking place in relativly restricted areas. In Bayonetta it's caused by force fields blocking you exit and in Okami it's caused by a wall of evil surounding you, creating a circular arena.
It's like The Legend of Zelda with the open world mechanics and dungeon system, most of them you're able to leave the dungeon at any time to visit merchants or do side quests and there's a variety of characters to talk to.
The art style is great, I think it's also why Okami aged so well. It doesn't try to be realistic, characters have usually only a few markings to show their eyes or defining features, it really does look like classic Japanese artwork come to life. It looks beautiful to me, even if it's on low quality for visuals so my computer can run it without problem. I can only imagine what it would look like on a top of the line desk top with ultra high settings enabled.
The characters may seem a little one dimensional at first (the sweet sake brewer, the perverted partner, the taunting rival) but they all have their hidden depths and secrets and the sheer amount of characters, all with different personalities and thoughts on the large white wolf barking at them. I think the only truely one dimensional character he is a side character who is literally called "Nameless Man".
The enemies are rather unique, though are divided into several classes of enemies (chimera, bull, and samurai are a few) with similar attack patterns and shapes. There's a bestiary provided that lets you read about their lore and tips on how to defeat them in a lore friendly manner. You also get a picture of said enemy in the classic Japanese style.
I only have one complaint about this game, and it's in the first cutscene in which both Amaterasu and Issun (essentially your Navi of this game) are introduced. I won't go into detail but it really didn't match the rest of the feel of the game and honestly, if you get past that it's smooth sailing from there.
Music's great too, I have most of the sountrack and remixes on my iPhone.
Also, while it took me a bit to get used to it, the Celestial Brush is great being controlled by a mouse. I'd recomend a keyboard for this game, I tried using a controller but wasn't comfortable with it.
One other thing, I couldn't figure this out at first but pushing F1 allows you to skip cutscenes. The first Okami cutscene isn't super long but if you've seen it as many times as I have it's nice to be able to skip.
Well, that's all I can say about it. It's a wonderful game to me both because of the nostalga I feel for it (I was nine my first playthrough) and because it hasn't decreased in fun as I got older.
TL;DR: I can finally see Rao's "rosary" in HD.

This is a game that's a bit complicated to talk about, and not because it's open world.
The gameplay is pretty good. If it's a story driven first person shooter you want, then it's got this down pretty well.
Character customization is also quite good. There are so many options that, by itself, could be worth dumping an hour of your time.
Codsworth has voice samplings for so many names, including naughty ones. You can name your character "Boobies" and that is what he will call you.
Settlement building is a fun little diversion if you like building your own custom towns. I wouldn't buy this game for the settlements, but it's pretty decent.
Bugs. Several times, I have ended up getting trapped in rooms because the loading zones suddenly stop working. The settlement info on the Pip-Boy is always wrong until you actually visit the settlement. I get assigned quests that can't be finished because the guy I'm supposed to kill never actually spawned. What was Bethesda thinking when they actually decided to release this game as it was? The fact that they're asking even more money to get the entire game (DLC) is insulting.
The sidequests suck and many of them aren't original. While there are some sidequests that are pretty good, being told to kill someone for some guy or find some object for some guy gets a little old. In a lot of sidequests, you can ask for more caps, but the huge abundance of ammo you can pick up and sell makes this kind of pointless outside of the very beginning of the game.
The plot, while it's not terrible, isn't very interesting. Perhaps giving more than four options (that all do the same thing but one or more of them offends someone) would have made sense. While there are several endings depending on which faction you side with, the storyline is exactly the same until near the very end. The DLC doesn't really get any better.
It's not a terrible game, but the asking price of $59.93 for an unfinished, buggy base game plus DLC is ludicrous, and there's no amount of money that would make me sell my soul to recommend that.

To start: I didn't enjoy Starbound when it first came out and since the stable updates ran dry. Since the game finally now had one, it was time to give it another try. The game has shown improvement since its early days and feels more fleshed out as a game, but it still falls short in feeling too placid of a game.
The game feels too static. The most common form of threats are planet fauna, which act too realistically like animals to be engaging. Some are neutral towards you - that's fine. But most are just casually patrolling and only aggro you when you get in their view. While that would be fine for some enemies, the problem is these are all the enemies. Take Terraria, for example: Enemies want to kill you. They spawn somewhere off-screen and give their 100% best effort to track you down and murder you. This gives a sense of alertness and danger that isn't seen in Starbound. The fact that events also aren't present in Starbound currently - things like Terraria's blood moon and invasions - makes the worlds seem simple and lifeless. I also don't like the idea of planet threat levels being related to their biomes. The most dangerous planets (and with the best loot) will ALWAYS be dead/volcanic planets. While it makes sense, more variety with different threat level biomes would be appreciated.
Another minus is the fact there doesn't seem to be any point to villages. Right now they only exist to expand your decorative prowess and to trade with some of the folks, but even trading has its downside of being almost pointless. Some of the vanity items are nice at least.
As for what it improved on: Actual quests and missions now. Although a lot of them are "get me x ores" or "get me decorative item y" it feels nice to know they're fleshing out the quest system into something with potential. Some of the missions can be pretty challenging going solo, so multiplayer is a big help for most of them. The ship upgrades are also a welcome addition and I hope more ship-centric events come out of them.
The game is more fleshed out than it was roughly a year ago. If somehow more life could be brought to a number of planets, villages, and the game in general, it could feel more like a Terraria successor. Just have to break that barrier, Chucklefish. For now it gets a recommendation because it's fun to play with friends, has a better sense of progression than it used to, and looks to be more promising in terms of future updates.

I would personally reccomend this game to almost anyone new to the MMORPG genre. The game is easily accesible to most players, and quickly and effectively introduces the rules of the game. However, this game may not be for everyone, such as people who are familiar with the genre. There is a ton of looting in the game, and I mean a TON.  Any dungeon requires you to go through your inventory, just trying to figure what the ehll you should do with your items. It takes a lot of intuition and comparing, which may turn of new players. If you do get over that "learning curve", then you'll be able to have fun while looting. Also, it's very difficult for you to get truly good stuff. For me at least, the appeal of the game kinda died out at the 230 hour mak, which is still extremely good on the game's part, since it kept me fully invested for so long. After you get to a certain point in the game, it get's a little bit pay to win, with a ton of grinding involved. First of all, you have to find a club that is extremely active, so you get have a regular way of getting through the shadow towers, and then you have to spend time doing the challenges so you can get dragon coins and dragon chests. It becomes somewhat infuriating when you are just waiting for an hour to pass so the challenge starts, only to complete and get a pitiful amount of dragon souls or coins (To clarify, dragon souls and dragon coins are used to get the various dragon mounts). It feels like it's pay to win, and if you don't decide to pay, then it devolves into a endless grindfest, making it relatively boring. In conclusion, I would reccomend this game to people looking for some quick and easy fun, or for people who have a lot of time and money to invest in the game.

You play an intergalatic bug-catcher.  I BS you not.
You explore your crash-landed world, build a butterfly net, and catch 2 bugs from your planet.  You build a bedroom and put the bugs in jars, leaving them in your bedroom.
You dig to the center of the planet to repair your ship so you can travel within your galaxy, getting more bugs from nearby planets.  You catch two more bugs from a desert planet and an ocean planet.  You now have 6 bugs and have to make a second shelf for more bugs in jars.
You save a mining colony from ugly, fleshy mutants.  It is a violent struggle.  They repay you by repairing your ship for intergalatic travel.  You harvest fuel from a moon.  You travel to different galaxies, exploring for bugs.  Along ythe way you find temples, tombs, villages, underground dungeons, and a variety.  You steal their furniture.
You now have a bug collection room, complete with shelves.  You have to start creating a catalogue and squinting to make sure you don't have two of the same bug displayed.  You've built more rooms for the furniture along the way.
In order to keep building your nice furniture and showing off your travels, you have a forest of trees and cacti on your left.  On your right, you have a farm of fruits, veggies, and coffee that spans five systems.
You have statues of Avian bird-gods, walls made out of dense "plantstone" that makes it looks like a forest, and a sandstone room filled with bookshelves raided from the robot race.
You expand your bug collection, color-coordinating them and moving them to the basement, since it is easier to expand as you find more bugs.  You make more lights so you can see these bugs.
You track planets to find the right ore for armor/robots/applicances.  You make a radioactive protective suit.  You use said suit to explore radioactive planets.  You hope these bugs glow in the dark.

Definitely one of my favorite games on Steam. I love it because it serves three purposes.
First, it's a great shmup. You have three weapons, including a sword and "bits" that lock on enemy targets, surround them and shoot them. All your weapons can be used with a destructive EX attack, which replaces the bombs you usually see on other shmups. You also have a rechargeable shield. There are no power-ups to pick up, but that's a good thing here.
Second, this game is perfect for fans of mecha anime. You control a mech yourself and will occasionally fight other mechs. All the characters in the game are voiced in Japanese. If you don't know the language, you'll need to read the subtitles while you play. The dialog is pretty anime-like.
Third, this game is really bullet hell for beginners. You have a prologue mission that teaches you the basics and then you also have several tutorials that will teach you every single aspect of the special mech you'll be controlling and even how scoring works. I think the normal difficulty level is pretty easy, it only gets harder on the final stages. So, after you complete normal, you'll unlock the hard difficulty level and that's where you'll face a real challenge. Seriously, if you never played a bullet hell before, this should be your first.

This game is disappointing and tiring.
The gameplay is not uniform. Once you watch a 10 minutes long cut scene and in the next instant you have to make a split second decision that affects your story. Not even enough to locate a keys on a keyboard. Sometimes you don't even know you have to do something. Movie just stops, and you have to guess that you're back in control. Sometimes this controll is limited to just one button, moving forward.
There is a lot of difficult choices in the game but more often than not, choices make no sense. This is no rpg. This is a train simulator. You ride along tracks and occasionally you can choose to turn right or left. Often there is even no way to guess where that would lead you. You cannot examine your options. Even if it's a rare occasion where you have time to do so.
Dialogues are similar. Sometimes there is just no right option. And sometimes even if you think there is a right option the tone of your voice is different than you'd expect. For example instead of calming someone it sounds like you are blaming them.
There is also problem with pacing. Once there is nothing to do. You spend a few minutes just looking around for that one action that would move the story forward and it's just boring. On other occasions there is so many things happening at once that you are just not prepared to handle it. Fortunately in the most hectic parts you have more that one layer of quick time events you can fail. However some of these QTEs can affect your story so don't count on that.
In conclusion this game reminds me a little of Resident Evil 4. Especially that one moment where you watch a 3 minutes long cut scene, you put down your controller, take some popcorn, a guy jumps on you with a knife, press LT+RT to not die. You died. And now imagine a whole game based around this concept.
This game would be better if it was just released as a movie. And even then, story is not that great. Just watch it on youtube if you must.

It looks nice enough, if very generic, but the music is utterly forgettable and the dialogue is incessant and literally never shuts up. The characters babble on about nonsense for the entire game, and of course, it's all in Japanese.

To all the upsides of the first XCOM reincarnation this game adds better graphics and more customization. But there are some significant downsides too:

I've played this game multiple times now. After beating it on my first playthrough on Veteran difficulty, I tried doing Ironman runs, but I rarely even go to magnetic weapons or plated armor (tier 1 upgrades). Frustrated, I deleted the game (even though I really enjoyed the first normal playthrough). When Long War 2 came out, I reinstalled it and tried Long War 2, but I quickly realized that Long War 2 is nothing for me, so I started a normal playthrough again, this time on Commander though. With everything I learned before, especially from my Ironman runs, I managed to get through commander fairly easily, so before completing that playthrough, I started another one on Commander Ironman. And I beat the game.
This playthrough was one of the most satisfying, terrifying and intense experiences I've ever had. In the past it always seemed stupid to me to have a mode like this for a game that is so RNG heavy, but if you know what you're doing you can play around that. And the game tells you that Commander is only for people who already know the game.
I also found out about all the little secrets the developers put into the game to make it as unfrustrating as possible. For example when you miss shots, an invisible counter goes up and increases your chances for your next shot until you hit something. When you are in combat against an enemy squad or two, the game will make other enemy squads move away, so you don't have to fight too many enemies simultaneously, and when there are too many enemies active at the same time, not all of them will try to kill you. Some will just run towards some cover, other will go into overwatch.
There is still plenty of times where you'll feel like the game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting you. You will miss 90% shots, you will get hit from enemies even though you were behind high cover and the enemy very far away.
The game also still has tons of bugs, some really annoying bugs and even some that affect the gameplay in a very bad way. Once I had a soldier on a roof, which got destroyed. The soldier fell down, but then got stuck in terrain. I couldn't move that soldier away from there, and it was an escort mission, so I HAD to evacuate that soldier. Luckily I could free that soldier with a grenade (which did damage to him), but that's obviously stupid. The game still struggles sometimes with performence, sometimes the game gets stuck for a few seconds because it doesn't know what it's supposed to do or something. When you click "Make all Utility Items available" the mission will just cancel a lot of times. There are multiple places where sounds can get stuck. The list goes on and on.
You have to keep in mind though how big and complex this game is. The game offers a great amount of enemy types right at the start, and for most games, that would be fine. No one would really complain if those were the only enemies in the game and if they just got more health and damage later. But no, the game keeps introducing new enemies right until the final mission, which is really impressive in my opinion. Those new enemies are also extremely crazy with devastating abilities and tons of health, but the thing is your soldiers will get SO powerful during the game that you will still be able to completely destroy them, and this is just awesome. It feels so satisfying, because you actually made so much progress with all your soldiers AND the enemies did as well.
The systems of the game are really well thought out. The base building, the world map, the avatar project. There is a timer that starts after a few hours, which if it runs out, you loose the game. But the timer is really generous and it is just there so that you can't just build and research until you get extremely powerful, but are forced to go for the enemy blacksite facilities every now and then. But as I said, the time is generous, and it brings a strategic element to your base building, like in RTS games, where you have to decide how greedy you want to be and what path to focus on. And there are plenty of ways to delay or lengthen the timer btw.
I think X-Com 2 is a brilliant game. Even the story was really cool. The character customization is very impressive for a game like this and makes your soldiers much more important to you. Also nice soundtrack.

This game truly is an underappreciated gem. I know the $20 price tag seems a tad steep for a 2D mech shooter, but I really think it's worth every penny. The controls take a bit of getting used to, but I have no sympathy for people who got turned off by the controls at the start. They're 100% functional and I've had no issues at all since I figured out all the little quirks. Graphics are good, combat is satisfying, vehicle and weapon diversity is great, and the tone and atmosphere are very well realized. It's by far one of the most well thought through indie games I've ever played. A relativly simple core gameplay system is surrounded by very well realized framework. the maps are richly detailed, featuring farms, monorail systems, neon-lit entertainment districts, train yards, highways choked with abandoned cars, and more. Every vehicle, weapon, and pilot comes with it's own little lore entry, and the nature of the setting gets more and more clear the further you progress through the game. Even if you're not much one for lore, the thought they put into the setting still fills out the gameplay like mortar around bricks, and it all comes together in a simple (but not as simple as it looks) but engaging and well crafted mech shooter.
In short, I can't recomend it highly enough. If you believe in supporting quality indie games, this is a must buy. It may not be for everyone, but I think all but the most unpleasable of gamers will find $20 worth of fun in this game.

In the vast ocean of potential content that is the fallout universe, one could take a dive into Fallout 4 without the fear of getting wet.
The game you've been waiting for for so long has finally come! ... and it sucks.
THe story feels very rushed and lack luster. I have no relationship to shaun yet the game wants me to care about him to the point of risking my life to find him. Factions are simple and exceedingly boring. Very black and white. If story or interesting factions are important to you I'd suggest Fallout:New Vegas instead.
Pretty much all RPG elements are gone or neuterd. Working within the confines of the character you made are gone, now you can level up anything and be all powerful in one character. Gone are the interesting dialogue choices. You get four options, of which 2 are yes,1 is no, and 1 is give me a little bit more info. You also have no idea what you're going to say since the dialogue options are cut down to give you the general idea, and fail horridly.
The world itself is really boring and shallow. Best example is Concord. Bethesda built it up like some awesome city that would introduce you to the wonderful world of Fallout 4. Instead it has nothing in it, a quest that gives you the most annoying companion ever,and some raiders. Yawn. This is how the rest of the world is. You have two major settlements that are nowhere near as interesting as Rivet city or Megaton, or New Vegas. They barely have that many quests or interesting parts to them.
They even have some elements of Bostons gangs and they don't even expand on it! How can you mess that up!?
Settlement building is clunky and feels incomplete. Once again another half baked idea rushed into a game that is trying to compete with EA for least amount of content on release.
Graphics are okay, but the visuals are bland and don't feel to me like they fit the Fallout universe. Yes Fallout has its cartoony side, however that doesn't mean everything needs to be cartoony.
DLC is a mess. You get two major DLC and a load of smaller ones that add either settlement stuff or a tiny quest with an addition to the game.
Far Harbor is pretty awesome. Still bland and shallow, but my god the idea and setting are awesome. Having extras with Nick just makes it better.
Nuka World is probably the best as it adds the most, and finally lets you be the bad guy in this game!
The two main small dlcs add the ability to build a robot and the ability to build a vault. Things that should have been in the main game and have boring dlcs to go with them.
Gunplay is the only improvement in this game, upgrading your weapons is interesting, if not dull and simple, and fighting is smoother than before.
The one thing they did do right is cooking. Best cooking so far in a Fallout game.
All in all I'd say get F3 or New Vegas if you want a Fallout RPG. Get this if you want Call of Duty in an open world.

On first glance this game looks like a space-themed top-down actioner in the spirit of Hotline Miami and others.
But this glance couldn't be more wrong.
Through the use of a pause mode the game gives way more room to planning and tactical decision making, while (mostly) taking out the need for split-second reflexes. You are always able to try and make the best out of a difficult situation by cleverly and creatively utilizing the various gadgets at your disposal, which leads to a much more cerebral gameplay approach.
The 'roguelite' elements in the game (random but persistant map with permadeath for player characters) help with keeping the action tense but never too frustrating. The game progress through station liberations works kind of like a semi-random technology tree, where you can plan your progress to try and optimize the possible loadout for your current and future characters.
Overall the game is very fun and, through randomisation, offers a very high amount of replay value.
Highly recommended.

I remember hearing good things about this game around the time it came out, but never had a chance to play it. Now that it's in glorious HD I can say all those good things I heard were true, this really is a great game. I wish Capcom still made games like this today...
It has some annoyances. It's not the best PC port, and as a result is best played on a controller. The menus are clunky and too difficult to exit sometimes (yes, that's a thing). Issun (this game's Navi) is freaking annoying - like really, you don't have to tell me every little thing I'm doing, and at no point in the game did I like having this dumb character attached to me. Some cutscenes have way too much dialogue, and you can't skip all dialogue in this game - some of it you have to sit there and watch it slowly type away. I can read the faster dialogue just fine. There's also a 15 minute cutscene at the beginning! So be prepared for a small movie.
The game's also pretty easy, I died once in my entire playthrough and that was because my controller died in a section of the game with stomach acid. The bosses are creative, and luckily most of the puny fights are skippable meaning Okami avoids the Final Fantasy tedium of having to fight the same enemies over and over again. Okami is really good at giving you new things to fight throughout the game.
But the story is great, the HD graphics are great even though the camera will argue with you sometimes, and the music is great. Pretty much everything is great about this game besides the above excusable annoyances - it is an old game, after all.

Pros: Stable, Smooth graphics and gameplay, nice effects
Cons: clunky controls (should have options for gamepad), lack of voice acting, lack of direction, top down view is disorienting
Thoughts:
It's easy to tell a lot of passion and effort was put into this game, it's just not my cup of tea and it definitly has some interface issues. I rarely post reviews but felt this one merited one.
I would like the "pause" menu to be called something else. "pause" kills immersion. Also, instead of pausing in and pausing out, how about an option for "holding" the key (or button/trigger if gamepad can be added) and then let go to get back into the action. There's the additional, disorienting effect of having the pause menu but also having a slowed-down framerate whenever I come freshly out of combat. Maybe this is just me. This was executed beautifully in DOOM with the weapon wheel.
Why are there cooldown timers? Just require a reload key'button from outside the pause menu to remind me that I'm empty. I forget about the cooldown and since they are different for every weapon I stutter over my tactics everytime I change weapons. Why have a primary and a secondary? You can only fire/use one weapon at a time, and you can change to ANY weapon at ANY time from the pause menu. Make weapon selection mouse wheel scroll or pad/bumper selection from the gamepad.
Switching between mouse controls for the pod and WASD for interior shop/station control also clunky and kills immersion. Again, with gamepad it could be done seamlessly between two joysticks so I never have to go from a nice smooth mouse to a Cherry MX mechanical key slap.
I think the reason for this review is that I don't want to write this game off, I think it has a LOT of potential and I'd like to see it progress, but for now I's just too unplayable for me, and I can't recommend it.

This game is disappointing and tiring.
The gameplay is not uniform. Once you watch a 10 minutes long cut scene and in the next instant you have to make a split second decision that affects your story. Not even enough to locate a keys on a keyboard. Sometimes you don't even know you have to do something. Movie just stops, and you have to guess that you're back in control. Sometimes this controll is limited to just one button, moving forward.
There is a lot of difficult choices in the game but more often than not, choices make no sense. This is no rpg. This is a train simulator. You ride along tracks and occasionally you can choose to turn right or left. Often there is even no way to guess where that would lead you. You cannot examine your options. Even if it's a rare occasion where you have time to do so.
Dialogues are similar. Sometimes there is just no right option. And sometimes even if you think there is a right option the tone of your voice is different than you'd expect. For example instead of calming someone it sounds like you are blaming them.
There is also problem with pacing. Once there is nothing to do. You spend a few minutes just looking around for that one action that would move the story forward and it's just boring. On other occasions there is so many things happening at once that you are just not prepared to handle it. Fortunately in the most hectic parts you have more that one layer of quick time events you can fail. However some of these QTEs can affect your story so don't count on that.
In conclusion this game reminds me a little of Resident Evil 4. Especially that one moment where you watch a 3 minutes long cut scene, you put down your controller, take some popcorn, a guy jumps on you with a knife, press LT+RT to not die. You died. And now imagine a whole game based around this concept.
This game would be better if it was just released as a movie. And even then, story is not that great. Just watch it on youtube if you must.

Ok, so make no mistake, this game is brutal - once you get your head around that it's awesome, but it can be tough getting to where you're loving it instead of throwing your hands in the air - especially if like me, you want to play in Iron Man mode (perma-death).
I played XCOM 1 & its expansion to completion at Normal difficulty (Iron Man), and it honestly feels like XCOM 2 starts where there one left off in terms of difficulty. I would honestly recommend to anyone who hasn't played XCOM 1 all the way through to start with that game first - otherwise you may not get the practice you need before you give up with this one.
Now I always play XCOM in Iron Man mode, because I believe its the way the game is meant to be played - not because I like pain or think I'm l33t, but because I detest games where you reload over and over to excuse bad luck. Not everyone has this playstyle, but if you do then DO NOT BELIEVE the descriptions of the difficulty levels! After 13 restarts on Normal (Iron Man), I finally conceded and started on Rookie level (Iron Man), and am finally able to enjoy the game. My advice is to anyone playing this game for the first time, play it on Rookie, and only if you beat it easily go back and choose a harder level.
So why is this game so brutal compared to XCOM 1?
Ignore people saying it's broken, or unfair, or completely random - it's not (I've encountered only 1 mission bug so far in 33 hours playtime). Nor do you need a completely different play style to XCOM 1 to beat it - unless your XCOM 1 play style was to either rush into everything or take 50 turns to complete a map. It's just quicker to punish your mistakes, and punish your mistakes it will.
There are many subtle things to be learned here that you may have only vaguely cared about in XCOM 1. Don't move too far ahead in one go - being isolated is often fatal. Don't group your troops too close together either. Worry A LOT about bringing extra enemies into a fight you have under control. Learn to ambush your first contact with concealment whenever possible. Learn to use grenades and grenadiers to shred armour first. Learn flanking, but don't flank and die. Learn that sometimes you HAVE to rush to your objective despite the risks, because NOT rushing is going to lose everyone. And so on and so on.
The learning curve of these critical subtleties is very steep, and I would say even if you've played XCOM 1, not because you have. The only thing you need to unlearn from XCOM 1 is being careless. :)
But what's REALLY brutal in this game, is deaths, particularly at the start of this game. Losing a Rookie or Squaddie early on in XCOM 1 was no big deal - you'd be winning the first 20 missions easily anyway. But the vicious circle even one death early on unleashes in XCOM 2 is harsh - even if you get out of that mission, from each moment thereafter you are behind the curve, trying to have soldiers with enough health and abilities to survive the next mission, and there's a good chance you will NEVER catch up, and everything you develop will be too late and too slow. I would go as far as to say if you lose more than 1 of your 'best' soldiers in the first 10 missions or so, you're going to really struggle.
So my recommendation? Buy this game, set difficulty to Rookie, and if you loved XCOM 1 you will love this more - there are so many neat polished touches over XCOM 1 and the added customisations of the soldiers is an XCOM 1 player's dream.
Just expect to restart (or reload), and do that again and again, and again ... until you learn how to be more careful. :)

It's hard to recommend or condemn this game for what it is.  It is a direct port of the mobile title. So, if you're used to playing on Facebook, you might miss a few optimizations.  If you're used to playing on mobile, you will confront the obvious screen size change (with the obvious sliding scale on all the graphics) coupled with using a mouse instead of your finger.  Going from a 5" screen to a large monitor without some form of optimization makes the mobile nature of the title VERY obvious.
As for whether or not you'll like the game, YMMV.  If you've already played it on other platforms, then you might as well install it and link your account for free achievements.  Maybe you want it just because your computer is faster than your phone or tablet.  If you've never played it before, just keep in mind that this is very much a collectible game where you either play fairly regularly to keep rankings and participate in events to get free characters and such, while knowing that those that put a lot of money into the game will always be better than you, or you're the one putting a lot of money into it.  I've put some money into the game, I admit it, but that's because I enjoy the game AND play it regularly.  However, if you play regularly and don't pay money, you will have plenty of chances to get purple and gold rank characters.  It may just take more work and time.

Brigador is possibly the most underrated game of all time.
Personally, I'm not too familiar with games of this style - e.g., I don't even know what genre this is, exactly - so I can't easily analogize "If you like game X, then you'll love Brigador."  I don't know what game could fill-in that blank; this game has been a very novel experience for me.
However, there are at least three things I can say with confidence about this game...
1.) This game has a steep learning curve for at least the first hour.  For me, this game was somewhat "inaccessible" at first.  It was hard for me to learn, and it was hard for me to get into it.
2.) This game is best for players who enjoy high-difficulty games in which they need to replay levels over and over before they get that satisfying buzz once they finally beat it.  I am that sort of player.
3.) This game just *feels* cool.  I can't pinpoint what it is exactly, but it just feels so freaking sick.  I also love the retro aesthetic.

One thing worth mentioning is that since the game was made in '98, it's bound to have its traditional 90's computer game look and feel, with the outdated graphics, weird choices, loading screens everywhere and some halls just remain entirely empty because of engine limitations. The game still holds up as a classic, something everyone should play.

This is actually one of the most fun RPG games I've played in a while. Don't let the graphics fool you because it actually fits with the style of the game. An interesting mix between Uplink and Street Hacker, for the price of ~10 USD is definitely worth checking out.
The game is pretty fun, some things require attention to detail and logical thinking, and the humor is pretty good!
However, the game launched with a very bad bug which might make your save useless: if you try to make two missions at a time, you won't be able to complete the first one. This can simply kill your save.
Also, even though the presentation is well done and the interface looks pretty, I don't see much advance over what other Hacking games did before (Uplink was released in 2001), so you really should approach this with caution. The biggest difference here is being able to use both a GUI and a Console - which is good news.
This doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the game, of course. But it does dissapoint if you expected anything more than that.
I haven't finished the game yet, due to the bug that probably broke my savegame. But about the plot: it's decently intriguing and will make you want to uncover all the secrets, as a hacking game should.
So even though I ended up pretty disappointed - it's 2015, yet there's little news here. Even Street Hacker, which is a decade old and terribly programmed, had deeper features; and Uplink had a more compelling gameplay and story - there's still some fun to be had and some jokes/moments actually made me laugh or smile.
I do recommend waiting for a patch before playing it, though. So rush it on your own risk.

A lighthearted story about a tomboy,who attends magical school near a small countryside town.Well,it's almost normal school,if you thought of Hogwarts,then you're a little off =) the point is,all students need an "elemental stone" to utilize magic.The problem is,it's not a cheap thing.Luckily for our little protagonist,there's supposed to be one in the cave near the town,or so the gossip says...That's a beggining of the story.
As for the gameplay-imagine metroidvania with some rather harsh platforming elements(harsh for those who don't know what NES-era platformers was like,that is ;) ),interesting combat system,which strangely resembles that of a "Tales of" series a lil' bit, to do any special movies you need to tap buttons,not hold them,which is  GREAT for keyboard users like myself.There's chain specials,combos,blocking and jumping and rolling...and you need to utilize all of that to stay alive on higher difficulty,at least.Also,there's a party members others than little sword-girl,in prologue only one available is Sana,which is your typical "cleric-type"-healing,killing and occasionly mashing everything close enough with her stick.You can give her a set of commands,which again force you to remember one of Namco's famous RPGs,because battle strategies menu is virtually the same.Did I mention that you can switch between party members any time,which will not only be useful in fights,but outside them as well,because this game also drawn inspiration from "Lost Vikings" or some game similar.Arche(that's the name of a little tomboy,yes)can push objects around,while Sana(cleric),can walk underwater.Both of them can pull levers,press buttons,or stand still if need be.Well,you get the
CONCLUSION IF YOU WISH TO SKIP THE WALL OF TEXT HERE:Metroidvania meets Lost Vikings and happily goes on a little epic quest.I strongly suggests you to try it.This game is nothing revolutionary,and it wasn't meant to be.Instead,it's just very,very fun.And that is what people play games for,right?

Darkest Dungeon really scratches my inner demons with satisfaction while delivering powerful dosages of stress and anxiety from the prospect of losing my fragile adventurers to the abominations that lurk around the corrupted hamlet and seek to crush their bodies and psyche alike.
Red Hook Studios delivered a solid yet merciless dungeon crawler with RPG elements, absolutely dripping with quality art by Chris Bourassa, eerie sounds, superb voice acting by Wayne June and overall a great haunting atmosphere. All accompanied by simple yet engaging gameplay.
The core of the game is party composition and keeping your adventurers healthy and well prepared in terms of equipment, consumables, skills and mental stability in accordance to whatever hell hole you're putting them through. Battle is done with a turn-based positioning system that dictates which adventurer classes go where and how they destroy their foes.
While out of combat but inside a dungeon, a careful eye must seek out traps, rekindle torches to light the way and diminish stress, decide either to open the abandoned chest in your path or leave it be, with the possibility of being rewarded with loot or infected with a debuffing disease, for example.
The only moment when the game eases up (a bit) is in town when upgrading the several buildings that improve the survival chances of the adventurers and ease their poor existence in this terrible place through relaxation or curing their physical and psychological ailments.
Often, in key moments, your late ancestor will melancholically narrate the events occurring, along with commenting some highlights of your dark quest. All from beyond the grave.
Once you've embarked on enough missions on a certain area, a boss must be slain. While your surviving adventurers toughen up, they'll eventually have to face the ultimate evil of eldritch, cthuloid nature and cleanse the hamlet of this wickedness once and for all.
I'd only point out the lack of more interactivity within the dungeon itself. More kinds of traps, rooms, obstacles and perhaps even puzzles and riddles. Just to make the crawl more varied.
Darkest Dungeon truly is one of, if not THE darkest dungeon crawler around in all its aspects and in the right way and never has the old saying "making the best out of a bad situation" been more relevant. For after losing adventurer after adventurer (or corpses, as the game suggests) to wicked monsters or episodes or pure dementia, you might start to question if maybe your own sanity hasn't dwindled a bit...
Maybe.

Starbound is a resource gathering, sandbox, adventure game. The difficulty curb is compitently put together, the music is nice and atmospheric, the entire experience feels much more like an adventure than it did before. It actually encourages exploration more than it did before which is something that the game desperately needed. New areas are opened as you progress through the game and unlock new abilities in a metroid fashion. (For example, you CAN visit the fire planet but good luck surviving without the fire protective suit, which unlocks more of the game in a very organic way) You now have missions which require you to visit all types of planets which is good for experiencing the entirety of the game. However each of these points has an asterisk that I would like to explain for you now.
The difficulty curb is compitently put together that is true. Never once did I die in an area more than once or twice, nor did it become too easy that I never took a pause for thought when deciding how many bandages I was to bring on each mission. There's just one problem I have with it and that's the combat is on the whole a boring experience in which my eyes glaze over. I get no satisfaction from killing enemies because all they drop are pixels (money) or weapons which are very seldom better than the one I already have and none of them really change up how I play the game or bring anything meaningful or interesting to the table besides an attack rate twices as fast and 5 times weaker. So the combat is virtually meaningless. There's really only one way to dispose of enemies. Fighting them head on. Nothing else. Sure you can take a couple of shots but that uses stamina and your just much better off using the sword. Take another sandbox for example like Skyrim or Dark Souls. Fighting enemies in Skyrim is gratifying because you can go about it most any way you like: sneaky, shield/ sword, dual wield magic, snipe, let a randomly spawned dragon kill everything, turn one of the enemies over to your side, etc. The entire experience being made all the better because of what abilities you've gained up to that point and the fact that you can tackle it in any way you like but there will always be a best course of action that you don't HAVE to take. So if you're bored of fighting enemies with magic, you could always try sneaking or shield and swording or whatever giving the combat great lastability because taking on a new fighting style has it's own rewards which can be gained through leveling up that ability by using it. In Dark Souls the gratification comes from the fact that the bosses and even some of the enemies are incredibly difficult to kill, so when you finally do kill them it's a very triumphant feeling. The combat is made slightly easier by objects you collect throughout the area which is rewarding of exploration but none of these upgrades really break the game to the point that the combat gets boring. Of these two methods, I'd go for the skyrim approach. Making your enemies harder to kill will only frustrate most people to the point they stop playing because your game has been desidgned to be more of an easy disposal of enemies, whereas having stealth elements or ability to use the futuristic equivalent of magic and having levels for each method of combat would add an enjoyable dimension to your sandbox's combat and keep people playing. Also maybe have enemies drop something other than useless pixels or useless weapons. Like maybe occasionally one of them could drop an item that triggers a sidequest.
The game does encourage exploration but not in a very clever way. It sends you to different places because that's the mission. Why am I going to this moon? Because the mission says I need fuel. Why am I scowering this planet for this ONE thing I need to turn into this guy? Because the mission says so. How about encouraging exploration for the player instead of doing something because the game tells you to? For example okay so we have this fetch quest here but once you get there you find there's a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of stuff to do instead of this planet being like every other planet you've been to thusfar and there's plenty to do in the way of sandbox mess aroundy funness. Like having fun raiding an avian dungeon that happened to be on that planet with the afformentioned combat system. Or for god's sakes let someone have a recipe or item that's actually useful to us and for god's sake^2 let us sell stuff. I NEVER once EVER bought anything in this game and that's just bad game design. Or how about each town has a loyalty meter and you can increase loyalty by completing missions given out in each hub town or even upgrading their houses. Put your creative engine sandbox to work for the game play. And unlocking more loyalty makes more of the town's merchant's inventory available unlocking access to bigger and better weapons and items? Sure maybe this will reduce one's desire to explore the universe if the player gets too invested in a singular town but as it stands the sandbox is boring to play through and exploration is already discouraged enough because the animation of going from one planet to another is tedious and annoyingly long. It might take a lot of coding but you could probably spice up the travel by having space battles randomly occur in FTL situations and they become easier as you upgrade your ship. It actually seems like missing an opportunity when you have a space game that is played primarily on the surface of planets. I might as well be playing terraria.
Now for the missions. There are two varieties in the game. The type that you can get and then access from your ship after you've proven you're worthy by arriving in the required armor set which encourages you to mine for resources if only to make the game progress. Realistically though the mission encourages little else, but it's definitely a step in the right direction and a few steps above the other type of missions you can take. And we're getting to em now. Fetch quests. Hey you remember that one tiny little item you saw as decoration in that avian village 5 planets ago and now you can't quite remember which planet it's on because every one of them is the ♥♥♥♥ing same? I'd like you to go fetch me one. So now you have a choice to make. Try and find out which planet you think you might have remembered seeing this one inocuous thing in, go to the wikia and find out what it is they're talking about and where you can find the thing they're talking about and maybe if you're lucky the item will actually be in the randomly generated village or dungeon because sometimes it isn't, OR put down the game, stop playing and forget about it entirely. I eventually chose the third option because I was tired of youtubing what I needed to find and where I could find them only to find out that sometimes they're there and sometimes they aren't. A quest marker wouldn't go amiss. Or how about this instead, require of us to go out and get resources in order to make a scanner for the ship which allows us to scan a planet before even travelling to it to see if it will be worth it to us to waste our time watching the entire animation it takes to get us there. While I'm thinking about it ship upgrades plays hand in hand with the space battles idea. You could do sort of an FTL battle system. Make us choose between which parts of the ship we want to upgrade or boost in order to maximize our effectiveness. Recruit different species for different benefits. Keep them around by doing missions that your crew gives you to increase loyalty and reduce likelihood of mutiny. And if you do lose a space battle you still manage to get to the planet. Your ship just gets downgraded and you lose crew loyalty.
The game is still very much a beta and has a lot of room to improve. Their latest update shows they know what they're doing but a few smaller updates more frequently would be better.
