It should be noted that controller support, atleast in the case for the ds4 in my experience, is well supported. The issue at first was that pressing x or o while the game loads does not activate the controller. Instead, one must press start. Seems odd but not a dealbreaker.
As for the game itself, its most certainly a fun game but i do have my gripes. Although my play hours seem low ive played for much longer in offline mode for personal circumstances. I have yet to complete the game but i think ive played enough this far to make a fair judgement.
First and foremost, the game has TONS of collectibles. You'll constantly find yourself backtracking to collect praise or stray beads after collecting a new brush technique. You have to feed animals, rejuvenate trees, and much more in order to collect praise, which you can call the equivalent to "exp" of sorts used to upgrade a trait of your choice. Praise can also be acquired from story progression for that matter. The issue is how ever that the amount you get for each one is rather small, counterbalanced by the sheer number of collectible praise. At some point it becomes a bit of a chore that takes away from being able to enjoy the main game. Of course you can just do any praise collecting thats happens to be in your path but why gimp yourself for the lategame? At the very least the game has lists of sorts for some of these collectibles, but not all of them, such as for rejuvenating clovers.
The game is also bogged a bit more by constant hand holding. Occasionally some hand holding is needed. For example, when your given the crescent brush technique to make it night time, youre supposed to make a simple curved line from top to bottom. I kept making a full backwards c from bottom to top, frustrated until the game pointed out exactly how to make the proper stroke. Japanese stroke order is serious business. Beyond that however youre constantly given text explaining everything even after its already obvious what solution is needed for a given circumstance. Some dialogue here and there cant be sped up, and constant story dialogue that tends to be needlessly long is peppered through out the game. I feel the game could be trimmed about a quarter of the total play time just by removing needless text and dialogue.
The game is also relatively easy. You'll hardly find yourself struggling against encountered enemies and bosses. Bosses tend to be slow and their gimmick as obvious as broad daylight. The game doesnt quite require the technical skill in combat as say zelda for instance. Bear in mind ive only fought 4 actual bosses thus far so perhaps its to early to say that other bosses may not require more skill, but when i havent gone below 75% of my health once the entire game the difficulty becomes questionable. Its laughable that theres a mechanic that once fully upgraded allows you to be revived up to 4 times(if i understand correctly) during a fight. I have to wonder if the team behind the game wasnt sure if they wanted a younger or older demoographic for the game during development, or if the play testers have never touched an action game once in their life.
Anyways, for the modest price of the game id still reccomend picking up the game. Even for a zeldaesque game it rivals smaller and older jrpgs for completion time. Enjoy the game and take your time making your progress while you enjoy the beautiful visuals of okami.

I want to love this game, it has so much going on for it, but in reality it's just your throwing a dice with every single action that you take.
The whole premise of the game is based on RNG (read: luck).
If you're the type of person to love gambling, then yes, this might be a feature that would not bother you, and in that case yes, I can recommend this to you.
But in general, or at least for me, I prefer a game that rewards me for my skill, for me doing good at the game. If I make a mistake, I learn from it, and do better the next time that I try.
In the case of Darkest Dungeon, though, I could do everything right, and still, purely out of a bad dice throw, I can lose everything I worked for hours upon hours. And in some cases, even if I do everything wrong, just out of pure luck I could still progress, which is not exactly what I would call rewarding.
TL;DR
Darkest Dungeon does not properly reward players for being good, but instead leaves too much to be decided by RNG.

Codename 47 is certainly an interesting nut to crack. I'm playing the Hitman series for the first time and doing it in order, so I can't compare to later games in the series yet, but I think this game is an experience worth having, even if it's not something I'd say everyone should rush out and buy.
The game's best and worst feature is that you can't save. In some levels, the more medium-sized ones that are more along the lines of "here's the level, here's your weapons, kill this target", this can make for a very tense, suspenseful stealth experience and you can find yourself resorting to some interesting tactics to just try and survive a minute longer, but as the levels get longer and longer, and as you experience levels that have certain things to be done in a specific order, it becomes incredibly tedious and frustrating. It definitely comes from the 80's school of game design that wants you to die over and over again until you get it exactly right, so think Cuphead if some of the levels took 3 times as long to master and you're on the right track for this game's difficulty. You do get two "lives" but the enemy's suspicion of you doesn't reset so you're still in a bad spot if you died.
I love the basic mechanics of this, the core controls are pretty bizarre and odd, but once I got into it, it felt fine and even useful in some places. I like that you can detatch your crosshair from the direction your character is looking then pop it back into place, that came in handy for lining up some rapid headshots in a couple situations. I loved wearing disguises and slipping into places I'm not supposed to be, and trying to take out enemies without anyone noticing. Every weapon is really satisfying to use too, which is nice. I also liked that you get penalized for killing innocents, which gives you some incentive to play creatively and try to keep things on the down-low, but also have to keep people who can catch you alive. Each level also has a great atmosphere, bolstered by an amazing soundtrack that fits each area well, and some levels, such as the Hotel look surprisingly nice even today.
The AI can be both stunningly aggresive and hilariously inept. Sometimes if you so much as carry the wrong gun when walking into a room, they'll put you down ASAP, but other times you can be standing behind a line of three guys, quickly headshot one and holster your gun before the other two turn around. They'll then turn around and inspect the body and walk away, then you can pull the same trick on the other two. Something that made the game magnitudes more entertaining was coming up with mental dialogues for what 47 could be saying in such absurd scenarios. BANG "Oh, my goodness! There has been a murder, do you see this body?" BANG "Oh my goodness, therer has been another one, what is going on here?" Another favorite tactic was to use noise to lure enemies into places I can't be seen BANG "Oh wow, was that a gun, did you hear tha-" BANG "Oh no! Another of our guards has been murdered!"
So yeah, the basics of this game are pretty fun. There are some odd points where it almost feels more like a 3D version of Contra (with all the player fragility that implies) and those can be fun and tense in their own right. What really keeps me from 100% saying you should play it, is that certain levels fall victim to tedium and cheap design. There's also times where the game requires you to know things you have know way of really knowing. There's one level on a Colombian Airfield where there must be upwards of 200 guys and there's only one blind spot at first for you to start picking people off. That level ended up probably taking 20 of my playtime hours just to beat, and I actually kind of ended up loving the experience of that one, since the goal was simple (kill the guy in the house at the center) and it was really satisfying once I finally did beat it, because I had learned the ins and outs of the level to such an extreme degree that I basically knew when and where everything happened, but that's a really extreme experience and I think most people would be put off. Later in the game, there's a level that, while not as dense with enemies, is probably three times as large and complex as far as what you have to do, and that was where I said "screw it". The level is a boat harbor which has you first traversing several real-world miles of land and guards just to get to the boat, optionally going even further to get something that can help you beat the mission, and then going into the incredibly well-guarded and convoluted boat to try and disarm a bomb and kill your target. This was too much for me. I spent hours on it and just got so tired of repeating the boring parts just to get to the interesting challenge, which was the boat itself. The level also had some inconsistent rules, such as each gate you can go through is guarded by a guy on the roof on the other side of the gate, but sometimes the guy on the roof wouldn't actually spawn until you went throughu the game, which means he gets the drop on you and you can't pick him off before going through. You can find alternate ways through most gates, which is cool and the game does do a great job of rewarding exploration with either stealthier routes or things that can help you, but this level was too much overload. I turned on God Mode so I could just get it over with and still lost because the bomb on the ship is tucked into such an obscure-easy to miss spot that I didn't find it in time. Other levels have these issues on a smaller scale, but that one was the most emblematic of the game's problems for me.
Codename 47 is at its best when it drops you into a sandbox with a bunch of interesting weapons and says "here's your target, have fun". When it makes you go through a bunch of hoops to get something done it drags significantly and kind of hurts itself with some odd mechanics. The lack of saving really hurts some of the later levels, but it also makes some of the earlier ones very tense and exciting in ways that you generally don't see from stealth games anymore. It's not what I'd call an "accessible" game, but it is worth looking at.

To start: I didn't enjoy Starbound when it first came out and since the stable updates ran dry. Since the game finally now had one, it was time to give it another try. The game has shown improvement since its early days and feels more fleshed out as a game, but it still falls short in feeling too placid of a game.
The game feels too static. The most common form of threats are planet fauna, which act too realistically like animals to be engaging. Some are neutral towards you - that's fine. But most are just casually patrolling and only aggro you when you get in their view. While that would be fine for some enemies, the problem is these are all the enemies. Take Terraria, for example: Enemies want to kill you. They spawn somewhere off-screen and give their 100% best effort to track you down and murder you. This gives a sense of alertness and danger that isn't seen in Starbound. The fact that events also aren't present in Starbound currently - things like Terraria's blood moon and invasions - makes the worlds seem simple and lifeless. I also don't like the idea of planet threat levels being related to their biomes. The most dangerous planets (and with the best loot) will ALWAYS be dead/volcanic planets. While it makes sense, more variety with different threat level biomes would be appreciated.
Another minus is the fact there doesn't seem to be any point to villages. Right now they only exist to expand your decorative prowess and to trade with some of the folks, but even trading has its downside of being almost pointless. Some of the vanity items are nice at least.
As for what it improved on: Actual quests and missions now. Although a lot of them are "get me x ores" or "get me decorative item y" it feels nice to know they're fleshing out the quest system into something with potential. Some of the missions can be pretty challenging going solo, so multiplayer is a big help for most of them. The ship upgrades are also a welcome addition and I hope more ship-centric events come out of them.
The game is more fleshed out than it was roughly a year ago. If somehow more life could be brought to a number of planets, villages, and the game in general, it could feel more like a Terraria successor. Just have to break that barrier, Chucklefish. For now it gets a recommendation because it's fun to play with friends, has a better sense of progression than it used to, and looks to be more promising in terms of future updates.

Game has several flaws that make it not enjoyable, despite its decent gameplay.
- Audio is Japanese only with a small bar at the bottom for subtitles.  You will hear Japanese throughout battles but you are focused on the battle, so rarely do you get to read any of the subtitles.  So if you want to know the storyline, you won't unless you understand Japanese.
- Targetting system is silly.  You can't turn off direction-based targetting so you end up trying to lock on to either the direction you are moving or the opposite of the direction you are moving.  The only way to target an enemy directly is not to move at all and hope the 'auto-lock' figures out the best target to lock on to.
- Attacking with multiple attacks will sometimes lock your attack in a single direction.  Not sure if this is intended, but it is annoying as ♥♥♥♥.
- "Special Attack" has multiple attack types but the tutorial is useless in explaining how you use them.  You want to do the mega-ultra-single-target attack?  Nope, aoe shield attack.  You want to do the aoe sheild attack?  Nope, random target attack.  Sweet!  I guess this is part of the very simple control scheme.   Instead of allowing you to assign each special attack to a different button, you have to do so combo, ie. button 1 + button 3, and if you fail it defaults to the aoe shield attack.
- Control setup is too simple.  It would be amazing if you could auto-fire and use the hat/thumb sticks to fire in a different direction you are moving, but instead you get a silly one-direction / direction-based targetting system that is counter-intuitive.
Pros...
- Decent graphics
- Voice acting if you like to hear Japanese
Conclusion: the game feels like it was made by some college game grad looking to make a game, but lacks the experience of game design to make the game fun to play.  The storyline might be impressive if it didn't require reading the subtitles or some other non-action cutscene... oh yeah, the cut scenes are awful.

I'm going to give you a serious low-down about Codename 47. If you don't like it, that's fine. I don't care about you.
Here is comes... My no holds barred take on the "classic" Hitman:
This game sucks.
At best, it's an excellent experiment that was perfected to its fullest in Hitman: Blood Money. At worst, it's a buggy, clunky, and dated piece of garbage that will only waste your time. I mean that. You can replay a mission over and over a hundred different times, with different stratagies, only to fail with one single crappy game design.
Did you make it through 98% of a mission on full stealth, only to try to hide that last body in a room and try to close the door, only to not have the spacebar close the door behind you, but instead pick up the gun your snuffed enemy dropped? Then right as you're correcting the mistake, another enemy walks right around the corner, sees your newly acquired weapon, and alerts the entire enemy force with his gunfire into your♥♥♥♥♥

Or fate could decree that your target is on the move, and just when you round the corner to pop him, there's an invisible map wall. Even if you plant a head shot, you still can't drop the evidence on his♥♥♥♥♥in order to frame a rival faction, thus failing the mission.
My all time favorite "WTF moment" is when you bust out the piano wire to silently kill a foe, only to have him magically aware of your presence as his back is turned. I mean, he doesn't even see you, then you come up behind him and he suddenly knows you're there without a sound or anything. It kind of defeats the purpose.
I enjoyed this game back when it was released on PC back in the days of oversized game boxes and game manuals. But I have to say, revisiting it was a giant disappointment. Perhaps I've been spoiled by its sequels, which are a vast improvement of the formula. Or maybe my tolerance for crap has changed, and now I set the bar a little bit higher when it comes to my standards. I dunno.
What I can say for sure is this: Codename 47 was a new thing back in the day, and at that time it was very much appreciated for what it was. Today, however, with all the improvements in its sequels, there is no denial that it is an obsolete model of the stealth-killer genre.
It's no wonder that there's no texture mods and improvements for this game, and that's because it's not worth the trouble.
Play Blood Money instead.

As an experienced MOBA player and all-round gamer, I recently picked this up at a friend's behest and decided to give it a try so we could play it together. Here is my initial impression after ~4 hours and about 12 or so matches.
Huge spoiler! This is not the true 3-dimensional space game it looks like. Your ship can only rotate 360° around the y axis and has a 'surface' and 'dive' button. Furthermore, the sense of being in space is ruined by magical friction slowing your ship far faster than your engines can accellerate it any time you let off of the gas. Best leave behind any dreams you had of skilled dogfighting techniques or drifting through space and executing some cool spaceship maneuvers. It's more like 3D Streets of Rage but with spaceships.
Fractured Space is, at its core, a very watered-down capture the point/MOBA hybrid with an old-and-busted pay-to-win mobile game cash shop bolted onto it. In-game, there are no skill choices or equipment to purchase, so there are no item builds to learn or ability to counterbuy to defeat your opponent. This means that comp and teamwork are paramount and coordinated groups will forever pub-stomp randoms. Fractured Space does nothing interesting or special that other MOBA don't already do far better. It is not a fair or balanced game at its core and it is very pay to win, although the P2W aspect appears relatively minimal and probably will not impact most players. For those who dig into the game, however, I'd venture that building a min/max crew could take 1-2 years of regular play or thousands of dollars.
If you're looking for a serious game to commit to learning and competing, then avoid Fractured Space.
However, it is a fun, casual free game that's probably good for a couple dozen hours at least before the novelty wears thin, despite all of its many flaws. So I can't help but recommend it.

Puzzles, reading, stress management... All in all, it's a fun and challenging game. Also a frustrating and annoying game. It sort of depends on your mood and attitude. There were times I was caught up by the puzzles and the challenges, and times where I wanted to throw my computer across the room. Then finally I caved in, looked at a guide and wanted to punch myself for not having seen the obvious solution for the problem.
So, playwise, it's a fun game.
I feel like there are too few tools. You learn to use a few tools and programs, but after the first 5 that's it, and you just solve the problems with the tools you have. For a better game: More tools.
Then there's the netmap, which is... horrible. The servers you connect to pop up somewhere random, and you can't hide the ones you don't need, so eventually the map is cluttered, confusing and worthless. I ended up with a notepad with the needed ip adresses beside me.
So, some things could be better, a lot of things could be worse. I'd recommend the game for people who like finding solutions to puzzles, quizzes and riddles. Creative thinkers who can digest a lot of text in a short amount of time (scan the text more so than read it), and who can handle flashing lights and preassure. I don't recommend it for the first person shooters, young kids (not that it's violent, I just don't think they'd be entertained much) or for light gaming where you're partially talking to your girlfriend, partially on facebook and partially gaming. It's not good for those types of situations.

I wanted to like this game, but there were just a few too many problems that makes me just not *quite* able to recommend it. Close... so close.
The biggest flaw is (mentioned a few time) - the lack of controller support. This game is really crying out for controller support and Big Screen mode. Other problems include some of the F/X (even when dialed down, the ball trail still makes things a pain to see sometimes), achievements not popping in game (less of a problem, since they all pop at once when you leave the game), lack of explanation of some of the power-ups (Shields? When does my laser come back?), and not-so-good control explanations. There needs to be a mite more power-ups *during* a level, but I can imagine that that might be a design choice (not one I like, but still).
Otherwise, there are good ideas here. For example, if you keep the ball in play long enough, there is a blast of energy that wipes out random 'blocks' (enemies) - especially great for when you just can't line up the ball and get that one last lone enemy (absolutely brilliant, and every Arkanoid-type game needs this from now on). The music is good for the type of game, XP-gathering adds an extra dimension, and there's lots of upgrades to buy (keeping one busy gathering XP).
A mythical Ionball 3 might be just the ticket to ironing everything out and getting a fantastic block-breaking game.

Okami is honestly the best game I have had the pleasure of playing. The fact that they remastered this game and the gameplay still holds up by today’s standards truly says something about this game. The multifaceted combat and puzzle gameplay mechanic and the truly amazing rendition of classic Japanese folklore tales just makes this game a true gem of games. I had 100% completed this game back when I played it on the PlayStation 2 and I was impressed by the graphics then but now I’m in awe at the graphical fidelity and to see the fine details of the games Sumi-e ink art style fully come to life. I haven’t had the opportunity to play this game a lot since I bought it but that mostly because of some IRL stuff that have been stopping me from playing but rest assured from my experience of completing this game back when it was on the PlayStation 2 that the game itself works very well.
A few things that would make this game better are such as a controller, PlayStation Controller or Xbox Controller either one works just fine but this is my personal preference so if you want to play with mouse and keyboard it will be just the same. Now another thing that would make this game a lot more meaningful is that you learn a bit of Japanese folktales such as “The tale of Princess Kaguya” or the legend of “Yamata No Orochi”. These explains things such as the relations between Orochi and Amaterasu the Sun God. With that I can assure you that you will have a good time playing this game with all its character. If you’re like me and want to 100% complete this game, then it shouldn’t be a full-time commitment like most modern games that try and suck all your free time and if you can’t find a particular item just google for hints or guide since this is an old game and a lot of people have made guides for it.
With all that in mind I genuinely recommend this game if you want an authentic one of a kind experience. Oh and before you say anything, yes Issun is really annoying like Navi from the Zelda Series

I have plenty of hours logged on mobile in this game and consider myself a reasonably high level player with great crew/ships to back it up, but wanted to get some thoughts and observations out there real quick if people are considering spending time with the game.
First, this is absolutely a mobile game. That means there will be a concerted effort to get some cash out of you fairly frequently. With that said, I've spent exactly $5 on this game once and spent the rest of the time just grinding for free to get where I am. It is not mandatory to spend real world money, but if you wish to, wait for a great sale and not a mediocre one (which the devs are more apt to throw at you more frequently)
Second, the Steam version of this game is convenient since I can check in on and maintain missions while on my home PC or laptop without having to drain my mobile battery. This alone makes it worth it TO ME, as someone that has invested a decent amount of casual time in the game. With that said, it might not be ideal for someone brand new to the game. For those individuals I'd still recommend it as a mobile "killing time" game, in particular if you enjoy the license.
It is also worth noting that the PC version, if it will be maintained here on Steam, needs a texture overhaul as well as at least 720p and above resolution options. As it stands, it is a straight up phone port, and believe me when I say its very obvious.
Ultimately, do I recommend the game? Yes, if you don't mine a "time sink" set in the Star Trek multiverse that now has the convenience of a desktop version. But if you're going into this expecting something OTHER than the Star Trek aesthetic layered on top of a mobile game's business model, you're setting yourself up for disappointment.

I'll be blunt: Okami, in my opinion, is one of the few games which HAS to be in everyone's Top 10 games of all time. Period.
Story: 8.0/10

+ Super lovely characters. Dialogues with the residents are interesting to read, too.

+ The final part of Okami (which still takes about 10 hours to finish) really raise the stakes.

Gameplay: 9.5/10
+ Similar to the likes of Zelda, Darksiders and other action adventures

+++The celestial paintbrush mechanic
- Playing it after 10 years, the camera movement could be somewhat more responsive.
- Really easy game, almost impossible to die. There's a workaround though: Don't upgrade your equipment/status plus refrain from using items and you'll be up to a challenge.
Final rating:

10/10 game.

If you're looking for an MMO, then Star Trek Online is where you need to look.
If you're looking for a game that can be played for a few minutes here and there, then this is probably better for you.
The game is designed for touch-screen operation so the interface can feel big and clunky of you use a mouse.
However, it's a well-designed game with beautiful artwork for the characters and astonishing visuals for the ship combat - especially since the game is so 'small' in terms of install size compared to similar items.
Missions rely on chronitons for 'fuel' and you have a limited supply of theis, but it restores over time.  This means that longer play-sessions will likely result in running out of chrontins.
You can buy more (pay to play) or leave the game alone for a few hours and let the chronitons recharge (free to play).
Of course, there is an ingame shop that allows players to obtain more powerful, premium characters, but many of these can be obtained by playing the various ingame events that run most weekends.
The game has its' strength on a phone/tablet but don't let that put you off playing it here, on Steam.

Astebreed is a bullet-hell style shooter that is driven by a deep and powerful backstory about loss, pain, love, and redemption. Like I said, the game is  short (I can blow through the easy mode of this game in about 30-45 minutes. Normal mode took me a couple hours. Haven't tried hard yet), but the story makes it a great experience. There are definitely some feelsy moments here. My only complaint is that the story unfolds as the game is taking place. Since the voices are all in Japanese, it's kind of hard to read the subtitles, shoot enemies, and dodge bullets at the same time. ~Trying not to spoil anything, so yeah...~ This game also isn't just a mindless button mashing game. In order to use certain special moves, certain circumstances must be met, as well as each boss has it's own sort of unique style to being beaten. I definitely recommend this game. In my opinion, worth every penny.

Assassin's Creed Unity. Ubisoft's biggest fail of 2014. They released a buggy, nearly unplayable mess to their audience, slapped some Templars in there, and called it an Assassin's Creed game. After the horrendous ♥♥♥♥♥torm after it, Ubisoft had to give free games out to calm the masses and not make people mad. It was a miracle that they weren't sent to the guillotine in the game. I finally played the game, and I got to experience it first hand. I know you await my judgement. You read the horror stories, you saw the caps with only the eyes and mouths showing up. You know this must be worst than the Holocaust. So how traumatized am I by it?
It was alright. Nothing too bad.
Yeah, I am playing this a year and a half after it was released, and they patched it, but it was honestly fine. Not the best AssCreed, I guess that might go to Black Flag or one of the 2's, and I think I enjoyed Rogue more than this, but I liked this enough. I'm sure you wonder what I talk about, so let's take a look at everything.
STORY: You're Arno, the second blandest character in ACreed history ever. Your master is murdered and you are framed. However, during the famed Bastielle escape, you get out of jail, join the Assassins, and go after the men who killed your master, who also happen to be pulling the strings of the French Revolutions. Kind of generic "get revenge" story, but it's not terrible or anything. It kept me interested long enough, and while Rogue's is more compelling, this was fine. It was neat running into Napolean and... that guy who invented sadism and... okay, I don't recognize most of these names, but I haven't had this lesson in school yet, so shut up xD. The modern day♥♥♥♥♥♥they throw in is pointless as always, and I wish they'd just get rid of it, but they need some link to connect the games together, so I guess we have to deal with it. It really ruined the mood here, though. Not the biggest mood killer, but I'll get into that later.
GAMEPLAY: Same ACreed, Different Game. Well, they do refine it a bit more since it's a new gen game. You have a skill tree to unlock what you had back in the last games along with the new stuff. There's a new lockpicking system, which is a neat addition. Stealth has been overhauled a bit, making it a better option depending on what you want to do. Apparently Arno is a lot less agile than the Kenway's or anyone like that, though, as combat is a lot stiffer and you can't just go in guns blazing. Or I guess swords blazing, but you know what I mean. Sadly, there's no ship gameplay, which was my favorite part of Black Flag, but I guess it wouldn't make sense to have that here.
GRAPHICS, LEVEL DESIGN, AND PERFORMANCE: So the graphics. Goddamn, Paris is ♥♥♥♥ing beautiful. Might depend on your preference, but this is probably the best looking ACreed I've seen. Paris feels so alive, and if you can run it on Ultra, do so. It's amazing to see it. While the game had performance issues at launch, they're fixed now. I heard some nonsense about a 30FPS lock, but that's nowhere to be found. Framerate stuck at around 60 for me, with some drops to the 50's or even 40's sometimes, but it was fine nontheless.
CHARACTERS, VOICE ACTING, AND DIALOGUE: Arno is kind of a dull protagonist. I mean, he isn't the complete and utter bore as Connor in AC3, who was known to bore any Templars who bought that game to death along with everyone else, but still, not very good. His companion/love interest Elise is much better, and I honestly think she'd be a more interesting protagonist, but I guess they did the "play as a Templar" thing in Rogue already, so ah well. Voice acting is good... kind of. While the actors are very good, I noticed something odd... EVERYONE HAD A FREAKING BRITISH ACCENT. It's fine if Arno and Elise had one, I wouldn't care. But do you mean to tell me that Napolean and numerous historical figures who lived in France their whole life had British accents? Around 40% of people who live in France today can speak some English, you couldn't get one of them to play some of these characters? It's not that I'm mad or calling racism or some stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥like that, but it kind of takes you out of the otherwise good atmosphere in the game. Other than that, I had no real problems with the game, voice acting was top notch and the script was alright.
SIDE ACTIVITIES: It's an ACreed game, of course there are a lot of things to do. You have a general idea of what there is? Yes? Well, that's it. No? Ask someone else, I'm too lazy to xD Though I will say that if you want to, you can sink a lot of time into it. I think this is the ACreed game I put the less time into, compared to the 27 hours (says 19 but Steam glitched out, it was 27) of Rogue and the two playthroughs I did on Black Flag on two different systems, so take that as you will.
MULTIPLAYER: ...oh right. ACreed had multiplayer. Um... I only played one co-op game, I think I remembered it being alright, but I don't have enough gameplay on it to make a good judgement.
FINAL THOUGHTS: Eh, it's alright. Graphically it's impressive, but other than that, it's just your usual ACreed game. 7.5/10, it's fine. If you can grab it for $20, that's probably a good deal. Enjoy all the ACreed games? Try this out for size if you haven't.

So we decided to play Fractured Space, and I'm glad that I did!
We ended up playing FS for 2-3 hours.  It was fantastic, It felt like we were coordinating real space combat.  The fights lasted long enough where we felt like we could make tactical decisions, we felt more in control of what was going on instead of what appears to be a very chatoic brawl that Dreadnought turns into.
I will probably be uninstalling Dreadnought and continuing to play Fractured Space.  Hopefully they will continue to support the game and add some more variety in their maps and game modes.

Update 03/12:
I now gave it another try after reading some guides and watching tutorials on YouTube. Bit by bit the game mechanics became more clear and I started to understand the interaction between the different classes. A big thanks to vasvaripeter95 and JWalker for their comments which made me give this game another chance, I'm glad I did!
Original Review:
I really like the gameplay mechanics, art-style, setting etc. There is that constant doom looming around the corner, tricky choices to be made etc. It makes you continuously weigh off pro's and con's and take decisions on the fly. This all combines to a very fun, challenging and nail-biting experience.
What bothers me however is the unfair advantage some of the bosses have. In one example I breezed through an entire level, arrived at the boss and got wiped. Getting wiped is not an issue if I understand what I, as a player, did wrong i.e. where I could have done something better. In this case however the boss got two actions per turn: one at the start and one at the end. Again, no big deal, that's why it's a boss. However in addition to the double action, the boss would use a skill which damages my characters for 50% of their health and targets multiple characters ... Needless to say almost immediatly I  lost two characters without having any way to prevent this.
I arrived to this fight with fully upgraded characters (weapons and skills) for their level and nearly full health. There is literally nothing I could have done to avoid the wipe. And that's my main gripe with the game: it feels as if it was programmed to make you fail, making sure the boss has such an unfair advantage that there is nothing you can do. I don't mind that I get screwed, have to start over, get wiped, ... as long as I see a way to overcome the challenge and to understand what I did wrong. In this case I couldn't have done anything better except for not playing this level in the first place. Yet the fact that I breezed through the level itself shows that my party was up to par with this difficulty.
Sure, you can treat it as a loss, continue, grow stronger and beat the adversary in another attempt, however the above totally ruins your motivation as a player: Why should I invest more time in this knowing that, inevitably, this will happen again and there is nothing I, as a player, can do to avoid it. Playing extremely good or just lousy in the end doesn't make a difference, you'll get wiped due to an unfair advantage anyway. This takes away any incentive for playing, but merely makes it a waste of time.
I now tried to get into this game on three different playthroughs, each time thoroughly enjoying the game until I again hit such a roadblock. If this is the way the game was intended then I unfortunately have to conclude it's not my kind of 'fun'.

TL;DR:
-like,
is a fun and challenging game of arcade action.
Lately, arcade games of old have been making a return in new clothes.
joins the fray, imitating such classics as
and
. In case you don't know those titles, in it you control a "paddle" that you use to ricochet a ball towards enemies. On hit the ball hurts or destroys them. You musn't let the ball fall off the stage lest you lose.
The idea is simple enough but it has been seen many times. Fortunately
introduces several twists to the common core, many of them a convenience.
There are several enemy types. Most of the droids are stationary and just wait there to be killed. Some are moving, others fly into the air to become effectively indestructible for a while since the ball can only hit stuff on the floor. Perhaps the most irritating one is the droid that keeps a shield made of droids that gets replaced as you smash them away. Interesting one is the indestructible wall enemy that dies only when you kill its special key droid.
There are also support droids that can only be targeted by specific weapons (more about weapons in a bit). For example: "the healer" fixes damaged droids and another shoots a blaster beam towards your ship, eventually killing you if you can't dodge. Especially one must watch out for death droids that rush down when hit and kill your ship instantly if not dodged.
To help beat up the droids there are occasional, fairly familiar power-ups: every once in a while an enemy will drop a power cell that either splits the ball into three or empowers it so it goes through enemies, insta-killing them on hit. Another nice feature is the super laser that automatically shoots droids at random. It's especially convenient when trying to hit that one last elusive droid and lets you finish levels faster.
Controlling a spaceship of some kind, you can also upgrade your ship and unlock weapons. They are bought with the experience collected from the beaten enemies. It's a nice idea to bundle with the ball game! Shop sells health and damage upgrades, paddle size and similar things as well as weapons that act like skills.
Weapons can be used once per level per life. They include stuff like laser beams, rail guns and kamikaze ball, as well as rockets that can only be used to shoot at some special enemies. A couple of weapons only affect the ball, e.g. equipping it with a machine gun or making it electric and thus causing damage over time effect on hit.
Weapons are a cool touch but being only able to use them once per life makes them rather limited. The annoying aspect of theirs is the way you have to cycle through them (mind though, there might be a keyboard shortcut that I just didn't find). It's inconvenient to find your desired weapon this way. Also, if kamikaze is your last weapon you have to be careful not to use it because obviously it kills the ball and consequently your ship.
Finally, there are bosses: special "monster" robots of huge size. The first one is quite classic since it's be killed by ricocheting the ball against its core but the two others are more special.
Bosses shoot and attack in several patterns, but in the later bosses you don't have the ionball to fight with but instead have to find the special means yourself, which is cool and different for a game like this. The ending boss is really tough though and needs practice to survive through.
It's obvious it's meant to be casual yet challenging game. The enemies and game mechanics are familiar enough but the ball moves fast and enemies explode in happy flashy displays (and thankfully if it's too flashy the FX effects can be minimized in the options). It's good there's two camera views for different players. The standard one made it hard (for me) to follow the ball and assess where it's going since the level is tilted. Thus I used the classic, over-head version that was adequate. Music is electronic style, pretty generic but very appropriate for the game.
It's not totally free of bugs. I experienced freezes a few times at the end of a level so that I couldn't exit the level or do whatsoever and was forced to ALT+F4. Fortunately it auto-saves between levels so it was just inconvenient at best and irritating at worst (after a longer or more difficult level). Once the ball was stuck exactly between armored shield droids and wouldn't move at all forcing me to restart the level.
The level selection is initially rather confusing since the level selection wheel consists of tiny flashing lights on the dark floor. Generally the interface has many numbers and symbols so it takes a while to get used to.
All in all, it's a decent, fast-paced action arcade game and a fun update on the original concept. The main game can be played through once in 2-3 hours but to unlock everything about two playthroughs are needed because of the large amount of upgrades - for me it took 6 ½ hours to 100% everything.
For the more competitive lot there's curiously named Assault Tower mode that one can play forever for highscores. There are no upgrades, instead you grab power-ups that both make you stronger and help you beat the levels faster. I found the mode challenging yet casually pleasant to play. It even has different levels than the main mode.
It's a cheap game for brief fun and short sessions of testing reflexes. It's also fast to pick up and quit if your real life demands it.

Note: This is a challenging, mildly technical, dystopian pixel game. Don't expect otherwise.
Overall: Haven't been this excited about a 'mech game since I was a kid playing MechWarrior 3. Not worth the $20(in my opinion), but definetly go for it if it's on sale.
Rating: 8.75/10
The game is a pixel 'mech/tank/hovercraft shooter where you can play a 'story' mode or a replayable mission mode where you can make money to acquire new stuff(lore, enemy briefings, vehicles, weapons). The thought put into this game is impressive, the pixel graphics are very well-done, and are easily one of this games many strong points.
This game's difficulty, at least, in the non-mission mode, scales based on the pilot the player chooses and vehicle they drive. Lighter, less offensively-geared vehicles means more cash, and higher level pilots means more cash, more enemies, and higher quality enemies. Difficulty in mission mode seems to be that smaller vehicles are harder, but that's somewhat a personal preference issue.
Loadouts in this game cannot be customized as highly as MechWarrior. There are two weapon slots per vehicle, and four(I believe) weapon categories. Weapons are furher divided into ballistic, energy, repeating, and something else which is purple(don't know what those are, explosive?). Weapons deal different damage levels to different targets(shields, health, structures). Energy weapons have low penetration(railguns are considered energy weapons in this game, but, realisticially, they're ballistic). Ballistics have high(er) penetration. Machine guns and explosives tend to simply damage cover(though explosives are much more effective).
You can also affix a special to your vehicle. The options available are EMP, smoke grenades, active camoflage, and Audio-Kinetic pulse(directional sonic death-cone).
This game is one of the four best purchases I've made on Steam.
(The others being Stardew Vallley, Cryptark, and Divinity: Dragon Commander)

Fortune Summoners: Secret of the Elemental Stone is side-scrolling japanese action RPG developed by LizSoft and localized by Carpe Fulgur. Story is set in the country of Scotsholm and follows an energetic 10-year old girl Arche as she and her family just moved in town of Tonkiness.
As you progress through the game, two more girls will join Arche - Sana, a water-type magician specialized in support and crowd control magic (beware of the nice ones - Sana gains insanely powerful offensive spells near the end of the game), and Stella, a fire-type magician specialized in offensive magic. Those two girls can as well be controlled (and will be required to pass certain point - you might easily get frustrated once you get to those points without them only to figure out you need them), albeit only one at a time - AI will control the other two and WILL ASSIST you. Playstyle with each of the 3 characters is different, so you can pick whoever you're most comfortable with.
Why did I emphasized "AI will assist"? Because, unlike most games with AI controlled partners, AI in Fortune Summoners is great at doing its job. Girls will attack and defend themselves, use magic, assist you with supportive spells, coordinate their attacks with you etc. You can also modify AI's behavior - how often will it use spells (none of the characters regenerates mana), which spells will it use and other parameters so you can configure the AI for each situation.
Opponent AI is equally good. Opponents will dodge your attacks, try to strike you from vulnerable spot, use their spells, parry your attacks, and do everything like human opponent would do. That alone raises challenge to 11, and on several places (beginning of the game, flying opponents, DAMNED HARPIES for example) it might get highly frustrating. Beating flying opponents is especially difficult as Arche learns Moonsault technique ("spinning sword in midair") fairly late in the game.
Controls need some time to adjust to. As you start with the game, there will be some difficulties in controlling characters - especially Arche, who uses sword to fight, and controls might seem to be unresponsive. However, there isn't any fake difficulty - manuevering through map and battles need a good timing on the button pressing, similar to the fighter games. Due to that, once you get a feel for controls, you'll just mow down everything in your path.
In conclusion, fun and interesting game. Graphic style might repel someone, learning curve as well. If you give it a try and some time, you might be satisfied with this hidden little gem.
Definite recommendation for anyone who wants a little challenge and nice story.

Heat Signature combines puzzling, sci-fi, and badassery in a tight, replayable package. The regular missions provide excellent variety, real danger, and great sense of accomplishment. The 'Liberator' missions stand out, as they are so tough that they make me fully explore each and every mechanic in the game, however you can replay them endlessly until you get it right. Can you knock out a room with 4 guards in before they sound the alarm, with just a blade and a short range teleporter? You will find out how, and once you've learned, you take those skills into the real world missions. Rarely have I played a game that teaches it's core mechanics in such an ingenius way. 10/10.
See story-time below.
I choose to accept a rescue mission. The mission is labeled a 'Mistake' and has the 'Ghost' clause: No deaths, no incapacitations, don't be seen. Just snag a guy and ghost the place. I pick my loadout, optimize it for stealth and throw in a few key cloners, as well as my trusty self-charging EMP gun, to deactivate any electronics that could detect me. I hop into my pod, and zip off in pursuit of my target. It's a ship belonging to the Offworld Security faction, so it's going to be close quarters.
I dock my pod with their airlock. They don't know I'm here. I sneak my way into a hallway. Ahead is corrdidor with 5 guards, one of them carrying a key. First I deactivate their shields and infrared detector fields. Then I use the key cloner to snag the key. That was the easy part, now it's time to get up close and personal. My stealth shield only has a 5 second charge, only works across 180 degree angle, and the approaching hallway is long. I don't know if this will work. It's go time: I activate my shield, and immediately start to move. I enter the corridor with 3 seconds to spare. Sneaking past two guards no problem. The  guard blocking the other entrance of the corridor is closer to the wall than I would like. I hold my breath as I squeeze past. He doesn't notice.
I use the stealth shield once more to sneak past an easier group of guards, and make it to the prisoner.♥♥♥♥♥♥ I can't carry the prisoner and use the stealth shield at the same time. I physically throw the stealth field generator down a hallway, the noise catches the attention of the group of guards. There's my chance: I pick up the prisoner, and dash past them. I run to a control room with viewing deck, which I passed earlier. There's no time for finesse, the guards are on their way back. I pull out my silenced shotgun and blast the plasteel glass window. It explodes outward, in a shower of glass and air escaping into space: We're out of here. I feel like a badass. Even as the vacuum pulls us through this newly created door, I start remote controlling my pod. First it picks up the prisoner, then myself. The package is secure, and I'm on my way home. They never even knew what was happening until I was long gone.

Fortune summoners is an action RPG featuring 3 cute little girls going out on an adventure. The story is pretty great, the artwork is polished, it has a memorable and fitting soundtrack.
The story talks about Arche, a girl who just moved over to the town of Tonkiness, and now attends the Minasa-Ratis school, where students are being taught about magic using their elemental stone. Not having a coin to spare for an elemental stone however, Arche ends up not being able to learn magic. As a result, she decides to go on an adventure with her new friends to find her own elemental stone.
The only thing that may get on the nerve of some players is the stiff controlls. This is NOT a button-mashing combat game. The delays are put in there on purpose, which raises the difficulty drastically. This game is still beautiful and fun as I remembered it. You play as a wolf, roaming the land to restore it to its former beauty. As a wolf you can do things like dig, bark, bite and recieve pat albiet only from  a few npc. Only dig have gameplay signficance but you can still prompt reaction from people. There a lot to do in this game, sidequest, collectable and even fishing. Your main method of gaining upgrade is aquiring praise, which you get for restoring land, helping people and feeding animals. As you progress through the story you unlock brush technique. There is a lot of interactivity with the enviroment that involve the brush technique thats worth disovering on your own. The brush technique lets you gain access to new area or treasures that were previously unreachable.
Combat is equally prominent in okami as you'll need to slay the demons that are contaminating the land. Combat is standard action hack and slash but what make it special the interaction enemy have with the brush technique. Enemy will have certain weakness/resistance to brush technique for example the red imp instrument can be destroyed with slash brush technique when its been raised to block attack. Combat is not difficult and rather forgiving, at least for me. Those who are struggling could always use consumable which there are plenty and can be bought. The real challenge is to obtain blossom ranking at the end of combat. The game rewards you with more currency for beating enemy quickly and not taking damage. It is very difficult to obtain blossom rank on boss fight assuming you don't plan on save scumming or retrying. Its in your best interest to not die in the game as there is a game performance score at the end of the game which grant rewards. Thankfully time is not part of the game peformance score so you can take your time beating the game.
It runs fine on low specs machine and even on low quality the game is still georgeous.  Graphic option are lacking not that you would need a lot, but I would at least like view distance. If you running low spec remember to set your option before you starting the game, you don't want to listen to Issun and Sakuya for an agonising half an hour of unskippable dialogue due to the lag.
As a port, the biggest disappointment is the lack of mouse support for the menu. You have to navigate with keyboard. It would of been nice to have a brush cursor. Otherwise the game runs smoothly and the controls work.
Edit*
I forgot to mention about the beautiful soundtrack. Its consist of traditional japanese instrument, the flute work is amazing. It works really well with the paint brush aesthetic.

Brigador offers a unique and very enjoyable experience.
I had this on my wishlist for a while, after reading a RPS article on its development.  Since my purchase, Brigador remains a very enjoyable and cathartic game.  The graphics are very detailed, with entrancing lighting effects, satisfying destructability and complex, but rewarding vehicles with which to to wreak havoc.   The ones I have encountered thus far include tanks, various sized mechs and hover vehicles, with each class having unique movement, stats, weapons, etc.  Admittedly, it takes a while to acquaint yourself with the controls, as most vehicles have separate movement and turret controls, which can be slightly disorienting at first, but these are quickly learned through addictive gameplay that doesn't punish failure.  If you die, just start the level again, maybe with one of the different vehicles permitted for the mission and try a different approach (smoke to hide your movement, or camo to sneak into position).
Another point of potential contention is that the game doesn't feature savegames.  The missions aren't typically that long, but are sometimes difficult and losing progress right near the end can be a little frustrating.  This frustration has not stopped me from diving right back in however, and there is a clear sense of satisfaction when completing the level, despite having died multiple times in the session.
I must make specific mention of the excellent soundtrack done by Makeup and Vanity Set.  It gives the action a great feel and I find myself nodding along, as I stomp, crush and smash my way through the levels.  I have since bought the soundtrack, as well as two other albums by MAVS and it is definitely worthwhile checking out.
For what it's worth, I highly recommend Brigador.

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in
computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.
You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.
The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. (
) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate a IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a
. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.
The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).
The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM, which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively.
------------------------------------------------------
Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.
Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)

quotes

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. (I mean, it's just ls, cd, cat, and mv really) Also,

I read the comics and watch the TV show and this game is a worthy entry to the canon of The Walking Dead.
This is basically an adventure game with a twist in that your choices will affect later chapters (and even the next season!), so unlike classic entries in the genre it has more replay value.
However, it doesn't have much in the way of puzzles like the oldschool games, so you won't find anything that taxes your brain.  Also, there are scenes with quicktime events, but none of them were difficult.
Although it's not a difficult game, the story is one of the best I've seen in the genre.  The characters are well-written and there were many moments when I was disturbed or emotionally moved by what happened to them.  I'd say the writing is better than most of what you see on the TV show, and is on par with some of the better parts of the comics.  The game also handles moral choices very well in that there will be many instances in which neither path you take will be the "right" or the "wrong" one, and that the consequences won't be revealed until much later in the game.
However, I did notice that your choices don't modify the main story significantly.  For instance, you can prevent a character from dying early on in a chapter only to have them die shortly afterward.  Although it's interesting to see how both choices play out, the ultimate results aren't radically different.
The DLC is also good.  It gives you a series of vignettes and then ties them all together in the end, and yes, the choices you make in this content will also modify Season 2.
Although this is more of an interactive story than a game, the story and characterization is interesting enough for me to recommend it to those who love horror and are fans of The Walking Dead series.

This is simultaneously the most immersive and immersion breaking open world game i have played recently. Paris has been lovingly recreated with a 1:1 scale, meaning when you walk up to or climb buildings they look massive and the same proportions as in real life, that makes a big difference from past Creed games.
Graphically it looks superb with everything maxed out and you can tell Ubisoft put most of their effort into making the actual city in painstaking detail. The amount of NPC'S in this is insane as well, usually open world games have far fewer people walking around the streets than you would expect. This goes the complete opposite direction, there is one mission where there are literally thousands of people you have to navigate through to find the target you need to assassinate.
This is however also what f*cked up the game and breaks the immersion for you as a player. Ubisoft hasn't managed to eliminate the bugs of NPC'S appearing and disappearing in front of you, and some characters still swap their clothes at will. I can't stress how bad this is in the game, because there are always large crowds of people on the streets it happens CONSTANTLY and was really distracting to me. I eventually was able to ignore it after about 10 hours, but by that time i was just trying to finish the story missions.
The game also still doesn't run that well because of (i assume) the large crowds of people. I would get between 40 to 60 fps with the settings all maxed out, and my pc is pretty good.
There actually is a f*ckton of side content to do, but the few side missions i tried were rubbish. There are these new detective murder mystery missions you can solve where you have to talk to people and accuse the right person who you think did it. At the start of this it warned me not to accuse just anyone and to be sure of who i thought it was, so i thought that all the evidence pointing to the guy who obviously did it was a misdirection by one of the characters planting the evidence on the guy.......but no it actually is the guy you think it is, so it's rubbish lol i didn't bother with the other murder mysteries.
I tried co op but the one time it worked for me the guy immediately left, so good luck finding people to play with.
Story wise it's okay i guess, although there weren't really any stand out missions that took me by surprise like in Rogue, also all the characters speak with an english accent.........in FRANCE lol, i was thinking about this and it's either have the voice actors speak with a sh*tty french accent like Joseph Gordon Levitt in The Walk and give the game some charm, or do what they did and not even try.
If you like Assassins Creed games and have a fairly powerful PC i would cautiously recommend this, the only bugs i witnessed were cosmetic, the game never crashed on me or had bugged missions like some past Creed games i've played. It's a shame Ubisoft fell at the last hurdle because the game does a lot of things well, it's just that the things it does wrong are so consistent that it ruins a big part of the experience.

Brigador is without a doubt one of the best isometric shooters out there, it is a solid start for those who feel curious about the kind of gameplay and an absolute must for dedicated fans of the genre.
Don't get fooled by the deceptively simple gameplay, which is about shooting things, because behind the layer of simplicity lies a set of layers that adds to the complexity of the battle system: damage type, weapon type, vehicle type, noise generated, terrain, positioning, even the factions you're up against only serve to create a cohesive, intuitive and intelligent battle design, so you'll find yourself dying constantly if you think it's about just going turret mode and shooting whatever comes across your weaponry.
The art style is absolutely gorgeous to look at, nailing that 80s cyberpunk look with a spritework that is just downright beautiful. The levels arent just some mindless details thrown into a box, many sprites dedicated to the different environments serve the purpose of giving life to the setting, and the effort is such that there's even sprites for small road traffic barriers and street lamps. The buildings, the debris, the vehicle models, the farms/countryside, even the small pedestrians running around, everything looks so good, it almost feels like watching a tabletop of very high quality models, and I'm particularly fond of spritework, especially the ones with this level of quality.
The soundtrack only compounds that 80s feeling with the neo 80s style it has, it's really cool and provides much of the feeling of being a kickass inside a vehicle blowing stuff up with the tension of being swarmed by enemy units and pulling off maneuvers to keep yourself alive and kicking. The main theme that plays when you boot up the game is only the tip of the iceberg regarding the quality of the music here.
Not only do the devs put in the effort of an excelent, buttery smooth gameplay and great audiovisual design, there's also a universe built around the game, a huge amount of lore and story details is put on Solo Nobre, it's factions, the pilots, even the weapons and vehicles are described in terms of the game's fiction, giving even more life to the setting. You can even read the contract's terms that the brigadors sign!
The game features a campaign (a series of missions played using specific vehicle builds) and freelance mode (missions set in districts in which you can use a vehicle build of your choosing), and while the gameplay is rock solid and responsive that definitely help freelance mode, the campaign is more of a challenge mode rather than a story since there are only small explanations an nothing more aside from the intro given at the end of the first story mission. It's not a bad thing per se, but there is just so much lore giving life to the setting that the lack of a proper story detailing the fall of Solo Nobre doesn't do justice to the existing potential. On the gameplay side, a little balancing could help the utility of the defensive abilities, as the active camo is way above the usefulness of the AK pulse and the EMP grenade.
However, those are small concerns I have that don't really detract from the excellent quality at display here, and with the devs showing even further support with the recent inclusion of different control schemes and a level editor down the line, only good things appear to be certain for the future of this game, which is a shame since this game deserves way more love considering the level of effort and execution.
TL;DR - It's a great game that deserves a lot of love, and I thoroughly recommend it to anyone. Well, at least if you're into isometric shooters anyway. So please buy the game to accept the contract.

Bridgador is a very satisfying, visceral mech combat game. It's the top-down tactical explosion bonanza you've been waiting for!
In Bridgador, you take command of one of several mercenaries of questionable mental health, tasked with what is essentially the terrorising of the planet Solo Nobre for monetary and political gain. The objectives don't change too much from level to level, and essentially boil down to destory everything while avoiding being destroyed - which can be a rather difficult task depending on the vehicle, loadout and tactics you choose to emply.
There are two modes of play, a campaign and 'freelance' mode. The campaign is more story heavy, as you might expect (although it's not obnoxiously in-your-face either), but my favourite mode is Freelance, where completing missions provides funds to buy new vehicles, pilots, weapons etc. Bonus money is awarded for taking weaker mechs (or more unstable pilots!). Experimenting with the weapons is a joy. A lot of it is imbalanced in a beautiful way - some weapons are terrible, some punch above their weight class, and it rewards experimentation.
The gameplay its-self is from an isometric perspective (reminiscent of Mechwarrior 3050 on the SNES for me), and the default controls are like that of a tank (AWSD to rotate and stomp forwards/backwards, mouse to aim). The aiming in particular is quite nuanced, as the mechs are often taller than the things they're shooting at, so you need to aim where you intend the projectile to hit, rather than in the general direction of the enemy. There are many interesting touches and lots of attention to detail.
All in all, the worst aspect of Brigador is that the missions tend to be a tad samey (especially in Freelance mode, the objectives are the same each time), but the terrain you stomp though and specifics of the fights you'll have to take keep things interesting. It's by no means a perfect game, but if you enjoy mech or future war themes, explosions or tactical shooty gameplay, definitely check out... BRIGADOR!

Brigador is good. I'm sure there are plenty of reviews already that explain the ins and outs of the game, so I'll just list what I like.
Brigador has very good art. You can see the care that went into every single sprite. The thought put into the engineering of these vehicles. There are three different factions in the game, each with their own sort of theme. The Loyalists are pretty standard Battletech/Starcraft Terran style that you'd expect from a game like this, with some creative twists. The Spacers have vehicles that look very high-tech and elegant, but still believable in design. Orange checkerboard patterns, thin lightweight legs, spherical wheels instead of tank treads, lots of moving parts. The Corvids (my favorite) have vehicles that are cobbled together from old truck frames, salvaged legs, and the occasional stripped out muscle car. Each vehicle has character and creativity in its design.
Brigador has a lot of variety. You choose a vehicle, bolt your choice of two weapons onto it, and roll out. There are many different vehicles in the game, each with its own list of statistics such as hull strength, turn speed, forward movement speed, chassis turn speed, etc. Each weapon does something different. The Abbot is a giant cannon that punches through armor through sheer concussive force. The Otomo is a giant, short-ranged sustained laser that can melt through metal like marshmallows over a fire, but takes a few seconds to focus in. The Gutterball is a giant ball of heavy metal launched like a catapult that arcs over obstacles and crashes through buildings like they're made of paper. The Harvester is a massive artillery strike that flies high into the air before splitting into a cluster of explosives and then destroying a city block as it lands. These guns are all unique and satisfying to use.
Brigador has unique and interesting lore.  It's mostly presented through vehicle descriptions and the backstory of the selectable pilot characters. It all paints a bleak picture of an interesting and cohesive world. Also, the developers have approached a professional author to write a book set in the game's universe. It's definitely worth a read. I think it's really cool that the game got this kind of dual release and wish more developers would do this sort of thing.

- Game gives you something other to do than picking boggers out of your nose when you're bored. You don't have your hands free anyway. Those are busy facepalming Picard-style a lot.
- The artwork for some of the crewmembers looks pretty decent. I liked the style.
- Deinstalling it was very fast because it didn't take too much space on my harddrive.
Cons:
- It's a mobile port. And a ferociously bad one at that.
- The space fights are very, very repetetive and boring after the first few times you do them. And they are short and hasty aswell. So even if the graphics were not a cheap failure by themselves, you wouldn't be given the time to enjoy them. Additionally the balancing of ships is arguably not comparable or somewhat carefully oriented on the TV-series or movies. You'll be beating Borg vessels with your weak starting ship and Warbirds, too. I just thought that was lame, so I wanted to mention it aswell.
- Game will force you to farm for a ton of items in order to procede. Your crew needs a bunch of items to unlock higher levels and thereby higher skills which again are needed to procede with the storyline (which was my main motivation to continue the game at all). So in order to get on with the story, first you'll find yourself farming like old McDonald. Farming in this game mostly means you have to repeat older missions which adds to the bordem generated by its repetetiveness allready. I didn't enjoy it much but it was what I did most of my ingame time.
- Linear progress of crew members. Doesn't sound like a problem but it managed to ruin my feeling of creating a unique team and making it better. It's just steps on a ladder which take you hours (mostly waiting hours!) to continue walking up, knowing that certainly everyone who started earlier than you, allready climbed higher. Maybe you get the idea.
- Game feels more like a Candy Crush Saga clone than a properly developed space-exploration game.
- Ingame currency made my eyebrows go up because I thought it was way too expensive and at the same time simply not rewarding enough. To be fair: They seem to offer a lot of deals to make purchases more appealing but just looking at the normal prices for simple speed up return times or various possibilities to gamble are making me want to place a #ripoff tag somewhere around here. Nothing wrong with making money by developing a Free-to-play title, but .... come on .... you got to give the people something nice extra for it.
- The menu is a maze. Trying to figure out what you need and what you have is surprisingly difficult. When you're still reading this and still want to play the game let me give you one last good advice: When you want to start a mission on the galaxy screen and the game seems frozen because you can't click on anything, keep in mind that you have to doubleclick there. Yea ... nowhere else you have to doubleclick anything but right there it's rather that or Alt+F4 because you think the game froze. The game is awkwardly counter-intuitive not just there but at a bunch of moments.
I could imagine that for some hardcore Star Trek fans, this game might be a good catch still. Mainly because it offers an endless opportunity to spend time and lose yourself in that universe, (which is something you honestly shouldn't do. The world has much to offer that is better than this game. No, honestly!), unlike most other Star Trek games I know of which have an ending somewhere. But it still isn't a good game.
It feels like some kind of browsergame with arguably slightly better graphics and a lot of flaws in balancing and ergonomics. It feels like someday in the past someone put a lot of love to detail in the characters and afterwards other people came to melk the cashcow dry. I really don't know if that's what you're looking for as a costumer. But good luck trying it if you feel like.
tl;dr: You better set maximum warp to propably just any other game in the Steam universe. Even the Borg wouldn't assimilate this title, because it offers nothing new at all. This game is so boring, it would make Janeway fly all the way back to the Delta quadrant just to be as far away as possible from it.
tl;dr non-Trekkie version: It's not a good game.
