Fallout 4 is a first person shooter loudly declaring that it's an RPG, despite all evidence to the contrary. It is also a giant flashing red warning sign of things to come in the future of Elder Scrolls and Fallout while under Bethesda's control.
Now I have to preface this by saying that I didn't actually HATE Fallout 4. In fact, as you can see from my playtime I put a lot into it and generally had fun in the process. But it was the same kind of fun that comes from loading up a Call of Duty or Battlefront style FPS just so you can run around and shoot things. And that's what this game is at its core. It's Call of Duty: Fallout and entirely built from the ground up to appeal to the Call of Duty crowd. But the problem arises in that Fallout is not intended as a shooting action game and is first and foremost an RPG. Bethesda releasing this game is like going to the same restuarant for three years and ordering lasagna, but the fourth year you go they give you a plate of pizza and swear to your face that it's lasagna.
And the state of Fallout 4 is an indicator of Bethesda's shift from quality games to just make-as-much money-as-possible The first hints were there in Skyrim, where the RPG mechanics were scaled back until it was really just a hack'n'slash with bad combat and the story woven into a childish power fantasy wherein the player is the most imporant special snowflake in the world. But at least you could ignore a lot of that. In Fallout 4 the RPG mechanics are so neutered that they only barely have any affect on the game whatsoever. And the story intentionally railroads you into a very specific path that is so rigid in execution that you cannot even roleplay within the confines of the forced story. For example say I want to roleplay as a bad mom who doesn't care about her kid and feels that the apocalypse was the greatest day of her life now that she's free of her crappy husband. But you can't, because said mom won't shut the hell up about her missing kid and how sad she is about it.
Bethesda no longer has interest in making games epic in scale and ambition. They now exclusively make games that appeal to the widest demographic possible. And I honestly can't fault them for that really. Businesses exist to make money and they've found a way to generate more revenue by making their games simple and generic. But as a long time fan who has been with the Elder Scrolls and Fallout series since their inception, it's a shame to see Bethesda tell me that I no longer matter. Future installments of these franchises, which were once "must buy" for me, are now simply "wait and see" or "grab it on sale years later". Pre-orders are certainly out of the question at this juncture. And that does make me a bit sad.
So congrats Bethesda, I guess? You told me to get lost but gained hundreds of replacement wallets that will throw money at mediocrity. You win.

This game has been out on other platforms for 10 years but in case this is your first time seeing it before, Okami is an adventure exploration game with light RPG elements like that of a 3D Zelda game. In fact I'd go as far as to say if you took the Wolf form from Zelda: Twilight Princess and put it in it's own standalone game with a highly stylized art style & Japanese Folklore theme, Okami is what you'd get.
Boasting HD resolutions and textures, the crisp visual quality is definitely a step up from the Playstation 2 version I originally played. It's still locked in a 30fps framerate, which, given the graphics/art it seemed just fine to me. If you're not used to low framerates like that it'll take time to adjust but it's well worth it. Dismissing this amazing game outright over a framerate debate is one of the dumbest arguments I've heard to not play this installment if you've never touched this game at all. This is one of my all-time favorite games and a classic. If you want a real in-depth review of the gameplay itself, remember this is a 10 year old game, there's plenty out there.
I'm just writing to highly recommend this game to anyone who loves the exploration & adventure genres. $20 for 30-60 hours of a beautifully crafted  & insanely fun gaming experience is well worth that price.

MyPark is awesome, play your story mode character online as part of one of three park teams, where you will level up playing against other members of that park on multiple courts in different game modes (2v2 half court, 21 with 3 players, or full court 3v3).  Eventually when you gain enough experience playing with fellow park members you will be able to travel to rival parks and represent your team in other courts.
I find the Spike Lee story of the campaign boring and somewhat annoying sometimes, and you might spend a lot of time on the bench (which you can skip through) especially early on.  It is a fun experience playing through a career starting in school and leading up to being an NBA professional though.
There is a more traditional play mode where you are able to swap between which player you control as well, if that is what you want to do.  This is also a great mode, and what I originally played because it was the most similar to what I'm used to in an NBA game, but like I stated at the beginning once I played MyPark it easily became my favorite part of the game.
The amount of character customization content is pretty astounding, there's literally hundreds of shoes, shirts, pants, and other accessories to choose from to customize the look of your player, as well as different animations and skills to purchse with the coins you earn from playing.
There is still lots I haven't done or seen in this game, and every time I play it I find myself learning more and liking the game even better.

Sometimes Arno won't catch the exact spot I want him to catch during a parkour ascent or descent and will get me (sometimes) in trouble. Also, in a couple really cramped instances Arno was putting away his weapon instead of parrying or attacking. Gear only helps mitigate your mistakes...and you will make mistakes. I love how the civilians will jump in from time to time and take some of the fire and steel off me. In fact in one particular mission I recall you can actually use several civs to start a riot, there-by allowing you a clandestine entrance to a certain location. This version of the series actually makes you have to plan your assaults, and I for one like the change from the almost super-hero like fighting abilities from Conner to Shay. Those were all fun and great games, but the combat system wears thin after so many titles.
Make no mistake, you will die alot at first, but you will learn if you stick with it.

Brigador is an Isometric shooter with an unique aiming system where you pilot mechs, tanks, 'anti-gravs' and powersuits though a fully destructible, neon-lit, dystopian city on the far away planet of Novo Solo.
The dictator known as 'Great Leader' has died and the evil corporation SNC has put out a 'Brigador' contract for anyone interested in making some money to take out the orbital cannons in the city of Solo Nobre so they can start their invasion from space.
The game has a very 'morally grey' feel to it and it's all presented though a cold, business like menus where you accept contracts from the SNC and buy new vehicles, weapons and powerups to do your bloody work with. You can also unlock (or rather buy) new pilots that function as a difficulty setting in the game. A more difficult pilot means more and tougher opposition but also a greater paycheck IF you manage to reach the spaceport and make it off-world in one piece.
All this corporate killing is represented in stylish retro '90ies graphics and goes along with a great Synthwave soundtrack. The soundtrack is available as DLC to listen to in your own living room and there is even an audiobook with great immersion and lore (which i HIGHLY recommend you listen to - it's awesome!). The audiobook is also available as an e-book. Even though bigger games came out this year,
Brigador is definately my personal GOTY (Game of The Year) title of 2016. I have more then 70 hours put into it and i still find myself coming back to it for just one more run. It is original, stylish, has original gameplay mechanics and (while it might seem a bit difficult at first) i would definately recommend you pick it up! Pure class.

When you first play the game, the one thing that hits you is the art style; Designed around the illustrations of The Walking Dead comics with a completely new cast of characters. The game is solely based on the decisions of the player, from things to say; to pivotal plot points, the game gives you a variety of options to choose from and a limited time to do so.
Throughout the game you can get very attached to the characters, one minute everything's fine, the next you're sent into shock as something may have gone horribly wrong. This is what the game does well and builds its story around this alongside the problems and drama you will face. This interesting point and click adventure asks the player to scavenge and be creative with how they handle situations;
Also the game has a system where each character will remember your actions and recall them later on in the story; this can be when you don't take sides with someone or when you don't agree with their ideas. This can lead to characters holding grudges or characters willing to back you up.
It's episodic format what originally helped the pacing of the game; each ending on a different note that will cause you to buy the next episode to continue those compelling moments of the story much like when you read the hardback comics. Although since all the episodes are out, you can buy all of them together and play through the them all.

Pros:
- mech game for mech enthusiasts
- lovingly crafted game engine
- great replay value
Cons:
- horrible control design
- story told through expository passages
- lack of character interaction
I have spent a long time deciding how to approach this review. As a huge fan of the MechCommander series, and isometric games in general, there is a lot to love about this game: intricate pixel art, newly built mech engine, deep storyline, great soundtrack, lots of replay value, approachable despite its depth. But for all its triumphs, there are some notable setbacks.
I can only imagine the courage it takes for a newly formed indie developer to create a new game engine from the ground up. A five year endeavor by Stellar Jockeys, Brigador has been a long time in the works and that work shows. I can’t recall the number of times I stopped to appreciate the level of detail. From mission structure to game mechanics to the surprisingly great AUDIO BOOK?! (more on this later), so much thought went into this game.
At its core, Brigador is a mission-based, real time, tactical mech game split into two game modes, Campaign and Freelance. In campaign mode, you begin as a soldier piloting a mech at the exact moment that the “great leader” of a planet wide totalitarian dictatorship has perished (not so subtly based on North Korea). The story then plays out in a string of missions depicting your desertion from the regime as you fight your way to becoming a brigador, a mech-piloting mercenary.
In reality, the campaign exists to get you acquainted with the game world. It’s where you discover whether your preference is sneaking your way through missions as you strike targets with surgical precision, or stomping across the battlefield, dismantling all that would oppose you.
And Brigador gives you that freedom. Impressively, the game engine is built as a mech sandbox: enemies perform patrols and exhibit behavioral patterns, mech and weapon choice affect how detectable you are by the enemy, and environments are fully destructible allowing you to forge your own path towards objectives. Once you are comfortable with the game’s foundation, your career continues as a mech-for-hire in freelance mode, arguably the heart of Brigador.
Surprisingly, the campaign acts as a prologue to Freelance mode. Freelance mode is all about the minutiae of mech-piloting. No longer restricted to the predefined load-outs offered during the campaign, the player is free to customize every facet of their mech: pilots based on skill, mech bodies of varying strengths and weaknesses, bi-pedal motion or hovering, weapons based on ammo efficiency and damage type. In short, parting out your ideal mech is where you'll spend the majority of your time.
As much as there is to say about the game, even more can be said about its atmosphere. The entire game plays out at nighttime, with lighting effects to match: enemy spotlights cause debris to cast shadows, industrial locations are bathed in an orange glow. Sound wise, hauntingly synthesized electronica elevates Brigador’s entire soundscape. Seriously, the soundtrack by Makeup and Vanity Set stupidly good.
What’s more, an audio book can be purchased alongside the game, allowing you to delve deeper into the game world’s origins. In a way, Brigador follows a three act structure, with the audio book serving as Act 1, the campaign as Act 2, and freelance mode as Act 3. It’s all kind of meta in a way.
But the game’s atmosphere doesn’t remain unbroken. It’s clear that certain sacrifices had to be made, limiting Brigador’s engine. For instance, every level is a completely flat surface suspended in a black void. The game (sans audiobook) is almost entirely devoid of personality. There’s a complete lack of character interaction and the only story to speak of is a page of text that immediately precedes each level. But most egregious are the controls; they’re tank controls.
I get the rationale; it’s a make a mech game with a control scheme to match. But tank controls died for a reason and should stay dead. Simply put, they’re ♥♥♥♥ing horrible. Movement in relation to the character, not the camera, was a necessity at the time, but a mistake today. To make matters worse, it doesn’t have just one set of tank controls, but two. Depending on the type of mech you’re using, you either turn left/right or strafe left/right. Even after playing through the entire campaign, I still felt like I had no control over my mech.
Despite all it has going for it, Brigador ultimately feels like a game out of time. What would’ve been a great game ten years ago, feels like a good game today. Oddly enough, while the controls stop me from playing the game, they don’t stop me from enjoying the soundtrack and audio book. It’s strange to say, but I think they both turned out better than the game.

This review used to say "What Dreadnought could have been." It also used to be positive. Not anymore.
Short version: It's a wonderful game being ruined by it's freemium economy, and shady development choices.
In the past few months the game has:
Nerfed the ability to obtain the premium currency in-game.
DOUBLED THE PRICE OF ALL IN-GAME ITEMS BOUGHT WITH THE STANDARD CURRENCY.
And nerfed the ability to obtain any cosmetics items.
For example at the time of writing they just let a new update out, one that adds a new playable ship at the price of 1.7 million of the normal currency. Assuming a good money drop rate for an experienced player, you would get about 25,000 credits a match. So in others words, it will take you just under SEVENTY games played to get the ship they just released. I'll remind you a few months ago it would have been less then 35.
Oh but every time you open the ship in the menu without the money it buy it it helpfully reminds you that you can just buy it with your real world money. Coincidence? I think not.
And cosmetics items are just as bad. Normal skins are now about a one in fifty drop chance, by the looks of it. And the premium cosmetics items? the "ultimate skins" that increase how much money you make? They have a ONE IN 666 DROP CHANCE.(3 in 2000) And that's not per match, that's per loot crate. You might get five of those in a day if you play for a few hours.
It's pure BS.
The game has been arbitrarily edited to demand your cash, and only determined players can stomach the endless grind to have things without shilling out real money for them.
Which brings us to my current opinion: don't waste your time with this game. It's not worth it anymore. And I seriously hope the developers of Dreadnought are looking at this and thinking about what not to do wrong, because this game is a perfect example of EXACTLY how to ruin a brilliant concept of a scifi capital ship game.

Dated it might be, but this game is definately worth a look. A fun, challenging, and quite honestly, punishing tactical game. You control a few different 4 man squads (squads can also be broken up into 2 man buddy teams essentially creating mini squads) and sometimes a vehicle or other special unit. The story and story dialogue is a little cheesy, but I honestly don't care. The gameplay is great and the combat dialogue is surprisingly responsive to what is actually going on. You task your soldiers with breaching rooms, moving to corners, taking cover, laying down suppressing fire, throwing grenades, covering a sector, etc. Even on easy difficulty the game is very unforgiving and can be challenging, especially when you're just starting out. Send your troops charging into the room recklessly? They're gonna get dropped by a bunch of AK-toting sand-dwellers. Have good ol' sarge run out from the corner into the street? He's gonna catch a tank shell in the face. Decide to jump out from behind cover and say boo? All your guys are gonna die. Or if there's an enemy with an rpg in a window and you decide it's not worth moving your squad from behind your lovely flowerbox, you're going to have to casevac an entire squad. Basically if you don't play it smart in this game, you will lose. It is challenging game and requires the use of real tactics. Have your LMG trooper lay down suppressing fire so you can move your second team into a flanking position. Lay down smoke so you can enter a building to get an angle on the enemies in cover. You get the idea. Great game, well worth the price.

If I was to recommend any game to a fan of Bullet Hell games, or SHMUP' in general; my first choice would most definetly be Astebreed.
There's something about this game that instantly clicks; and it does so many things right that there are very few flaws if any at all; and below I'm going to tell you everything there is to love about this game.
1. The camera; initially it might feel a bit jarring seeing it pan and zoom at various intervals but the good thing about this is that it does so in a flawless and seamless manner that it never really becomes an issue; there's the standard top/down view, a side-scrolling view and a rather well done third person view which alternate between set sections to really give a bigger impact instead of sticking with just one camera view. It's this concept that makes Astebreed unique and gives it that kick to make it stand out.
2. The graphics; Graphic wise, most Bullet Hell games tend to stick with the 2D format, pixels on a moving, otherwise repeated background yet that isn't the case here. The graphics are some of the best I've seen from an indie game; they're smooth, clean and incredibly crisp and despite all the madness that goes on screen, it doesn't deter you away at all; you can always see where your ship is, and most importantly the backgrounds are eye-dazzling; each one changing from the next although it implements heavy sci-fi elements AKA flying robots of various sizes there's always a new design for each enemy you come across be it big or small although certain enemies are more visually appealing than the rest each of them has something unique to them.
3. The Story: This is, something of a hit and miss but what this game does is actually make a damn good attempt at actually telling a story amidst the carnage. Essentially, you are a Rookie pilot sent on a mission to finally end a Galatic war between mankind, and the Filune; a race of alien creatures that; for reasons unknown is hellbent on wiping humans from extinction. I won't go into too much detail, but it's surprising how good the story is even if it's a little cliche. The characters interact with each-other constantly, giving advice or being a general nuisance and the voice acting to go with it is some of the best I've heard; despite the fact that it's in Japanese only. The only flaw to go with this though, is that you can't really pay attention to what the characters are saying, unless you know Japanese; if not you most likely won't have time to pay attention to the subtitles at the bottom left corner amidst all the shooting and dodging you'll be doing, this is just a very minor flaw though.
4. The Music; ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic, is a good term for this. Granted, Bullet Hell games have always had catchy music; whilst not the most memorable Astebreed has a soundtrack that suits perfectly with each stage and boss encounter. There's always a set tone whether it's a more upbeat tone for the initial stage or something more desperate for the stage bosses; the most enjoyable one for me is the entirety of the stage 5 theme, which I personally believe would've suited the final boss better but that's just me.
As of writing this review; I've put plenty of time into this game; despite what the hours say. If I ever want to keep myself occupied and entertained without really getting bored I'll boot up this game and waste a few hours blowing things up like a complete lunatic; and there's nothing wrong with that. This is the sort of game designed to keep you hooked for hours on end, whether you play it casually, or if you're like me prefer to beat all the high scores in the game and top the Leaderboards for bragging rights.
If you've ever got the time, and the money to spare; give this game a try; you most certainly won't regret it.

Good looking game, with some really weird bugs/features.
My perspective is from someone who has been belaying World of Tanks/Warships a lot. I also play Dreadnaught Beta and this game has the same concept. However;
I am not sure why, but aiming at someone, be that zoomed in or zoomed out, is very frustrating in this game. No matter how much I adjust sensitivity, it still feels clunky. Also, when zoomed in, there is no option to increase the mouse wheel sensitivity, so roiling the mouse wheel to zoom even further is very slow.
Seeing target in range is way more difficult in this game than any of the above mentioned games. The game offers a tab target option, which I guess is good, but you only see the targeted ship, when you’re really close. It also has this weird red outline, which outlines the obstructed targets and I can’t say weather this is helps or makes things worse.
In Dreadnaught, the battles are mainly near a planet or another surface, so the lack of flying up and down with your ship fully tilted up and down looks somewhat realistic. However, Fractured space battles take place in space, near some asteroids.  Having ships not fully animate the X axis tilt makes  it look very weird, like flying a log. It has this weird feeling of constantly “strafing” up or down, while staying relatively horizontal.
Why are rockets/torpedos so big and bright? If you fire rockets at someone while in a zoomed in mode, your screen gets obstructed by your own rockets and sometimes they cover the entire damn screen.
This game has the most weird and uncomfortable menus. It gives you daily login rewards, which pop as soon as you log in. Trying to locate that daily reward window afterwards is impossible, until the next day’s popup.
The only place you can take a look at all of the ships available is in “Hangar” menu. However, it doesn’t even say how much the ship costs when you select the ship. You have to press “purchase” then it shows the cost in credits, but not in platinum, if you don’t have enough. Are they going for a “element of surprise”?
The active players count always show 300. Not sure if it’s a homage to a movie but, sometimes I sit in queue over 30 min, but the active player count never changes.
With all this thing said, this game has some very nice graphics and sound effects.
P.S. why the hell the AI is so strong in this game. I end up playing co-op against AI, because PVP queues are crazy long and I have yet to win against an AI. Every game feels like we’re against the damn Skynet.

: This game feels like classic Pong-meets-Space-Invaders. You're not so much shooting bullets as 'catching' them via your thrown ball. You need to defend a space tower & destroy some alien vehicles. All the while keeping track of your ionball.
: Replay value is good (so far). I've played around 25 different levels of this game and I've found most of them interesting & challenging. When I lose all my lives & it's "Game Over" I don't feel utterly beaten & ready to quit. Instead, I feel eager to try again. It encourages me to hone my reflexes and peak my curiosity over what the next level might bring. I feel the end-goal is far less about 'winning' the game, although there is a Leaderboard you can compete in if you want to try.
: Graphics are up to date in this decade, with a 3D-look over a 2D format. There are two viewing/playing options but my fav is Top-Down; in the style of the old arcade shooter/pinball games. I will note that beginner players may easily get confused with all the sparkly bits & lose sight of their fast-moving ball. If you're getting frustrated, turn down the graphics to 'Fastest' & then raise them up later to a fancier setting once you've gotten the hang of the game. Focus first on enjoying & progress, rather than perfection.
: From what I've read this game is not compatible with joystick or controller. It is intended to be used with a mouse, and thankfully it works well. You only need to tilt the mouse side to side & left click to fire your first shot at each new level (or use the menu). The great news is it's also a simple one-handed game; so if you've carpal tunnel in one hand you'll still be able to play with the other. Although playing this game with your off-hand will be a good challenge. :)
: I got it during the holiday sale, so it was under $2 for me. It's easily worth $10, however. If you're not sure that it's even worth $10 then add it to your wishlist & wait for a sale. That said, you may end up feeling like I did though; a bit guilty about getting such a good deal.
: This game saves your progress after each completed level, so if you lose all your lives & hit 'Game Over' you can still continue where you left off (although there is a score penalty). You can also opt to start a new game to try to raise your score higher (and reduce your # of deaths.) As said before, the replay value is good.
: I'm sure nearly every fast-paced game on Steam would have this warning but I'll say it anyways. As the levels progress, the game gets far more flashy & intense.
. If however, you suffer from very mild seizures and still want to try this game then put all the settings down to minimum, take plenty of breaks & stop if you feel strain or headaches. It's fun to play, but it can get very intense, very quickly.
.
: I personally feel this game is meant to be used with peripherial(rod) vision. Focusing straight on the ball (which most people tend to do) may cause you to lose sight of it very quickly as colours & movement clash together. I recommend instead that you relax your eyes & look 'through' the screen about 1 foot behind it - like you would with the old 3D Magic Eye creations. With a bit of practice, this method will give you a wider field of vision & allow you to react faster to changes. It will also reduce the chance of headaches if you're prone to them.
Now if you'll excuse me, I shall end this review & go back to playing... :)

Overall incredible game, and I've bought it 3 times. Really one of the better zelda type games to ever exist. Other's have written better reviews but I'll give some info about fixing the controller issues.
This game uses the steam controller API, which overall is somewhat poor in detecting controllers, and implimenting the features. If you experience controller issues, launch the game in BIG PICTURE mode which handles controllers and games that use the Steam Controller API much better. Big picture mode will check constantly if you have plugged in a controller, and will switch inputs on the fly for you. I launch in big picture every time and experience 0 issues, and the game is pretty much a flawless experience, even bluetooth ps4 controllers are supported in big picture mode.

Ah, the beginning of an era in the stealth/action game genre.
is where the revolutionary
series began in 2001. Being a fan since
, when I saw the series on sale, I was delighted, and am now in the process of playing through them.
The
series' use of difficulty and required creativity have their beginnings here. You
have to pay attention to guards, their movements, what they react to, and their overall patterns. Some are quick, some are not. I'll admit, the gunplay in
is lacking, but not by a huge margin. You really do manage to get used to it after a while of practicing.  There are also additional bugs that may have to be worked around when encountered. The stealth mechanics, though, even for its age, are well kept. Dragging bodies, disguising, slitting throats; what's
to love?
This is where it all begins. Agent 47's long trail of bodies begins as he wakes up strapped to a bed, and explores more about his past and origins through the game. As far as an origin story goes, he's got quite a load here.
The graphics, mediocre even for the game's time, are nothing to guffaw at, even for nostalgia fans, and this particularly where the game falls short. Textures are dull and sometimes conflict with each other. Severely pixelated and blurry textures are not uncommon.
Overall,
, despite its age and its shortcomings, can be thoroughly enjoyed through the nice tint of some rose-colored glasses.

This game-serie was recommended to me already a looong time ago, but never had the time to step into this hitman series. Recently there was a sale of hitman games on steam, so I decided to buy the first 4 games. And of course, I started with the oldest: Codename 47 from the year 2000.
I read some reviews after finishing the game, but 1 thing I should have read before playing the game:
Open Hitman.ini in the game's installation folder.
Add these lines:
Resolution 1920x1080
Window
StartUpperPos 0,0
I played the game in 800x600, because otherwise it didn't work. With these lines (i checked it), you could play full screen and the game looks better as well. I also changed the keys, because the standard keys are not playable for me.
I think Codename 47 is a good entry point for the series so that you learn who Agent 47 is and how he came to be. I am used to play games in 2000 as well (heck, already since 1987), so I am used to bad A.I. like in this game. Although sometimes situations in the game really don't make any sense. Read the story very carefully before a mission, because that is the only help you get and there is many times some hints and clues how to fninsh a mission.
+ good music
+ good atmosphere
+ sometimes multiple ways to finish a level
+ still worth to play
- opponents shoot very accurate, once detected you can start over the level
- no savegames
- some levels are very dificult to finish without checking for some hints and tips
- your second life/respawn is in many cases worthless since you are already discovered
- figure things out on ur own by dying and dying and dying
Once you know how to beat a level, it will take you next time between 5-15 minutes. But before you know that, it can take you hours by finding it out by dying. There are some levels that you can finish the first time you play it, but most of them will take more tries, and some of them many, many more tries.
Not a highly recommended game, but if you play newer versions of hitman and you like it, you should also have finished the first one.

I remember Syndicate. I was probably too young for the game, but I remember the feeling I got in my minds eye: of relentless rain, neon, egg-shaped cars and random citizens in gunfire that they did not order with their brainchip. I remember torching trees, and trashcans, occasional bystander and shooting every window.
I remember Syndicate Wars, which apart from being badly reviewed, was an extremely well-made continuation of the premise. You go into environment, do your stuff and there is collateral. The interesting collateral in Syndicate Wars were the buildings.
Now Brigador. This game is the game, which I have always wanted to make myself. Buildings coming down, lights going out when the sonic wave from my towering behemoth machine levels a few neighbouring blocks, bombarding a far-away train-yard, waiting for a second, then sending a next volley to devastate the investigating troops.
This is an old school clever shoot-em-up game with the feeling that Syndicate evoked at the time. With more lights and more destruction and way less story. I'd like to have more story, but as a culmination of my ever-lingering hope for a game in which I can go around and level a city-block in neon lights and in which the map tells a story of a location which turns into a war-zone.
If you love the visuals of the trailer and destruction of buildings I would hope, that you like Brigador. If you hate repetitive missions you might get bored. Look through two levels of a let's play if in doubt on that front.

Each unit comes in three classes (mechs, tanks, and air) with a large variety of weapons; several special abilities are also available. Brigador is played from an isometric perspective; controls are handled using the WASD keys to move and turn, with the mouse reserved for aiming the weapons. Handy firing arcs are shown for both the primary and secondary weapons. The AI isn’t smart as much as it is numerous. Adept use of the controls, along with intelligent use of special abilities and weapons, is key to success. Brigador is a challenging mech game with lots of action that desperately needs adjustable difficulty.

This game feels like a huge step back from its predecessor, Black Flag.  I bought this game after a year it came out. When I heard about all the issues, I told myself I would pay no more than $20 for this game. I got the game for $16, and I feel like I still paid too much for it. This is the worst put together Assassin's Creed game I have played (I've played all the main ones up to this point, including Rougue), and after getting about half way through the main story, I don't think I am interested in ever playing Assassin's Creed Syndicate. There are probably too many points to hit, but I'll discuss the ones that seem the most bothersome.
- Free running does not flow as well as it use to. The free run up and down feature was a nice touch, but what you consider to be ascend, descend, or static running may not be the same as the game's idea. I kept getting stuck in places that I would never have a problem with in previous AC games
- Everyone has guns and everyone is a perfect crackshot with them. Each bullet takes about a third of your health (even with decent armor loadout), and you will be shot by someone off map and die a lot. The combat in general just seems a bit unfair. Either Arno is the worst assassin ever, or Ubisoft made the combat too steep.
- The interface constantly interferes with gameplay. I completed a mission but was surrounded by enemies when it did, and I died because the combat does not work properly until you close the end-mission dialogue box. Hints would pop up over other dialogue boxes, making you wait for them to go away before reading information on side quests and such. May not seem like a big deal, but it happens enough to become super annoying.
- The camera in combat is awful. In older AC games, the camera would automatically adjust to keep enemies on screen. Now it just sits there and you have to move it manually like you do outside of combat. This leads to many enemies being off screen and attacking you without much warning. With the combat already being unfair, this just adds more frustration.
- Although many of the bugs have been fixed, there are still a lot in the game. I constantly get stuck in walls and have the either fast travel or wait to be shot to death to escape. I died more times from bugs than I'd like to admit on any game.
- The main story has not really been about the French Revolution at all. I'm only half way through the story, so maybe the game does get more involved with what is going on at the time, but half way in it has just been it's own seperate story that happens to take place in Paris during the time of the French Revolution. In AC3, you at least are somewhat a part of the American Revolution (Boston Massacre, Battle of Chesepeke Bay), and in AC4 you pirate with Blackbeard in some missions. The big advertising for Unity was the French Revolution, but the assassin order does nothing to take part. This story could be copied and pasted into any historical time and not change. Again, have not finished the main story, but so far, nothing

My impressions:
- Stompy mech combat that is a perfect balance between arcadey and tactical. The game pace is snappy and combat is fluid, but so far hasn't been relentless or overwhelming.
- Battles are intense with lots of variety catering to different play styles. Scrappy engagements punctuate maneuvering and objective-hunting.
-Not really sure what to think about the “plot” (backstory may be a better term?). There's a lot there, but it seems a little fractured- not sure if that's on purpose or not. I am having trouble following along- it's confusing and a little dry for my taste, but that's okay because the actual game is fun enough that I don't need a justification for blowing everything up.
- The tank controls are awkward at first, but I think it translates nicely into how you would expect a giant mech to move. They definitely add to the unpredictability of the combat (in a good way). Surprisingly, I feel I have been my most graceful when I stop thinking about movement and just let my fingers do their thing. Trust me, if you do it too, you'll suddenly stop stomping around in circles after about 15 minutes. Just get through the tutorials- the real learning happens in the first few missions!
- Is Brigador worth $20? IMO Brigador offers enough content, variety, balance, and polish to justify the asking price.
- Great effort by the dev team! There's no reason why this game shouldn't be a Steam indie favorite.
- Happy stomping!!

The interface is great on this game, and the scale of combat is what I've been looking for.
That said, I'm going to go ahead and complain about some things. It's a shooter. Despite having hulking capital ships full of guns and fighters, you, the captain, are really running guns. While things feel strategic overall, they've moved away from the slow and thoughtful naval battles to something more arcade action focused. Hopefully they move away from that.
The biggest weak point for this game is the matchmaking system. It uses the same tired arena combat in which players have to be prepped in a lobby, matched with similar 'level' experience, and grind for ship purchases. I get the grind, it leads to a possible income source. But for something with this kind of player base, the segmented matchmaking system just doesn't work. Having larger battles with a wider range of skills, allowing drop in and drop out during battles, and possibly adjusting so high and low level players can play together would fix a lot of these problems. People have created mathematical models to describe active player bases needed for games like this, and it's simply unrealistic. The fun of the game depends on a lot of people connecting on line, and if we're being honest most players want their shooters on the ground, not in space. So that will never happen.
The developers did an amazing job creating an innovative design that properly captures the feel of capital ship battles that all of us scifi nerds have been looking for. Hoooo, boy. Quite possibly Bethesda's most controversial game yet. Such a polarising game; some say, it's bigger than a Fat Man's nuke. And there are others that say, it has tanked our retro-future Apocalypse Now. All we know is.... It's not called 'The Stig'! (I miss old Top Gear :(...) So let's settle with "War. War never changes..."
The Good:
-Running, the glorious action that everyone can do (Overwatch characters who aren't Soldier 76) that makes getting aroung the overworld of the Commonwealth that much easier. Fallout 4 has done that better than previous games.
-VATS, Fallout's fine-aiming extravaganza which is immensely fun and cool.
-Power Armour (ain't for p*****s, Duke), the walking tank that makes you feel like Iron Man on Bane's Venom. While its power source may be a bit lacking compared to previous accounts, it makes Power Armour feel more like a last resort/ use for danger resource rather than a stronger piece of armour. It feels like you're in a suit of armour with its little animations as you climb in and out of a suit, and it retains that old survival trait: maintaining equipment.
-Crafting tables, allowing you to modify your weapons, armour and clothing for more damage, durability and/or extra perks, like making you more stealthy.
-The Overworld, the Commonwealth is a B-E-A-U-tiful land to explore and traverse.
-The enemy AI, like all games it can sometimes be a little bit dumb, but when it isn't it is great. Feral Ghouls dodging your gunfire feels authentic, Radscorpions burrowing under the ground to surprise you is f*****g infuriating (but intuitive) along with those Mole Rat buggers.
-Gun-smacking, need I say more?
-The companions, while some of them aren't intriguing or fun from the get-go (see later), the rest of them are interesting and a joy to have along for the ride. For me, it also makes the game feel like you have friends in the world. And even though they can't die (unless some of them turn hostile due to plot), this makes them even better. It's why in Fallout 3 and Skyrim I never want to take anyone with me, I'm too worried about losing an interesting and unique character forever.
The Bad (or Neutral points):
-The fully-voiced protagonist... A
I actually liked this. For me, having a voiced character adds me into the world just that little bit more than games where your player avatar says ".........." and "..........." and not much of anything else. I actually feel invested in the world, and not having a voiced... well, voice feels like I'm just playing a blank slate in this world. While the lack of options and the cinematic flow means dialogue can be chosen ineffectively or incorrectly (and that your character feels more heroic than they can potentially be in previous Fallout games), I feel that Bethesda shouldn't shut down the idea of having another voiced protagonist in the future simply because this was their first try, and not everyone liked it.
-The base-building, something that starts off confusing, then becomes intrguing, and then becomes frustrating because you never have enough resources. Luckily on PC, console commands are at your service, load up some batch files (not too many, you'll kill the game!) and make building easy again! Hooray!
-None deteriorating weapons armour and clothes, while it isn't as stressful anymore, you might still end up picking up a copy of what you've already got because you've forgotten you're not playing Fallout 3 or New Vegas, and you may lug it around everywhere because you keep forgetting if that is your ace item or not.
-Adding value to junk; now it can be used for building or shooting teddy bears and bicycles at Deathclaws with the Junk Jet. Fun! But it also means that there's less of a steady way of making money in the game. S**t!
-The story, while interesting, is a bit formulaic and cliche, and doesn't allow for many morally-questionable options that other RPGs (not just previous Fallout games) offer.
And the Ugly (the true Bad points):
-SOME of the companions aren't that intriguing. Despite one companion (MacCready) returning from a previous game, I have never really been interested in bringing him along for a ride. Similar story for Strong, who if you play a more moral character, is next-to-impossible to please, and X6-88 is basically the T-101 Arnie-nator from the Terminator franchise only not as cool, terrifying or Austrian, thus making him a flat rip-off. Finally, Deacon. While quite possibly more entertaining over the previous three, not intriguing or entertaining enough for me to bring along during storytime.
-The Institute, a bunch of t***s who live underground and say they're the future of mankind in the post-apocalyptic Wasteland, and yet they kidnap people from the surface and spy on them, and don't try- oh, you know- HELPING THEIR FELLOW HUMAN BEINGS. It's hard to support the Institute from the standpoint of a gamer looking into the story, and the character in the events of the story; all they do to you is treat you like a guinea pig. Which leads me onto...
-Opposing the Institute, probably the more satisfying part of the story, and yet, it feels really hollow as well. Even as he knows he's about to die, the Director of the Institute still believes that your actions if you oppose him will doom mankind forever. It feels really empty as there isn't a way to even try and convince him of anything else. I know that the Institute is his life, but come on! He's a scientist with no experience of the truth, not a shell-shocked war vet whose seen everything! It would a kind of ironic twist to his character if you could convince him of his ideology faults; one of the smartest men in the world, yet naive and gullible? Or even genuinely open to ideologies that he never thought of despite his intelligence.
-Some of the Settlement choices are extremely lacking. Seriously, Sanctuary is the only place that's actually decent, and you can fill it up pretty quickly. Like, one's a boathouse (with a garden for space), many are farms (with a garden for space), and Jamaica Plain, one that I looked forward to unlocking for the first time, was... a corner of an entire town that could have been equal in size or scope as Sanctuary. WAIT, WHAT!?!?!?!?! To be fair, the Castle is pretty decent (and cool!), but most of the settlements aren't great. Speaking of settlements....
MEME TIME ALERT!
-"Another settlement is in need of help." -Preston Garvey. F**K OFF, PRESTON! FOR F***'S SAKE! DO IT YOURSELF! I'M THE BOSS OF THE MINUTEMEN! WHY DO I HAVE TO DO EVERYTHING!?
In conclusion, I have enjoyed playing Fallout 4. Sure, it has flaws. It may not be as great as Fallout 3 or New Vegas, or the first two games if you've played them. But I can't say that this was a bad game.

Fallout 4 is a first person shooter loudly declaring that it's an RPG, despite all evidence to the contrary. It is also a giant flashing red warning sign of things to come in the future of Elder Scrolls and Fallout while under Bethesda's control.
Now I have to preface this by saying that I didn't actually HATE Fallout 4. In fact, as you can see from my playtime I put a lot into it and generally had fun in the process. But it was the same kind of fun that comes from loading up a Call of Duty or Battlefront style FPS just so you can run around and shoot things. And that's what this game is at its core. It's Call of Duty: Fallout and entirely built from the ground up to appeal to the Call of Duty crowd. But the problem arises in that Fallout is not intended as a shooting action game and is first and foremost an RPG. Bethesda releasing this game is like going to the same restuarant for three years and ordering lasagna, but the fourth year you go they give you a plate of pizza and swear to your face that it's lasagna.
And the state of Fallout 4 is an indicator of Bethesda's shift from quality games to just make-as-much money-as-possible The first hints were there in Skyrim, where the RPG mechanics were scaled back until it was really just a hack'n'slash with bad combat and the story woven into a childish power fantasy wherein the player is the most imporant special snowflake in the world. But at least you could ignore a lot of that. In Fallout 4 the RPG mechanics are so neutered that they only barely have any affect on the game whatsoever. And the story intentionally railroads you into a very specific path that is so rigid in execution that you cannot even roleplay within the confines of the forced story. For example say I want to roleplay as a bad mom who doesn't care about her kid and feels that the apocalypse was the greatest day of her life now that she's free of her crappy husband. But you can't, because said mom won't shut the hell up about her missing kid and how sad she is about it.
Bethesda no longer has interest in making games epic in scale and ambition. They now exclusively make games that appeal to the widest demographic possible. And I honestly can't fault them for that really. Businesses exist to make money and they've found a way to generate more revenue by making their games simple and generic. But as a long time fan who has been with the Elder Scrolls and Fallout series since their inception, it's a shame to see Bethesda tell me that I no longer matter. Future installments of these franchises, which were once "must buy" for me, are now simply "wait and see" or "grab it on sale years later". Pre-orders are certainly out of the question at this juncture. And that does make me a bit sad.
So congrats Bethesda, I guess? You told me to get lost but gained hundreds of replacement wallets that will throw money at mediocrity. You win.

Astebreed is arguably one of the best Bullet-hell games/Shoot em ups in existence. It is technically very basic and the story is told mostly through the dialogue (so if you only speak English you will probably be mashing buttons while you read the text), there is no customization, minimal variability in terms of actions and simple projectile mechanics (can be blocked, and can't be blocked). This however isn't a complaint as it makes the game more accessible and although definitely on the easier side, for even novice gamers the experience is not diminished. The game offers first and formost impressive visuals, both models, backgrounds and cutscenes for its genre. The combat takes place in a variety of styles (top down-, behind-, third person views), that all mesh together nicely unlike some games where it seems forced. These mechanics add to the immersion along with the winding environments and dramatic pauses done by the camera and mech making everything one cohesive experience.
The story is moderately good although relatively vague, it leaves much to the imagination and seems rushed, mostly in terms of execution. Its not often one desires more padding, but they could have easily through in some generic missions to stretch out the experience. That is really the only gripe with the game, that it is too short, and within 2 and a half hours you will be done and wanting more. Its a solid ride and is on par with playing through a cinematic experience/movie, but it needed more content. Overall a full recommend for fans of the genre and the uninitiated alike.

When you look into a game of this type, The most important thing is
you can do.
So let me tell you a story.
I was playing the Personal Mission. You only get one of those per character, it's a "losing is not an option" type of thing. I had to rescue a target, using the stuff I found throughout the game.
Only thing, I never found an armor-penetrating gun. So I got creative.
Used a key-cloner to avoid contact with the first group. Snuck by a couple of guards with a stealth shield. Found a short-range teleporter, distracted a guard and stole the cell key.
When I entered the cell, one of the guards saw me. Immidiately I saw a swarm of shotgun blasts directed at me. It was bad. Luckily, at the last millisecond, I placed a teleporter trap, before falling down, bleeding. So everybody who tried to pick me up (and throw into space to die), got trapped in space himself. Ok, I got the target, time to get out.
And then another ship attacked.
The extraction point was demolished in seconds. I was honestly about to give up. But then a crazy idea passed my mind.
I took out the last gadget I had: a one-use time slowdown for everyone except me. Turned it on, picked up the body, and ran towards the window.
As the slowdown stopped, it became clear how fast I was
running. I threw my target through the window like a goddamn superman. Immediately we both got sucked into space.
On my last bit of oxygen, I turned on the remote control for my space pod. I directed it towards us with the rear door open, and saved both myself and the target.

Jump right into the middle of five guards. Kill the first, throw your sword at the second, teleport the two now unused swords into your hands to kill the next two guards and throw one at the last, before any of them even realised what just happened.
Every character comes with their own bit of backstory and motivation, defining their personal goals. They all work towards the common goal of freeing their little patch of the galaxy from four different factions. Characters that are captured can be freed by others and played again.
The beginnings are humble. But as you progress your equipment gets better and you grow bolder, which can lead to both, hilarious failures and epic successes.
While the missions don't vary that much the bonus targets and randomly generated ships and crews bring in enough change that things don't get boring.
With time you're not just playing some guy trying to pay off his sister's debt, avenge his mother or free his buddy. You're playing a force of nature. And just when you think you know all of the game you find a new way to apply a known mechanic. I can absolutely recommend this game.

I was skeptical about buying this game at first. Around January 15, Negative reviews filled the "most helpful" section. Still, I gave it a go. I was amazed at first, but then a little disappointed. I just kind of said, "Is that it?" The exploration was nice, but I figured that all the planets were just the same: Forest, desert, snow, and the occasional volcanic. (I was wrong, but I didn't know that).
Then came the Late January Update AKA The Winter Update. This completely changed the format of the game, and, to me, created an entirely new game. This time I chose the Novakid, because, hey, he's the new guy, and entered the world.
One thing, that was plainly obvious about Starbound was the building. At first it doesn't seem much different from it's predecessors (i.e. Minecraft and Terraria), but later in the game, especially after you get the Paint Tool, you become able to make fortresses and houses that you never even dreamed of (with the help of decorations found in dungeons). It also has some of the best building mechanics I've seen in a Side-scrolling game.
Starbound also has an awful lot of weapons to choose from. Just before writing this review, I was on a snow planet and discovered a minigun-like contraption that shoots snowballs. There's a huge variety of swords, hammers, spears, guns, pistols, axes, and more to choose from. With the help of Tech like the Jump Boost or the Energy Dash, you can easily jump around your enemies to turn the fight in your favour.
The navigation in Starbound is ridiculously large for an indie game. I couldn't see myself exploring more than 5 solar systems, maybe 6. And yet there seems to be 100 or likely more out there! And travel isn't cheap, either. You need to travel to a moon and start mining there to fing Archius fuel. To pick it up, you need to upgrade your Matter Manipulator, one of Starbound's brilliant concepts. Or you could collect Uranium from hazardous planets. The 5 different types of Stars, Gentle (Beginner), Eccentric (Moderate), Radioactive (Master), Frozen (Expert), and Fiery (also Expert) all come with their own unique planets to explore.
Don't let the art or the 2D fool you. Starbound is it's own little gem in the Survival genre. The game isn't even past Early Access and it's easily worth $25, in my opinion. I would indeed recommend this game to any fan of exploration, survival, fighting, or Rouge-like games. 9.2/10
Notes:
This game has indeed been in development for more than 2 years now. It has evolved a lot from it's original state, but the community has only grown more impatient. You see, the Starbound devs go about development a bit differently than most. By the way, in my 44 hours of playing this game, I have not encountered a single bug. Not one. Anyway, the Starbound devs produce content in large, stretched-out patches. One of them released today. It is called PLeased Giraffe. I'll copy about 1/10 or less of the changelog here for you:
Colony System
Colonize your worlds! Create a home, decorate it nicely, then place a Colony Deed to attract a tenant!
The type of NPC who moves in will depend on the type and quality of the home’s furniture and decorations. Decorating a room with several objects from the same theme (such as a biome or material tier) will attract a tenant themed to match!
Keep your tenants happy and they’ll periodically offer you gifts, some cosmetic and some very useful
New Outpost Store: Frögg Furnishings
Sells Colony Deeds as well as a variety of furniture in many themes
The set of specialty furniture available will rotate each (out of game) day, so make sure you keep coming back to see the full selection
Each furniture set can be used to attract a particular tenant that fits its theme
Improvements to NPCs
NPCs will now interact with each other and with many different objects in the world. Depending on their personalities they might get sad, excited, fall in love or do all kinds of different things in different situations!
See who your tenants are and what they’re thinking! (press Alt to activate)
Added many unique NPC dialogue options and updated some old ones
Further improved NPC movement and pathfinding
NPCs now switch between ranged and melee weapons in combat depending on their available energy, range, and whether they can reach the player
Groups of NPCs now coordinate in combat to attack from different positions and divide themselves between ranged and melee
Surface Biomes and Sub-Biomes (Tiers 1 – 4)
Major visual improvements to background parallaxes
All biomes have several types of unique critters (60+)
Added a huge number of biome-specific microdungeons (450+)
Added many new biome-specific cosmetic armors and other items
Randomly generated monsters will now have color palettes that generally match the biome they spawn in
<End Changelog copy>
As you can see, this is a lot of content. Visit the site for the whole thing:
This patch changed the game (again!). No doubt soon many of these reviews will turn to positive, and then 2 months or so later will revert back to negative. That's how Starbound works. In my opinion, they should call it done with this update and then keep releasing this content, which would please those which seem to have been angered by this development.
It's still a 9.2/10 game. You really need to experience it for yourself.

It’s not a hard game by itself (except the last mission) but what makes it frustrating, is the planning part of your mission. Clearly there is one intended solution and it can contain a rather easy to miss element. These sorts of obstacles are not fun to figure out and on a few cases, led me to follow a walkthrough instead. There were a couple of fun missions, but most of them are a grind. As far as combat is concerned, it is the most inconvenient system I think I’ve ever come across. Also the controls are f*cking mental. Combine those two things and it is virtually impossible to shoot your way through any mission, or out of a sticky situation for that matter (on hard difficulty). And to top it off, the stealth thing I found is very inconsistent. You could die wearing your suit, respawn, acquire like a triads robe or smth (undetected of course) and you will still be shot on sight by some enemies. Generally this happens when you’re following the unconventional path and the game I guess tries to cut you down for it. The ‘check-point’ system in this game is more of a nuisance than help. And it crashes constantly right before some cut-scenes. Extremely infuriating if you haven’t reached so far into the level before. The story, mission layouts and soundtrack are all good though. I realise some of these issues are really down to the fact that this is a 17 year old game, but If I had known those things beforehand, I wouldn’t have had to waste 16hrs to find out. I think if you want to start the hitman series, then you needn’t worry about playing the first game.
PS. No need to be alarmed by the negative review. If you are interested, don’t be afraid to buy the game.

First off, I love the 2K basketball series.  In my opinion they've offered the best basketball game on the market year after year, and I started with the 2K college hoops games in 2006.  I still wish the NCAA would drop EA deal and allow 2K to return.
As anyone who's played the 2K series knows, every release is usually the same game as before.  So I'll go right ahead and say, 2K16 makes some of the biggest improvements over the last game that 2K has released in YEARS.
Graphically, much better.  Environment and atmosphere is a massive improvement.  Level of detail is spectacular.  Gameplay is tweaked a bit but pretty similar.  And the AI plays like an actually basketball team, making adjustments and responding to the flow of the game.
There are a few minor flaws in tthe game itself.  I know alot of people are upset with the MyPlayer career story.  Which is really trash, but isn't a game breaker by itself.  It would have been nice to see an option that lets you play MyCareer without the BS Spike Lee cliche.  But the story wank is short and afterword it's the same old MyPlayer people love.
My problem with this game is optimization.  It's the worst optimized AAA game I've ever seen released.  And the most insulting thing is that this isn't reflected in the recommended specs.
Just as a baseline, I can run Alien Isolation and similar demanding titles on ultra settings.  On 2K16 I set all the graphic sliders to medium go to play a game, and watch in terror as the opening commentors lag to a halt.  The damn commentator cutscenes don't even play correctly.  And then when the game starts at tip off, I knew I was getting my refund.  Watching the ref throw the ball into the air, only for it to slowly hover for about 10 seconds before falling.
Don't buy on PC is all I can say

After deciding that the game just flatout sucks and I will never play again, I gave it another chance... 7 months later. However, I was pleasantly surprised by some aspects which I didn't try before and ultimately lead to my choice of actually recommending the game.
My first gripe with the game was the combat, which has been changed significantly and you are now... well... underpowered, to say the least. To me at least, the combat was infuriatingly annoying throughout my first playthrough and through those blackbox assassination missions, of which we will talk about soon. However, a bit of practise does make perfect, and the combat just becomes really easy after a while. However, make sure to always upgrade your gear while playing, and always - ALWAYS - make sure you are carrying full health potions and full smoke bombs. Hell, fill everything.
The story mode is pretty decent, but nothing extraordinary. It is one of the weakest Assassin's Creed stories, and overall, why should you care. It is some boring and cliché revenge tale with some love bits thrown in, and a rather dull ending. The story isn't the highlight, but surely enough - the story is well acted (with no French accents) and you can get at least a bit of fun out of it.
The city... is absolutely gorgeous. It is pretty big and the amazing graphics blend in very well with this game. Unfortunately, this isn't the best optimized game out there and I thought Batman Arkham Knight ran much better. However, this is pretty much a whole new AC, on a new engine, and the gameplay is wildly different to, say, Assassin's Creed IV. The parkour and climbing is so frustrating at times, with my character not doing what I want him and doing the wrong things at VERY inconvenient times. The series long frustration is not gone with this game.
The game is actually quite lengthy. It is longer than, say, Shadow of Mordor or Batman Arkham Knight, or the tipical AC game, but I think my playtime increased significantly due to my awful fighting. There is a lot of content in this game, and most of it is decent at best, the overall package comes out really nice.
One of the best things about the game are the blackbox assassinations which give you several options to defeat your targets...... BUT! The stealth in this game is just absolutely ridiculously bad, it is finicky and it... oh my God. I would say Metal Gear Solid V is the best stealth game of all time, and this - by comparison - is just disgraceful. And the combat was made tougher probably because they wanted to encourage stealth. That is a shame, since the stealth rarely works, and you can't even do much. And when you do get into fights, the camera is so damn awful in tight corners in these BBAs that it made me rage quite infernally, leading to many undesirable deaths. So quick recommendation: GET MGS V! It is literally one of the best games I ever played!
The big highlight to the game, and the thing that made me enjoy it a lot more, are the cooperative missions which are absolutely great fun and I really recommend this game if you have at least 1 friend to play with because my God are they fun and varied. There are quite a bunch too, so you and your buddy will get hours to enjoy! They are easily replayable and really fun, if you can - of course - get past the maleficent things noted in this review.
So overall I am almost mixed about this game, but I would say get it ON A SALE. Anything else would be completely regrettable. But simply the sheer amount of fun I encountered in the game made it easily worth the £12 I paid in back in December 2015 for the Winter sale. The game is a 6/10 or more, it did leave a bad taste in my mouth after the first playthrough but your playthrough may be better and more fun, so I will leave it at that.

Brigador is the love-child of Virtual On and Syndicate Plus, after a diesel-soaked romp on Gibsonian streets. Dozens of unique vehicles to suit any play-style, enough lore-dripping killpower to kit them out with, core defenses for ambushing, disabling or annihilating *everything*, and an utterly relentless sandbox experience to pit your choices against. SNC, NEP, or Corvid, you're going to die. An awful lot. In delightfully dystopian ways. Brigador will mop the floor with you, your first few throwaway lives. It won't matter; Grab another loadout. Try something else. Eventually, something will click just right, and Solo Nobre comes apart for you, deliciously crunchy gun-chaff all wrapped up in Brigador's bombastic soundtrack.

Desert Strike and Syndicate have a neon-tinged HD baby in this visually arresting tank shooter, featuring a wonderful soundtrack and enormous customizability.
Novo Solo has been under the reign of a tyrant known only as "Great Leader" for as long as anyone still alive remembers. His sudden passing has left the capital, Solo Nobre in turmoil. As one of many "Brigadors" hired on by the definitely-not-evil SNC, you are tasked with staging sucicidal assaults throughout the capital in one of nearly fifty tanks, aircraft, and walkers customizable with over eighty weapons, ranging from explosive autocannons to repeating lasers.
Although the game certainly is among the pricier indie titles on Steam, let me assure you it's been worth every penny so far. A twenty-one mission campaign introduces you to the basics of combat, but the real meat lies in the game's freelance mode, which lets you loose in a series of open-ended, completely (and I mean COMPLETELY) destructable playgrounds. You have one life, and the only limit is how far you're willing to push your luck for more cash. BRIGADOR rewards proper planning as well as deadeye precision, boasting a full visibility and stealth system. You don't always have to outshoot your opponents if you can outwit them.
There are a few quibbles prospective players should consider, however. The controls are definitely non-standard, being quite literally "tank controls", where A-D turns your vehicle around in a circle, with the mouse controlling your turret. Even with multiple indicators I've gotten mixed up as to just where my wheels were pointing, and a second of confusion is all it takes to blow a mission in this game. But, with a few hours practice it should become second nature for the most part. The by-default dark graphics can make it hard to see smaller targets, but it can be fixed in the options menu. The tutorial is insufficient for much beyond the first ten to fifteen missions, but there are much better tutorials available on the game's Steam Forums. For nerve-wracking, pulse-pounding vehicle combat you can't do any better on Steam.

Thought Unity had a shaky release; as we all know, with incredible lag spikes and numerous other problems. The game now, is pristine. In Unity you play as Arno Dorian through Paris in the 1780s during the french revolution. A wonderful view of the city is seen around every corner. Whether you're looking at the old church of Notre Dame, or just witnissing the crowds gather and sing and yell for a change. I do believe I sat in Versailles watching people get executed for 10 entire minutes.
The story mode can be challenging in some portions, big fights make life difficult so the classic Assassin's Creed stealth requirement is returned because you want to do your best to avoid these massive 6-to-10 on 1 fights. Gameplay is quick and exciting as Arno proves he can do many more things than Ezio, Connor, and Edward. Climbing is faster, combat is faster (and cooler I might add).
Side missions and Side puzzles are in numerous variations and levels of difficulty all around Paris. I am not that good at Puzzles but if you are any more intelligent than me (which isn't hard to do mind you) then take a crack at it. Where I love the gameplay most is Co-op missions.
I'm hooked up with anywhere between 1 and 3 other assassin's where we tackle missions together in the coolest ways possible. I never thought I would ever see such badassery when we plan a mission perfectly and pull of the sweetest combos. Every mission is just like the trailer I promise you. Nothing feels better than running into a room with 3 other badasses and taking out a room of 16 guards so swiftly and easily. You won't be able to press F12 fast enough to catch it all!
I won't even get into all the customisation features to make your very own Arno look far better than any other Arno, representing your class and playing type the way you want to.
I would highly recommend Assassin's Creed Unity to anyone who is new to Asssassin's creed, and to anyone that has followed the series from the beginning.

The Hitman series is one that helped to revolutionize stealth games by introducing a brand new spin on the concept; putting players into the shoes of not a military personnel, not a sniper, but a hitman for hire. The franchise got its start in 2000 with the release of Hitman: Codename 47, which was developed by IO Interactive and initially published by Eidos (the same guys responsible for Deus Ex), though Square Enix would take over publishing rights in 2012 with the release of Absolution.
The game follows a bald individual known as "Subject 47", or later referred to as Agent 47, who wakes up in the basement of a sanitarium. He undergoes weapon and combat training (the tutorial level) before the game drops you into his life a year later, as he's in Hong Kong. By this time, Agent 47 has been hired as a hitman for the ICA. Although his first handful of assignments end up leading him to the assassination of a Triad leader, it's merely the first in a series of hits he will perform. Though much of the story seems to flow with no rhyme or reason other than contract killing, it does come with a surprise, somewhat horrific, ending that's definitely worth playing all the way through for. In fact, there are two endings in total.
Let's just go ahead and address the elephant in the room: Hitman: Codename 47 is U.G.L.Y., but luckily it has an alibi... it's entertaining; stick with me here. Even back in 2000 this title was considered graphically outdated, especially when taking into account the Playstation 2 released earlier the same year and had games that were far visually superior to this eye scarring swatch of PC master race shame. It's slightly above par with the original Resident Evil titles, but the first handful of levels will leave you feeling like you're making a big mistake even bothering with this game since the maps keep offering the same buildings and layout time after time.
Though Hitman: Codename 47's true saving graces lie within its musical score, atmosphere, and a unique gameplay system. Despite the repeating, flat, blobby textures, there's quite a bit of fog, haze, and mist that gives the game a gloomy vibe. There are 12 levels in the game, and each one has a track that's uniquely fitting; for instance, the first 4 missions take place in Hong Kong, and the music has a traditional Asian theme to it. Other locations you'll venture to are the jungle, a mental asylum, and a shipyard; so there's quite a bit of variety, once you get past the initial cityscape.
The gameplay is hit and miss in many aspects. The good thing about this title is that there are a number of ways you can complete each mission; whether you want to go in with your guns drawn, or try to work the situation out as stealthily as possible. There's a good amount of replayability because of this, since the more you explore different ways to complete your objectives, the more cutscenes and dialogue you'll inevitably end up uncovering. It really does take outside-of-the-box thinking in order to get through the game, though it's nowhere near as advanced as later Hitman titles. Mostly, you will be using disguises to infiltrate areas as opposed to formulating any real strategy. Let's also take a moment to be thankful for key rebinding, since either of the two default key layouts in this title are completely insane.
Some of the stunts that you have to perform in order to see a cutscene or complete a mission as intended are extremely obscure, no matter how uniquely you may be thinking, which is one of the major pain points of the game. Another downside is that there is no saving or checkpoint system; meaning if you die mid-mission, or fail an objective, it's back to the beginning. There's usually no indication on your in-game map of where to go, so you have to run around the abnormally large landscapes to find your next progression point. Worse yet, there's no way to check your objectives mid-mission, leaving you to rely on memory alone as to what you're supposed to be doing. As for the AI, the enemies in Hitman: Codename 47 are as dumb as bags of hammers. They can't see more than a couple of feet in front of them, and you can practically be mounting their butts without them so much as noticing your happy stick poking them; they don't react to footsteps, or much noise at all really, but they will raise alarms if they find dead bodies.
Even though Hitman: Codename 47 fell out of the ugly tree and hit every branch on the way down, and although it has some harsh shortcomings such as the lack of a save and checkpoint system, it's still a pretty fun title once you know what to do. Discovering new ways to complete objectives that end up following the correct path feels genuinely rewarding, especially when it involves getting some new dialogue. Suffice it to say that this isn't the best Hitman release on the market today, truly what makes this game worth playing is its great atmosphere and chilling ending(s).

So first and foremost: As someone who works with computer systems as a profession, I must admit that I am one of the few odd ones that really, *really* dislikes terminal based stuff. That being said, this game not only forced me to use the terminal, but actually gave me a reason to get used to using it, which has helped with my work.
This game is enjoyable, extremely so. Going into this game with mixed feelings, especially with what I felt, at the time, was the most important plot element being spoiled (Bit's death) I wasn't really sure how to feel about it, but I quickly forgot all about that as I began tackling missions and getting used to the world. On my first day alone I clocked nearly 6 hours of game time, which is almost half of the time that I've spent on this game to date so far. I simply could not put it down. While it's not completely realistic, the concept is really well executed and it's definitely one of the more real hacking themed games that I've seen compared to others.
The game play starts off rather simple, and there isn't really much challenge in the beginning, but for those who aren't really computer savvy this gives them time to learn how to do some of the essentials while also testing their skills and improving. I think the first time I actually struggled was after getting counter-hacked by Naix and getting thrown into Terminal Mode, although I was freaking out over that because up until that point I had been really successful at avoiding any security in place; I was confused as I was positive that I had deleted everything in the logs dir and couldn't understand how I had been found. I wasn't aware that it was a scripted sequence until later.
One thing I wish the game did a bit better though was when you failed to DC in time and were tracked. There was *so* much going on in the short amount of time you have to reset your IP that the first time it happened to me, I panicked and almost failed, resorting to closing out of the game (because what is cheating, right?).
While there are a few issues with the game's missions, namely you being unable to complete missions if you've managed to wonder off to another one, overall I feel the game is extremely polished for something that started off as a small project. The missions are all enjoyable, the music is fantastic, the story is overall impressive (and the small logs scattered throughout the computers is a pretty enjoyable addition as well), and it just feels good as a whole. I haven't gotten around to playing the DLC yet, but if it's anything like the rest of the main game, I'm sure it won't disappoint in the slightest.
I would strongly recommend this to anyone who is looking for a bit of a more "realistic" hacking game. It makes you think, and teaches you some terminal basics, all while having fun in the process.
