It's on sale so I'm pretending that my opinions on video games are worth anything
Unlike most steam reviewers, I will assume that you can read and that you have read the description of the game, so you have an idea of what it is.
The game is pretty fun, all things considered. It's not like real hacking, but it is the type of experience that is engaging and does make you solve problems that are similar to ones that you'd have to solve with actual hacking. That being said, a lot of terminology is thrown around loosely so if you're an autist you'll probably find a problem with that, as it's something that doesn't affect the actual gameplay at all but is easy to feign your superiority with.
For everyone else, the game is entertaining. The story is okay, but the DLC's story gets good towards the end. The game challenges you to think outside the box on occasion and this progresses the story further. It also keeps in character a lot, considering that the game is supposedly it's own "hacker" operating system, and this affects the experience inside the game and out of it, as anyone who's played it will agree.
TL;DR the game is pretty fun if you're not a prick about it. The DLC and user campaigns will add more content as time goes on, though the game's format can become repetitive after a while. It's nothing that's worth more than the Ultimate edition when it's on sale, though.

A challenging 'brick ball' game, Ionball 2 can become downright masochistic to play at higher stages, where the difficulty spikes considerably. It doesn't alter the standard formula of 'bounce the ball against the bricks' considerably, but a wide array of activate-able and passive powerups, unique enemy types, and levelling skills keep the game fresh, even past the point wherein it becomes tedious.
The controls are a bit slimy, and I ended up frustrated several times as I nudged my mouse to move the platform just a smidgen and had it slide too far beyond the target spot, losing the ball and a life. The menu screen transitions are not particularly smooth, either, and it can take anywhere from 15 - 30 seconds to pass through the menus from death to rebirth, which might frustrate gamers at higher difficulties, where death occurs constantly. Graphically, the game combines 'gritty industrial' with 'neon eyegasm' so you might be turned off by the visual style. All in all, unless you like punishment, you'll likely grow weary of this game within a few hours.

So after playing for a short while and considering my interest in cyber security, this game does really pull you into a different perspective altogether, especially if you're unaware of the concept behind malicious activities. This game puts you straight into the seat of a hacker, where cracking, executing and advanced computer knowledge is your weapon as you progress through the story in stages. At the start of the story, you begin in a tutorial stage which walks you through basic commands and how to hack a port and delete tracking information. As well as disconnecting from systems. The tutorial is well constructed and written, which helps the player understand what to do and how to do something to advance. The story also has no voice acting, but relies on text as if some anonymous user is contacting you - an example would be the in-game email system and intermissions. When it comes to presentation, it definitely makes you feel a part of something outside your comfort zone, as the hacking environment really does look and feel as if you're breaching unsecure or secured networks.
Overall, Hacknet doesn't fail to impress me and it's worth checking out if you're into cyber security or computer coding.
My Verdict - 8/10.

Full disclosure: My main motivation for even reviewing this game was the introduction of the Creation Club. With the addition of paid mods that leave the modders at a disadvantageous agreement, blatant misdirection on the part of Bethesda. The use of microtransactions that force you to buy an additional currency designed in a way that you will always either need to buy more, or waste money is deplorable to me. For this reason alone, I cannot recommend Fallout 4, however, I think that it's only fair to give the game an actual review to decide for yourself if you want to buy it.
Fallout 4 is by nearly every metric a decent game: the story is passable, the map is large but not nearly as dynamic or interesting as that of GTA V, and the variety of gameplay is above average. Firstly, the story is rather simple, and is nothing new: it checks the boxes and does it's job of introducing us to the world and little else. I doubt you would feel particularly thrilled or moved by anything that transpires along any of the storylines simply because there isn't really anything to glom onto with any of the characters. The map in fallout 4 is quite large, however the diversity is something to be desired. If you want any of that I can recommend Far Harbor and Nuka World which both offer a refreshing change of pace and scenery from the base game.

The map is beautiful as beautiful as a ravaged, and barren Boston Commonwealth can be. The city feels massive, and well scaled, the small outlying suburbias all have a unique charm to them, and everything seems to fit well. I would like to see more color in the plant life, as I can only assume that after so many years nature would "find a way" so to speak.

My main gripe with the game in it's base state is the lack of variety in equipment, Bethesda made the choice to forego raw variety and favored customization above all else. The main weapons you will find are: Laser, plasma, pipe weapons, combat rifles, assault rifles, revolvers, Gatling style guns and 10mm pistols for ballistic weapons, and for melee you will find rippers occupying the 'very fast' category, combat knives in the 'fast' category, baseball bats and machetes in the 'medium' category, and boards, sledges, and super sledges in the 'slow' category. All of these barring a few unique weapons. A few of these weapons can actually change their archetype: in that they can be customized into pistols, carbines, and precision rifles with a simple change in stock and barrel. But beyond this there is little else to customize, most of the customization lies in linear improvements over previous options, making it not as much customization as weapon based progression. The most variety you will find is generally in the top four receiver upgrades that determine how the weapon functions in rapid full auto, moderate full auto, and semi auto. Everything else simply comes down to picking the last part in each list which is generally an upgraded version of another part i.e.: drum mag vs quick eject drum mag, or long barrel vs fluted long barrel, or marksmen stock vs recoil dampening stock. The weapons also serve themselves to different skills which is a topic in and of itself.

Speaking of which: The progression in this game is a MAJOR departure from previous entries: the game has dropped specialized skills in favor of simply having different levels of perks under the SPECIAL tree. Most of the perks are pretty niche, but in terms of specialization you have: four levels of upgrades in damage for semi auto, full auto, pistol, explosive, and melee, and four levels of upgrades for various forms of resistance to rads, energy, ballistic, less damage whilst moving, and less damage whist still. Each stage increases the efficacy by what feels like a staggering amount and after four upgrades you can effectively double the potency of a given spec. There is NO depth or progression to any perks. Each perk is in a column and the only thing barring them is how many points you invest in the actual trait. There’s no specing into melee for instance, and eventually narrowing it down to heavy melee. The simplification goes so far as to not have any downsides for any perks, after roughly 120 levels I have fully spec’d semi auto, rifles, and stealth, but also invested partially into full auto and a perk which allows you to take less damage whilst standing still. Me being a stealth with precision weapons has no impact on other play styles and hypothetically, if you played only one character you could feasibly max out all trees and be a master of all. In fact, aside from playing different storylines, there’s no reason to not do this. When you spec into Semi auto, it’s just a bonus for that there’s no downside and you don’t feel like there was any investment in what you were doing.

So, Fallout 4 is a decent game, but I would not call it a good Fallout game. This game is by far and away the weakest entry in the franchise, which I think speaks more about the franchise as a whole than this game in particular. If you want a simple RPG that is mindless and simple to grasp, or if you just want a game to play to pass the time, this is going to be a good choice. I would wait for it to go on sale if you are considering it as your next purchase.

Absolutely superb isometric mech action. One can sense genuine effort and artistry that were poured into it, from its satisfying and responsive action (once one gets used to tank controlls that grace most of game's vehicles, something we rarely see today) to its gorgeously crafted visuals and remarkable soundtrack.
While most folks will understandably start with game's campaign mode, freelance mode is where the real fun is. Unlike campaign mode, which oft gives choice between few predefined vehicles for each mission, freelance mode offers insane variety of vehicles and weapons one can purchase through credits earned in each mission, as well as variety of meaty new missions to unlock. Weapons differ vastly in their properties and behaviour, and are mostly really fun to use, so that already high replayability is additionaly enhanced with player's desire to try out all those different ways of unleashing glorious mass destruction upon the world.
Game is also oozing with olden style cyberpunk mood and is trully gorgeous to look at, especially once action is at its pinnacle with gratuitous explosions and laser beams filling the screen, and with game's destructible environments showing their crunchy best.
All in all, remarkably well crafted game, and one that is chock full of content. I've played this game about 30 hours right now, and I like most of it so far. Although there are a few (not even minor things) I really dislike about this game.
First of all: it doesn't work properly on Windows 10 after installation, you get a crash every 10 to 15 minutes. It is easy to fix though, but it is quite irritating at first. You can stop it by searching for
, you will get probably 3 results. Move or rename the one in Windows/System32, and you will have no problem playing the game anymore. (you won't have sound during the UBISOFT logo video, but there are no other problems with this.)
Now during the combat they changed a few key things:
They removed the human shield ability, I don't know why, but it's bad. You will get in combat with maybe 7 soldiers, maybe 2 will start to shoot at you, and you can't do anything about it. And, when you are in combat and throw a smokebomb, you have to keep using your primary weapon (i.e. sword, axe or spear thingy), so you can't just stab them with your hidden blade, which is just totally ridiculous. Also, a lot of times, you will get spotted. And when you are spotted, you cannot air assasinate enemy's, so far so good. BUT: when you jump on them, they get knocked down, and
, you just have to wait for them to get back up. You can only stab them on the ground after playing a large part of the story, after which you have to use ability points to unlock the ability to stab people who you knocked down on the ground. (
why did you think that was a good idea?)
Now I do like the Paris they made, it's a pretty big open world with a lot to do in it. It's also really nice you can customise they way you play by changing parts of Arno's costume. Also the lighting is sublime, The castles and palaces are just beatiful with the glossy marble and golden detailing and the beautiful art pieces on the walls. The story is good so far (only played until sequence 6 yet)
Short version of my review:
Pros:
+ really nice and beautifully created Paris, they put so much detail into it.
+ random events on the streets of Paris
+ lot's of quests/side missions
+ you can customise Arno's costume, with each part contributing to different abbilities
+ lot's of different weapons
+ when you have to assassinate a major person in the story, you can take a lot of different routes to get to them
+ nice brutal finishing animations
Cons:
- crashes every 10-15 minutes on Windows 10 after install, easy to fix though, but Ubisoft should've already fixed it.
- can't stab enemy's who are in a smoke cloud
- they removed the human shield ability
- can stab knocked down enemy's only after playing a big part of the story

Today marks the release of the Up-Armored edition. As flamed as I was by the community for suggesting improvements, it seems the devs took note (of mine or others criticisms), and added much value to this game. As a result it no longer feels "rushed out of EA", and is well worth your time. I will leave the old review as it still has some relevence.
---------------
Rushed out of EA and not sure why. A few more months, a little more feedback and I think this could have been a real gem.
The game has a cool story trapped behind a cold game menu through which it is told. This is made more frustrating after they went to the trouble of having someone write and voice an audio-book but didn't include a single sound bite in the game.
There are a couple dozen unique drivers each with their own stories and "traits" that effect your final score. But those stories are so coldly told through the games menu that the driver becomes nothing more than a score multiplier.
A few cut scenes similar to what you might find in cryptark or invisible inc. Simple text and pixel portraits could have really gone a long way in connecting the player with the avatar.
The unlock system feels a little blind at times, you'll often spend a mill on some lore and a few mill on a driver only to feel like you just stuck your hand in a lucky dip or played pin the tale on the donkey, with the only consolation being that all the prizes were pretty crap so what difference does it make what you get.
Now if the lore had been audio logs, or part of the audio book along side the menu text, it would have been worth a mill.. and that driver, if it came with 3 or 4 personalised text boxes expressing their motives for risking their lives, placed next to their portraits at the start of the first 3 or 4 Freelance missions I took 'em on, maybe I'd care about them and be inclined to learn about another.
Some of the stories told through the menus are emotive but feel like a chore to connect with. It's a real shame.
The game looks great imo, music is perfect, it's that new retro wave.
Controls are perfect imo also, some people complain about them, but if you give them a chance and think about the logistics they work well and make sense.
It's in the variety of vehicles and weapons that this game really shines, while missions can feel similar (due to having little to no investment in any of the characters or the story), it's the loadout that makes a run unique. Vehicles have their own feel and can't all support the same mounts, so with weapons ranging from explosives with arch like firing arcs to machine gun lazers, there is absolutely an incentive and desire to experiment.
+ Beautiful game, lovely lighting
+ Lots of unlockables
+ Great ost and sfx
+ Lots of lore (though poorly implemented)
+ Fun guns
+ Strong level design
+ Interesting vehicles
+ Fair amount of content
+ Multiple ways to finish your mission
- Feels rushed
- Some bugs (known about since EA)
- No ability to zoom in on the lovely pixelated mechs and weps, not even through the Acquisitions menu
- Poor use of wonderfully crafted lore
- Missions can feel the same, with little to no investment in any of the characters or the story
- No Auto forward key (trust me it needs one)
- No level editor
7.5/10 Pretty good, could have been so much better. Could still be, with some work
Recommended

Just to be totally upfront: I haven't played a shoot em up game since Gradius III.  That said I had a lot of fun with Astebreed.  I got a real sense of being in control of a one man army as I locked my homing lasers onto dozens of enemies and watch them explode, while using my machine's hilariously oversized sword to swat their shots out of the sky.
The game is a bit on the short side as I beat it on easy (because I'm a pansy who doesn't play shootemups) in about an hour and a half.  That said there are harder difficulties to play through as well as different mecha to play through the game as, so I don't feel cheated with the length.
My main complaint with the game is the way the story is presented. It is mainly told through dialogue in the missions and this dialogue is entirely in Japanese.  While it is translated in text at the bottom corner of the screen, it is difficult to both read the text and keep an eye on the action of the game.  It almost makes me wish the game was dubbed, but from a production standpoint that wouldn't have been worth the extra cost.
The story itself is fairly cookie cutter for real robot anime, with some stuff about loved ones on the other side of the war and the morality of people being used as weapons.  Nothing to write home about at all, but decent enough to provide a backdrop for an entertaining game.
Overall if Astebreed looks at all interesting to you or of you like either giant robots blowing stuff up or shoot em ups that aren't controller-breaking difficult, I'd recommend you give it a try.

X-Com 2 is clearly a game that the developer put a lot of thought into. I do want to say that they are to be commended for experimenting, and leaving the game open to community modding so that some of their design choices are now completely optional. Ultimately I have to give it a thumbs down, but this is speaking as a hardcore X-Com fan, and someone who did enjoy the game. I don't want to harp on X-comm 2 that much, It's clear this game did make some meaningful attempts to innovate the rebooted franchise. However it's important to understand why hardcore X-Com fans consider this game a step backward.
1. Number of Soldiers: In the original X-Com you get tons of soliders on each mission, perhaps even too many. This gives your strategies more interlocking parts, and gives the game more depth. While you still become attached to soldiers in the original x-com, it's not super frustrating if a few dudes die. In fact, on harder missions, you can basically expect 4-6 casulties. Losses are normal in the original X-Com, and you don't feel too punished by them.
In the new X-Com, while every effort was made to make the soldiers customizable and unique, the fact that you can only take a small number of soldiers with you means that the loss of a single solder is a huge punishment. At the start of the game, the loss of a single soldier will cost you 25% of your total force. The original X-com made you attached to your little hero mens, but that attachment meant so much more because that soldier had distinguished himself by climbing over a pile of dead chumps, picked up a grenade blew up an alien or something similarly heroic. In the new X-Com, you are TOO attached to each soldier. Losing a single one can cause you to ragequit, in a weird way you become less attached to them because they are all so important to your combat efficiency, game pieces.
2. Strategic Map: In the original X-Com, the strategic map was a very important aspect of the game. It was very flexible at accomodating different strategies (tall vs wide, all-in vs slow buildup, etc.). Most importantly there was a meaningful symbiosis between the tactical and strategic modes. As yatzee said about the original reboot, "gee I'm sure glad I can build these guns so I can kill more aliens. Gee I'm glad I killed those aliens so I can build new cool guns." That core loop is the essense of x-com.
In X-Com 2, any pretense of an in-depth strategic mode have been lost. Air combat has been removed entirely, as have most of the logistical features of the original games. The core gameplay loop has essentially been broken. While X-Com has always been a sort of tactical and strategic board game, the original felt more inspired by simulators, the new X-Com feels much more abstracted like a boardgame, and this hurts mah 'mersion.
3. Missions: While the original x-com missions can get repetitive, each type of mission had an important purpose and context. Bust open UFOs and get the goodies inside, prevent aliens from terrorizing the earth, and most importantly, defend your base from a direct invasion. These different mission types have enough diversity to keep the game replayable.
In the new X-Com, it is clear they wanted to make more varied missions for the player in order to increase mission diversity and overall replayability. However I don't think the things they added make the game stronger than the things they removed. The missions still feel generic (go here, perform action/defend X), and can often get in the way of what your actually want to do, kill aliens (no, the game tells you, you must escort this VIP instead!). Part of me feels that if they had made the strategic mode more engaging and the mission system interact with it more, they could have fixed this. Don't even get me started on turn timers.
4. General stripping down of complexity: This is really the essence of why X-Com fans can't accept this game as a true successor to the original, and where most of the criticism about the reboot come from.
TU: Yes TU was clumsy, but it felt more real that each individual action cost a set of time units. The new "2 moves" system is far too simplistic. I admit TU was clumsy and more time consuming, but I still miss it.
Soldeir Stats: That guy you named after your co-worker, he's a♥♥♥♥♥♥shot, but he's the best damn grenade-chucker in X-Com. Your girlfriend's character on the other hand, is an amazing sniper, but lacks bravery. All these individual stats really mattered for you tactics and made each soldier feel unique. Soldiers are more customizable now, but they all start from this boring, generic base of mush.
Inventory: Strong soldiers used to be able to carry all sorts of stuff, while weak noodle arms could barely hold a rifle and enough ammunition to stay alive. If you wanted, you could just give a guy a grenade in each hand, and a belt full of grenades. ♥♥♥♥, you could even adopt a policy of C4 kamikaze dead-man's switch suicide bombs for your... less stat endowed soldiers. All this inventory customization basically allowed you to make your own classes. The new rigid system of "you get 2 slots and your class weapons" is really limiting by comparison.
I don't think X-Com players want to see a completely faithful remake of the original (maybe they do, but that's why we have Xenonauts) but hopefully I have illustrated why they feel TOO much of the core-gameplay loop and original formula of the series has been lost in translation. Hopefuly the devs continue to innovate and make the game more accessible and pretty, while looking at what really made the original X-Com such a unique experience that long-time fans still consider an icon of strategy gaming.

This game is... mediocre. The gameplay is monotonous and unchallenging, the storyline is fractured and uninspiring (it's even harder to take seriously since you're playing as a script kiddie), and the material is extremely far from reality.  As an actual Linux sysadmin, I am in particular annoyed by how poorly implemented common UNIX utilities are.  "ls *" and "rm ./*" fail, but "rm *" works? No "cp" or "mkdir"?  No way to delete directories? I can go on and on. Literally, I programmed more coreutils in a single college project than there are in this game. Couldn't they have just used busybox or something?  It certainly would have solved the issues the game has with file duplication in directories, since it'd be using actual files, rather than what is presumably a stack/queue/list/whatever.  And I would kill for io redirection.
Also, I'm mildly triggered by the executables being .exe files, but I'm definitely amused that you BSOD instead of kernel panicking.
I bought this game for a song, but I don't think I'd even recommend it if it were free, because in the time it takes you to play this game, you could have learned all sorts of actual UNIX commands in an actual terminal emulator on Linux, something that actually is free -- and you'd probably have a lot more fun, too.

Astebreed is a good mecha shoot'em up game that has a reasonable amount of content and one of the first I have played. The gameplay is pretty fun and it's easy to learn the basics even without the guidance of optional tutorials. In combat, you have plenty of options like simply shooting bullets, lock on enemies to shoot them with bullets, cut your way through with a powerful blade, and heck using a quick short insurmountable blade dash. Although the story isn't so amazing, the fact that most of the dialogue is spoken during the game can become an annoyance since you have to focus on destroying your enemies but sometimes you may feel the need to read the English subtitles (dialogue is in Japanese only) and that may be a bother (not so much for me personally). The dialogue is not terrible though, the voice actors did a good job voicing each character. Another thing that must be noted is that once you start the game, you have to finish it completely (like ever shoot 'em up game) because you cannot load from where you left off. However, there is a Chapter Select option that allows you to play chapters you have at least completed but if you care about certain achievements then you would have to stick to playing the game in one go. You can play the game on Easy, Normal, or Hard but be warned that Hard mode is really challenging (I tried and failed miserably). One last letdown is that the game is rather short, I was able to beat the game in about an hour and I really wished there was more to play.
Despite the negatives, Astebreed is still a good game to try out. Aside from the great gameplay, the art done in this game is great. Speaking of art, this game offers extras that allow you to see in-game art, concept art, 3-D mecha art, and more. The characters in the game are tolerable and you can also know more about them in the extras along with pretty much anything. To me, the price seems a little reasonable considering what the game offers so if you're a fan of shoot'em ups, mecha, and anime then I would definitely recommend picking this game up. Before I wrap up this review, I also highly recommend using a controller to play the game.
That concludes my review on Astebreed, looking forward to hopefully seeing more of this game in the future.

I manage to sneak past the guards for most of the mission, but now I'm in a right tight spot.
2 full kit squads of 4 guards are nearby, and one of them is nearly in view.  Firing up my trusty Sidewinder I glitch past the guard and make it to the loot, finally fulfilling my lifelong goal.
Just one problem.  That was the last charge on my Sidewinder, meaning it's dead until I get back.  Or...well...die.
I'm not kitted with a stealth shield.  Just didn't have one but sure wishing for it now.  Then a thought strikes me.  Break the window.  Nothing standing between me and freedom but fragile glass.  Well...that and an endless vacuum of nothingness waiting to make my eyes explode.
No airlock nearby...no way past the guard...too many guards to book for the exit...I pull out my shotgun, take careful aim, squeeze...
And hold my breath.  And start the timer.  20 seconds.
The glass shatters and vanishes without sound.  After all there's no air in space.  19 seconds.
The maw of nothingness slurps me into the void, and my breath is almost stolen from me.  18.
And I'm free.  Well, free to die.  I put my breacher on autopilot.  It takes longer than normal.  Too long.  13.
I see the lights.  12.
It's still so far away...11.
I blink...and loose count.  My lungs start to burn.
And just when I cannot hold my breath anymore...the breacher scoops me up and I am GONE.
While normally I wouldn't mind taking a shot and getting carried to freedom...I don't have any blood to spare.  I'd die the moment they put me out the airlock.  And bullets sting worse than stun rounds.
As I look back, I spot another little prize.  No...too risky...and yet...
The sheer satisfaction of riding in on someone's elses ship just can't be beat.

Approximately 9 to 10 years ago, I purchased Okami for the Wii, its first re-release since the original on the PS2.
Frankly, I was disappointed initially. The opening sequence, including a very, very long unskippable cutscene, was extremely slow, and it felt like an endless wave of tutorial after tutorial. While the visuals were unique and attention-grabbing, it was not quite enough to sustain my interest.
I put the game down in boredom and disappointment, and did not plan to come back. But I did, months after on a slow day, and boy am I glad I did so. I trudged through the remaining slow parts of the opening, and the game steadily picked up its pace.
I became absorbed into its massive, sprawling world beautifully designed with meticulous care to detail. The accompanying soundtrack was at times catchy and at other times emotional, but always appropriate and gorgeous in execution, defying the technical limitations of being initially developed for the PS2. Characters were humorous and filled with personality in writing and in visual design. Combat was simple but satisfying. And of course, the Celestial Brush mechanic continuously impressed in its creativity and implementation.
A few minor annoyances have not been fixed since even the PS2 days. The choppy and abrupt "voice acting" was perhaps tolerable in 2008, but not so much in 2017. Drawing with the Celestial Brush can be frustrating at times when the game simply refuses to recognize input. Some dialogue is still (seemingly arbitrarily) not skippable, leading to a feeling of being bogged down when I'm reading way ahead of the characters "speaking".
Of course, the remastered visuals haven't been a case of simply flipping a switch to change the game's native resolution. Many textures have been significantly bumped up in clarity, and many particle effects are much cleaner in appearance. The game's unique thick brush stroke outlines are sharp and defined. The end result is a game that I'd readily believe is a modern 2017 release, albeit not of the same AAA calibre as it was. New options like bringing back the PS2 loading screen minigames are also appreciated.
Special mention needs to be made about the game's controversial 30 fps lock. As someone with a 144Hz monitor and who is usually a stickler for higher framerates and refresh rates, I genuinely do not find it diminishing my experience too much thanks to the game's unique artstyle and specifically designed animations. However, it definitely was and still is a slight bummer that the now-universal 60 fps has not been implemented into this game's third re-release.
The keyboard+mouse implementation is acceptable. Some keybindings are strange (thankfully this is changeable in the menus) and the game's menus are not exactly mouse-friendly, but it wasn't too intrusive for the most part. In particular, drawing with the Celestial Brush felt extremely fast and intuitive, allowing me to draw at at a speed and accuracy far surpassing the Wiimote, much less other traditional controllers.
Do I recommend this remaster of Clover Studio's masterpiece? Unequivocally yes, especially to the folks who have not yet experienced the game in any form. Fans of the original PS2/Wii release would surely appreciate reliving the experience with vastly improved visuals and perhaps a new method of input. For the owners of the PS3 HD remaster, this is really much of the same with 4K and keyboard+mouse input, so it really boils down to a judgment call.

While I haven't beaten the PC version yet, I remember this game fondly from beating it several times as a kid while it was out on the PS2. I was looking forward to this release for some. However, now that I'm a bit older and have time to actually review the game, I will say there there are some things lacking that I may of "tolerated" in my youth. Aesthetically, the game is flawless, it's beautiful,  the characters are very nice and combat is pretty flawless. It's easy to grasp without losing it's challenge.
So, not to scare you too much, I'll say a  lot of the pros here first and the cons will come later.
-The Characters are memorable
-The Music is ABSOLUTELY beautiful
-The scenery is beautiful
-There is a lot to do, small minigames available to play, side quest a'plenty, and plenty of demon scrolls to kill
-Secrets a plenty, this game has a lot of replay value with a New Game+ Mode that makes the game easier and more fun with the abilities, weapons, etc in tact as well as bonus stuff at the end.
-Yes, you CAN be petted and called a good dog.
-The story is memorable and I have yet to NOT cry near the end from how beautiful it can get.
-Each location is beautiful and unique, from the very first city you go to at the start of the game to the last area, you won't find anything about the locations  repeating themselves enough to be annoying.
-Each boss brings something unique to the fight, normally dealing with clever ways of using the new brush techniques you learn to beat them.
-Combat has a very nice flow to it, I haven't really died in the game yet, and only in more difficult fights like facing new enemies that I'm unfamiliar with do I have to worry about a prolonged fight. It's fast, it's quick, it doesn't break up the flow and some encounters can be avoided outright, as the random encounter fights - represented by flying red demon scrolls - can be avoided if you do not want to fight at all.
The pros outweigh a lot of the cons, but there ARE still cons, which I will try my best to  point out here.
-The Characters are memorable...but annoying. The small not-Navi  Issun is annoying, stating things over that you already know, constantly pointing out the obvious, and repeating what people say to make sure you get it. Very rarely is any of his advice actually useful and you will normally be quickly clicking through even dialogue you haven't heard as it's normally just him repeating what another character has said.
-The controls are very obviously made for a controller and I've found that my playthrough with a keyboard and mouse is...awkward, to say the least. After fidgeting with the controls a bit in the menu, I've gotten it more or less under control, but it's still awkward. Platforming is somewhat difficult, but the real con I've found is using the "Celestial brush", it's wonky, jagged and doesn't really respond well with a mouse, you get a more natural flow with a controller while you'll find yourself having some minor challenge in just drawing a circle with a mouse - I won't deny that this might just be my mouse's fault, but this is my experience so far.
-There are far too many pauses in the game. You'll find that while you're running through the beautiful world of Okami, it has a poor habit of stopping the entire game to show you a short cutscene of it pointing out something obvious, like buildings, places of interests, etc even though you can see them normally quite clearly. Combine this with the fact that every pickup besides money will pause the game and give you a brief description of what it is you picked up, even when you've seen it a thousand times over, it gets pretty annoying and you'll find the flow of the game interrupted quite a lot.
-Certain character motivations are a bit...strange. I won't spoil anything, but there are times in the story when it seems like the evidence behind a character's motivation was left out, or something was just added in as a secondary thought. This can leave you a bit dumbstruck at times, as you wonder why no one pointed this out to begin with or "how the heck did you jump to THAT conclusion?"
-The plot is amazing, but some things are predictable. Good guys are obviously good, bad guys are obviously bad. Even when the story tries to paint it otherwise to fool you, you can normally tell if a character is good or evil pretty quickly. It tries to do this thing with keeping characters in the shadows until a big reveal, but it's pretty easy to tell who is who.
-This is more a personal thing, but people treat a random white wolf walking into their city pretty...casually. Issun - I would imagine - is suppose to be there to sort of bridge a gap, since your character cannot talk, but people just spill out their life's problems to this random wild animal that doesn't bite them instantly, even when he's not hopping around and talking. Plus, your Godhood rarely comes out, even when people realize you're a God, it's just passed off casually. Maybe I'm just missing something, but it sort of irks me.
Those are the few cons I can really think of off the top of my head. I hope this review helps you in whether or not you buy the game, as you might of noticed, I recommend it and I honestly do think that despite the flaws stated, this is a journey that you shouldn't pass up. It's a beautiful game with a beautiful atmosphere. Is it perfect? No, but games don't have to be perfect for you to enjoy them.

I was skeptical about buying this game at first. Around January 15, Negative reviews filled the "most helpful" section. Still, I gave it a go. I was amazed at first, but then a little disappointed. I just kind of said, "Is that it?" The exploration was nice, but I figured that all the planets were just the same: Forest, desert, snow, and the occasional volcanic. (I was wrong, but I didn't know that).
Then came the Late January Update AKA The Winter Update. This completely changed the format of the game, and, to me, created an entirely new game. This time I chose the Novakid, because, hey, he's the new guy, and entered the world.
One thing, that was plainly obvious about Starbound was the building. At first it doesn't seem much different from it's predecessors (i.e. Minecraft and Terraria), but later in the game, especially after you get the Paint Tool, you become able to make fortresses and houses that you never even dreamed of (with the help of decorations found in dungeons). It also has some of the best building mechanics I've seen in a Side-scrolling game.
Starbound also has an awful lot of weapons to choose from. Just before writing this review, I was on a snow planet and discovered a minigun-like contraption that shoots snowballs. There's a huge variety of swords, hammers, spears, guns, pistols, axes, and more to choose from. With the help of Tech like the Jump Boost or the Energy Dash, you can easily jump around your enemies to turn the fight in your favour.
The navigation in Starbound is ridiculously large for an indie game. I couldn't see myself exploring more than 5 solar systems, maybe 6. And yet there seems to be 100 or likely more out there! And travel isn't cheap, either. You need to travel to a moon and start mining there to fing Archius fuel. To pick it up, you need to upgrade your Matter Manipulator, one of Starbound's brilliant concepts. Or you could collect Uranium from hazardous planets. The 5 different types of Stars, Gentle (Beginner), Eccentric (Moderate), Radioactive (Master), Frozen (Expert), and Fiery (also Expert) all come with their own unique planets to explore.
Don't let the art or the 2D fool you. Starbound is it's own little gem in the Survival genre. The game isn't even past Early Access and it's easily worth $25, in my opinion. I would indeed recommend this game to any fan of exploration, survival, fighting, or Rouge-like games. 9.2/10
Notes:
This game has indeed been in development for more than 2 years now. It has evolved a lot from it's original state, but the community has only grown more impatient. You see, the Starbound devs go about development a bit differently than most. By the way, in my 44 hours of playing this game, I have not encountered a single bug. Not one. Anyway, the Starbound devs produce content in large, stretched-out patches. One of them released today. It is called PLeased Giraffe. I'll copy about 1/10 or less of the changelog here for you:
Colony System
Colonize your worlds! Create a home, decorate it nicely, then place a Colony Deed to attract a tenant!
The type of NPC who moves in will depend on the type and quality of the home’s furniture and decorations. Decorating a room with several objects from the same theme (such as a biome or material tier) will attract a tenant themed to match!
Keep your tenants happy and they’ll periodically offer you gifts, some cosmetic and some very useful
New Outpost Store: Frögg Furnishings
Sells Colony Deeds as well as a variety of furniture in many themes
The set of specialty furniture available will rotate each (out of game) day, so make sure you keep coming back to see the full selection
Each furniture set can be used to attract a particular tenant that fits its theme
Improvements to NPCs
NPCs will now interact with each other and with many different objects in the world. Depending on their personalities they might get sad, excited, fall in love or do all kinds of different things in different situations!
See who your tenants are and what they’re thinking! (press Alt to activate)
Added many unique NPC dialogue options and updated some old ones
Further improved NPC movement and pathfinding
NPCs now switch between ranged and melee weapons in combat depending on their available energy, range, and whether they can reach the player
Groups of NPCs now coordinate in combat to attack from different positions and divide themselves between ranged and melee
Surface Biomes and Sub-Biomes (Tiers 1 – 4)
Major visual improvements to background parallaxes
All biomes have several types of unique critters (60+)
Added a huge number of biome-specific microdungeons (450+)
Added many new biome-specific cosmetic armors and other items
Randomly generated monsters will now have color palettes that generally match the biome they spawn in
<End Changelog copy>
As you can see, this is a lot of content. Visit the site for the whole thing:
This patch changed the game (again!). No doubt soon many of these reviews will turn to positive, and then 2 months or so later will revert back to negative. That's how Starbound works. In my opinion, they should call it done with this update and then keep releasing this content, which would please those which seem to have been angered by this development.
It's still a 9.2/10 game. You really need to experience it for yourself.

There is much to love and hate about this game. You send party members to the theater of war that is your evil-ridden ancestral estate. They fight, scream, bleed, and curse you for the horrors that they put up with. Many die, but somehow they are better off than the ones who survive.
The mechanics, lore, and overall mood of the game make this worthy of its name. It is not a fair game; fate sometimes has a way to make mincemeat out of your party before you even get a turn. When your ancestor reminds you that overconfidence is a slow and insidious killer, he means it. Sure, you can justify your way and blame the game and the numbers for getting you killed; perhaps that is fine, too.
Perhaps the best way of describe Darkest Dungeon is Fantasy Armchair Commander Simulator. How you play the game speaks volumes of your morality and character should you be placed in a position of authority and responsibility. Sure, you can treat willing adventurers either like comrades you would live with and die for, or discard them like pawns to be sacrificed at convenience. The game will not judge you, but can you live with yourself?

Hitman: Codename 47 is a game developed by IO Interactive and published by Sqaure Enix. As the enigmatic Hitman, you must use stealth and tactical problem solving to enter, execute and exit your assignment with minimum attention and maximum effectiveness
One of the finest stealth games of its generation, it puts you in the role of Agent 47, a shadowy assassin who is equally capable of slipping in and out of target locations un-noticed, the game provides a wealth of memorable situations you will talk about years down the road.
However, the game is not without its flaws. For a game nearly 10+ years old, gameplay mechanics can be somewhat clunky. Probably the biggest gripe however is the in-game saving option, which does not exist. If you are spotted in the middle of a mission or die, you will need to start the mission over. While not a big issue in the earlier missions, this can become extremely frustrating on the later missions where you need to navigate a huge mansion with tons of guards and one mis-step means you're killed and need to restart
However, Hitman: Codename 47 is a brilliant stealth game for its generation!

Full review:
TL;DR:

Depends heavily on tight time windows and scripted scenes/routes. Instead of rolling with the punches and playing how you want, you can fail missions entirely and use "continues". Most missions are constant scripted events where you have to make sure things constantly line up at the right place and time. This could potentially mean waiting a few minutes for a target to go into position. If you fail, you're going to have to wait for however long it takes for the scripted event to happen.
In later Hitman games, this was why the Quicksave was a welcome addition. Some will argue about Quicksave systems, that it'll simply be easy to cheese through the entire game. But with Codename 47's rather languid pace for missions, this is simply for the sake of streamlining it and making it more convenient on the player's end. Codename 47 isn't a particularly difficult game, it's just extremely punishing whenever you fail. Most of what you do in Codename 47 is wait, when you fail... you're forced to wait longer.
To address the issue of waiting, there's the continue system (yes, I found this design choice to be fairly jarring for a Hitman game) which allows you to respawn in the map with all of your items in your inventory and whatnot. This was a pretty awkward choice, mostly because enemies can still be on the look out for you. You'll keep whatever you had in your inventory and enemies will still stay around where they killed you.
This was Hitman before it found its way as the artsy stealth sandbox that we came to know and love. Still a worthy entry regardless, but if you're coming from Blood Money or hell, even Silent Assassin without being aware of the series' rather rigid roots, you could be in for a shock.

XCOM 2. What can I say? The same good old XCOM. The combat system is still outdated but it works. You can't interrupt your movement to take an action and there aren't any free/bonus actions. The game is still giving me a good vibe but the combat system is kind of outdated. Yet, I still enjoy the game. The feeling is like driving a manual stick shift car which you enjoyed but after driving automatic you know that manual is a bit clunky. I have yet to finish the game so I'll add more later. The false RNG is a major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ The AI simply decides if you can win or not, skill is not a factor. There isn't even a legitimate random chance. If the game wants you to miss, you will miss 100% of the time. I have a save with guaranteed misses on a 50% chance shot where I reloaded the game just to see if I would hit. 8 times reloaded, 8 times missed.
Additionally, the cool combos from XCOM were removed and the poor Sharpshooter has been greatly nerfed in XCOM2. There isn't a combat drone either. Berserkers work very differently now. They no longer move when they get hit. You no longer kite them with 2 different units, now they are just big fat slobs of meat that get "Enraged" and die. You just use a Ranger with the Untouchable skill and has killed a unit to stand in front of it and get it to miss at POINT BLANK RANGE. Alternate cheeses include blocking the ladder and making it fall from the rooftop.
Conclusion, it feels more like you want me to lose on purpose to create a false sense of urgency. Instead of a tactical RPG, it's more like my choices are fixed. Even the UFO attacking the XCOM base is pre-fixed into a destroy the Disruptor mission. What valued choices am I really making?
17/11/17: I decided to complete the game on Rookie. That is the only way to play it for me. I gave up on normal. Thanks to my first playthrough, I know where the crisis is going to pop up and in what order. This saddened me greatly as I thought there was not going to be linear gameplay. After completing it, I feel much better but the artificial events just scream bad game design and a form of railroading. You also learn to never scout ahead. Just learn to wait, Overwatch and let the Aliens come to you. It wastes their turn and gives you the advantage.
1. Tactical Strategy
Tactical turned base combat. XCOM is great at this. An outdated model but still fun.
2. Alien Multiplayer
You get to use the aliens for combat. There are quite a few missing though. They do not include models from XCOM. E.g. Avatar, Heavy MEC, Ethereal (XCOM), Thin Man (XCOM), Outsider (XCOM), Cyberdisc (XCOM), Mechtoid (XCOM), Seeker (XCOM)
1. Can't Interrupt Your Movement
Same problem from every XCOM game. There still isn't the ability to interrupt your movement to shoot and then keep on moving. Board games have already progressed with this. It is surprising to see XCOM still using an old model. Basically, you can't move, shoot, then move again. If you shoot, you end your turn.
2. Graphic Bugs
Minor issue but it's still bad. E.g. The hostage is invisible.
3. -40% High Cover
I don't really get this one. How does this occur when you're at higher elevation. Was this in the old XCOM?
4. Slower Game Pace
Did they slow the pace of the game down? I was surprised that the rocket launcher still wasn't with my heavy despite all the game time. Laser sight is also picked up from the ground and not free. It feels a little more draggy this time.
5. Direct Counters
Somehow you can't help but think that the game AI is designed to artificially limit your progress. If you get too much science research, something that will impede research will pop up.
6. False Random Number Generator ****
I tested it out on a scenario with a 50% chance to hit. I shot the alien, missed and reloaded the stage. I did that 8 times and each time, it was a guaranteed missed. Please do not use this fake RNG generators to try to manipulate the game. Just let the game play normally, don't try to stage a scenario so that the humans will lose and pretend it's not. We can find ways to detect it. If you reload the same stage after shooting an enemy, the damage can change. E.g. Sniper shoots a tower, it deals 4 damage the first time. Reload the game, it does 2 damage.
This kind of forced scenarios are extremely stupid. The game doesn't play properly and you code an AI that tries to ensure losses. It is very dumb in XCOM2. After checking on the forums, there isn't a satisfactory answer except that the developers just decided to add it in.
7. Grenade Trajectory
If you toss a grenade, there is an awkward situation when you have to toss it in buildings. I took screenshots to remember the incident. E.g. Grenade doesn't go through glass except in special conditions.
8. Grenade AOE
Grenade explodes but no one gets injured. Huh? I believe it maybe a potential bug or a situation where the developers coded immunity for the enemy. I took screenshots of this one too.
9. Railroading
The game design railroads you towards a certain path. Where to go, where to build your relays, what to do, when to research. etc.
1. Gradation of odds♥♥♥♥♥damage
There are very unrealistic scenarios like shooting someone at point blank range and missing. There should be a 100% scenario that occurs at point blank and a gradual drop from 100% when you factor in things like
a. Range
b. Cover
c. Physical barriers e.g. walls, another enemy in between
d. Abilities e.g. Good Aim
e. Moving targets e.g Fast/Normal/Slow
f. Size of target
2. 0% hits
It's fine to have a scenario where you can't hit the enemy. It's so stupid to shoot through 2 walls and hit an enemy.
3. Missing at Point Blank
Can you just add a modifier that says "Point Blank +50%". It will only occur when you are 1-2 squares from the target. It is high risk, high reward and you will find that this will solve all the RNG complaints online.
4. Weak Skills - Covering Fire
I think the Specialist has an ability that lets you Overwatch on enemy actions. Covering Fire is the name. Why would have a skill that fires at the enemy in hiding? Logically, the enemy is still in cover and in the same spot. If the enemy is in the same spot, why didn't you just shoot him immediately?
5. Anti-Overwatch Units with the Fast/Evasion Ability
Some Aliens just can avoid fire by moving really fast. Slow lumbering hulks have high hp but they get hit all the time. Differentiate the Aliens by speed types as well.
6. Air Support
Can I call in some AC-130 Gunships? Artillery Strikes? If you don't want to scale up to vehicles, at least allow for some flying drones.
7. Using Intel
It was only on the penultimate mission that I was given the opportunity to use the intel to buy special buffs for the mission. I felt that this was the correct move. It made Intel valuable. I would suggest spy networks and using Intel to buy map vision, unit count, unit types, unit strength, hints, stealth insertions.
8. Stealth Missions - Invisiblity Cloak
Try making just 1 stealth mission in the campaign. Just 1 ranger, tasked to sneak into a compound, avoid patrols and plant the bomb/hack/turn off the detonator. For immersion sake, please make an invsibility cloak that can be equipped. You can look at similar square grid games like Invisibility Inc for some inspiration. There is no real stealth in this game. The only "stealth" is concealment before the ambush.
9. To Leave or Not To Leave - Secondary Objectives
Create missions with partial objectives where the player is allowed to Skyranger early and evac. This will give far more choice to the player. Oh, they completed the main objective? But what's this? If they probe further they might get some goodies. However, more enemy reinforcements will jump in. So, do they want to complete the secondary objective? Well, it's the player's choice. Risk vs reward, the perfect game design.

Shmups have never enjoyed the same success in the West as over in Japan. I suppose the need to be efficient, deadly and flawless just doesn't sit well with western gamers. Astebreed does it's best to rectify that with a few key changes to the shmup format that make it a lot more accesible.
Don't take accessibility as meaning the game is easy. If you cannot learn to adapt, the last boss will destroy you (FINALLY! A game where the last boss is the hardest thing in the game). Instead of just throwing endless enemies at you and expecting you to figure it out, the game features a rather in-depth tutorial mode.
Astebreed also has regenerating health. While that may seem pointless, it works wonders for getting out of tough situations. There are also specific enemy shots that one can only dodge with good, old fashion reflexes. Astebreed gives the player some different projectiles and a sword; this sword can dodge any attack that is yellow.
When you encounter a red shot, you have to dodge. There is more than one way to accomplish said dodge, but you still need to get out of the way. You cannot simply spam your way through this game (I tried in a few spots, so I know!). For as much as can happen at one moment on screen, the game still feels entirely in your control.
There is also a pretty interesting story, even if it's a bit short. The game can be finished within a few hours, but the cool anime style and constant dialogue make the journey worth it. Once the campaign is over, you get harder difficulties, different ships and the ability to check out a gallery full of artwork and 3D models.
For the casual gamer, just skip this. Astebreed could be a jumping off point into Shmups for you, but it doesn't possess a huge amount of content. For anyone else interested, buy the game. It's well worth the price.

Tl;dr: a good game if you like XCOM.
To elaborate: this game does have its problems. It isn't particularly well optimised; load times are pretty high; you'll get your fair share of minor graphical glitches, and apparently now and then actual bugs (though I haven't had that happen to me yet).
Personally, I've only experienced one or two crashes ever, and that's after installing a bunch of mod then disabling a few (which has a high chance of making your save unstable).
Now for the good bits: it's XCOM. It's updated. Whether it's better or worse than EU is up to opinion - I know some people that still swear by UFO Defense - but I don't think it's fair to claim that the older game is objecticely superior, as some reviews do.

I have loved this series since the original, and I especially loved the previous XCOM installment for PC. It modernized the gameplay of the original and kept alive the feeling of saving the world with the power of good planning, management, strategy and combat tactics. You could choose your path, to an extent, and there wasn't always one clear "best" decision to make.
XCOM 2 removes all of that.
There is always only one clear goal to accomplish, and only one way to get there. All of your choices are limited by this. For example...
You have to raid the facility.
To raid the facility, you first have to contact the region.
To contact the region, you first have to contact the region in front of it.
To contact that region, you have to build a comms facility.
To build the comms facility, you have to clear out debris and collect resources.
So all of the management decisions from XCOM are gone now; In XCOM 2 you're just checking off bullet points and jumping through hoops when they appear. Overall you'll generally feel like you're catching up and not in control.
As for the combat, it is much less balanced. It is sometimes boringly easy and sometimes frustratingly unfair. For instance many of the enemies you encounter have mind control and/or instant knockout abilities that can take your team members out of the battle instantly and unexpectedly WAY too easily and way too early in the game. They don't even have to take advantage of your poor planning; Sectoids only need one turn of line of site to ruin your entire team. All it take is for them to successfully take control of a melee ranger or a grenadier and you're doomed.
The challenge level and randomness of this game feel like they'd be more appropriately suited for your average indie roguelike. You're always one die roll away from a disaster that will make your progress essentially doomed.
This feels out of place in such a large-scale AAA game and it really adds to the feeling of lack of control. It's all up to the dice and you'll find yourself quitting or save-scumming way too often. There's never a sense of balanced challenge to be found; just success or disaster with nothing in between.

The Gameplay
For the gameplay I would say it is really really good. You can select some classes throughout the game. You can be building on: Health class, Stealth class, Ranged class and meele class. If i remember correctly. I like playing stealthy. You can really make your game so that it fits your prefered class, by choosing the correct weapons, skills & equipment. If you want to build on a class you can get all these things and the gameplay with any class is fun and great. For the fighting mechanincs I would say its great, you have enough time to parry attacks if you are good enough and you can counter attack after you parry. You can choose between what weapons you want, one handed, long, heavy, pistols,rifles and the
rifles with the axe blade on them ( I forgot what you call them lol :D) The gameplay with all of those weapons are great, some have advantages and some have disadvantages. If you buy a really expensive weapon then the work really really well.
For a bit of stealth...
The stealth system has been upgraded fully. Now you can get into covers next to a wall or table or pretty much anything, also you can switch covers silently wich both looks cool and is useful. And there are new ways to kill people too, like cover assassinations and stuff. And the enemy's hearing has been added. Then can hear you if you run behind them, or if you jump, or if you kill someone right behind their back or shoot a gun. Theres also a really good "spotting system" added wich is that if you are walking around the enemy a bit closer to them in the line of sight they will start being suspicious and a yellow ! mark will appear above their head, if you hang about or walk closer to them they will stard walking towards you and threatening you and pushing you away to guard a restricted area for example. If you hang about for too long the ! mark will turn orange and then they chase you for a bit and shout at you.  also if you do anything more suspicious than just walking around like running or climbing walls or something they will spot you and the ! mark turns red and they are going to chase you and shoot you and try and fight you. If you kill someone right infront of them the ! mark turn red right away because obviously you just killed their mate and thats a bit suspicious if you ask me, also in restricted areas if you walk right towards them they will attack straight away, if they only see you for one or two seconds then they will start to get suspicious and go to check out whats up. Also the difficulty of the enemy is a good system as well. LVL 1 enemy are really easy to kill and parry and you can kill them easy with a good weapon and as the LVL of the enemy increases the harded it is to parry and kill. Also the difficulty of the enemy depends on the difficulty of the district, for example in a difficulty LVL 1 district you will encounter difficulty level 1 or 2 enemy. Also for a bit more stealth the smoke bombs and other bombs work well and there is a last known position feature added wich is that wherever the enemy saw you last there is a white ghost that appears to mark where you were, this is useful for stealth.
Interaction
The world and the game became a way more interactive. For example you can walk into most houses and blend into massive crowds etc... There are also random crowd events like killing criminals that are marked, or tackling a theif to get a purse or something back or protecting a guy from extremists and many more, and if you complete all of the Social events in one district you get a prize. The phantom blade , wich is a mini crossbow on your wrist that you shoot bladed out of, this is really useful when you wanna kill two people that are away from eachother and you want them both dead because you dont wanna get into contact with them, you shoot one with the phantom blade and assassinate the other. After playing 100 hours in this game and loving it, I want give it a comprehensive review.
So is it worth trying? YES, absolutely.
The game is a very unique take on the MOBA genre with giant spaceships flying around in 3D space. It very focussed on multiplayer and general MOBA gameplay. That means you will have to fight your way down lanes in order to capture enemy outposts before you can attack their base. The game is extremely tactical and even more team based. This is mostly due to two facts:
1. There are more than 30 ships, which have their strength and weaknesses. Your ship choice defines your role in the team. Leave that role - you lose. Go solo - you lose, as you will meet your hard counters and be taken down instantly. These ships are not mere stat variations, they are playstyles and strategies which you have to master. So far after 100 hours of playing, I would say I can fly 3 ships decently and another one ok: A. The Raider - a fast scout ship with surprising survivability, B. The Paladin - basically a support healer, C. The Leviathan - a heavy fortress and D. The Brawler - a strong close combat fighter with no effect on longer distances. I wrote those down to give you an example about ship variations and roles. That said it somehow is expected taht you learn your ship in Solo vs AI mode, before you enter a match unprepared and weaken your team. Each new ship is a new game for you. To sum it up: You will have about 50 hours on the clock for learning three ships or maybe 500 for trying out 30. That is alot of gameplay time.
2.The map is devided into seperated sectors. You need to hyper-jump to these sectors which consumes valuable time and can't be done while engaged in a fight. Therefore the team has to be very well distributed among the sectors (2 possible lanes ALPHA / BETA). If you get 4 ships in ALPHA and one in BETA, the enemy might overun BETA. On the other hand pushing hard in one lane while neglecting the other might overwhelm a weak defense. To make things even more interesting, a special sector (GAMMA) will open up every five minutes. As this base is very valuable, all ships will jump there for a centerfight. To sum this up: Coordinating your ship distribution, flight formations and packs within the team is imperative and fun.
Is it free to play or pay to win? FREE.
Before I start on this, I want to state that I think developers have to earn money. They need their paycheck to create and support the game. Nobody works for nothing. Therefore I do not complain if there are mechanisms in a game which allow you to buy stuff. F2P in its best form allows you to try out the game before investing real money or builds up the player base needed for an multiplayer game by including players which otherwise would not give it a try. So again: Is it pay to win? NO. You can absolutely enjoy the game for free. There is no distinctive disadvantage for players which did not invest a dime. Everyone can compete.
The major disadvantage you will have as a free player is that you wont have many ships to start with. But the ones you have are in every way balanced with all other ones. I saw very experienced players returning to the first ship everyone gets (the PIONEER) as it is currently slighly OP and very versatile. So yay, you will only have about three ships. But as I said, I played 100 hours and can hardly say I am good at flying three. Getting new ships involves grinding for credits. For every match you play and win you get about 8k credits. That means you will have to play  13 games (two evenings or less) to get a tier 1 ship, 30 games to get a tier 2, 60 games to get a tier 3. That's totally ok, for the Tiers do not indicate better or less capable ships. The higher tiers are just newer and thus more interesting for players which have been in the game for long. That said I managed to ramp up the credits for the most expensive ship class twice. It's doable and good for the team as you will know your ship, before jumping to the next. Every ship is like a whole new game and unlocking one feels like birthday. I would even say that going F2P is very rewarding and even better for your skills. Take your time and learn the ships you have until you can compete or find your role in COOP. Ask other players which ship they would recommend to unlock next and try them out in SOLO (all sjps unlkocked there). Then when you gained the credits and have exhausted the mechanics of your old ones (not gonna happen), unlock the next and restart your learning experience.
That said. I bought the "Armada Pack" for 30 bucks to unlock all ships (excluding the three newest). Why? Because I feel that this is the full price of the game and the pack unlocks nearly everything. I love the game and think the devs need money to work on it. And paying the price of a cheap AAA title is totally ok for me if I get 40 hours of gameplay time out of it. I already have 100 hours now and am just starting to learn the game. So yeah. Why not buy the game. The thing is: You do not need to. Just try the ships you think about (unlocking with credits) first in solo, grind a bit and ou will have a decent fleet of 5-8 ships. That's not all, but that's all you need for 100 hours of playing. If you can't wait to won more ships, just pick the lower tiers. 100k of credits are gained during 2-3 evenings, and that's not half the time you will need to explore a ship.
Then there is crew and implants. Given, they implement another grinding mechanism which allows for ship improvment. But thats not to critical in the early stages of the game. After all the game has to give players, which have bought the game or progressed over level 50, something to invest their credits. The same is true for loadout (slight variations on ship systems). Loadout allow experienced players to adjust the ships to their playstyles. But each comes with its benefits and drwbacks, picking a loadout does not make any player OP and is targeted at experienced captains.
And there are skins, which you can only buy for real money or receive during events or rare rewards. But they are not gameplay relevant and mostly targeted at high level players which love their ships and want some cosmetics (supporting again the devs).
Is the community decent? YES, I can recommend the community. I met few toxis, as the game is so team-dependent that being an a...hole just does not pay off. There are currently not too many players  and matchmaking takes a while (3 minutes mostly). But that's okay. Matchmaking needs to be improved, but this depends on the player base. Therefore I do not complain and write this review instead, to motivate others to join the awesome experience this game is.
THIS GAME IS HARD BUT REWARDING
You will definately need your time to learn this game and the initial matches can be quite frustrating. This is due to the matchmaking MMR when playing against AI. Bots are very hard if you have an experienced player in your COOP team. But this is exactly what makes the game so rewarding and interesting on the long run. There are other games out their for casual play and quick rewards for every click you do. That's what Clickers ar developed for. They bore me and don't give me the feeling of achievment. FracturedSpace on the other hand is like playing in a sports team. Yeah, getting in can be hard and there is this presure to improve and match the skills of your mates. Got this game for free in a giveaway.
I was sure something was wrong, when in a promo video, for a retro-style video game, they used a modern dubstep tune.
Dead giveaway. Deeeead giveaway!
You listen to dubswtep music in a promo video and you just KNOW that people TRY to promote it.
I hate it when people use all the trends to draw attention and to show off things in a more fancy way.
On the other hand I can't blame marketing people for doing their job right.
So let's take a look at the actual game.
It is a 2D style game but it is implemented in 3D graphics.
It is like a fusion of old school Arkanoid  and space invaders.
You hit aliens with a ball that bouces through walls.
Fancy and nice graphics.
Everything merge together in harmony.
Everything except explosions and gameplay. I will talk about this later.
Music:
Well... it is Electronica. I listened to tunes that you can call trance, some could be a merge of other styles like techno house beats. What is sure is that the sound is not retro, which is not a bad thing, since the music is well compressed and gives you that "action" feeling.
So what's the bad thing here?
Gameplay. It is really hard to play it even from start.
The idea would be nice if the ball wouldn't bounce SOOO fast.
Add explosions that cover the position and the direction of the ball sometimes and you got a really bad experience.
Anyway, this doesn't kill it as a game, since you can farm for lives.
At the end of each stage you get an extra life.
What kills this game is flow.
You press play, select a level, then what? It loads all right. You play it...
you end the level... and you have to WAIT to load for the next menu.
Maybe SSD HDDs have no such performance issues, but standard HDDs  make this significant.
This get ou out of the gaming experince.
Not to mention that instead of floating the user through a bunch of levels, you throw him out on a menu...
WHY? You can implement upgrading on the start of each level keeping the gaming feeling alive.
On contrary we see our fancy 3D ship flying away with great animation then what? Wait and then get out of the gaming experience to enter a menu. Think of it. It looks really bad in my opinion.
Tell you what, you touch such retro concepts to make a new innovative game. That's good!
So your target group is people who recognize these games.
Right?
Most possible scenario is that modern day kids will not even give this game a chance.
You just forget one thing though.
Gamers of that era, people like me, were used to a world that serious gaming companies were making games working PERFECTLY out of the box. No patches, no fixes, no sorries, no nothing. Even renting a game for a weekend would be a bad experience. Gamers having a ruined weekend back then, would really discuss how BAD a game was. No excuses, no sorries were accepted. Nowadays people became softer. Good thing for them. I am not as soft as they are though. And many people of that era are like me.
Let me see the price now...
Oh! 7 Euro???
I can recommend that ONLY on a 90% discount then.
Seriously, I can understand that people worked on that, but as a consumer I wouldn't give more than that for this game.
I believe that games that work and give some joy always deserve some money.
A game will get my rate down ONLY if ut is worthless, broken or REALLY BAD in my opinion.
Every other game, I will give a recommendation even on a huge sale, like here.
It's not bad, but it isn't a game that is better than the competition.
That's always my personal opinion.

Brigador is a difficult but rewarding isometric shooter.  It's difficult in that the levels present challenges that force you to think about your approach; you can zoom in and lay waste, but you better be prepared for the backlash.  Or take it slow and pick off groups.  Best to get good at both though, as the campaign mode will demand it.  Freelance mode gives you a chance to customize your loadout and play with exactly what you want, but also to experiment and try new combinations.
And it shines with the combinations.  There are 4 vehicle types, many vehicles per type, and multiple weapon classes to load up with.  All weapons, not to mentuion the vehicles, have their pros and cons, although I'm fond of the war-crime-in-a-can that is the Ploughman.
The atmosphere is the big standout for me.  It's set on an isolationist totalitarian planet where the leader has just died, and a mercenary group has decided to take advantage and destroy not only loyalist targets, but competitors as well.  The visuals, details, and especially the music stress the amorality of your mission and your actions, and the game is richer for it.
Just so this doesn't seem overly fawning, the controls do take a little getting used to.  It does use tank controls, yes, but you are driving futuristic tanks, so I can't really fault them there.  The enemies do have a tendency to swarm after the first few shots, but the devs seem to be working on that, and honestly, it makes sense that firing heavy artillery draws attention.  Really, it's difficult to call them faults so much as an acquired taste.
So all in all, I recommend Brigador to anyone who likes a challenge, and especially anyone who likes the cyberpunk aesthetic.

If you missed out on this first installment and have stayed away due to the clunky controls and awful missions, I'd still recommend it for two reasons.
1) Lee Hong Assassination: This may be one of the most impressive maps of the series, with vibrant and contrasting settings - The opulent and colorful restaurant, the exclusive "den of inequity", grimy underground tunnels filled with armed gang members, as well as Lee Hong's well guarded mansion. It all comes together to create a remarkable video game setting, and while long and tricky, it's a joy to explore. (The Contracts remake doesn't come close to capturing the feel of the original, unfortunately)
2) Traditions of the Trade: This may still be my favorite Hitman level of all time, and where IO first really hit the sweet spot of the Hitman formula. The open, luxurious hotel complete with thermal bath is really a fun place to explore, and the dozens of hotel rooms and winding staircases make for some thrilling hunter/hunted chases as you frantically change outfits to stay one step ahead of your pursuers. This is your quintessential "swiss cheese" Hitman map.
Yes, the controls are awkward at first but easy enough to get used to, so don't let that hold you back.
Here is what I'd recommend. Play the Hong Kong sequence leading up to the Lee Hong Assassination, then look up the cheat codes to unlock all the levels and play Traditions of the Trade. You'll have experienced the best of Codename: 47 without the headache of those terrible jungle and shipyard missions.
TL;DR - worth it for Lee Hong Assassination and Traditions of the Trade.

As the enigmatic Hitman, you must use stealth and tactical problem solving to enter, execute and exit your assignment with minimum attention and maximum effectiveness. For a price, you have access to the most devious devices, but how you use them will determine if you retire as a millionaire
One of the finest Stealth / Strategy RPG's of its generation, it puts you in the role of Agent 47, a shadowy assassin who is equally capable of slipping in and out of target locations un-noticed as he is of pulling out a pair of chrome-plated 'Ballers' and taking absolutely everyone out. With a broad range of missions from the 'Lee Hong Assassination' (Rooftop Sniper takedown) to the 'Massacre at the Cheung Chow Fish House' (No one comes out alive), the game provides a wealth of memorable situations you will talk about years down the road.
The game is not without its flaws - for a game nearly 14 years old, gameplay mechanics can be somewhat clunky. Probably the biggest gripe however is the in-game Save option, which does not exist. If you are spotted in the middle of a mission or die, you will need to start the mission over. While not a big issue in the earlier (shorter) missions, this can become extremely frustrating on the later missions where you need to navigate a huge mansion with tons of guards and after 20 minutes of perfection, one mis-step means you're killed and need to restart.
All in All
is a very nice Retro Game!
