Darkest Dungeon is an interesting beast. A rock-hard RPG with complicated and unforgiving systems designed to make the game an uphill battle. You will lose, you will die, and you will wonder what went wrong. To be frank, the game is honestly rather unfair, and yet, I cannot seem to stop playing it.
Darkest Dungeon is a turn based RPG with position based gameplay. That is to say that you make a party of four heroes, each filling one of 4 slots, and they each can only use certain moves in certain slots on certain enemies in other certain spots. Each hero has unique attacks, functions and general roles within said party, meaning that party composition is paramount to success. Each hero has different quirks and stats which affect how they function. Each hero has their own stress meter which fills up as the horrors of adventuring mount, causing negative debuffs which can be game ending if not managed. Each area has a different feel and theme of gameplay, meaning that there is no ideal party, and each enemy and boss is it's own challenge. Many reviewers take issue with RNG in the game, which is an understandable issue, although, what I believe they fail to realize is that the RNG is totally manage if prepared for, and that is part of what makes it so compelling.
Darkest Dungeon is the kind of game that either grabs you or pushes you away, you'll know almost immediately whether you'll be continuing.

"Curious is the Trapmaker's art; his efficacy unwitnessed by his own eye."
Alas!  How this was the eulogy of so many of my heroes, as they met their end upon a cruel spike trap, or vicious sawblade - and only two rooms from victory.
The Darkest Dungeon will test your mettle as a player.  It will not forgive your mistakes.  It will not let you forget your failures.  It will punish you at least as hard as it will reward you, and often in the same stroke.  Every bloodstained coin you earn will seem precious.  Every single point of experience your heroes gain will seem like a large sum of learning.  Every point of damage you give, or take, will seem like a substantial wound, and is frequently the difference between life and death.  Make no mistake about it; this game is very difficult, even on a lower setting of difficulty.
But you cannot advance without falling back.  You cannot win this game without losing along the way.  Enjoy your heroes.  Treat them well.  Train them right.  Do not be afraid to spend money on their betterment.  And do not be afraid to lose them in the Darkest Dungeon.

I've played Heat Signature for at least 20 hours offline. It's a fantastic game. Basically, you fly about in a little pod, board enemy spaceships, take out everyone aboard, and return to your base. Really, there are different sorts of missions available, such as "steal the thing", "assassinate the dude", or "steal the ship", but effectively it usually comes down to, "go about and take everyone out, then do the thing" as the most expedient method. Sometimes you can't kill anyone, but that's mostly just a gear check, requiring a wrench instead of a sword or a concussive gun instead of a lethal one. The tactics don't change much. They do change some, though, and deny you the use of cool things like traps that teleport enemies into space, as they'll suffocate. It actually reminds me a lot of how a non-lethal Dishonored run made you unable to use many of the cool gadgets. It's similarly a bit sad, but as in this it's on a ship by ship basis, it can be a nice change of pace. Unless you have a bunch of cool lethal weapons you're itching to use and instead have to go about knocking people out with a wrench like a lamebutt.
And if you're like me, you must get past its graphics. They're quite ugly, to my eyes. Less subjectively, it can often be very difficult to tell what objects in a level are passable set dressing, and which block movement and line of sight. I got shot a few times due to this, expecting enemies to not see me and instead being shot as I tried furiously to backpedal. However, characters are immenently replaceable, so even the one I lost due to this I didn't mind too much.
I have other gripes - many, in fact. The AI's patrol routines are far too exploitable, which can make missions meant to be hard (or even "audacious" or "mistake") too easy, but slow and boring. Forcing you to play suboptimally to make the game fun. Never a good thing to the force the player to do.
And the enemies could use some variety. They're all humans, with a handful of pieces of equipment available to them - mostly just shields, teleportation, armour, and explosives that go off if they die violently (though if you knock them out and THEN kill them, for some reason they don't explode - perhaps you're disarming them? I dunno.).
There are also only two types of enemy per level. The mooks have one combination of gear, the "bosses" have another, usually one that makes them a little trikier to deal with. But not remotely deserving of the title "boss."
The changing combinations of gear in each ship do provide a good deal of variety. Hours worth of it, even. And combine this with the changing gear you have as you retire characters and start new ones, and your playstyle will change often, keeping things fresh a lot longer.
The ship layouts are also quite boring. Mostly square rooms, the occasional bigger rectangular room, connected by straight hallways. It gets old.
If they put out a DLC with more enemy types and fights on planet surfaces or something - anything with more open, chaotic environments that made you think harder about each new level - I'd jump on it so fast. Which goes to show how happy I really am with the game. I've gotten my money's worth, even if I may be done now.
The joy of teleporting dudes into space, hijacking a turret so it takes everyone out for you, or just being a timestopping badass shotgunning and slashing your way through a horde in under a second is just so great. The core gmeplay loop is very enjoyable.
I wish there were more just because what there is is so fantastic, but that just means it's worth the price and worth buying any theoretical DLC in the future.

I doubt I need to say anything, it's all been said a million times. But it's a great casual game that still has just enough achievable goals and activities to keep you from getting bored, a common problem with most casual games where they give you virtually nothing to work towards except whatever you feel like doing. It might be boring for a really, really hardcore gamer who needs really intense experiences, and it might be too much for the super-casual Bejeweled player, but virtually everyone inbetween can get some enjoyment here. If I had to criticize anything, I guess I'd want a little more detail with characters and scenes; they feel SO short and underwhelming that you immediately forget about most of them. With the sprite graphics and 90% of the gameplay being repetitive (in a good way, mostly), I feel like longer, more intricate scenes with more character development for the townsfolk would have been welcome, but also not really all that hard. There's also some info lacking from the game that you have to get from wikis, and that seems wrong in a casual game, at least to me. But it's fairly minor stuff, it's still a very fun game for quite a long time.

As a teenager, I used to obsessively play the Future Cop: LAPD demo on PSX. Before that, I used to obsessively play Desert Strike on the Mega Drive. Now, I can play Brigador! Except not obsessively, because adulthood sucks. :(
Brigador is an isometric, vehicle-based action game with light stealth elements and destructible terrain. If either of the two names above ring a bell, you'll have a rough idea what you're in for (although it doesn't play entirely on super narrow corridor maps like Future Cop). If not: you control one vehicle (a mech, tank, or jetbike/antigrav) armed with two out of ~40 guns (split into different mount sizes, with each vehicle having two predetermined mount types) and have to make it through a series of maps with escalating difficulty. The maps are all ridiculously beautiful, hand-crafted, neon-soaked, sci-fi urban/rural landscapes. The fights are fun and fast, and fairly tactical (especially on higher difficulties) since you have to make sure you don't get overwhelmed and that spotter units don't sound the alarm, which would make all enemies activate their shields and beeline to your last known location.
There are no RPG elements or anything, but completing an "operation" (a fixed playlist of anywhere from three maps with the option to quit and cash out early, to "run through all 20 maps twice over with ever-escalating difficulty and no way out until you beat the entire run") or the campaign missions will reward you with Solo Nobre Dollars you can spend on unlocking new guns (of the 40, only 6 are available from the start), vehicles (there's 45 or so total, and the starting mech is one of the best vehicles in the game), operations (so you can play to earn money to unlock harder operations to earn more money) or pilots (the game's difficulty selection mechanic - each pilot has stats that dictate the difficulty of the first map in an operation, the difficulty increase per subsequent map, and a payout multiplier at the end of the run, so you can control difficulty in a farely fine-grained way).
In short, it's a fantastic game with great visuals, a ton of replayability and that is just generally really fun to play. The tank controls for all vehicles (except for antigravs, which can strafe, but with A/D always read relative to the vehicle orientation instead of the camera) take a little bit of getting used to, but once you've mastered them, you'll feel like a complete badass, stomping around town in your 200-ton superheavy mech with two artillery cannons strapped to its back and optical camo.

Contrary to popular belief, if you are going for A+, 64.2 is the hardest level. Now that we got that out of the way.
64.0 is a fantastic game for people with an average of -3 second reaction times. It is a game based around coordination, skill, and sheer willpower as the levels are basically the same patterns, but from different directions, sometimes. Practice makes perfect with this game, and it is a true test of patience.
If you have anger issues, I do not recommend this game.
If you have epilepsy, I do not recommend level 4.
Basically, enemies (who are transparent), come from a direction, and you shoot them with your guy (gray/white cube in the center). Allies (who are colored), also, come from a direction, and you don't shoot them. Luckily, there are only 4 directions. Unluckily, they come from all 4 directions.
Firing and hitting nothing resets your streak.
Firing and hitting an ally ends the game.
NOT firing and hitting an ENEMY ends the game.
Each level is approximately 64 seconds, and if you fail to be a master, you restart at 0 seconds and try again.

If you're looking for some fast-paced difficult arcade-style action, 64.0 is a pretty good choice for its price.
Most importantly for a game of this kind, the controls are very responsive.  The screen shakes satisfyingly when you shoot, which gives everything a satisfying feel of weight.  When you die--and you will die--no time is wasted allowing you to try again, maintaining a good feel of flow.  Even the minimalist graphics work in the game's favour.  You have very little time to choose what to shoot and what to leave, and the simple style helps there.
Obviously, you shouldn't get this if you're not willing to play something that demands good reflexes, pattern memorisation and a willingness to die over and over.  Other than that, there is little to criticise here.  There are only five levels plus endless mode, but each level will take at least an hour to beat.  Also, the level editor and community levels offset this.  The one thing that did annoy me is that every time you start the game, there's a screen telling you "the music is awesome!"  You've already got my money, 64.0, and I'm quite capable of deciding the quality of the soundtrack myself.
Given the price you can't expect too much from this game.  Honestly, though, I've had less enjoyment from plenty of more expensive games, so I'd definitely encourage you to check this out.

Full disclosure: I am acquainted with the developers of this game.

It demands a steady hand, cool nerves, and balls of steel and is uncompromising in its pursuit of delivering a tough but unique and stylish action game. Some words of wisdom for fans of games like Binding of Isaac and Enter the Gungeon: at a first glance this game might seem to have strange controls and a deceptive aim assist. Keep in mind that there are tangible benefits to having direct control on the direction your vehicle faces: you are vulnerable in your rear and sides but protected at the front, and the same goes for the enemy. Additionally, manual control of where your shots go is key to ambush and stealth tactics but also means you must "think in 3d" and adjust your shots to hit flying or small targets.

At first the game looks like a run n' gun top down shooter. It's certainly possible to play it that way, but you probably won't achieve great success. It's a little slower than that, a bit of a light sim. To truely shine you need scheme and ambush. Pop through trees onto unsuspecting baddies, dash around corners to stomp sentries to death before they can call for help, toss long bomb artillary from several city blocks away on top of a tank group, drop smoke and turn main street into a killing field, that sort of stuff. It becomes increasingly satisfying as these little thing become second nature, and you find yourself rending armies into heaps of burning wreckage without a scratch.
There's a lot to do and unlock in this game. There's the standard campaign mode where on most missions you'll choose from one of four vehicles as a sort of difficulty selector, and then the freelance mode with a seemingly endless combination of vehicles and weapons and dozens of maps. Enough to keep you busy for awhile. They did a good job on the varity of vehicles and weaponry as well. While some certainly feel similar to others they never feel copy pasted.
I really like this game. It's great to hop into for 30 minutes and have a quick bit of fun, and it's also got that "well just one more time" hook that has you looking up and realizing you've been playing for 6 hours. It may seem a bit fiddly at first, but give it some time, get the feel for it, and remember that you're piloting a vehicle not hoofing it around. Be sure to try out all the different vehicle classes since they all control differently, and you maybe all thumbs with a mech, but a natural in a-grav. I'd personally recommend starting off with the tank type since I think it will feel more familiar to most people. Also the distance you aim controls the altitude of the shot, so if you want to nail that a-grav in your face you need to aim far past them.

This is bullet hell done right, and that's coming from someone who's definitely not a fan of the genre.  The game is short (an experienced player can easily clear it in a single sitting), but the gameplay and full 3D rendering with impressive artwork and varying camera angles put it well above most competing titles.  My biggest gripe is that the story is practically impossible to follow, and not just for the usual reasons: following along would require reading dialog balloons while dodging bullets and lasers, which is a tall order.  If you want to figure out what the story's about, your best bet is to beat the game, and then read through the codex that unlocks at the end.

Really enjoyed this game and its very impressive in scope. There is so much to see and do but it can get pretty daunting. I wish they hadn't focused so much on quantity, the list of side missions and collectibles end up looking like clutter on the map [ that thing deserves a review in itself, it represents the endless addition of features added to Assassin's creed drawing away from the focus on improving the chore mechanics/ story , in that its difficuly to recognise your own character key from all the clutter , side quests, relics, co cop missions, main quests, assassin's guild, chests( every chest in the dam game so literally hundreds, viewpoints, tunnel entrances .... ] It's somewhat hilarious and at times feels like a call for help from the entrapped ubisoft staff, being forced to add content and given no creative freedom make something great.
Doing my best to ignore the endless side clutter the main story line never did anything I didn't expect. Come on this is revolutionery France and again they give us tired old story of a murdered father spurring revenge ! Put me on one of the sides, maintaining the monarchy or have be as part of a revolutionery group.  Put the whole templar / assassin thing in the background if you wan't one on either of the two sides, anyway a complete missed opportunity that would have made the stunning demonstrations significant to my character rather than a backdrop.
This last point brings me to what I liked most about the game. The city of paris, recreated prior the creation of the modern boulevards, is the best environement I have ever experienced in an open world game. The combination of old medieval Paris with the narrow streets combined with the beatifully recreated monuments like notre dame or sainte chapelle make this worth the asking price alone for me. The crowds of demonstators are also really impressive, there are often hundreds/ perhaps thousands of characters rendered on the screen at any one time taking part in public executions, book burning or just general protest. Although interaction is limited the level of detail of the environment, the archictecture and the people make it feel like you really are walking the streets of revolutionery France. Also the missions are great, they are multistage and really promote stealth and movement, all the traditional features of assassins creed. However the weakpoint is combat, which is very basic, block or mash the attack key is the basis of it. Despite some failures to address long standing issues like combat, thankfully movement is much improved and is almost perfect at this stage, the game is a fantastic experience.
Lastly I want to address the games performance and bugs which is the reason for the majority of negative reviews. By the time I started playing the game has seen many patches, I came across one glich ( a floating NPC ) in my 11 hours of play. I also ran this on a gtx 660 which maintainted stapble frames ( above 30 ) on high.
Hope this review helps, If you are not entirely convinced I'd recommend waiting for a sale, but If you have time to do everything this game has to offer the full asking price is pretty good.

I have played this game since alpha.
One thing I see current reviews saying is how the game has changed for them which I find silly because that isn't going to be the experience that new players need to hear. If you're a new player then I recommend jumping right in. The visuals are spectacular and the gameplay is incredibly addictive. Clearly I'm an optimist about this game but I won't deny some faults, namely that you can jump into a match where the players are toxic or refuse to strategise.
For a F2P game, this one is very good. If you haven't been enjoying it after a match or two once you get the hang of the strategy then uninstall it. Period. I don't understand this "bad matchmaking" criticism I've been hearing. I play from europe and I've never had to wait more than 2 mintutes to find a match. And after that I've never been dropped from one.
This game really shines when you have 2 teams with good humour and spirit who will listen to each other. But it also involves some very satisfying tactics depending on the different ships and you will find yourself either using your abilities to turn the tide of a battle or a dogfight or making a narrow escape to heal or regroup.
People complain about this game being a grind. But unlike war thunder or world of tanks, you aren't grinding to get always better ships, you're grinding to get different ones. After I had rounded out my collection a little bit I was just playing to have fun. Sometimes I'd have the massive surfboard and lumber up to a control point and absorb fire while fighting off up to 3 enemies while my team could offer me help, other times I used the artillery cruiser to snipe, or in frontline mode I'd use it to quickly flank and deliver a massive shot to the enemy team's healer killing him outright or making him move out from cover. So yeah, I had a ton of fun even when losing and I would say that if you play this game to grind out all the ships then you're doing it wrong.

The Walking Dead is a dialogue-based adventure set in the same universe as The Walking Dead TV series and comics. Don't worry if you're unfamiliar with TWD, you won't be missing out on anything if you start here. The story progresses really well and does a great job of pulling you in. Well-designed quicktime event keep you involved in cutscenes and the game gives different respones from NPCs based on how you act. I really liked that sometimes doing or saying nothing at all could be just as significant as making an action.
It's not perfect though. There are some tedious and slow parts, and there are hiccups from time to time where a character does something that doesn't make sense (or that's just
stupid). Also, in case you're not aware, the gameplay is mostly dialogue choices, exploring, and some light puzzle solving, it's not challenging and this type of game isn't suppposed to be. You play this game for the story, the gameplay is there to get you involved and invested.
If you're a fan of The Walking Dead already then you'll probably enjoy this game; it has the same style and feel but plays out in its own unique way. If you've seen both shows, it's like the main series TWD compared to Fear TWD. Same universe, same style, but (mostly) different character archetypes and plot devices.
+Unique characters
+Good story with lots of variety
+Progresses and develops and a satisfying rate
-Lacks polish
Despite the minor frustrations this game was a thrill to play and fits in well with the rest of the series, I rate it 8/10.

It's honestly the perfect melding of two games.
Now, going into this game, I was really skeptical. A friend bought it for me on GOG. He knew I liked Harvest Moon and told me I'd be excited to play this. That... doesn't get me excited. People tend to miss what made those games great.
Harvest Moon's focus on character building, slow progression and loving care for your farm was always out of grasp for most games. This? Captured it perfectly. I was so into this game that after months of play I bought the Steam version just so I could play it with friends on Steam whenever the multiplayer option comes about.
Now, when I say perfectly, I mean it.
The slow drudge of clearing your farm, getting to know evryone, memorizing their schedules, build resources to make your farm better, it's all there.
What make this game good for me is they combined Rune Factory and Harvest Moon.
You see, Rune Factory is Harvest Moon with combat. Mostly combat. Almost purely combat.
Your farming is just a side bit that kind of occurs occasionally with the ability to have some monsters as animals on your farm, and your farm is VERY limited in space. They basically wanted a dungeon crawler with Harvest Moon tacked on.
You still talked to people and built relationships, but questing, combat and monster study took over.
Stardew Valley found the balance it needed. Harvest Moon with just a bit of nice combat. This game FEELS like what it should, and it adds a few things HM and RF never  had with who you marry, how you go about events, the world unlocking more as you progress and an honest feel that choices matter.
Oh, and choices matter! You can ctually be the bad guy for once, go the corporate route, sell-out and help the cold steel take over the natural order, it's amazing.

I can't recommend this game highly enough.  It is solid, cute and well written.  The cooperative play aspects are well done, and the challenge level makes it enjoyable without being frustrating for a wide skill set of gamers.
While it's fair to say that it's an evolution of games like Terraria, it is a huge one.  The concepts of building and exploring in other games are taken an enormous step further with Starbound.
One of the principal mechanics of the game is your personal space ship, which you build into a mobile base.  This ship remains with you even when you go to other servers, or play in your single player game - providing consistency and backdrop for your other adventures.
There is a great deal of cosmetic design you are able to do in ships and planetside base building, lots of varied and interesting enemies, mining, crafting and wire-based logic design.  It really is quite an interesting game.
I'm a gaming dad, and this is one of the games that I've played with my kids.  If you're a gaming dad, wait until it's on sale and get a 4-pack and gift it around.  It really is a great experience to let your kids see that side of you, and to guide and grow with them in games as a virtual peer.

Easily one of the best story-focused games I have played. Well done TellTale Games!

Episode 1 was kind of slow in the start but seeing as its meant to introduce all the main characters I don't mind that much, by Episode 2 you're just dragged into a more and more interesting story-line all the way up until the final episode.
Overall, The Walking Dead: Season 1 is a nice change of pace from the run-and-gun FPS zombie games like Dead Island or Left For Dead. Do not be turned off by the "comic like" graphics because in my opinion it gives the game that extra sense of "originality" (yes IK there are other games with "comic like" graphics but still) and atmosphere.

In Okami you play as Amaterasu, the sun goddess from Shinto mythology, taking the corporeal form of a legendary wolf in order to battle Orochi, an 8-headed demon that has poisoned the land. Along the way you'll use your legendary divine brush techniques and natural abilities to battle demons, purify nature, and solve puzzles.
The closest analog in terms of gameplay would be Zelda, though it's definitely its own game. Combat is fun and engaging; every enemy type requires different tactics to defeat, and there are even fancier ways to beat each one in order to receive better rewards. It's very humorous with a great deal of levity throughout; there are some darker bits in the background, but for the most part it's all very light-hearted. It's also packed to the brim with references to ancient Japanese culture, though if you're playing a game about one of the more powerful deities in Shinto you shouldn't be too surprised about that.
I own the original and the Wii version, and I by far prefer this PC port to either of them. As astounding as Okami is, it always felt like it struggled with its own controls a bit, especially with the painting mechanic. Now that you can use your mouse to paint with everything finally feels smooth and natural, and the keyboard controls for movement are just as good. The PC is definitely where Okami belongs.
As far as it being HD, it's definitely beautiful. Okami was always gorgeous, with bright, vivid colors and an art style intentionally reminiscent of traditional Japanese woodblock paintings, but the fuzziness was something of a pain to look at after a while. Now that everything is clean and sharp, it really brings out a lot of the game's life and artistic energy. I've read some people mentioning it being locked at 30FPS, but to be honest I haven't noticed, or at the very least it hasn't impacted my enjoyment of the game in any way. I certainly wouldn't shy away from a purchase just because of it.
All-in-all, I heartily recommend buying Okami HD on PC. If you've never played it before, this is definitely the best version to date, and if you own it on other systems, then this version is worth it for the controls alone.

Despite the big blue thumb above this text, I can only recommend this game to some. It's quite an old game (Older than myself), but old games can still be good, Doom being the prime example. But the thing is with Hitman: Codename 47, it REEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEALLY hasn't aged well, the controls are strange and archaic, but with some fiddling, you can get somewhat modern controls. (The run button is completely independent of the walk forward, so you hold it to run, without holding the W key, which is weird at the start.)
Now, onto to pros and cons:
Pros:
Quite big open levels.
A nice roster of weapons.
A purchase screen at the start of some missions, which lets you take what you need for whatever your playstyle maybe be. (Though some missions don't give you this option, and instead carry over weapons from the previous mission.)
The story tells you about 47 and
.
There's a fair few ways to go about things, gun blazing (wouldn't recommend it) or all stealthily like.
Some missions have RNG to spice things up, like the safes in The Lee Hong Assassination.
Pretty sweet music!
Its levels are all quite different visually, each hit (Which consists of a mission or possibly multiple.) takes place in a different place. One takes place in a Columbian forest looking for a lost relic, getting around a tiger and breaking into a camp to kill a Tony Montana wannabe. While another takes place in a Chinese restaurant/brothel in Hong Kong. Plus, unlike some games *cough cough*
*cough cough*, the NPCs have accents. I can't really gage some of them, but to me, they mostly sound good. (Though the Budapest accents sounded a little strange.)
Cons:
The graphics are pretty yucky, with pixel heavy textures.
The controls. Ohhhhhhh, golly God, the controls! All hail rebindable keys.
The AI is very... Unpredictable. Sometimes, you can do something, say stab a guy and get no indication anyone heard, no guns firing or any of that, but then you round the corner and somebody shouts something like "Alarm! Alarm! He's packing!" annnnd, your health bar magically empties. The end. Bye.
Wacky resolutions from 16 years ago. So, if you're planning to record this, it's going to be shrunk in the corner doing its thing. (At least with OBS)
Not the friendliest with it mechanics and such, I mean the tutorial is all right, and it serves a story purpose but besides that, ehhhhh.
Not a very good entry point to the franchise, if you're new to the series, stay away unless you become a big fan who wants to see where their beloved series was born. (In a mechanically awkward, poorly textured house. Even for the time.)
No checkpoint system. You die, back to the load out screen. Yeah, it's real annoying.
So, in conclusion:/TL:DR;
This, at least I'd say, is a good game. Good ideas, some levels really are quite nice (Such as the Thermal Bath hotel in Budapest, that's my favourite level.) but ultimately it's aged horribly and can be a chore to slog through at times, but overall it's a good game. If you get through the gunk, of graphics, controls and it's generally archaic nature, it can be pretty fun. But, if you're new, I hear Contracts remade some of the best levels from this game, so go check that out, or, if you do fancy getting this, you may as well pick up the Hitman Collection like I did! It includes all the Hitman games, pardoning the new, weirdly released one.

- Way, way, WAY too many worthless side quests and activities. It's all time-wasting padding to disguise the lack of a compelling main story arc. The little jumps to different time periods are weird, pointless little arcade diversions. The main story is boring and predictable, and the main character (Arno) is devoid of charm or depth.
- The "leveling" system is confusing; there isn't really a coherent EXP tracking system, but quests have a "recommended" level. Perks and abilities are buried in a bewildering stack of sub-menus.
- The controls are clunky and feel like a step back from games like Black Flag. Switching weapons is difficult, and the dynamic abilities that change based on your proximity to an enemy, such as melee vs. assassinate are clumsily handled ... I have hidden blades selected and try to make a stealth kill, only to punch the guy instead, alerting the guards and failing the quest.
- I've played all the AC games, and I've never seen an AC with more arbitrary and frustrating quest restrictions (don't be seen or the quest fails, don't kill anyone or the quest fails, etc.) They're just there as a pacing speed bump, not because there was a compelling story-related reason for them, and it feels forced and speaks of lazy quest design ... "let's forbid you from using all the hard-earned weapons and abilities that would be most useful for this quest, and make you complete it like a noob, stumbling through crowds and past guards to kill some guy like you never made it past level 1, because we, the developers, were too lazy to find a more natural way to make quests more challenging."
I never bothered to finish this game, and I never will.

Hacknet is a fantastic hacking game with an interesting story. The interface is built around a set of simulated command line tools very close to the real Unix environment which is generally easy to use although the game map can get crowded in the late stages of the game. The atmosphere really does create the impression of being a hacker finding a target system's weaknesses, digging through your target's files and investigating what your contracts require. The gameplay rewards exploration and the game itself is peppered with lots of flourishes and attention to detail that really shows the love and effort put in by the developers. It recreates everything from private conversations to stupid corporate communications and IT practices (and even in-game OS crashes) realistically which makes for a very authentic game world.
While there are occasional typos and part of the gameplay loop migh seem repetitive, the flow of the game is very addictive and many times what starts off as a short session ends up taking up several hours. The game can definitely be enjoyed by non-computer savvy users although those with command-line experience are sure to find some amusing little touches that enhance the overall experience. The music and visuals are also very pleasant.
All in all, highly recommended and looking forward to playing the expansion!

Successor to the great Gmod Tower, Tower Unite is a stand alone version with an almost an endless stream of new possibilities to offer. Tower Unite IS in early access as I currently write this which leads many to say it is "not worth buying right now." Despite it being under construction the dev team works around the clock to bring quality content and beautiful visuals. The plans they have for the game down the road are amazing and I'm beyond excited to see them unfold.
Both the game play and social aspects are very diverse and very fun. Sometimes I think of Tower as an amusement park, or a playground. They provide us with the tools, and it's up to us the players to enjoy ourselves and encourage one another. The core of Towers players are amazing, passionate, diverse, friendly, and wonderful people. It's hard to play this game and not make a few new friends along the way.
I have the utmost faith in Tower Unites developers to bring quality  content in the future. They're amazing hard working people who listen to community feedback and understand that respect and understanding are powerful tools to make a great community.
TL ; DR : Early access or not, Tower Unite gets a 10/10

Ionball 2: Ionstorm is a AAA 3D Arkanoid / Breakout clone that features hardcore Arkanoid and Breakout like game-play and introduces many original concepts to individualize itself in a crowded genre.  The game's difficulty and speed are jacked from the very first board. The speed of the game is extreme and powerups and weapons take some time to acquire making the game at first somewhat difficult to acclimate to.
In Arkanoid and most clones, weapons drop as each board is played. Ionball 2 implements an XP system where XP is released from defeated enemies and needs to be caught with the "bat".  Upon board completion the XP becomes your currency to which you can use to purchase both passive and active upgrades for use on all boards.
There is a scoring system as well as a continue option if you trigger game over and which will deduct from your running tally if utilized.  The Steam Punk levels are hub based in that you may play any of the 10 boards in the current hub in any order. Once completed, the final level of the hub will need to be completed to advance to the next hub.  The game features over 60 levels and 3 boss levels.
Ionball 2 is intense and requires serious concentration especially with the crazy particle effects employed in the game. Outstanding graphics, sounds and a pulse pounding musical score complement the well animated enemy designs.  Many boards are littered with different droids which have distinctive responsibilities.   Some for example may replenish life of worn down enemy units.
With Arkanoid clones there was always the issue of the last remaining enemy. Many clones just leave the enemy on the board until hit. Ionball 2 rewards you by eliminating an enemy if you've kept the ball alive.  This is applicable not just for the last enemy but from the start of the board to it's completion. Given the speed of the game, this mechanism works as a reward to the player for keeping the ball in play.
Ionball 2 features spectacular effects and explosions. While the game is just marvellous to look at, all of the pretty effects may interfere with your concentration and thereby increasing the difficulty in an already difficult game and jacking the intensity.
Ionball2: Ionstorm, challenging, polished and overall an indie gem.

It's a shooter, it's tactical, there's a lot more variety than it looks like on the surface. Guns blazing/stealth is a real choice. Death comes swiftly if you're careless, and is a wrench after a long level.
Two ways to play - campaign missions are varied, short and hard, and unlock in sequence. Freelance lets you choose your risk/difficulty/reward payoff and play longer missions.
Fundamentally the gameplay is really solid - you need to plan your approach and get through without burning through all your ammo or getting cornered and obliterated. There's more than one way to do it, and it can take a few goes to find the approach that works for you. Getting the hang of aiming and using cover is key.
I melted a bunch of robots from the other side of wall using a black hand irradiator, it was great.
More hours in, I keep coming back for the fundamental gameplay. Because you're rewarded for risk, taking out the smaller vehicles and higher difficulty pilots and trying to get through the freelance levels alive is really good fun. Effective combinations of weapons tie in to your strategy, as does ensuring you can scavange enough ammo and shields to keep going.

This is a game that thrives in a dark and foreboding atmosphere with a presentation that is absolutely sublime. The character models and backgrounds are delightfully macabre, perfectly complimented by the soundtrack and the narrators grim mien. The gameplay induces a sense that there are threats around every corner and yet urges you to calculate and brave the risks of the realm with the promise of great reward.
It also fosters imagination as each "hero" in your company will have their own personality traits and quirks that directly effect their abilities on and off the field of battle. You WILL watch some of your greatest heroes be laid low when they cannot cope with the horrors they face and you WILL watch the weak and cowardly stand tall in their darkest hour when you need them the most.
In essence, we are talking about we are talking about an RPG that has a very defined line between what is under your control and what isn't. On the one hand, preparing your party with items, skills, and propor mental health will help you fight past seemingly unwinable situations. The combat is brutal, yet tactical with an emphasis on making sure that the heroes abilities synergise with each other. On the other hand, the RNG (or simply put, random elements) in the game will certainly spice up every adventure you go on with either new tools or obstacles that you must face along the way. With the right amount of forethought, you will find that you're capable of handling most encounters. However, when things start to go wrong, it doesn't just rain, it pours. This is where the game shines in my opinion.
When an adventure goes smoothly, you'll get to pat yourself on the back for a job well done. Nobody got remotely close to death and you got exactly what you wanted from the dungeon, so send your heroes to celebrate their victory in various ways before going on to the next one. Inversely, when an adventure goes poorly, the panic sets in. Your mind will be racing as you try and think of a way to get the rewards you so desperately need without losing all. Do you give up so that this particular batch of heroes can live to fight another day despite the penalty? BORING! It is at this point that every decision becomes that of life or death. Every enemy you face may be the one to bring this adventure to an end so you will be comanding your heroes to battle with every trick in the book maybe even hoping that lady luck will smile at you just long enough to make it through. Every random stockpile you see may hold the items that make the treck onward just a little more possible, or deadly traps to hinder you further. It is in those moments when you see that your healer is nearing the limit of mental stress and you direly need them to show their true courage, when any hard hit could turn the tide of a battle to either you or your enemies, and when you are practically praying that your kleptomaniac crusader will FOR ONCE not grab that F&$%ING SHINY THING THAT IS OBVIOUSLY A TRAP that the game stands completely apart from anything else on offer. Then the dust settles. In success you feel a mix of elation at your conquest mixed with the grim reality of your mounting losses. In failure, the game beckons you stand back up and try again.
IN CONCLUSION/ TLDR
This game is tough and unforgiving at times, but there are also moments when luck is on your side and things can get downright comical. For players who want to play a tactical rpg unlike anything else out there, this game will be good. For players who are willing to do all that then fail and try again, this game will be great!

Running on Amd 8320, Gtx 970, 16GB of ram.  The game has bugs, but none i encountered were game breakings.  The npc would sometimes be floating and did some weird stuff during cut scenes.  The combat was hit and miss and felt sluggish, as if there was a delay between when I pressed the button and when the game responded to my button press.
The game looks georgeous and the number of people on screen at any given time is incredible.
The story is bit on the boring side with a fairly simple revenge plot.  It would have been nice to see the characters from Assassin's creed rogue make an appearence.
The gameplay is fairly typical of an assassins creed game.  I really appreciated some of the added mechanics for traversal such as holding a to climb and holding b to indicate that i wanted to drop. Entering windows was sometimes a difficult task with my character jumping everywhere but in to the open window(The game indicates that you can press LT to enter a window, which only occassionaly behaved as i expected to).  The combat in this game is brutal, you cannot engage a large number of enemies and live through the encounter most of the time.  This is actually a welcome change which forces you to sneak around a bit more and make more well thought out decisions which brings me to another change, the game has finally added a sneak button(llow profile).  That was really a long time coming.  If you do get into a bad situation, a smoke bomb is uaully all you will need to recover.
One huge addition to the game is the abllity to buy individual armor pieces; head, chest, arms, legs, and belt.  I really liked this addition since it allowed me to customize my assassin to my liking. I don't like the default assassins outfit in this game, but there are several choices that i did like.
The game did feel a bit tedious at times, requiring me to run around for extended periods of time and repeat sections that a failed.  Buying the best armor will take a long time because of how long it takes to aquire money. There is a lot to do, but i wasn't really interested in a lot of it like the murder mysteries and tracking down the weird symbols hidden around the city.
Lastly, the multiplayer is kind of a neat addition but difficult to get into since there are so few people playing at this time.
Overall, This feels like a natural evolution for assassins creed and I recommend it to fans and probably new comers as well.

Undoubtedly, I'm well overdue to write a review, especially for Stardew Valley. It's been my favorite game for the last year or so, and ConcernedApe absolutely deserves my public thanks for his very entertaining game. I'm sure lots of reviews talk about Stardew's Harvest Moon (which I haven't ever played) roots, the beautiful pixel art, the dating simulator, and most certainly the music, so I'll not elaborate on that.  I'll just say I make friends with people mostly because the empty friendship hearts bug me, and I rarely bother with marriage because it doesn't seem to add much to the game. Also, in most games, I end up turning off the sound and/or music after a short while. I've never done that in Stardew. I love how it sounds.
Typically, I'll play to about the end of the second year. Then I get bored with that save, because the farmer is pretty well established, and I'll start a new save.
What draws me back over and over to Stardew is that it feels like an idealized version of my home. I grew up in a rural part of the Pacific Northwest on property given to my parents by my grandfather. We didn't farm on the scale of Stardew, but we had a huge garden, all kinds of animals, and I have cleared plenty of stones, trees, and brush by hand, often without the benefts of powered machinery. It was hard work that came with plenty of bruises, aching muscles, blisters, sunburns,  blackberry scratches, poison oak rashes, and so on. However, I do have a lot of good memories, too, of family and laughter and pranks and stories and the satisfaction of seeing stuff get built. Stardew somehow taps that nostalgia and the love I have for working out on the land while it leaves out all of the really not fun things. Maybe my digital farmer gets digital blisters, but my digits are just fine! I suppose that, growing up, some of that work my family and I did was play. In Stardew, I just get to play, and sometimes that's really nice.

Very good game overall!
On the technical and visual side there are some nice and colourful environments to explore. The animation of the "Kid" is great and fluid and he has a nice number of weapons and special abilities to choose from, making sure the game doesn't get boring. Combat is quickly learned but takes some time to master. There are some training areas (proving grounds) specific to each weapon (10 in total) to help you achieve this.
Difficulty becomes perfectly adjustable and customizable. As you play you find idols which provide powers and abilities to your oponents (and greater bonuses to XP and coin to you when you defeat them) which can range from resistance to damage to more feroucious attacks. There are in total 10 idols which, when (and if) you activate them all, you are faced with a great challenge (with matching reward) to overcome.
The dynamic narration (one of the selling points of Bastion) makes it a lot of fun to play as it reacts to what you're doing in real time. The narrator, Logan Cunningham, does a great job in conveying drama and sometimes a hint of comedy when appropriate and you never get tired of his great voice.
The story is good with well developed characters each with an interesting background story and the last playable moments of the game provide for a great narrative. I was surprised on how... poetic the end of this game can be, depending on your choices.
Last, but certainly not least, a lot of emotion is conveyed by the wonderful soundtrack, produced and composed by Darren Korb and winner of the Spike's 2011 VGAs. I know some of the winners have been met with raised eyebrows (to say the least), but this soundtrack is absolutely fantastic.
Even at its full price of £11.49, this is a great buy as it gives you 10-15 hours of gameplay and it does have some replayability value (I'm on my second playthough) as you are allowed to continue to gather XP and improve your weapons from where you left off.

Few games have had a visceral effect on me like Stardew Valley. When I hear the start-up music, I can feel my muscles relax and my focus grow soft. Most games that I fall in love with draw me in, demanding my full attention and requiring subsequent play sessions. Stardew valley is not one of those games.
In Stardew Valley,  the main character is tired of their day to day life and are looking for an escape from responsibility. This causes the player to leave their job, move to a small town in the middle of nowhere, and operate their own farm.
The player has the daily option of farming, fishing, mining or foraging. They can setup their crops however they want, with the season being the only limiting factor. You can intereact with the local townsfolk by giving them gifts or carrying out tasks for them. Occasionally, there are even town wide events such as the egg festival. Activities during these events are varied, but they repeat every year.
The most relaxing thing about this game is there's no wrong way to play. You can become incredibly efficient at farming and fishing, or you can take your time. The game has no fail state (as far as I can tell), no hard timer, and no obligations. Money is easily earned, also not particularly vital. It's only real use is buying crop seeds or upgrading your farm to provide more daily resources. If you end a day with no money, it's simple enough to fish and forage til you've got what you need.
Stardew Valley's mantra is "Stress-free." It takes a while to get used to that idea. When I first started, I was concerned with making sure I always had some money, in case I desperately needed it. I also wanted to make sure I was being absolutely effiicent in what I did everyday. That's one way to play the game, certainly, but I don't believe it offers the most  complete experience of the game.

Fractured Space became such a disapointment for me, I can't recommend it in its current state. I'm a Forerunner from the alpha days and I have to say the FS is nowhere near as enjoyable to play as it was back then. I loved FS for that feeling of captaining a gigantic lumbering capital ship and using its awesome firepower to wipe out my foes, but now after Conquest 2.0 the scale of FS has been completely ruined for me. Maps now feel extremely cramped and there is no sense of strategy anymore thanks to the modified respawn times. Positioning and setting up your attacks are much more of a non-concern now since battles for mines always end up in a huge cluster♥♥♥♥ within minutes of jumping in and penalty for death has been greatly reduced. I think EdgeCase definately achieved their goal of making the game "faster paced and more action-packed" but at the cost of the strategic space battle experience.
I enjoyed Fractured Space more when each ship had its role and the playing field was equal. I could choose my favorite ship and play skillfuly against other similarly skilled players. Now I have to worry about having to setup the proper crew implants to give me and edge in battle, wich greatly detracts from the overall gameplay experience for me. Implants are just another thing to keep me in the menues reading guides and trying to choose the right ones.
Overall, the visuals and sound are amazing and I love the art design. But theres no sense of scale or strategy anymore and it's starting to feel like your typical free-to-play grindfest. For me fractured Space is now in the same boat as Dreadnought from Six Foot and Yager, promising in the early stages but now a huge dissapointment.
Edit: The game has improved noticabley and in its current state I can recommend it. Plenty of content, considerable pricing for crew and implants and daily and weekley missions that give out a plentiful amount of rewards.

This is the first time I feel that I should give an in depth review on this game. Bear in mind I haven't even beaten it yet, this is my first time playing, and I played the sequel when I was younger.
I have been wanting to play this game for quite some time after beating the sequel, OkamiDen, multiple times because of how much I loved it. Never got the chance to, but then Okami got released on PC and here we are now. This game is a true gem, something that feels like it was created out of love rather than as a money grab. It's jaw dropping how much detail was put into this game, and it will leave you hoping that it won't end yet.
The characters, the story, the silly dialogue... it's all very charming, and on top of that everything feels fresh and unique. You'll be getting to know so many characters in this game rather than being limited to only a handful like most games. I'm left speechless on what I could say really as there's just so many great things about it. It's been a long time since I've enjoyed a game so much, and for $20? This game is a steal as you'll end up getting more time out of it than the price listed.
Honestly the 30 FPS doesn't bother me at all, this game runs extremely smoothly and if you're contemplating on getting it just because of the lock then go for it, you won't even notice it. Yes controller support is a little funky too but all you need to do is go through Big Picture Mode to get it working, and hell I might even recommend keyboard + mouse over controller because it makes it a lot easier to use your brush techniques (Which if you're like me will be using a lot). I'm using a controller but it's a little slow compared to the couple of minutes I used a mouse and keyboard, however both work perfectly for this game in my opinion. My only complaint is the camera can be a little cluncky at times but it's so minor that I can't even be frustrated with it.
So to sum is up.
Pros:
- Unique gameplay
- Engaging story and characters
- Stunning art style/graphics
- A large world where everything is your canvas
- Multiple sidequests and extra goodies if you want to sink in even more time in this game
- A wonderful soundtrack that fits the game perfectly
Cons:
- Funky controller support (Easily fixable with Big Picture Mode)
- Camera is clunky sometimes
- Brush techniques are a little finicky at times (There's a stray bead with lots of percision that this might frustrate you)
I recommend this game for anyone who loves puzzle solving games or the Zelda series, and I hope you can fall in love with everything this game has to offer just like I have. 10/10 would play again.

Played this game from more or less day one and I waited for the right time to write a review.  With the newest update and about 6 months between my last play session and now (about 5 hours in two days) the game has changed dramatically.  I dont have to fight a UFO and sniper penguins with a bow and arrow and I can travel from planet to planet without so much as  coal to power my engines.  Individual residents of areas offer quests and the scope of items to buy/craft/steal is much larger.  Finding that first cluster of planet fragment ore was satisfying.  Using my raygun to suck up oil from pools puzzled me.
Overall this era of Starbound is more complex and more confusing.  Going for 2 hours building a crafting table, furnace and anvil only to have me waste resources when the onboard computer quested me to do so through a specific menu and didnt recognize that I had already went far beyond these items.  The mobs on planets are still satisfyingly cute and random.  The melee weapons have more flexible aim and the magic xray effect of the matter manipulator allows me to see through walls to find ore deposits once again.  I am glad to see my favorite parts of the old builds return but some of the new content concerns me only in so much that it adds what feels like an artificial layer of additional materials and items to pad upward movement and throw more turmoil and misdirection and struggle into the game.  Its implimentation is simply frustration in comparison to the old flow of the game. However if I had never played this game until today I would simply accept these demands as another grind forced on the player.
Overall I give starbound a 8.5/10 rating at its current incarnation.  Good humor, mechanics, art, and delivery give it a cheery warm exciting exploration and gathering feel that I find very refreshing.  The only negative aspect to me in this current build is that I feel the creators are in transition to find a broad enough scale of gathering, a growing list of progressive item refinement, and enough variety to force players to go far and wide to complete the search for resources new and old.  In comparison to older builds this is entirely more laborious and almost numbing however the improvements in every other aspect (interactions, growing of depth in NPCs and variety of systems and introductions of gates etc) are a breath of welcome fresh air to the game.
I am optimistic this game will be a solid wonderful experience in time and has made leaps and bounds of improvement since its early inception.  Recommended 100%

This game is just a mix of minecraft and CS:GO. However, that does not make it a bad game. BLOCKADE lets you fortify a base to survive from people and zombies which is pretty fun trying to hide/shoot you're way out of trouble being a one man army. You can BUY weapons, but they are just reskins mostly. You always feel surrounded and if you are new, everything feels so pretty and calm if you know FPS already. Leveling up takes time which makes players get used to weapons before leveling up and getting more weapons. Guns do ALOT of damage and healing can only be done sniper vs sniper or if you won a fight with the guy you just killed. You learn quick and levels are destructable and fun to destroy.Also, FREAKING TANKS!!!! BUT, this game does have downsides. When you start out, all you need is the M14 which 3 shots people unless it is to the head. Buying things replenishes things like grenades, tnt, ect. much faster than leveling up. Helmets DEFEND from headshots and are very and unbalance gameplay. The uzi, m14 and most LMGs need a very big nerf. And spawncamping is a BIG deal right now. Also, the game does not have ANY unbalanced team support and can pit 3 people against 6. Controls cannot be tweaked in any way so if you use y to chat NOPE!  Teamwork is not a factor in this game in anyway and is taking pot-shots at people across the map. This is countered by headshots and enemy's who built a tower in front of you're spawn, which MAKES you work with you're team so it is not a big deal ATM.
I am aware this game is early access, and that it has a few bugs, but don't you think that helmets are OP AS HELL?! Sorry. Overall, this game is a great non-computer intensive game to pass the time. Killing people feels rewarding, and it is being constantly updated. I am sure most of the downsides will be fixed, but for now, it is P2W but all means. And be glad the way it is currently, they are not asking 5 dollars to play an indie game. I rate this game 7/10 but, it does need a few fixes. I recommend this game to anyone who wants a relaxed style of FPS or are a fan of minecraft/cs:go.

DayZ is a mod for Arma 2 that turns the base game into a zombie survival simulator. DayZ is one of the most detailed, if not the most detailed, and immersive zombie survival sims available. When you play DayZ, you create a character and spawn on a beach with nothing but your clothes and from there you have to make your way inland and try to find the tools you need to fend off the undead and to survive in this new world. Generally you are looking for things such as a melee weapon, medical supplies, light sources, food and you might even be lucky enough to find a gun or camping gear.
As you make your way through formerly populated areas like villages, farms and the three large cities, you will run into hordes of zombies that you will have to deal with. You can lose them by running into buildings or otherwise breaking line of sight with them. But the zombies are actually not the real threat in this game; the biggest potential threat comes from the other players who are attempting to survive just like you. Some of them will try to help you or trade with you, but usually in exchange for something of equal value, or if you are both being attacked by zombies or other players and you band together out of desperation. Most players though, are bandits, which you can tell by their clothes and covered faces. These players are out for your blood, and only want the stuff they can loot off your dead body.
You want to be very cautious in approaching other survivors that you do not know in DayZ because a lot of bandit groups will try to bait victims by having one of their number pose as a "friendly" and then when the victim runs over to trade or help, the rest of the bandits ambush him or her. Players in this game have gotten very paranoid in the last year and a half, and so a lot of times players will shoot each other on sight rather than risk losing their gear to a potential bandit.
So what do you actually do in DayZ once you have your basic weapons and tools needed to survive? Well you want to find a safe place that you can use as a home base. Generally you want to be far away from areas frequented by zombies, so somewhere in the woods usually. You want to be close enough to a town that you can raid it for supplies every few hours but far enough that zombies and players will have a difficult time tracking you home.
Once you have your things safely stashed, the best thing you can do is band together with your friends or any friendly people on the server you can find and get a vehicle. A bicycle is great for solo scout and loot missions to town, but a car, truck or SUV will provide cover from bullets, a large inventory and quick transport for multiple people. Focus on getting the necessary car parts you will need to fix up one of the junked cars you find laying around. After that, once you get enough loot and establish a territory, you can even build a house in some versions of DayZ and barricade it against zeds and meddlesome players.
At some point you will get into a fight with another player. Most of the time these fights aren't fair. Maybe a group of players rolled up on you while you were looting and shot you as you came out of a house. Other times you'll follow someone and not realize that they have friends with them and their friends flank and kill you, or you just get shot by someone while you are running from zombies that have aggroed you. All of these things will happen to you on a regular basis, and since everything stays on your corpse when you die, chances are they will loot and take your stuff. But other times you get lucky and you kill a guy with a huge gun that you need because you were lucky enough to catch him with his pants down. So now you have a big gun, and then when you go around the side of the house he was in, you find his giant military truck full of more guns and supplies. Now you are a zombie slaying god and you can bring all of that back to your base.
It is very easy to either get very, very mad at this game and ragequit or try to keep deaths in perspective, play smart and take all the opportunities you get. If you are observant and patient in every situation you will do well. If you run into a building without checking the surroundings for players watching or for zombies that will attract attention to you, you will die a lot. If you take your time and all necessary precautions you will catch somebody making a mistake and profit from it, and continue to survive the apocalypse.

Astbreed is a game that leaves a lot of story to the imagination, the 'how' & the 'why', go largely unexplained. However the action is by far a crowning achievement, as a sidescroller, Astebreed goes to great lengths to create changing dimensions during play. You may be charging headlong into enemy fire to find that the enemy is now behind you, or drop down on a foe & fly circles around them during combat.
During combat you have Spread Shot/Spread lock-on, Focus Shot/Focus lock-on, Blade Flurry/Blade Dash, EX Nova/ EX Blade Storm/ EX Wild. The shot & blade techniques are a simple difference between holding down the required button, however the EX attacks vary depending on how many targets your locked on -if any- & lastly if you've locked every weapon you have on a single target you go EX Wild.
The game has difficulty settings, chapter select, & leaderboards as part of the replay experience. It also has a gallery of all sorts of unlockable images to award your exceptional efforts.

As if the game was on shaky enough ground as is with the sub-par gameplay and further divergence from actual RPG elements that made the series famous, Bethesda had to bring forth Paid Mods 2 in the form of the 'Creation Club', swearing on their lives that it wasn't paid mods and are instead 'mini DLCs' despite the blatant evidence showing otherwise. As if the general idea isn't bad enough, CC is considered mandatory to even play the game, being made in a way that's somewhat hardcoded to dump all the files in its library into hard drives and other equivalents to get around a limitation on the console versions. The kicker in that part is that the files are borderline useless in-game unless the corresponding item is purchased in the CC, the credits only able to obtained with real cash, solidifying that they are indeed paid mods.
I used to play this game a lot in the past, though my play time pales in comparison to the more hardened veterans who have invested in far more time than I have. Despite such, I grew bored with it since the game did not have the same charm and atmosphere as previous Fallout installments did like New Vegas or Fallout 3. While the engine is better, the streamlining and trimming to the immersive mechanics made it almost impossible to actually feel...well...immersive. There are the pockets here and there where it's possible, but it's very, very brief and often broken when an enemy comes out of nowhere for the sake of keeping things 'interesting'.
It's difficult to feel as though the player could insert themselves into the game. Everything about your character is decided from the start; The male is known as Nate, a retired soldier, with the female being Nora, a graduate from a law school. No chance to develop a character from scratch other than the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats, and the skills are similar to that of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, where you gain experience to level up and pick whichever skill you'd like. This kind of leveling though suffers in that the level cap is limitless, leading to a character being a master of everything after enough time has been invested or if one cheats with the console commands(outside of Survivor difficulty that is since it's disabled for whatever reason), resulting in whatever builds out there eventually merging into this omnipotent survivor of the wastes capable of doing everything whenever it's needed.
Back to the CC, rumors have been going around that the folks that contribute to the library of it aren't even given a fair share of the cut, getting as little as twenty-five or so percent of the profits. I'm not entirely sure on the accuracy of these claims, but if they do hold true, just shows on how anti-consumer and anti-modding that Bethesda has become over the years. Folks have made mods for their games for years, often in the form of community patches to fix up the numerous glaring bugs and breaks in their games. To turn their back on modders would mean the death of their products and future releases, if their track record of broken and buggy games holds true.
As of the day of this review, on 9/16/2017, I do not recommend getting the game, even on sale. The day that the CC goes is when this will change, if only slightly.

Fractured Space is a true f2p space moba like no other. In this moment you can choose between 34 (very nicely designed) different ships, each one having its own unique abilities and equipment. The equipment customization is very superficial (weapons and abilities are very similar), but by playing  around a little bit with the ship's crew you can change its behaviour and create unique builds suitable for your playstyle. Also keep in mind that every ship has its role and they are all very balanced for their purpose (with very few exceptions) so it's up to you to make it shine!
The matchmaking is as bad as in every other single moba out there so if you are familiar with that kind of games don't expect to find a better or worst situation here. It's exactly the same. Reguarding the time it takes to find a game, i have to say that the maximum i had to wait was 6-7 minutes till now. Generally i start a game in less than 5 minutes. Maybe you should check in the server selection all the servers and the maps in order to speed up the proceedure.
As i've mentioned above this game is true f2p. You can buy everything just by grinding (except for the skins) and you will never have that feeling that someone is better than you because he paid for something.
A thing to consider is the high ping that i've experienced during all this time. I've never had less than 130ms in all the servers i've tested. Generally my ping median in this game is around 200ms, but in the end it's not so important since this game is more tactical than just fast reflexes.
In conclusion i higly recommend Fractured Space to all the fans of moba and space combat games. After all it's free so give it a try and see for yourself.

I'll keep it brief. I do not reccomend getting this title, especially during Early Access.
This game is a bundle of dissapointment. The shady developers are a group of rag-tag novices with more artists than programmers in desperate need of a Project Manager.
The game is unstable, very incomplete, unsatisfying to play, and very frustrating as a whole. There are many poor design choices in the game that keep it from being good, as well as many missing features after over 2 years of development.
Pros:
Lots of customization
Interesting lore and worldbuilding for races & setting
Lots of tools to work with for functional and vanity building.
Interesting take on Terrarria's formula
Meh:
Art style is unappealing to me
Soundtrack is very hit-and-miss, sound design as a whole ranges from acceptable to outright out of place or dissapointing. These is no track switching, once a song plays it plays all the way through.
Cons:
The game is very, very, VERY unstable; any patch they release is almost 100% certain to break more things than it fixes along with hamfisted balancing. Expect constant crashes no matter the OS, hardware, and programs you're running.
Game has become cripplingly linear (Which is a major issue, given the main draw of the game, and their tagline, is to 'explore an infinite galaxy'.)
In addition to the above, the game borrows Terrarria and Minecraft's resource-tier-progression; with the aforementioned linearity this also means that once you have a star-type's resource, you're done with those stars effectively permaneatly unless you need something specefic from them.
Over 2 years of post-funded development with minimal content added; most features implemented are left unusable or just half-finished
Developers continue to butcher content already in place; tons of content is left in unfinished
Devs have priorities♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ing-backwards, including things like extra dungeons and cosmetics when basic functions are left incomplete.
Equipment progression is incredibly barebones and flawed, randomly generated items always outscale player-made equipment. Coupled with the game's linearity, this means place the player out-scales become completely trivialized.
Tons of visual issues, the poor art style constantly clashes with itself due to poor scaling/placement of items, etc
Enemy AI and randomly generated enemies in general are very lackluster despite them supposedly pouring thousands of manhours into them; every fight in the game can be beaten by jumping up and down and shooting the enemy; exluding the bosses which only show up in 2 set quest-missions and nowhere else.
Combat is effectively crippled, there is no variation between weapon types and playstyles as they all involve jumping around like an idiot because the AI can't hit you and walking through the enemy while beating/shooting them to death. In multiplayer fights are decided by simply backpedaling and dodging every attack or being struck multiple times at once by an individual monster.
Enemy design as a whole is lackluster, procedural enemies almost always look like garbled trash and they all play the exact same (land/flying, melee/breath attack; no exceptions); there are no interesting enemy types to be encountered outside of very specific dungeons/underground spawned structures.
New quest system is awful, requires every character to go through a grueling set of stages to progress and upgrade your ship as well as to unlock the ability to visit most of the content; while at the same time locking the player onto the railroad tracks that basically nullify all previous content. Some quests rely on pure RNG or are otherwise stupidly easy to do. (IE: 'get me my script' when it's less than 10 seconds away to 'get me this one specefic type of furniture' with no idea of where or with what race it may spawn, if at all. Quests/Missions also lock interesting things like bosses behind ♥♥♥♥♥♥ non-scaling instances.
Races and setting lore, while enticing, are nowhere near ♥♥♥♥ing finished and are basically non-existant for some of them; everything is left absolutely unexplained, dropped and never spoken of again, or seemingly written off by some other piece of lore in an unsatisfying, conflicting mess.
Customization is limited by developers in both not continueing to complete features (dyeing armor/clothing colors is in the game, but is unusable by players and only has 3 colors) and just outright disabling them outside of very limited circumstances (paint tool cannot be used outside the ship).
Despite dev's claim to have released the game on Early Access for fan input, the developers have been absolutely vile to any criticism of the game, it's coding, or it's design choices. This had led to them outright censoring the steam forum, banning users for posting about game flaws, and treating parts of the community like dirt for not choking on their♥♥♥♥♥♥♥for waving around this half-baked product.
Don't give these chuckle♥♥♥♥s any more money, they need to get their goddamn act together, hire the people they need, and get a Project Managar to smack them into order so they can actually get♥♥♥♥♥♥done.

Exactly what the doctor ordered after a long day: insanely customizable robots with amoral cyberpunk jockies tearing up a city and earning mad cash in this 80-future sci-fi top down tactical action game.
The aesthetic, music, and blurbs of story surrounding the game are awesome, but it's the gameplay that really shines. With a dizzying array of weapons and base mechs the game is a playground for anyone with destructive tendancies. Some loadouts are all about mobility, hitting and running and whittling your enemy down. Some are about stealth, moving quietly from point to point while you gun down lone patrols. And of course, some times you have to heap on heavy weapons that wake up the whole neighborhood as your blowing it up.
What makes it great is that what sounds like simple mayhem becomes a ballet of drawing enemy attention, destroying and perserving cover to funnel enemies into spots where you can pick them off, and figuring out how to survive when the alarm goes off and the entire map wakes up on you.
The base missions offer some well built challenges that act as sort of a test run for certain configurations of weapons, but  the bragging rights come from stacking on challenge modifiers on top of taking long multi-map contracts in freelance mode (the challenge of each mission set in freelance is further modified via pilot choice, an inspired game design idea)
With a glut of games showing style over substance, it's great to find something that has both in ample amounts.

It's always great to see a game that at first glance seems like a mass of mindless, superficial details, but ultimately ends up defying your first impression.
Brigador has much more to offer than just a mech-grind of mass destruction. No, the attention to detail in this game has astounded me, and I've only barely begun. To be completely honest, the game's interfacing confused me at first. There's a lot of information. However, it takes nothing more than one calm breath, and an agreement to focus on what the game has to offer. Once you burst out of the tutorial levels, the tactics and skills the game has taught you thus far are vital to your success in merely accomplishing the mission. Onward!
The levels have a sandbox design, allowing you as the player to choose how to approach each portion of the mission's map. Understanding the special defense abilities, weapon types, and vehicle you're using attributes to the tactical precision necessary to carry out your mission. This game doesn't play around with free rides, you'll have to earn your success.
The lore of the setting, and all its inhabitants is an impressive collection that unfortunately leaves me yearning for a voiced narrative of certain details, but the presented format is well fitted to the entire experience.
Brigador is a fun game, and you'll soon find yourself wrapped as tightly inside its dystopian future, as the game's fundamental mechanics are tight.
