Without spoilers, I can not go into detail. The motivations and backgrounds of most characters are not introduced, keeping you guessing in the worst way possible. Not "Wow, crazzy. Why did he do this? I want to find out, hopefully next chapter..." but "WTF? Who is this dude, what do they refer to and how does this tie in with the story?". Only three characters get an in depth introduction - seriously, three? C'mon, XCOM made me feel more attached to my soldiers and that's a turn based, top-down squad game were soldiers die and get replaced on a regular basis. Oh, and the enemies - you will face the same enemy faction everywhere, no matter how the quest flavor text lables them. Extremists, templars, thugs, smugglers, mercenaries, all the same 4, 5 guys multiplied in the hundreds, wearing the same uniform.
No surprises here. Simple Assassins VS Templars, no moral grey areas as in most previous AC titles. Not even any big turns or revelations. After the first hour, how the story plays out is obvious. Mentioning the tie ins with the story above - Paris does not change at all in between each chapter. You are in one of the most troubled times in French history, yet I did not feel that. The situation did not really deteriorate. Most demonstrations were identical (often, the mass was shouting and waving fists at an empty square, a bridge or a wall - wtf?).
Oh, and you have no choices. Not one. A really outdated game design choice. Moreover, apart from the main missions, the game is grind. Collectibles in the hundreds, dozens of basically identical side missions completed in 30 seconds... Why, Ubisoft, why?
One bright side: They managed to make a great love story for Arno and Elise!
The whole main story and almost all side missions play in identical looking areas of Paris. There is one tiny slum, some really tiny swamp areas and a big field where an army is camped. The rest is a monotone mix of houses, churches, placaes etc.
Ubisoft worked on expanding your options and easing the control especially in free run mode since AC1. But this time, it took a turn for the worse. Unresponsive controls (hanging on a lamp post, not being able to drop for 3min; blocks not activating), being stuck on a chair (Yay, great assassin, go! Reload last checkpoint...), over-use of some keys (E is one case where Arno often did things I did not intend; another case is Ctrl - ever tried entering a window for a few minutes, giving up frustrated and choosing the main door?) or the inability to activate certain abilities (ever tried to role when being shot at while running away? Arno simply jumps and gets shot in the back) make it hard and immersion breaking to play the game. Yet they become game-breakers in multyplayer.
It's not really Assassin's Creed. Stealth is underpowered, badly designed, hard to control and above all - not rewarded. Charging in through the front door (remember, Arno often simply does not like the window... Yay, great assassin, go!), haking everybody to pieces, casually looting the corpses and then walk up to your objective is the way to go. Easier, less buggy, more reliable and more Creed Points. Yes, more creed points. Apparently, hack&slash style combat finishers and pistol headshots are more in accordance to the Creed than stealthily avoiding any combat.
Assassination targets sit idle while you slaughter their household, partys go on with dead bodies everywhere, guards freak out verbally when finding their dead mates only to return to their post within seconds, bystanders shed away from dead bodies with a  delay of several seconds whilst not being bothered be me murdering other people right next to them, quest followers draw dozens of enemies while telling me to be stealthy... I could go on and on here.
Dying is inconsequential, cash is abundant, enemies are easy. The hardest part is finding some of the collectibles. I mean, they are marked on the map - easy right? Well, sometimes you have to go underground and make your way through a maze to find it. Yes, an underground maze! Awesome, right? Complex parcour, cool puzzles and the like... No, wait, this is AC Unity we are talking about. The maze is only five junctions with often all but one way blocked.
Not really Assassin's Creed, most of the content is collectibles, shallow characters, one great love story, hack&slash combat, bad stealth. I enjoyed it only because I loved the previous AC titles and was on a constant nostalgia trip.

I thought it important to warn those who have, and those who have not yet purchased this game, to be completely aware NOT to trust the Uplay Sync Services in keeping your game saves supposedly safe...
Uplay sync services is known for being unsafe in some Ubisoft/uplay titles. Take for example this game; As soon as Unity creates a save, Uplay attempts to upload it to the cloud to create a current back up. Since Unity creates a new save every 5 seconds (or almost every time you complete an action in game), Unity is constantly creating and Uplay is constantly uploading new 'overwritten' saves to the cloud; this creates large opportunities for your saves to become corrupted in the cloud or on your computer during the upload or rewrite phase.... This is essentially a huge fault in development, which was overlooked and unchangeable after the games release. Ubisoft has gone on to fix this problem in later games, such as syndicate, by only having the game upload the save 'after' the user has quit the game; this of course, gives time for the game to completely finish editing the saves before they are ready for upload.
I myself, got half way through Unity when I got a warning from Uplay that read something like "Uplay sync services has failed; please quit the game and restart"... After restarting, my game opened with the beginning intro, and I had realized that my save was gone. After searching my computer in the normal locations, I found that the save was deleted entirely and that the cloud was no longer downloading my previous save and instead, it just wanted to keep starting a new save... I of course, then came to the conclusion at this point that my save was just entirely gone. After turning off sync services and then continuing to play, I have had no issues and have been rather enjoying co-op gameplay with my friend.
It should be equally understood, that when you turn off sync services, some games (such as syndicate) do not even load local saves unless it can acquire a copy/clone from the cloud. After playing Syndicate half way through, and then turning sync services off to play unity, I then went back to syndicate but could no longer load my saves; they were of course, being loaded from the cloud (which was turned off at this point). Once I closed the game, turned the services back on, Uplay then asked me which save I wanted to use after loading syndicate back up; I chose my previous save from the cloud, and the game opened as normal...

All in all, though Ubisoft has been working on Uplay extensively lately, it is completely apparent that Uplay sync services still suck... I highly advise using another third party software to backup your saves, and don't use the Uplay cloud at all; or, use the cloud until it crashes; just be sure to have local backups of your saves or you’re screwed if something goes wrong.
Finally, even with syndicate; if a new save is created without sync services enabled, the save will be created and stored in its normal location where it usually can be found; such as in the Documents folder, as well as the Ubisoft/uplay folder. Unity seems to store two copies of the save; 1 online, and 1 locally. Syndicate on the other hand, seems to only load from a save if the save was first created offline/without sync services enabled, otherwise it wants to load from the cloud; if it can't find one, it loads a new save.
- The rest of my review for this game can be found below -
Unity is what I see as a reasonable addition to the Assassin's Creed collection. Not only does it stay on point with Templar history, but it also brings to light specific conspiracies and traditions about the Templars and their affiliate orders.

In comparison to previous titles, a lot of people were disappointed with the story and were confused why certain aspects were chosen; I personally, being an avid individual who studies Templar history, found this game to be rather enjoyable and quite accurate for what Ubisoft was trying to portray. Yes, the game does not go exactly with the first three or four Assassin's Creed titles, but it does stay pretty accurate to Templar facts, myths and legends for the time period. To not spoil anything, I'll refrain from explaining this point too much; just bare in mind that this game is exploring further points of Templar history. The below part may or may not be considered as a spoiler, so I've blacked it out; read if you want, but you've been warned.
And a Syndicate spoiler, I guess...
So, with my final note on the story of Unity, the game seems to be accurate enough to Templar history to enjoy it...Just don't expect anything fancy what so ever compared to previous games.
- As far as gameplay goes, there is a leveling system and multiple weapons to choose from. Some skills, and clothing boosters. Many missions, and what feels like 3x the amount of side missions. Co-op is fun and seems to work flawless except for where there is someone with bad ping (which seems to affect everyone in the game).
- The mobile companion app, which you can download for your phone or tablet, is essentially a 2nd screen that allows you to see your map at all times (like a GPS). You can see your character as you walk around the city, boxes you have not yet opened or collectables you have yet to unlock, it displays available missions and waypoints, you can set a waypoint by holding down on a specific spot of the map, and you'll then see the location in game. With this method, you can set two active waypoints by using the app, as well as the map in game. By completing small glyph puzzles in the app, you can unlock additional chests and content in game including some outfits and weapons. Due to updates to the game, you are no longer required to use this app.
- Performance - Though there appears to be a textural issue that causes textures to become blurry at a given (small) distance, I have been playing the game just fine with a healthy 40-45 FPS; all settings are set to high, except for a few such as antialiasing and texture quality. I attempted to set textures to ultra, but it supposedly said it was maxing my 4Gb 970, so I turned it down to "high" where I'm able to sustain at least 40 fps. More testing is needed before I can say whether other settings can be turned down or off, so that I can turn textures up, which would be preferable. Yes, I have enough hours in game that I should be able to answer these questions, but once I first tinkered to get 40 fps, I didn't mess with it again after that.
I probably would have added more to this review, but I ran out of space. I could summarize, but it’s not really necessary.. Thanks for reading. Other than Uplay sync services losing my save, I enjoyed Unity, and would play it again.

Do you like oldschool sci-fi cheese? Do you like twinstick shooters, but they are too basic for you? Do you like grimdark atmosphere with a little splash of neon and black humor? Do you like mechs, tanks, gravtanks and killdozers? This game is for you.
Pros:
-It plays a little bit like a twinstick shooter, but with more complex aiming (the aiming is 3D).
-There is a ton of customisation - you can choose your vehicle, weapons and a pilot in freelance mode. In campaign, you can choose between preset loadouts (different for each mission).
-Your loadout can heavily influence your playstyle. You can be a stealthy hit and run ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. You can speed around in a flying tank and avoid hits like crazy. Or you can pick some superheavy monstrosity and methodicaly annihilate any oposition with hard hitting doomsday weapons. The choice is yours.
-Even though there is no difficulty setting, you can influence the difficulty by your loadout. In freelance mode, your pilot choice functions as a difficulty modifier.
-The campaign is decently long and if you plan to finish every mission with every preset loadout, it will keep you entertained for some time.
-Mission descriptions and encyclopedia entries are hillarious.
-The music is great.
-The audibook (DLC) reminds me of those old Battletech inspired books. Unrelenting torrent of action, mayhem, and cheese. Its a delicious junkfood for your brain.
-It's visual style is great and it manages to strike perfect ballance between retro feel and responsive gameplay. Vehicles are sprites with very retro "choppy" animations, but the game itself runs at high framerate with all that responsiveness we want from our modern games.
-Devs are active on the forum and they are eager to help with technical problems and bugs. And they are still working on the game.
Cons:
-The game can be really punishing, before you get used to the aiming mechanics.
-My cats hate the soundtrack.

Another fun little game from the people who gave us Ether Vapor.
The game is surprisingly easy on Easy and Normal, and beatable without learning most of the mechanics. Hard mode is where the game actually shines though, and playing for high scores is a matter of skill and timing. There's a pretty deep, interesting system for combat that doesn't get really touched on unless you're going for scores. My main complaint is the game doesn't really do well with it's difficulty transition, going from "You can beat these without trying to much" for most of the game (although you'll probably score poorly if you dont know what you're doing) to a sudden gutpunch if you aren't prepared near the end.
Some controls could be better (dash-melee takes some getting used to without accidentally pulling out a combo you didnt intend to do), but are more than adequate for the most part. Some camera angles make using some shot types really annoying, but your sword will be doing alot of the legwork anyway. Another quibble is that until you get used to the game, there's alot of visual noise that, while pretty, makes it easy to lose track of what is going on.
While it's a nice the game has alot of side and backstory to it, some of the parts that allow dialogue to make sense require you to beat the game so you can read up on the side details. This part is unimportart for play really, nor is the plot particularly amazing or profound, and this complaint only matters for the first playthrough, but it's something that bothers me slightly.
Either way, it's a good, fun thing for anyone who enjoys shooters.

So there I was, creeping through a small abandoned town just outside an Industrial village. Frantically searching houses for a gun, or maybe an axe. I could hear them coming closer and I still had nothing but bandages and a box of pain killers. I didn't look long, but it didn't take long before I knew it was time to get out of this town. No sooner do I start moving, I hear them growling. They're running for me now.
I sprint into a small house and out the other side, jump a fence and stop in the shadow of a house. It was there that I found my first gun. A simple pistol with one mag. They're not chasing me anymore, I've lost them. It's time to leave the coast and head for the woods- At least this is what I had hoped I had done when a voice broke the silence. "Hey buddy, you can put that gun down. You're coming with me." Said the sniper, standing calmly in the wasteland.
My day had just begun. My first day in Day Z.

Stardew Valley isn't just about farming. It's about developing relationships, building a life for yourself in this small quiet town, and discovering the different environments and areas of the valley. The biggest part of this game though is how you're not the main character. You aren't there to save the day or be the only functioning member of the town, you're just another citizen. You'll find yourself doing simpler things such as fetching goods for others or simply tending to your farm animals. This isn't an exciting game, it's an immersive game.

As if the game was on shaky enough ground as is with the sub-par gameplay and further divergence from actual RPG elements that made the series famous, Bethesda had to bring forth Paid Mods 2 in the form of the 'Creation Club', swearing on their lives that it wasn't paid mods and are instead 'mini DLCs' despite the blatant evidence showing otherwise. As if the general idea isn't bad enough, CC is considered mandatory to even play the game, being made in a way that's somewhat hardcoded to dump all the files in its library into hard drives and other equivalents to get around a limitation on the console versions. The kicker in that part is that the files are borderline useless in-game unless the corresponding item is purchased in the CC, the credits only able to obtained with real cash, solidifying that they are indeed paid mods.
I used to play this game a lot in the past, though my play time pales in comparison to the more hardened veterans who have invested in far more time than I have. Despite such, I grew bored with it since the game did not have the same charm and atmosphere as previous Fallout installments did like New Vegas or Fallout 3. While the engine is better, the streamlining and trimming to the immersive mechanics made it almost impossible to actually feel...well...immersive. There are the pockets here and there where it's possible, but it's very, very brief and often broken when an enemy comes out of nowhere for the sake of keeping things 'interesting'.
It's difficult to feel as though the player could insert themselves into the game. Everything about your character is decided from the start; The male is known as Nate, a retired soldier, with the female being Nora, a graduate from a law school. No chance to develop a character from scratch other than the S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats, and the skills are similar to that of The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, where you gain experience to level up and pick whichever skill you'd like. This kind of leveling though suffers in that the level cap is limitless, leading to a character being a master of everything after enough time has been invested or if one cheats with the console commands(outside of Survivor difficulty that is since it's disabled for whatever reason), resulting in whatever builds out there eventually merging into this omnipotent survivor of the wastes capable of doing everything whenever it's needed.
Back to the CC, rumors have been going around that the folks that contribute to the library of it aren't even given a fair share of the cut, getting as little as twenty-five or so percent of the profits. I'm not entirely sure on the accuracy of these claims, but if they do hold true, just shows on how anti-consumer and anti-modding that Bethesda has become over the years. Folks have made mods for their games for years, often in the form of community patches to fix up the numerous glaring bugs and breaks in their games. To turn their back on modders would mean the death of their products and future releases, if their track record of broken and buggy games holds true.
As of the day of this review, on 9/16/2017, I do not recommend getting the game, even on sale. The day that the CC goes is when this will change, if only slightly.

*IMPORTANT!*  TodayEarly Access ends, this long review will be updated in time
This is going to be a big review, so sit and enjoy! Will avoid spoilers if possible.
Bought this game two weeks before "Upbeat Giraffe" update, played a bit on stable then started to play the unstable - crashes were bound to happen, but it's part of the fun.
My fiancée liked the game so much that I gave him a copy and he played twice my gametime O_O
In the game, you can be a human or one of the other six races (or any other, since you can mod - more about it later) just got out your planet to a random of the incredbly large number of planets.
Much of the universe background you'll by talking to NPCs, reading books; at the moment it's easier to get to a Wikia or the SB forums.
The story starts (at the moment the game does not give much, Chucklefish will change on coming updates) depends on which race, that are; Humans who got Earth shattered in pieces by a Chtulhu-esque gigantic tentacle monster, Novakid (Western gunslinger nomads with train-shaped ships), Apexis (ape people from the dystopian totalitaristic 1984's), Floran (plant-based humanoids who see everyone else as food), Avians (Aztec-llike bird-people - with some religious stuff added), Glitch (mechanical people stuck on medieval culture) and Hylotl (three-eyed fish people with ancient Japan culture)
Note: CF will change the beginning when version 1.0 is out, no more different beginnings for each race (a pity, imo)
Anyway, the game start with you in a planet's orbit with a broken ship and an A.I. that helps you to get it working. When you fix and upgrade the ship and your gear, the whole universe is open to you: Quests to achieve, items to find, crafts to do. You can create cities, fill it with NPCs and they will give quests.. the sky is no more the limit.
Mysteries are abound - there is a place where you find some holograms and murals that makes you think about, and some random portals you find underground where you can get some good items.
Chucklefish did a great work on random universes - you can spend (literal) centuries exploring and doing whatever you want.
About the mods:
If you don't like the original races, the biomes, weapons or whatever? Not a problem, you can mod the game or just get one (of the hundreds) on Starbound library (I recommend the Fracking Universe mod, one of the best IMO, and his creator keeps it up to date).
Early Access phase is ending soon (no idea when). Update releases tend to delay a lot for the stable version, Nightly (unstable) is updated very frequently and of course, is prone to glitches (I mean bugs, not the sentient android race).
What may I say? Its a very enjoyable game, with very cool visuals (akin of Terraria), with a HUGE and friendly community.
If you like games like Terraria or Craft the World, most probably you'll like this one - Enjoy!

The Hitman series of games was one I had always meant to get around to.  I owned three of the games for quite a while, but after picking up the last two (Contracts and Absolution) I finally decided to start playing through them.  Going into the first one, I fully expected it to be underwhelming.  It is old after all (released in 2000).  But even that didn't adequately prepare me for some of the infuriating old school design choices this game uses.
First off, the game has occasional moments of brilliance.  The Hong Kong missions and the Budapest mission are shining examples of the potential of the Hitman premise.  But all the missions surrounding it are slogs to get through.  And it all comes down to one simple problem.
Often, Hitman: Codename 47 doesn't seem to understand what the word "stealth" even means.
Take, for example, the third jungle mission.  You're tasked with taking out a drug lord.  But he's holed up inside a mansion inside of a fenced compound crawling with guards.  There is literally no way to take him out silently.  The room he's in has only one entrance, and the moment you open the door he grabs a big machine gun and starts shooting up the place.  And if you leave any nearby guards alive, they will start shooting you immediately.  Sure, you have a couple respawns, but they don't do anything because the moment you get close to the guards that killed you they recognize you and sound the alarm once again.
And it was in this mission that I finally realized how inconsistent the AI is.  Sometimes, they're incredibly stupid.  You can kill a guy on the other side of an open doorway from another guy, and that guy won't even notice.  However, sometimes you silently choke a guy who's in a completely different room (behind a closed door no less) from another guy, and the moment you walk through the door that guy somehow knows what you did and immediately starts shooting.  And there's no checkpoints so if everything hits the fan guess what?  You're starting that twenty minute long mission
.
This wouldn't be nearly as much of a problem if it wasn't for the randomness of it all.  The guard who psychically knows that I killed his friend?  A large portion of the time, it doesn't happen.  And there's no logic to it.  Sometimes he knows.  Sometimes he doesn't.  And this is endemic throughout the entire game.
Then there's the mission design, and that's where the game will occasionally get incredibly lazy.  For example, one mission involves getting through a bunch of gates to get to a boat where your target is hiding out.  Unfortunately, no matter what disguise you are wearing (even if it's the same exact one as the guards protecting the gates), they won't let you through.  They yell at you when you get close, and if you try to pass, they start shooting.  It makes even less sense when you consider that EVERY OTHER GUARD CAN WALK THROUGH JUST FINE.
I feel like a lot of the people still praising this game are feeling nostalgia because they played the game when it was new.  Considering that I haven't, maybe I'm just being overly critical because I'm more used to modern game design.  Whatever the case may be, I do
recommend this game, especially considering that I've heard Contracts remakes the best missions from this one (namely Hong Kong and Budapest).  I honestly would have skipped it if it wasn't for my masochistic completionist ways.
I do plan on reviewing the rest of the franchise as well.  I'm interested to see how it evolves over time.

I want to reccomend Starbound so badly. The premise of this game is amazing. It looks and sounds great, but terrible mismanagement from Chucklefish (the developers turned indie publisher) has completely soured my ability to reccomend this game.
Starbound was originally an offshoot project from a former Terraria developer, and the timing was great, since Redigit (Terraria dev) went off the deep-end, refused to support Terraria anymore, and jumped ship. Starbound promised the same, yet improved gameplay, and features galore. Three years since starting "Early Access", and Starbound is in a worse state today than it was in 2013. Ever since Redigit decided to pull his head out of his♥♥♥♥♥and support his cash-cow, Starbound has been the inferior game. Terraria has great Steam integration with drop-in multiplayer, while Starbound still has... terrible online functionality that requires finding stable servers and awful compatibility issues.
Starbound has no direction. The developers have no idea what they want their final product to look like, which was expected early on, but is absolutely unacceptable THREE YEARS later, with over $4 million in sales. From a business standpoint, it is obvious that Chuklefish invested this money into other indie projects and promotion, rather than actually developing Starbound. Infrequent game updates have dumbed down mechanics, and ruined the feels of combat and exploration entirely.
I saw so much potential in Starbound that I invested in the Solarium tier of preordering. This cost $1000, and promised some nifty stuff in the finished game. Three years going, and I have never been contacted by Chucklefish - I will probably never see my name in the credits, or the unique in-game hat and weapon that I designed for implementation.

For the first 10 or so hours, I quite liked Heat Signature. The gameplay is fun and unique, without being too gimicky. It scratches same itch that Hotline Miami does, with fast paced, top-down combat, and encouraging multiple ways to get through a level. The game world feel conquerable and populated but without losing the vast emptyness of space. Outside of this initial experience with the game, I won't list every pro and con; there are many other reviews and blogs that have that covered. I have played many more hours of Heat Signature than my 10ish hours on Steam would indicate (I bought the DRM-free version from Humble Store).
With the most recent update, several features have been added, seemingly to make the game easier. One of my major gripes with this game is how easy it becomes after liberating a few stations. Unlock just a few decent weapons and tools and you'll be good to go on any new character. Several of these changes simply modify in game textures to make certain types of npcs and bits of terrain easier to distinguish, and that's fine. In fact, all of these changes were fine, even the 'cheat' to turn off permadeath. All these features appeal to at least some of the player base.
What I would have liked to have seen in addition to these changes, would be some options for increasing the difficulty and challenge level. In my main save file, even losing my most geared up character isn't a huge deal, because after a few missions I can afford the same 'rare' gear that I've unlocked from liberating stations. Retiring a character, and being able to leave a custom named heirloom behind for other characters, while a very cool idea, doesn't really work in the context of the game. The drop rates are too low to be likely to find one before you unlock the exact same weapon in the shop.
One thing that I find very concerning, is a line from the changlog of the most recent update (at the time of posting).
"This update is a one-off, we don’t plan to do updates like this on a regular basis. We might add items from time to time, but only buy the game if you want the game as it stands – we don’t make promises about future content."
This game as it is currently, is lacking content. Adding a new gun every once and a while will not provide enough new and exciting action to support, what is already a game that is too repetitive. I would like to see at least one major content update (even as a dlc expansion), or support for modifications.
I very rarely find a game that makes me excited to wake up the next day in order to resume playing it. I can honestly say that Heat Signature was one of those games. Considering the most recent update addressed many 'fair points' brought up by the community, I have faith that the developers are listening and willing to make changes where it's deemed necessary. As the game is now, I cannot recommend it, at least not at the current price, with the knowledge that major content updates are not guarenteed, or even in the works. I have a huge amount of respect for the developers, especially for developing the game for three years before release, when so many others pump out half finished games in early access, and settle for the cash grab. I look forward to rewriting this review in the future, and giving the game my recommendation.

Bastion is what I consider the ultimate example of pacing in a videogame. The game hits you hard with major challenges early on, and steadily ramps up the difficulty while also providing a lot of new weapons and concepts to the player steadily. What's more, the game never keeps you pinned down in one spot for too long. There's always some new interesting weapon combo to try out, and new challenges to try them out on. The narrator and story presentation tie into this perfectly, keeping the storyline moving at a good stint along with the rest of the game. Bastion isn't a very long game, but it's a very dense experience - there's a lot to take in during that short time period, on all levels.

It's better than 1, it has Armor, it has new units, the graphics are extremely good and everything is nice and dandy, except for that one thing that keeps this game from being actually great:
The Spawn and Engagemechanics for the aliens is broken. The way it works is you "activate" a squad of aliens as soon as you see them. Depending on how far you are in your turn this deems your squadron either to doom or to an unfair advantage for you. It's hard to explain, contrary to the old originals the enemies don't really roam on the map independently. They have their attention radius and they attack all XCOM operatives in that radius but they don't care if their mates are fighting or dieing, as long as they don't see an XCOM operative they don't care.
This leads to several weird, stupid situations:
- If you go in closecombat with an alien to finish it off it can be that because you moved close to it you just triggered an alien group behind that alien that now will position itself. Because you probably just finished your activation this group gets a full turn of actions.
- Oftentimes you have concealment at the start of a mission, let's say you see 2 alien squads relatively close to each other just move in a way where you don't see the other anymore barely and then attack. That squad won't lift a finger even if they are an arms length from their dieing comrades. It makes absolutely no sense.
Lets say it's the other way around,  you didn't finish the alien in Melee but with ranged weapons, now this alien patrol accidentally walks into YOUR attention radius. They position themselves but in their turn and you get a full turn to react to them giving you a relatively unfair advantage.
Just like in XCOM1 it discourages you from splitting up your squadron and truly flanking your enemy because normally you just active another Alien Squad which completely negates the aspect of flanking.
I'm pretty sure they tried to fix this weird gamedesign with the introduction of constant timepressure in missions to avoid the constant baiting one tile at a time gameplay. Doesnt really work, tactical games like this shouldnt have 90% of these types of missions just to cover up this glaring issue of gameplay. It feels like you're gaming the system, encouraging you to either safescum or losing all your soldiers to stupid mechanics that you cannot influence no matter how skilled you are. You have to cheese the system and then you are fine, it doesnt feel like you master tactical combat, it feels like you abuse the spawning mechanics and that's it.
Before you jump on my neck, i finished the first one in classic ironman and i'm doing relatively well in this one but i just can't get past this very important gameplay aspect. It feels out of place, it swings the favour way to much either in your or against your enemies way and it strips the game unfortunately alot from many tactical decisions.
This is, like Xcom 1, a "good" game but ultimately missed the mark in how combat works. It's definitely not holding a candle to the old titles that got this just right, but suffer from old gameplay. It's a shame as they fixed and introduced armor to the game that works really well for instance.
Hence i cannot recommend XCOM2, i'm not sure i keep playing but i feel underwhelmed by what it is even though the production value is very high across the board.

The ring of hard-edged steel and pleading whispers resonate through the darkened halls, almost sinister with promise. Always leading us and solemn, Balian feared not the horrors that slither over the strangely smooth stone. His life was one of luxury, torn asunder by the creeping disease wracking his existence. Veriel's razor sharp daggers and even sharper eyes made sure no treasure or crumbled earth left unturned. Her dark humour almost fitting to the labyrinth we wandered through...she was my favorite. Priest Illith never far behind me, quick to care and even quicker to light a new torch. The gods had fled these lands, but they still hung over her providing cheap respite for us heathens.
The days had passed and halls blurred together, when we gazed into the darkness...it too gazed back. Screeching flesh, gnashing teeth, and scuttling terrors overwhelmed our camp. Balian stood fast and cleaved through the beasts, sending them back to the abyss that bore them forth. His bronzed plate deflected blow after clawed blow as they tore him apart. A pooled mess of tattered cloth and broken steel was all that remained of him. Illith tried desperately to sustain us as we fled through the eldritch arcades beneath the manor. She fell too...as did our torchlight. As the blazing light of day pierced through small holes before us, we tore at crumbled stone and encased bone. As I heaved the last boulder away, a tentacle wrapped itself around Veriel's leg and wrenched her from my grasp into the growing blackness. Her screams filled existence as she disappeared from view, I ran bleeding and weeping into the safety of daylight. The tavern and endless mugs of ale are lonely once more, but I do not feel alone...her screams are always with me.

Astebreed is a bullet hell shoot ‘em up (SHMUP) from Japanese indie developer Edelweiss.
First note to cover: this game looks absolutely stunning. As a proper SHMUP, Astebreed does not fail in delivering intense, non-stop combat, and players will stop blinking and breathing as the screen fills with beautifully rendered bullets, missiles, lasers and explosions. All the eye candy the game provides certainly helps in giving itself a high replay value.
Astebreed’s combat mechanism is very intelligent and complex. Players have three types of basic attacks at their disposal: spread shot (ranged), focus shot (ranged), and sword (melee). Two aforementioned ranged attacks also have additional homing mode (activated by holding the attack button for some time and releasing) that locks onto enemy units and increases the damage dealt. When the gold meter under the player’s mech is filled, additional attack option called EX attack becomes available that can dish out huge damage to enemy units. Like the ranged attacks, EX attack can also lock onto enemy units, dealing more focused, devastating blows.
While blindly mashing attack buttons may work, using the right attack at the right moments will allow you to take out the enemies quickly and keep your health bar up higher. Mastering the large arsenal game provides is challenging at first, but you will be feeling like a true badass when you are clearing the screen from hordes of enemies in a blink of an eye with cleverly picked and placed attacks.
For a SHMUP, Astebreed is pretty lenient on the players, providing frequent checkpoints and unlimited continues. This saves some tears of blood and frustration dance whenever your mech succumbs to the non-stop rain of enemy bullets. Game has three difficulty modes (easy, normal, hard) and I found these modes to be pretty accurately assessed (I’ve played SHMUPs where playing in easy mode made me drop the controller and sit in the corner of my room for hours).
The game does have a storyline. Humanity is at a losing war against the technologically advanced alien race known as Filune. Players take on the role of Roy Beckett, young pilot who operates a mech called XBreed equipped ex-human AI named Fio. The story develops in a predictable, anime cliché way (which is not necessarily bad), and in the end, Roy Beckett saves the humanity from Filune while scoring some loli AI love.
If there was one small complaint that I could raise, it’s that much of the story driving dialogues happen in midst of intense battles. While voice acting in the game is excellent, it’s in Japanese and I certainly don’t have time to look at the bottom corner of my screen to read the English subtitle when enemies are constantly trying to feed my face with death beams. I ended up missing most of the plot during my first playthrough and was only able to put the story together during my second playthrough.
Overall, Astebreed is one of the best SHMUP I’ve come across. The game is visually pleasing, intense, and adequately challenging.  Add this game on your list of “must play.”
Pros:
+Stunning visuals
+Voice acting
+Complex and rewarding combat
+Adequately challenging
Cons:
-Hard to keep up with the plot during intense gameplay
Score:
9 out of 10

Fractured Space has come a long way since I first started playing this game. At the time of this review I have 155 hours played since it’s free to play release. Here are my thoughts on the game:
While loosely formatted around a MOBA, it doesn’t necessarily feel like I’m playing a MOBA. Rather, FS plays more like conquest in Battlefront 2: you fight the enemy for control over certain areas, which leads to gaining control of the battlefield and eventual victory (I have yet to play Battlefront 3 so I can’t make a comparison there). While the mission doesn’t change, the way you play can widely vary based on your ship selection, and team compositions. Each ship feels balanced, however some ships or classes of ships (read stealth and snipers) have steep learning curves on how to actually contribute to the game. Unlike some other games, when Edge Case reveals new content, especially new ships, I get excited to play again. Unfortunately, with a lot of new changes comes bugs, many of which have been persistent. There are also some features which I feel should be included but aren’t. In game voice chat would be huge, as well as a server browser to allow players to fill in for an AI pilot. That being said, I feel like Edge Case has been putting forward a lot of honest effort to get the game to where they and the players want it to be.
Pros:
•	Fun – blowing away capitol ships is awesome
•	Gameplay rewards skill and teamwork
•	Balanced ships and content (mostly) means this avoids being a pay to win
•	All ships available on standard currency, and currency grind is fairly easy
•	Relatively consistent updates with exciting content
•	Great communities available on Reddit and Discord
Cons:
•	Bugs
•	Lack of certain features such as voice chat or server browsing
•	Premium currency (Though with this being a FTP, I have no problem supporting the devs)
•	Salt
Closing Thoughts:
My review here is lacking some information as I have never actually played the second game mode, Frontier. While this is an incredibly ambitious game, it falls short in so many ways as to be an ill-advised purchase for, well, anyone.
After playing through a good chunk of Spike Lee's Super-Special Spike Lee Career Mode by Spike Lee, I have to ask myself, "Is this really the same guy who directed 'Malcolm X?'" The writing is about as sharp as a pair of safety scissors and cuts with all the intensity of a butter knife. There is zero investment in anybody in this "story," and I really wonder how much he was involved in it other than getting paid to put his name on marketing materials. Characters are introduced at random points in my career without any explicit reason for being there or knowledge of how they came to know my character, or, for that matter, why my character's last name is "Vibrations." Despite this, Visual Concepts managed to dramatically improve the pacing of career mode since it was introduced in 2k10... but still maintained the miserable slog of spending hours stuck in neutral.
My draft stock plummeted inexplicably as I tumbled from a top 10 pick to a late first round pick with no explanation as to exactly how my above-average performances were impacting that status or what was expected of me. I wasn't given the choice to play a second year in college to see how I could improve, either. The atrocious teammate grade system is back yet again, because no one at Visual Concepts has watched an NBA game in at least 10 years. It's ironic, too, because teammate AI is horrible: I frequently catch a ball-handler standing around doing nothing until the shot clock is under 10, at which point he jacks up some stupid outside shot that would get me benched. The teammate grade's penalties for bad play - because bad play isn't its own penalty - mean it's possible to play an entire season and not actually progress as a player at all. It takes forever to see any real improvement as you must start out from virtual rock bottom - a 55 overall compared to players in the 70s and 80s is asking for an♥♥♥♥♥♥kicking - and now spend in-game currency to upgrade your player's attributes. This is, of course, part of a ploy to get players to spend real money on microtransactions to accelerate performance. The whole operation is a millstone around the game's neck.
But the fun doesn't stop there. God help you if you wanted to add multiple custom teams to the game for the GM or Season modes. Now you get one, and you have to add players to it by purchasing trading cards with, you guessed it, in-game currency. This is VC's take on FIFA's Ultimate Team system, which I also don't like in the least and never use, so one of my favorite parts of the game is now essentially gone and replaced with something I detest. But, hey, you can design your own shoes that look llike crap and won't be replicated faithfully in-game!
The GM mode is passable, but most of the things it tries to do have been done before in different, usually better ways in other games. Attempts at depth in a variety of things - including relocating a team, which a GM would never, EVER have control over like he does in this game - just come off as tedious diversions that ultimately detract from the experience. Your GM and the people he interacts with are given character models that don't do or say anything interesting when you're interacting with them. (Your GM also has a really awful slouch when he stands up, but that's another discussion.)
I've been putting it off, but there are things this game does well. The presentation is second to none. The curated soundtrack is full of excellent, atmosphere-building selections. The TNT studio crew (Ernie Johnson, Shaquille O'Neal, and Kenny Smith - no Charles Barkley, sadly) is usually interesting and funny, especially Shaq. The play-by-play commentary by Kevin Harlan, Clark Kellogg, and Greg Anthony is the most seamless and immersive I've ever heard in a video game. Doris Burke is here as a sideline reporter as well, although she doesn't add a whole lot. There are even cut-aways to pre-taped interviews, something that actually happens on NBA broadcasts and gives an extra wrinkle to the TV-style presentation.
Unfortunately, that's all lipstick on the proverbial pig, which is ironic, since none of the character models got working lips during their stay in the Uncanny Valley. The controls are sloppy, and I noticed a lot of lag with my gamepad, frequently leading to players getting their doors blown off on defense. Players move less like people and more like out-of-control 18 wheelers; the "Pro Stick" is little more than an easy way to turn the ball over; the passing mechanics are horrible, and play-calling is tedious and unrewarding. Why should I go through all the effort to draw up and run an offensive set when I can just run around and wait for the AI to trip over its own feet?
Then there are all the little things that just get annoying. Refereees dawdle with the basketball in their hands. Players have to physically go get the ball after a made basket, which ends up taking close to 10 seconds. The fancy TV camera angles and instant replays can't be bailed out of to get back to my guys for the inbound pass. It's almost as if the game wants as little player input as it can get and will give the player every reason not to play at all.
So I won't, and neither should you.

Hitman: Codename
47 is the first entry of the series and lays down the core mechanics for future Hitman games.
It's not surprising that Codename 47 is the least played game of the entire series.
Although it's not uncommon for people to completely skip the earlier games of a series in favor of a more updated and relevant experience, C47 is without a doubt a classic.
However, like many underappreciated classics, you have to ignore some of the game's flaws in order to reach the best parts of the game.
The controls are a bit strange at first, but after rebinding keys to something more intuitive, the only thing you have to get used to is pressing a separate button to run forward. The main flaws of C47 are the completely oblivious AI, the lack of an extensive rating system, and the sometimes linear level design.
The enemy AI functions more like walking sentry guns than actual guards. No matter how many times you run up behind someone the AI never turns around and the moment you acquire a disguise you're free to run around restricted areas without any suspicion.
Even if the stealth isn't rewarding, the fact that 47 isn't a bullet sponge will encourage a more strategical approach. The game shines because each level plays out like a puzzle. The reward of figuring out how to assassinate your target without any prior knowledge is unlike any other game.
Some of C47's best levels include Traditions of the Trade and The Lee Hong Assassination because of the expansive, non-linear level design and multiple approaches to completing the objectives. The sheer replayability of these levels are what defines Hitman as a series.
While Codename 47 is noticeably flawed, it provided the framework for future games of the series to refine. The AI is forgiving, but at the same time the levels will require multiple playthroughs in order to find the solution. The age of the game may put some people off, but if you're really interested in the Hitman series, Codename 47 isn't a bad game to start with. At least, it's definitely better than Absolution.

Checkpoint’s evacuated as I roll into Old Cascais in my Rounder tank. Between me and a ticket off this rock is an up market walled off residential are where Great Leader housed a lot of the top brass’ families. Now it’s inhabited by a detachment of angry Corvid fighters sporting homemade mechs and tanks and a myriad of things in-between. Beyond that, a commercial district which also services the spaceport behind. Therein lies the goal.
I cycle the Rounder’s cloaking field and shimmy forward a few hundred yards. Before the field disengages I’ve got the Zeus Railgun and the Crambo machine gun aimed at a squad of Corvids oblivious to my position.  The rail slug pierces through machinery and flesh alike, half the hostiles gone in a blink. I send the Rounder back and reengage the cloak as the remainder of the squad races towards my last known position. Instead of launching another precious slug I aim the Crambo at the fuel station that runs adjacent to the street. Second half of the Corvid squad evaporates in the explosion, except for some little mech that manages to get a signal out before I shred it.
Sirens.
Engines.
Big mechanical footsteps.
Sounds that are fine in moderation but as the saying goes, you can have too much of a good thing. I shunt everything into the engine and pull a hard right, plough straight through a concrete wall and burn towards the spaceport. Every street I pass by is chock full of armour, far more than the contract suggested. The outside of the tank flares blue as tracer fire is deflected away from the hull of the tank. Rockets streak overhead cratering the path I’d taken. Buildings collapse and explode and then sixty seconds later I find myself in sight of the tug that’s going to take me to orbit, along with mech nearly as tall as an orbital cannon. A mech that has two Zeus railguns like mine.  Aimed at me. They flash.
Instinct kicks in. The barrier between my flesh and my Rounder tank disappears. The first slug blows the shields out while the second blows at hole somewhere in the hull that lets light from outside leak into the cockpit. Sparks shower my bare shoulders, the smell of burning metal fills my nose. Somehow the cloak still works and I disappear. The mech’s torso swivels, trying to recapture a lock. Instead of turning tail I tear straight for it. My face slams into the control panel as the tanks hull impacts the mech’s leg, it stumbles. I fire my final rail slug point blank into its ankle.
And that’s what a couple minutes in Brigador is like.
10/10

Starbound was originally an offshoot project from a former Terraria developer, and the timing was great, since Redigit (Terraria dev) went off the deep-end, refused to support Terraria anymore, and jumped ship. Starbound promised the same, yet improved gameplay, and features galore. Three years since starting "Early Access", and Starbound is in a worse state today than it was in 2013. Ever since Redigit decided to pull his head out of his♥♥♥♥♥and support his cash-cow, Starbound has been the inferior game. Terraria has great Steam integration with drop-in multiplayer, while Starbound still has... terrible online functionality that requires finding stable servers and awful compatibility issues.
Starbound has no direction. The developers have no idea what they want their final product to look like, which was expected early on, but is absolutely unacceptable THREE YEARS later, with over $4 million in sales. From a business standpoint, it is obvious that Chuklefish invested this money into other indie projects and promotion, rather than actually developing Starbound. Infrequent game updates have dumbed down mechanics, and ruined the feels of combat and exploration entirely.
I saw so much potential in Starbound that I invested in the Solarium tier of preordering. This cost $1000, and promised some nifty stuff in the finished game. Three years going, and I have never been contacted by Chucklefish - I will probably never see my name in the credits, or the unique in-game hat and weapon that I designed for implementation.
I am not bitter at this game because I paid so much for it. I am beyond that. Starbound may be worth the $15 price tag. Good luck seeing it for any less, since the devs refuse to put it on sale, but definitely grab it if it's sub-$10. The sole reason I cannot reccomend Starbound is because over time, it has actually become a worse game, and Terraria is the clear superior title - as it is a completed game, feature complete, and has substantial updates.

is an action/stealth game, originally released in 2000, and the first entry in the popular and well-known
series.  You take on the role of a genetically-enhanced human clone assassin named "47", using stealth and tactical problem-solving in order to complete contract hits for your employer, the Agency.
This game uses a third-person perspective, but plays more like a first-person shooter in relation to controls and movement.  And the general idea is to use stealth and silent kills to eliminate your target without raising any alarms.   While it's possible to complete missions by other means and with more collateral damage, it will cost you financially (ie. clean-up crews, ammo and weapon cost, etc).
A very fun and intriguing concept, to be sure, and clearly a success considering
games are still being made to this day.  But does the original
stand the test of time?
++ Tactical Problem-Solving
+ Perspective/Camera
- Trial and Error
-- Controls
-- Ridiculous AI
-- No Save Feature in Missions
= Cool concept and interesting gameplay, but the game has way too many issues that make it almost unplayable at times.  If you are hardcore, like me, about playing games in order then get it cheap on sale, but otherwise I can't possibly recommend it.
-- Personally, I find the entire game concept, specifically the use of problem-solving skills in order to complete assassination missions, extremely cool.  There are some downsides in the execution, which I will get to in a minute, but overall I really enjoyed this aspect of the game.  It was surprising to see so much complexity and variety in each mission, and when I was finally able to execute my plans flawlessly it was extremely satisfying and rewarding.
Even the perspective style was creative and interesting: third-person view, but with controls and movement that felt like a first-person shooter/stealth game.  Mostly I could only see the back of my character's head, neck and shoulders.  I almost wish the game never showed his face except when looking in bathroom mirrors, giving him an even more mysterious quality, but their method works well too.  Not sure how exactly, but this perspective really made me feel like a stone-cold assassin.  Maybe it was such stiff, emotionless movement and the default walk speed (I only ran when I had to), but whatever it was, it certainly immersed me in the role.
-- Unfortunately, there's quite a few bad traits in the game that I just couldn't get over.  First of which, the controls.  They felt awkward, clunky and slow, even after I customized the key bindings to my personal preference.  Combined with the fact that I constantly had issues with getting certain things to work correctly, like strangling someone with fibre wire, I almost quit the game before the end of the second mission.  It was that bad.  Thankfully, I got used to it somewhat, but not entirely.
The next thing I noticed was the ridiculous AI.  NPCs were incredibly stupid, but at the same time uncannily omniscient.  A guard blocking entrance to an area would stop you and say you can't enter (as he should), but stand there and watch as you walk behind him and then wait patiently for you to slice his throat.  THEN other NPCs would walk up and see you next to the body and not suspect you in the slightest.  On the other hand, you can walk into a room unnoticed and have all NPCs with their backs to you, but you even THINK about drawing your gun and the entire building knows it and immediately comes down on you.  Extremely frustrating and immersion-breaking.
Finally, game turns into a big "trial and error"-fest.  With what information you're given walking into the mission, there's almost no way you could complete the contract in one attempt, unless with the aid of some sort of guide and you have incredible luck.  In a way, 47 becomes uncannily omniscient himself, because by the end, as the player, you know exactly how events will unfold and where the enemies are, etc, and are already ten steps ahead. (Suddenly, the new Agent 47 movie makes a lot more sense lol.)  Add the issues with controls and NPC AI -- not to mention the game crashing on me a lot whenever I try to open the map -- and the fact there is no save feature within the missions, the game becomes a frustrating and repetitive nightmare.
--  Before this, I had never played any of the
games and had only seen the movies,  but the newest installment in the series looks amazing, so I decided it was time I finally played the previous ones.
is very interesting, I'll give it that, but there's so much wrong with the game that it's almost unplayable, making it a painful experience that I would save other players from if I can.... which is why I can't possibly recommend this game.  If, like me, you have a thing about skipping games in a series, then at least catch it on sale (got mine for $1.75 or so).

When Hitman Codename 47 first came out in 2000, I was fascinated by the concept of playing a hitman for hire. It was like a modern version of Thief which is another favorite of mine. Now that I am finally able to play it, the experience is quite different from what I imagined.
In Hitman Codename 47, stealth tactics are required to get to your target and take him out and you will have to complete other objectives too. However, it is very difficult to complete the entire mission without being detected and you will often have to shoot your way out without dying. Many of the tougher missions are trial and error virtual suicide missions where there are only a few ways to finish and if you do not figure out exactly what to do, you are dead. Game breaking bugs only further increase the difficulty.
Yet considering these flaws, I was still motivated to finish Hitman and it is so rewarding when you figure out what to do. The challenge, atmosphere and incredible music by Jesper Kyd is what allows me to recommend this; most likely the hardest game in the Hitman series.

To top it off, the game has a superb soundtrack, blending japanese instrumentals with sweeping orchestral movements, each track filled to the brim with emotion and heart. Bastion is simply a beautiful game all over. The stunning gfx and prima soundtrack, already gives you good bang for your buck, but wait, there's more! Most importantly, the gameplay is great, and the difficulty settings are balanced - you can essentially make it as challenging as you want, by adding handicaps. The weapon selection, enemies and environment make sure the game stays varied, and it's easy to tailor your character to your liking with the many various stat bonuses and weapon alterations.
The unique setting, with the world being rebuilt as you walk around, is cool on it's own, but it also has a narrator. This may sound cheesy, but it actually adds a lot to the lore and storyline, without being annoying at any point.
This game gets my "balls to the walls"-rating (that's the best one!), and should be in any game collection. At the very least try the demo - you won't regret it. The game will give you many hours of joy, be you casual or committed gamer.

Okami is a cult classic that's beloved by many. It plays very similarly to games like Ocarina of Time and Kingdom hearts, with an added paintbrush mechanic that lets you shape the world like a god would. The game invokes a classical Japanese style in both visuals and music, and makes for a very artistic experience. However, unlike most modern art games, this comes with plenty of gameplay challenges.
This is a game that's been on my list of to-plays for a while. Wasn't willing to buy a new console for it and finding a copy for PS2 is near impossible. Really glad it's come to PC.
The port is very good, no graphical glitches or other bugs as far as I've seen. Runs just fine on a GTX 960.
The game works seamlessly with an xbox one controller plugged in, but I honestly would recommend using the keyboard/mouse controls instead. While the movement might feel a bit clunky with WASD (as opposed to a stick), the paintbrush mechanic feels so much smoother, which IMO improves the experience drastically.
The only downside I could find is the dialogue speed. The writing is good, but the lines are delivered very slowly, which can make cutscenes frustrating. For some dialogue, you can hold down the left mouse button to speed the text up, but this doesn't work for key cutscenes. An option to increase dialogue speed would be greatly appreciated.

I know there's a lot of LEL MINEKRAFT CODDD AWFUL statements about this game, but I genuinely enjoy it.  I've been having more fun with it than I probably should.  It's sort of a mindless fun kind of game, and I take the bad (certain p2w, some lag issues) in stride with the good.
First thing's first, the p2w can be kind of silly concerning the top tier weapons (the sniper that literally costs 8 dollars or something) but aside from that, the only money I've spent on "performance" was a (permanent) helmet and body armor.  I do think that's questionable in itself... but it was 2 whole dollars on something I'm enjoying, and I do very well in matches.  Aside from that, unfortunately the weapons aren't very varied, but they're mostly satisfying to use, and viable enough all around, but there are obvious better ones.  There is extremely little to no recoil or spread among weapons, but that doesn't bother me and I kinda like it that way - especially since it's a block game.
The block mechanics feel nice compared to other Callofdutycrafts.  You can't spam them in excess in one life, they feel just tough enough to act as cover but they don't feel like an impenetrable titanium wall, and you can effectively "battle build" if you're wary of your surroundings.  There are explosives, but those don't just completely wreck everything you've ever done in an instant, and like the blocks they're limited per-life.
A note about the spawncamping complaints, you're immune to damage for like the first 5 seconds of every life.
Might update later, as the game is in early access yet, and I might have something else to point out.  Bottom line - the game is far from perfect, but it's enjoyable for what there is.

Xcom EU was my favourite game for a very long time, so I had high hopes for Xcom 2.
It was a very close thing as well. But as I played this game I relised that most of the good parts of the game were the same as EU.
So first of all the Pros:
- They've made the world view much more interesting. You don't simply click a button and watch the world spin; now you click a button and watch a dial spin.
- There are more character customisation options.
- There's a new class; the specialist!
- It has some things in common with Xcom EU.
- You can finally choose classes...if you build the facility.
And now the Cons:
- You remember in EU how if you healed a soilder and they had enough armor then they wouldn't be injured at the end of the mission? Well that's no longer the case!! Medic sub-class loses about half of its value.
- Remember snipers? Of course you do, they were gods in EU. If you didn't bring a Sniper then there's something wrong with you. Well because of the time limit they aren't that useful any more. In fact you can just forget bringing them on half of the missions that you go on. The grenadier and specialist are the only good classes in Xcom 2, since Rangers require you running up to enemies and revealing more groups.
- There's a lot of bugs in this game. Like a huge amount of UI bugs; buttons change randomly, icons show up incorrectly, pressing the "Make All Items Available" button kicks you back to the world map, and of course there's the cliping through objects that we had in Xcom EU. These bugs happen every minute or so. They're minor bugs, but very annoying.
- The performance of this game is horrible. Why the hell does it tank the framerate when the squad jumps out of Skyranger?
- The AI in this game is really REALLY stupid. In one turn I made ALL the wrong moves. I was flanked multiple times! If an enemy is flanking me then it shouldn't think "Oh let's go and try to shoot that sniper behind full cover!". Every single person should have died in that mission; but none of the enemy took flanking shots, even though they were a few spaces away from the person they were flanking!!!! Turning up the difficulty just gave them more health, it didn't make them smarter.
- There's no Mecs that you can use. Only the enemy has Mecs. This means the developers didn't bother to keep something from Xcom EW, for some reason. Don't use the excuse of "it's a resistance, Xcom doesn't have the resources to build Mecs", because they clearly do.
- There's no Second Wave options. Again this is something which they just haven't bothered with.
- There's nothing more irratating that shooting the floor of the roof and then falling through it and taking fall damage, because for some reason your soliders want to shot the enemy through the thing that they are standing on.
- What grenades damage isn't very well shown; sometimes they will take away full cover that didn't show as red, other times they won't.
- Multiple items aren't described very well. What are the stats of an enemy hit by a flash bang? How much area does it cover?
Some of the negatives existed in Xcom EU as well. But they haven't solved any of them, and they haven't kept the content of the previous games.

I've played a lot of bullet hells. I went into the game expecting this to be a bullet hell but instead found a traditional shoot-em-up with health points.
You'd think with the large amount of bullets, the law of bullet hells apply (you can evade bullets), but the truth is, you have an attack that destroy bullets. However, it has tons of recovery and you lose mobility to evade other bullets. Good thing this isn't a bullet hell game.
The controls for teleporting is a little bit sluggish. Sometimes, I activate it accidentally but I've never done it on purpose. I can see many attack patterns where it would have been very useful. I wish they put the teleport into its own button.
Gameplay wise, its solid. The graphics is beautiful. The controls are not perfect. The story is average at best.
As for difficulty, I've finished the game in 2 hours. Its not that hard EXCEPT for the last boss. The last boss is divided into three parts and its difficulty reaches SNK-hard difficulty even in Normal. I'm sure there's a pattern that can be exploited but because of the sheer amount of particle effects, lack of feedback if you got hit or graze an attack, and large amount of recovery from blade attacks, its hard to get into position where you won't get hit.
At the easiest difficulty (with cutscene skipping), I finished the game in roughly 33mins.
Summary: Don't expect this game to be bullet hell. Its a shoot-em-up that pretends to be one. Its a short game, but the production value is well worth the money.

Hacknet is a fun and intriguing hacking puzzle game. Unlike many other games that are controlled by command line, such as TIS-100, Hacknet does not feature any actual programming. This is simultaneously kind of accurate to what a lot of "hacking" is, and also makes the game more accessible.
Individual puzzles will have you hacking into one or more computers to achieve some goal, often as contracts. A simple request might be to delete a file from a computer. But there might be a variety of obstacles in your way: You might not be given the location of the computer, and have to find its IP address elsewhere. The computer might be heavily protected. The file itself might be hidden.
As the complexity of the puzzles ratchets up, so do the stories behind them. The main storyline involves a security company developing dangerous hacking software. A particularly memorable one-off mission, should you choose to accept it, tasks you with euthanizing a terminally ill patient.
